Proof: `git grep -n -E 'IR_RUNTIME_ROUTES|route\.export' -- Compiler` prints nothing and `jet test Compiler --profile golden` passes on o0, o1 and o2. (was #6615 c8)

The compiler's effect-scope covers check reaches the runtime's one covers rule through the jet.runtime.authority binding `covers` (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Public/Authority.jet, export jet_authority_right_covers), not a C import. Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Policy/EffectScope.jet declares no #Import(c) and no #Unsafe, Tests/Guards/c_imports.jet has no CI_ALLOWED row for it, the C-string export jet_authority_covers is gone, and jet test Compiler/JetFoundation/Tests/Policy/EffectScope.jet passes the 33-row covers table on a jet built with it. SUBs: G8Scope-1c (any train), then G8Scope-1d (after a seed with 1c). Placed on #6615 rather than #6129 so this follow-up to G8Scope-1b's interim CI_ALLOWED row doesn't hold G8's closure. Proof: `jet test Compiler/JetFoundation/Tests/Policy/EffectScope.jet` passes the 33-row table and `git grep -n jet_authority_covers -- Compiler` prints nothing. (was #6615 c11)

Sema classifies the reachable Prelude closure into core, alloc and hosted layers (D-FREESTAND-PRELUDE1=A), and a program that reaches a layer its target lacks is refused with a registered error. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter freestanding_missing_layer_`. (was #6615 c16)

cards.title: Continuous landing cycle: Land.jet cycle runs census, batch compiler and full suite as one loop
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-15 ~15:30: fix the landing bottleneck and codify the efficient process durably. AGENTS.md (Delegation) now states the cycle. Until Land.jet carries it, Main runs it through scratch scripts (cycle.sh, suite.sh). The bottleneck was: two compiler builds per cycle (census build plus a separate batch build), the full suite only every three or four batch compilers (regressions found across ~50 commits and bisected by hand), generated-file conflicts returned to workers, and stages started by hand, leaving the heavy slot idle.

log.text: Cycles p189b and p189c ran this process with Main's scratch cycle.sh. p189 (16:00): the census went red in 1 minute, but the script built the unchanged tip for 20 minutes; fixed so a red census exits at once. p189b: a door-2 ICE held 1 submission. p189c: 20 landed at 15:57; the census build was the batch compiler; the full suite against p188 gave 18 new and 956 fixed rows, each new row routed to its owner by 16:20. Land.jet's generated-diagnostics retry landed in 488d251515 (c2 partial: its fixture proof is still open). The suite worker (c4) is GoalsB-5-2's queued SUB.

Finding 15:58: Land.jet serve and batch already set aside failing jobs and land the rest (bisect), publish the census-verified compiler as install-latest (the batch compiler), regenerate runtime generator outputs, and run each job's tests plus ui and golden for compiler changes. Main had been landing through scratch scripts instead of the service; that, plus intake.md rule 3 ('Full suites belong to milestones'), was the bottleneck. Real gaps in the tool: (1) the whole suite (cases and core included) on each train's compiler after landing, with new and fixed rows against the previous train, routed to that train's jobs; (2) DiagnosticRows regeneration for a conflict only in generated diagnostic pages. SUB Main-landing-cycle-intake fixes intake.md rule 3 and the AGENTS.md broad-suite line. Next: switch landing to Land.jet serve from cycle 190 and add (1) and (2) to batch.
Cycle 189 runs through Main's scratch cycle.sh (census build as batch compiler, full suite in parallel profiles, new.txt against suite-p188). c1 lands with SUB Main-landing-cycle in it.

criteria.text: AGENTS.md (Delegation) states the continuous landing cycle: one census takes every ready submission, the census build is the batch compiler, every batch compiler runs the full suite against the previous cycle, and the next cycle starts at once. Proof: the landed commit's AGENTS.md text.
criteria.evidence: 86a16f68f6 (AGENTS.md Delegation: the continuous landing cycle: one census takes every ready submission, the census build is the batch compiler, every batch compiler runs the full suite against the previous cycle, the next cycle starts at once) and 7610172909 (intake.md: affected rows first, then the whole suite on every batch compiler); 6e9f9e2849 (submissions leave generated diagnostic copies out)

criteria.text: Land.jet cycle applies every ready submission, drops only one whose hand-written source does not apply, and regenerates generated files instead of refusing a submission that conflicts only there. Proof: a fixture with one generated-file conflict and one hand-written conflict lands the first and returns the second.

Land.jet cycle keeps the census build as the batch compiler when the landed tip's tree equals the census snapshot, and builds the tip otherwise; one compiler build per cycle. Proof: the cycle log names the batch compiler's source and the tree comparison.

Land.jet cycle runs the landed submissions' proof lines and the whole suite (cases beside ui, golden and core) on the batch compiler, writes fails, new and fixed against the previous cycle, and names each new failure's candidate submissions. Proof: two consecutive cycles' new.txt and fixed.txt.
A census failure holds back only the submissions it implicates (by the files of its rows), and the rest land in the same cycle. Proof: a fixture census row on one submission's file lands the others.
Main's scratch cycle.sh and suite.sh are retired once Land.jet cycle passes c2-c5; the lander uses only Land.jet cycle. Proof: cycle logs of two consecutive cycles run through Land.jet cycle.

cards.title: Types are interned TypeIDs: one Interner for names and hash-consed types, threaded through sema, registration and IR
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-15 ~20:30: the type-representation switch is G6's first step, done before G6 adds new type forms (const generics, reflection, generation) so they are written once on the new model. Moved from #5479 c7 (its S3.3 part). Groundwork landed or landing: the shared Name/TypeID model (c7-shared-ids, p198). The switch is a multi-part set (s33 parts 1..N, each clean under jet check against the parts before it); the mechanical threading of `types: &Interner` (about 740 checker signatures, about 10k Type sites) is done by a throwaway codemod whose command is in each part's message; semantic changes are hand edits. Owner: GoalsA-1-4.

log.text: Moved G6 → G11 (owner order 2026-11-15 ~23:00: speed/size work goes to G11). The card's payoff is self-compile speed (c2). PrecompiledCore-4 sized the remaining part as days of type-directed hand work, not a codemod: about 5.6k sema Type lines, 1584 construction sites, 157 Type fields, about 1.4k IR lines, about 100 fields across IR/driver/foundation, and a writable &Interner chain with about 25 fork/merge task sites. s33-1 (the single Interner in TypeIDs.jet) lands in p203. s33-2 (the 4992-function interner threading codemod) is held for this card's G11 batch, because alone it adds 525 unused-parameter warnings.

criteria.text: Sema, registration and IR represent every type as a TypeID from one Interner (hash-consed, with worker-local ids merged deterministically for parallel phases); the `Type` enum survives only as the interned row form, and no checker carries a parallel Type tree. Proof: the s33 set lands on dev; `jet check Compiler` diagnostics are byte-identical before and after; `jet test Compiler --profile ui` and `--profile golden` show no new failures.
The switch's speed is measured, not assumed: a self-compile receipt before and after the set reports CPU-µs/line and wall time (expected -15 to -25 µs/line). Proof: the two receipts on this card.

cards.title: #Inline(Always) is a guarantee, not a hint: every direct call is inlined on every tier, or sema refuses it
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-15: "#Inline(Always) must be a guarantee not a hint". Today (dev d304f826ac) it is honored only at O1/O2 and only when the inliner agrees: OptInline.jet runs at O1 and O2 only, so O0 (jet run, jet dev, compile-time code) never inlines a marked call; the `inline: off` build option and `--inline=off` drop marked inlines too; and the inliner silently keeps a marked call when the callee writes a parameter, is a last-owner routine, reads context.trace, has stops in another file, or reveals a fixed value to a public result. Sema refuses only recursion (E0917), address-taking (E0918) and size (E0919). Nothing proves that zero marked calls remain.

log.text: All 4 criteria met; c1 proved on p233 (dev 22b864b785).

c1 is still open on dev 78f4541780. The evidence so far is IR Lint call.marked on ir.build (O0), ir.opt (O1/O2), CoreLibrary and eval.batch, plus the InlineContracts golden with inspect choices on O0/O1/O2. Missing: (1) a committed test that runs the zero-marked-Call census over Examples, Core and Compiler on each tier (the lint stops a build; no test counts); (2) the web path (calls from the JS partition into a marked #Export(wasm) function).

p206 (dev fe8c7b89ef): census-r3 dc38cfa29d (the call.marked IR lint, E1016/E1017, E0917 for cycles, guarantee text) and core-abs f9128ac736 landed. golden Contracts/InlineContracts passes; the suites show no new exit-101. Three ui snapshots fail: inline_always_scrub has a wrong fixture (ReadOnlyValueNotOwned fires before E1016), and cycle and reads_trace need their real spans blessed. Three O2 .err.out files cite shifted Math.jet lines. One fix SUB from PrecompiledCore-4; c1, c2 and c4 are met after it.

p205 (dev 16c1bda2d9): inspect-choices JSON line landed as 583f538540; cases build_entry/inspect_choices_shows_each_inlined_call_and_why passes. c1's census and golden, c2, c3 and c4 are queued for p206 (inline-always-refusals-census-r3 and core-abs-inline-always), with a full suite and self-build that must show zero new exit-101s.

p204 landed c1's first SUB (686cdaaee7), but its proof case inspect_choices_shows_each_inlined_call_and_why fails on the p204 batch compiler: 'JSON value differs: expected 7, got 4' on jet inspect choices -O2 --json. Sent back to PrecompiledCore-4 as its top priority.

criteria.text: Every direct call to an `#Inline(Always)` function is inlined on every tier: O0 (jet run, jet dev and compile-time code), O1, O2 and web where applicable. No build option removes a marked inline: `inline: off` and `--inline=off` cover only unmarked calls. Proof: a census after inlining on each tier counts zero Call ops whose callee is marked over Examples, Core and Compiler, run by a committed test; an example with golden output on O0/O1/O2 whose `jet inspect choices` lists every marked site as inlined.
criteria.evidence: p233 batch compiler (dev 22b864b785), commits 6bbd1eed99 (the inline_census suite) + cc69028f04: jet test Compiler --profile inline_census rc=0 PASS (Examples, Core and Compiler at O0/O1/O2 count zero Call ops to #Inline(Always) callees); jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter Contracts/InlineContracts PASS on o0/o1/o2; jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter inspect_choices_shows_each_inlined_call_and_why PASS (jet inspect choices lists every marked site as inlined).

criteria.text: The inliner never quietly leaves a marked call: each reason it refuses a site today (a written parameter, a last-owner routine, a context.trace read, stops in another file, a fixed value revealed to a public result, and any other) is either handled by the inliner for marked callees or refused by sema with a registered diagnostic (what/why/fix and a UI snapshot), so a marked call that reaches codegen uninlined is an internal compiler error (exit 101), never a silent call. Proof: one UI snapshot per new diagnostic and one test per former refusal reason.
criteria.evidence: Landed c9a590769f (p213, dev 78f4541780). p213 batch compiler: jet test Compiler/JetIR/Source/OptInline.jet rc=0, with one test per former refusal reason (written parameter, last-owner routine, context.trace read, stops in another file, fixed value revealed to a public result, foreign body). The foreign body, the reason that was silently accepted, is now refused by sema as E1021 (registered, what/why/fix); ui --filter inline_always 7 passed, 0 bad, including the new inline_always_foreign snapshot. A marked call that reaches codegen uninlined stops the build through IR Lint call.marked (ICE). DiagnosticRows --check and DiagnosticCensus --check pass; the census is clean (jet check Core: no E1021 in Core).

criteria.text: Marked bodies cross module, package and precompiled-Core boundaries: a program that calls a Core or another package's `#Inline(Always)` function (for example core.math abs) gets the body inlined, with no call to it in the image on O0/O1/O2. Proof: `jet inspect choices` and an image symbol census for that program on each tier.
criteria.evidence: p206 batch compiler (dev fe8c7b89ef; core.math.abs marked #Inline(Always) in f9128ac736): jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter build_entry/inline_always_crosses_package_and_core_boundaries → PASS 1 FAIL 0. The case calls abs, Int.abs() and a dependency package's marked gap across module, package and Core boundaries. It runs jet inspect choices on O0/O1/O2 and builds an image on each tier that holds neither core_math_abs nor geom_gap. The p206 suites show no new exit-101 (cases: the same 44 lines as p205).

criteria.text: The marker's reference text and its diagnostics say guarantee: the Markers spec and E0917-E0919 state that every direct call is inlined on every tier or the program is refused, with the full list of refusals. Proof: the spec text and the UI snapshots.
criteria.evidence: Landed c9a590769f (p213, dev 78f4541780). p213 batch compiler: the Markers reference text and every refusal (E0917-E0919, E1021) state the guarantee in their Why: every direct call is inlined on every tier or the program is refused, with the full list of refusals. ui --filter inline_always 7 passed, 0 bad (six re-blessed snapshots with the guarantee Why, plus E1021); cases inspect_choices_shows_each_inlined_call_and_why 1/0; golden InlineContracts passes in the p213 golden suite (0 FAIL).

cards.title: Memory placement: the compiler puts values whose lifetimes nest on per-thread scope stacks (Goose learnings)
cards.body: Owner discussion 2026-11-16 on the Goose and Lobster mining run (Docs/research/mine-for-jet-2026-10-23-goose-lobster.md once landed). Goose keeps every growable value on compiler-assigned data stacks: an address reservation with a bump pointer, freed by one store at scope exit. It pays for that with restrictions (one growable per stack, no growable array elements, restricted recursion, whole-program specialization, wasm growth checks) and its own record shows prior region systems retreating to a collector or ownership. Jet already has the explicit route (#Context(allocator:), D-ALLOC-SITE1=A), the default heap (D-ALLOC-DEFAULT1=A) and the scratch escape rule (D-REGION-ALLOC1=F). The open question is what Jet does for code that names no allocator. Ballot D-PLACE-DEFAULT1 carries it; whichever option wins, the build's first criterion is a passing adversarial review in Docs/audits.

criteria.text: A dated adversarial review in Docs/Audits attacks the ratified option of D-PLACE-DEFAULT1: it states Goose's, the ML Kit's, Cyclone's and Rust/Zig arena practice at their best case with sources, and tests every claimed gain with a runnable probe or measurement (allocation cost, peak memory on a long scope, web checked growth, task-crossing values, recursion). Every gap ends on a criterion here or a ballot; the build starts only on a passing verdict.

cards.title: Ballot D-WARM-SET1: how an app names the reads a device loads ahead for offline screens
cards.body: Owner ballot for #6868 c12 (warm coverage per screen). The build must know which live reads a device keeps warm so it can fail an offline screen that reads outside them. Options: A, a warm function in .offline(.Queue, warm: fn ...) with a compile-time coverage check; B, a .warm() screen mark; C, no warm set. Recommendation A. Ballot file: decision D-WARM-SET1.

criteria.text: After D-WARM-SET1 is ratified, build its outcome (moved from #6868 c12, which waited only on this ballot): Warm coverage per screen (sync review gap G10): the build reports, for each screen, which of its live reads are in the warm set and which are not, and a check fails a screen marked offline that reads anything outside it. Proof: a case with one covered and one uncovered screen, and the check's output for each. (was #3709 c27)

cards.title: App menus, context menus, the tray and the macOS menu bar on macOS, Windows and phones
cards.body: Platform half of #6799 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6799 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: App menus, context menus, the tray and the macOS menu bar on the native app host.

criteria.text: The tray from examples/tray.jet stays after the last window closes on Windows and macOS, and its menu follows the live project list as on Linux. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/tray_menu_follows_the_live_project_list` on Windows and macOS hosts.

On macOS, native.menu_bar becomes the menu bar with the app, Edit and Window menus and their key equivalents; on Windows the same value becomes the window's menu. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/menu_bar_maps_to_each_desktop_platform` on macOS and Windows hosts.

native.context_menu opens on right click on Windows and macOS and on long press on phones, and an item's Err reaches the app's error surface. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/context_menu_opens_on_every_target_and_reports_errors` on those hosts.

cards.title: Notifications on macOS, Windows and phones: APNs, FCM and local notifications
cards.body: Platform half of #6800 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6800 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Notifications: local notifications on desktop and phones, and push through APNs, FCM and Web Push from one typed server call.

criteria.text: app.notify reaches every Apple device the account registered through APNs and every Android device through FCM HTTP v1, from the same one server call as Web Push; native.notify shows a local notification on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter WebApp/notify_sends_apns_fcm_and_web_push_payloads` (local fake provider endpoints check each payload).
A tap on a notification opens the open: state through the one route table on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android.

cards.title: Background work on phones and on macOS and Windows: BGTaskScheduler, WorkManager and login items
cards.body: Platform half of #6801 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6801 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Background work: deferred and periodic jobs on phones (BGTaskScheduler, WorkManager) and desktops; browsers run none (server jobs and push cover the web).

criteria.text: native.background(every:, run:) registers per platform. On iOS it is a BGAppRefreshTask whose identifier the build writes into Info.plist BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers. On Android it is a WorkManager PeriodicWorkRequest, with every: raised to the 15-minute minimum. On macOS and Windows it is a timer while the app runs, or a login item.

A run that passes the system's time budget is cancelled as an ordinary task cancellation, and its cleanup runs. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/background_run_past_its_budget_is_cancelled`. (Moved from the Linux card: only phones set a budget.)

cards.title: Files on macOS, Windows and phones: native pickers, content URIs, security-scoped URLs and persisted folder access
cards.body: Platform half of #6802 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6802 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Files: native open and save pickers, folder access that persists, and the browser's file pickers, as one typed API.

criteria.text: A PickedFile is backed by a path on macOS and Windows, a content URI on Android and a security-scoped URL on iOS, and import_tasks in examples/files.jet imports the same CSV there as on Linux.

native.save_file writes through the system save dialog on macOS and Windows and through the document picker on phones. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/save_file_writes_where_the_person_chose` on those hosts.

Access to a chosen folder survives a restart through security-scoped bookmarks on macOS and iOS, persisted URI permissions on Android and the folder path on Windows. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/folder_access_survives_a_restart` on those hosts.

cards.title: Camera, sensors and location on macOS, Windows and phones
cards.body: Platform half of #6803 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6803 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Camera, sensors and location as typed streams behind declared device permissions.

criteria.text: After native.ask grants access, native.take_photo gives a PickedFile photo and native.location a Place on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/camera_and_location_give_typed_values_after_a_grant` on those hosts.

native.location_updates and the motion sensors stop with their scope, with no listener left registered, on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/sensor_streams_stop_with_their_scope` on those hosts.

cards.title: Deep links on macOS, Windows and phones: iOS universal links, Android App Links and single instance
cards.body: Platform half of #6804 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6804 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Deep links and app links: custom schemes, iOS universal links and Android App Links land on screen state (D-ROUTE-ONE1).

criteria.text: An iOS universal link, an Android App Link and crewboard://tasks/<id> on macOS and Windows land on TaskView{id} through the one route table. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/every_link_form_lands_on_the_route_state` on those hosts.

The server output serves /.well-known/apple-app-site-association and /.well-known/assetlinks.json, written from the phone output's id and signing identity. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter WebApp/app_link_files_are_written_from_the_phone_output`. (Moved from the Linux card.)

A second launch on macOS or Windows hands its link to the running app, which focuses its window and opens the state. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/second_launch_hands_its_link_to_the_running_app` on those hosts.

cards.title: System share sheet, clipboard and drag and drop on macOS, Windows and phones
cards.body: Platform half of #6805 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6805 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: System share sheet on phones and desktop and the Web Share API; clipboard and drag and drop reach app screens from core.ui.host.

criteria.text: native.share opens the system share sheet on phones, macOS and Windows. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/share_uses_the_system_sheet_or_copies` on those hosts.

native.copy_text and native.paste_text round-trip on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/clipboard_round_trips_on_every_target` on those hosts.

ui.drop_zone<T> refuses other types and offers a move without dragging on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/drop_zone_refuses_other_types_and_offers_a_move_without_dragging` on those hosts.

cards.title: Device permissions on macOS, Windows and phones: Info.plist, AndroidManifest and typed grants
cards.body: Platform half of #6806 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6806 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Device permissions: declared in package.jet, prompted at first use, with a typed denied result on every target.

criteria.text: The build writes each purposes: line into Info.plist usage descriptions and AndroidManifest.xml uses-permission entries.

native.ask gives Granted, Denied or Restricted on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android, prompts only at first use, and native.open_settings opens the app's settings page. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/ask_gives_a_typed_grant_on_every_target` on those hosts.

cards.title: Accessibility on macOS, Windows and phones: UIA, NSAccessibility, UIAccessibility and AccessibilityNodeInfo
cards.body: Platform half of #6807 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6807 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Accessibility build-out for D-A11Y-EXPORT1: AccessKit on desktop, phone providers, semantic HTML on the web, and compile-time checks.

criteria.text: kit views export their role, name and state through AccessKit on Windows (UIA) and macOS (NSAccessibility), through UIAccessibility on iOS and AccessibilityNodeInfo on Android; move_button is a button named "Move <title> to <status>" on each. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/access_tree_names_kit_views` on those hosts.

ui.announce is a polite announcement that keeps focus on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/announce_is_polite_and_keeps_focus` on those hosts.

cards.title: App lifecycle and saved state on macOS, Windows and phones
cards.body: Platform half of #6809 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6809 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: App lifecycle events (start, foreground, background, suspend, terminate) and saved screen state on every target.

criteria.text: start, foreground, background, suspend and terminate reach the app through scenePhase-equivalent events on phones and window events on macOS and Windows, and native.lifecycle(on_resume:) runs on resume. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/lifecycle_events_reach_the_app_on_every_target` on those hosts.
ui.saved state survives the phone ending the process in the background.

On resume, live queries resubscribe and the offline queue sends with no app code on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/resume_resubscribes_and_drains_the_queue` on those hosts.

cards.title: Desktop install, auto-update and signing on macOS and Windows: MSIX, notarized DMG, and phone asset packaging
cards.body: Platform half of #6810 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6810 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Desktop install, auto-update and signing: MSIX, notarized DMG, AppImage and Flatpak, with signed delta updates.

criteria.text: The desktop output writes an MSIX on Windows and a signed and notarized DMG on macOS, signed with the identities named in outputs:. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter BuildEntry/desktop_output_writes_signed_installers` on those hosts.

The same one-line install works on macOS arm64 and Windows x64 (`irm … | iex`), and `jet run hello.jet` prints the greeting on both. Proof: the release gate's committed install receipts for both hosts. (Moved from the Linux card; was #5950 c7.)

The getting-started commands are the same on macOS and Windows beginner hosts and run as documented, and the toolchain channel lists their releases with digests for `jet self`. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Onboarding/beginner_path_` and `--filter SelfUpdate/` on those hosts.

The app's ui.asset files are packaged per target: an iOS asset catalog with Info.plist entries, Android resources with manifest entries, and the macOS and Windows bundles. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter BuildEntry/assets_are_packaged_per_target` on those outputs.

cards.title: Native sessions on macOS, Windows and phones: refresh tokens in Keychain, Keystore and the Windows credential store
cards.body: Platform half of #6818 (owner order 2026-11-16): #6818 keeps Linux and the web in G9; this card holds macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A governs both halves, and the Linux half proves each shared API first. Original scope: Native sessions: short access tokens, refresh tokens in the system keychain, revocation.

criteria.text: Phone, macOS and Windows apps sign in with a short-lived access token and a refresh token stored in Keychain, Keystore or the Windows credential store; revoking a device ends its refresh within one access-token lifetime. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter app_native_session_` on those hosts, with the same output on O0, O1 and O2.

decisions.title: Game asset handles
decisions.gist: Choose how game assets are declared, loaded, and diagnosed.
decisions.story: Lena makes a platformer. She wants a typed `player_sprite` handle everywhere and a Jet diagnostic if a PNG is missing or used as a sound.
decisions.inWild: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Scene asset registry with typed handles
options.detail: Assets load through `scene.assets`, returning typed handles tied to scene identity.
options.code:
player :: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?
jump :: scene.assets.sound("assets/jump.wav")?

options.name: Top-level loaders
options.detail: Flexible, but weakens scene-owned diagnostics and editor identity.
options.code: player :: game.asset.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Manifest asset catalog
options.detail: Strong packaging provenance, more ceremony for one-file games.
options.code: targets: { game: { assets: { player: "assets/player.png" } } }

comparisons.note: Resource handles are editor-friendly; Jet should keep them typed and source-owned.

decisions.title: ECS over Scene
decisions.gist: Choose the component and query API that layers over `Scene`.
decisions.story: Omar starts with a simple scene, then adds hundreds of enemies. Components and queries should be another view over the same scene data, not a second engine.
decisions.inWild:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.query(Position, Velocity)

options.name: `component` declarations plus `scene.query`
options.detail: Components are typed declarations; queries are scene methods, preserving one scene identity.
options.code:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
loop item in scene.query(Position, Velocity) { }

options.name: Struct marker components
options.detail: No new declaration form, but component intent is less visible.
options.code:
struct Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.component<Velocity>()

options.name: System functions over query parameters
options.detail: Concise for experts, but puts scheduler vocabulary before the beginner scene story.
options.code: system move(pos: Position mut, vel: Velocity, frame: Frame) { }

comparisons.note: Typed queries are strong; Jet should hide scheduler complexity until needed.

decisions.title: Game input bindings
decisions.gist: Choose how input bindings and per-frame snapshots are named.
decisions.story: Aya wants keyboard today and gamepad later. Replay files should store actions, not raw device quirks, so logic is deterministic across dev, CI, and builds.
decisions.inWild:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Scene bindings plus frame snapshot
options.detail: Bindings live on `scene.input`; frame logic reads deterministic `frame.input` snapshots.
options.code:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Global input map
options.detail: Short, but weak multi-scene/editor isolation.
options.code: game.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])

options.name: Typed action enum
options.detail: Explicit and replay-friendly, more ceremony for tiny games.
options.code:
enum Action { jump }
frame.input<Action>().pressed(Action.jump)

comparisons.note: Action maps are beginner-friendly and replayable.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: Game replay contract
decisions.gist: Choose the replay API, file format, and determinism contract.
decisions.story: Ben gets a physics bug report. The player sends one replay file; Ben runs it under `jet dev` and compiled mode and gets the same frame transcript.
decisions.inWild: game.Replay.record("runs/bug-142.jreplay")

options.name: `game.Replay` API plus `.jreplay` artifact
options.detail: First-party typed artifact contains input actions, seeds, fixed-step timing, backend identity, and budget events.
options.code:
game.run(scene, replay: game.Replay.record("run.jreplay"))
game.Replay.play("run.jreplay", scene)?

options.name: CLI-only replay
options.detail: Keeps source clean, weakens tests that need replay facts.
options.code: jet game record game.jet --out run.jreplay

options.name: User serialization hooks
options.detail: Expert control, but no shared deterministic contract.
options.code: scene.on_snapshot((frame) => writer.write(frame.input))

comparisons.note: Input-stream replay is proven; Jet should type and version the artifact.

decisions.title: Game backend selection
decisions.gist: Choose how renderer, audio, and editor backends are selected.
decisions.story: Sana starts with a no-op CI backend, develops on raylib, and later targets wgpu. Gameplay code should not change when backend changes.
decisions.inWild: game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Typed `game.Backend` value
options.detail: Backends are explicit typed values passed to `game.run`; beginners can omit for the default headless/no-op path.
options.code:
game.run(scene)
game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Manifest target backend
options.detail: Fits packages, but single-file games need hidden defaults or a second path.
options.code: targets: { game: { backend: { renderer: core.raylib } } }

options.name: CLI-selected backend
options.detail: Useful for CI, harder to audit from source.
options.code: jet run game.jet --game-renderer=core.raylib

comparisons.note: Plugins are flexible; Jet should keep one stable Core scene API above replaceable backend packages.

decisions.title: Game budgets
decisions.gist: Choose how frame, memory, asset, and draw-call budgets attach and report diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nico ships a handheld build with strict frame, memory, and draw-call ceilings. Violations should be Jet diagnostics with replay context.
decisions.inWild: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Scene/package budgets, same model
options.detail: Budgets attach to scenes for one-file games and package targets for projects; sema/runtime treat both as one fact model.
options.code: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Package-only budgets
options.detail: Clean for CI, but one-file games lose budget diagnostics unless packaged.
options.code: targets: { game: { budgets: { frame: 16.ms } } }

options.name: Runtime watcher API
options.detail: Dynamic control, weaker build/dossier/CI facts.
options.code: budget_watch.attach(scene)

comparisons.note: Budgets work best when CI can fail deterministically.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: jetos Studio launch command
decisions.gist: Choose how users open jetos Studio.

decisions.inWild: jetos studio

options.name: jetos studio (recommended)
options.detail: Studio belongs to the OS engine and keeps package-manager verbs out of OS UX.
options.code: jetos studio

options.name: jet studio --os
options.detail: One Jet umbrella command, but blurs engine boundary.
options.code: jet studio --os

options.name: Editor command only
options.detail: Friendly inside IDEs, weak for docs, CI repro, and support.
options.code: Jetos: Open Studio

comparisons.note: Discoverable but not scriptable; jetos needs both.

decisions.title: jetos Studio default editing view
decisions.gist: Choose Studio's default editing view.
decisions.story: Ren enables Steam and SSH. They want safe toggles first, then the exact module diff before saving.
decisions.inWild:
Studio -> Services -> SSH -> Enable
Diff: module system.laptop { services.ssh.enable: true }

options.name: Guided control center plus source/diff (recommended)
options.detail: Panels for common tasks, source and provenance always one click away.
options.code: Services -> SSH -> Enable -> Diff

options.name: Source-first IDE
options.detail: Powerful and honest, but weak beginner onboarding.
options.code: edit system.jet

options.detail: Strong visual consistency with #182, but OS settings are usually forms and provenance trees.

decisions.title: jetos Studio local state boundary
decisions.gist: Decide what Studio may persist outside Jet source.
decisions.story: Priya arranges panels and filters proof logs. She does not want those UI choices to become semantic config or noisy PR diffs.
decisions.inWild:
.jet/studio/cache.json
system/laptop.jet

options.name: Generated cache only (recommended)
options.detail: Studio may persist view prefs under .jet, never semantic settings.
options.code: .jet/studio/cache.json

options.name: Committed .studio.jet metadata
options.detail: Reviewable UI metadata, but another source-like artifact.
options.code: .studio.jet

decisions.title: jetos Studio activation proof gate
decisions.gist: Choose how Studio blocks risky activation.
decisions.story: Mara changes kernel and filesystem settings. Studio must tell them whether VM boot and rollback proof are required before switch.
decisions.inWild:
Risk: boot + filesystem
Required: plan, VM boot, rollback proof
Switch: disabled until proof passes

options.name: Plan-only warning
options.detail: Always allow switch after diff approval. Fast, weaker than D-WD8 proof intent.
options.code: warning only

options.name: Risk-based hard gate (recommended)
options.detail: Boot/kernel/filesystem/service-risk changes require VM and rollback proof; low-risk changes require plan/diff unless policy says more.
options.code: switch disabled until proof passes

options.name: Always VM proof
options.detail: Simple and safe, but over-applies proof to trivial edits.
options.code: VM required for every switch

comparisons.note: Offers VM/build tools but leaves policy to user habit.

decisions.title: jetos Studio plan/proof schema stability
decisions.gist: Decide whether Studio proof/diff artifacts are public schemas in v1.
decisions.story: Owen wants CI to show the same plan, risk, and proof result that Studio shows before activation.
decisions.inWild:
jetos plan @laptop --json > plan.json
jetos prove @laptop --json > proof.json

options.name: Public schemas from first write flow
options.detail: Studio and CI share stable JSON immediately.
options.code: jetos plan --json

options.name: Internal GUI schema first
options.detail: Faster GUI iteration, but CI cannot trust the same artifact.
options.code: internal schema

options.name: Public after read-only Studio (recommended)
options.detail: Stabilize once projection fields prove out, before activation handoff.
options.code: public before switch flows

comparisons.note: Plans are useful because CI and humans inspect the same object.

decisions.title: Declarative containers and microVMs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos declares containers and microVMs under one proof model.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.
decisions.story: Walter runs Postgres in a container and a risky service in a microVM. Both need network, storage, secrets, health checks, and rollback proof, but they should not become two unrelated config languages.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.

options.name: Hybrid: workload declarations with container/microVM profiles (recommended)
options.detail: One workload.<name> mechanism declares isolated workloads. The backend enum selects Container or MicroVM; shared fields cover image/package, ports, mounts, secrets, health, resources, proof, and rollback. Backend-specific knobs live under nested profiles. Beginners see one concept; experts control isolation depth.

options.name: Separate `containers` and `microvms` trees
options.detail: Matches ecosystem words and keeps backend specifics obvious, but duplicates policy/proof fields.
options.code:
containers.db { image: image.postgres }
microvms.sandbox { memory: 2048.MiB }

options.name: Packages only
options.detail: Treat containers/VMs as packages launched by services. Reuses service machinery, but hides isolation/proof semantics.
options.code: services.db.exec: package.postgres_container.run

comparisons.note: Powerful but split modules; Jet can unify proof concepts.

decisions.title: Hardware profiles and specialisations
decisions.gist: Choose the surface for hardware scans, reusable device profiles, and boot-selectable variants.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.
decisions.story: Earl installs on a laptop with NVIDIA and a desktop with GPU passthrough. He needs hardware facts generated once, community profiles applied explicitly, and specialisations selectable at boot without duplicating a host.
decisions.inWild:
jet os init devhost
// emits what? how do variants compose?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.

options.name: Hybrid: scanned hardware modules plus reusable profiles and specialisations (recommended)
options.detail: Hardware scan emits hardware.<host> source. Systems import that source and can apply first-party/community hardware profile packages. Specialisations are named boot variants over the same host and generation, with option-priority/explain output showing what changed.

options.name: Inline hardware in system
options.detail: All facts live in system.<host>. Fewer modules, but generated hardware and authored policy mix noisily.
options.code: system.devhost { hardware.gpu: .Nvidia }

options.name: Profile packages only
options.detail: Hardware profiles are packages users add. Good sharing, weak for local scan facts and drift reporting.
options.code: packages: [hardware.nixos-hardware.framework-13]

comparisons.note: hardware-configuration.nix + nixos-hardware + specialisations are separate conventions.

decisions.title: Declarative disks and impermanence
decisions.gist: Choose how disk layouts, encryption, filesystems, and persisted paths are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.
decisions.story: Inez wants btrfs subvolumes, LUKS, an ephemeral root, and a precise persist list. The installer must show exactly what will be destroyed and what survives rollback before touching a disk.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.

options.name: Hybrid: storage tree consumed by installer and activation (recommended)
options.detail: One storage tree declares disks, partitions, encryption, filesystems, mounts, ephemeral roots, and persistence. The installer uses the same source for destructive actions; activation uses it for mounts and persistence proof. Guided install can draft storage source, never own hidden disk state.

options.name: Separate `disk` and `impermanence` modules
options.detail: Mirrors existing tools. Clear boundaries, but persistence and mount truth can drift.
options.code:
disk.main { ... }
impermanence.persist: ["/var/lib"]

options.name: Installer-generated only
options.detail: Installer records disk facts outside source. Fast first install, but not reproducible or reviewable.
options.code: jet os install --guided

comparisons.note: Community tools solve each half separately; Jet can make one proof-backed source.

decisions.title: Declarative theming
decisions.gist: Choose the source surface for wallpaper, palette, fonts, cursor, and per-app theme projection.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.
decisions.story: Doris wants one wallpaper and palette to drive GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, and the display manager, with per-app opt-outs and Studio preview. It should be first-party source, not community glue.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.

options.name: Hybrid: reusable theme profiles with inline host overrides (recommended)
options.detail: theme.<name> modules are reusable theme profiles. A system references one and may override specific targets inline. The theme engine derives/apply palettes across GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, DM, and Studio preview; per-app opt-outs stay explicit.

options.name: Inline system.theme tree
options.detail: Fewer modules, but themes are harder to reuse across hosts/variants.
options.code: system.devhost { theme.wallpaper: file("forest.png") }

options.name: Per-app theming only
options.detail: Each app module owns colors/fonts. Flexible, but no single source of truth.
options.code:
programs.ghostty.theme: ...
programs.helix.theme: ...

comparisons.note: Community module proves the demand; Jet can make it first-party and proof-backed.

decisions.title: Declarative Flatpak and foreign app ecosystems
decisions.gist: Choose how Flatpak remotes, apps, permissions, and reconcile policy are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one Flatpak authority graph, ergonomic per-user app use, and proof-gated reconciliation.
decisions.story: Sam currently has an activation script that adds Flathub, installs desired apps, removes undeclared apps, and updates them. Jetos should plan that change, prove it, and roll it back like everything else.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one Flatpak authority graph, ergonomic per-user app use, and proof-gated reconciliation.

options.name: Hybrid: central Flatpak policy plus user-app projections (recommended)
options.detail: apps.flatpak declares remotes, refs, pins/tracking, reconcile mode, and permission policy. User environment app modules can reference those Flatpak apps for per-user install intent. Activation computes one plan/diff/proof and rollback path.

options.name: User-env app modules
options.detail: Flatpaks are just per-user program modules. Good integration, but remotes/reconcile/permissions become scattered.
options.code: user.user.programs.discord.source: flatpak("com.discordapp.Discord")

options.name: Activation script bridge
options.detail: Keep a generated script. Preserves today’s behavior, but diff/proof semantics stay opaque.
options.code: activation.script("flatpak install ...")

comparisons.note: Community module exists because NixOS lacks first-party Flatpak reconciliation.

decisions.title: Kernel and performance tuning surface
decisions.gist: Choose how kernel profiles, sysctl, zram, sched-ext, initrd, and bootloader tuning are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: friendly profiles for the default path, exact typed knobs for experts.
decisions.story: Hank wants a safe laptop default, a CachyOS performance profile for gaming, zram, one sysctl, sched-ext, and a quieter initrd. These knobs affect boot and performance, so they need typed source and proof.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: friendly profiles for the default path, exact typed knobs for experts.

options.name: Hybrid: safe profiles plus typed expert overrides (recommended)
options.detail: Beginners choose profile enums such as safe/lts/performance. Experts override typed boot/performance families for kernel params, sysctl, zram, sched-ext, initrd, and bootloader. Every override carries risk/proof classification and explain output.
options.code:
performance.profile: .Gaming
boot.kernel.profile: .CachyOSLatest
boot.kernel.params += ["quiet"]
performance.zram.memoryPercent: 50
performance.sysctl.vm.swappiness: 10
performance.scheduler: .Scx("scx_lavd")

options.name: Free-form kernel option map
options.detail: One map for all low-level knobs. Flexible, but loses type checks and explainability.
options.code: boot.options["vm.swappiness"] = "10"

options.name: Profiles only
options.detail: Choose safe/lts/performance profiles; no individual knobs. Great beginner path, insufficient expert control.
options.code: performance.profile: .Gaming

comparisons.note: boot/sysctl/zram/scx are powerful but scattered across modules.

decisions.title: jetos fleet target and authority surface
decisions.gist: How fleet hosts name remote machines and authority.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: tiny label defaults for beginners, explicit reusable authority facts for real fleets.
decisions.story: Mara deploys to web1, web2, and db from CI. The fleet already says which system each host runs, but jetos still needs to know the SSH target, user, privilege boundary, and host identity without hiding authority in shell scripts.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: tiny label defaults for beginners, explicit reusable authority facts for real fleets.

options.name: Hybrid: host target fields with label defaults and reusable target refs (recommended)
options.detail: Each fleet host carries typed target/authority fields beside its system. If omitted, the friendly label can be used as a safe SSH default. Reusable deploy.target refs avoid duplication for bastions/CI. Host key policy, privilege boundary, and identity are proof-visible.

options.name: Host label is SSH name
options.detail: Use `web1` as the SSH target by default, with few knobs. Very small for beginners, but weak for CI, non-DNS labels, alternate users, bastions, host-key policy, and audit output.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
# jet push prod uses ssh web1

options.name: Separate deploy.targets map
options.detail: Fleet topology stays pure and a separate map binds labels to SSH details. Explicit, but splits one host's deploy facts across two places and creates ordering/debug friction.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
deploy.targets.web1: ssh("deploy@web1.example.com")

options.name: External inventory file
options.detail: Read SSH targets from YAML/JSON/SSH config. Familiar to ops teams, but Jet cannot type-check or explain the full authority graph from source alone.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
# targets loaded from inventory.yml

comparisons.note: Node deployment facts live in node config fields such as targetHost and targetUser.
Deploy nodes bind host names to SSH user/host details and profiles.

decisions.title: jetos fleet rollout and rollback policy
decisions.gist: How fleet push sequences hosts and rolls back failures.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: safe magic default plus exact rollout choreography for experts and CI.
decisions.story: Olive pushes a config changing OpenSSH and a service port. She needs jetos to stage hosts safely, prove health on each machine, stop on bad health, and roll back the failed host without leaving a mystery half-deploy.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: safe magic default plus exact rollout choreography for experts and CI.

options.name: Hybrid: staged proof-gated rollout with plan/stage controls (recommended)
options.detail: Default push is staged and proof-gated with rollback-and-stop. Experts can choose batch/canary/dependency order, health timeout, and stage-only/continue flows using the same rollout object. All-at-once is an explicit policy, never the default.
options.code:
rollout: .Staged(
    batch: 1,
    canary: [web1],
    health_timeout: 60s,
    on_failure: .RollbackAndStop
)

$ jet push prod --plan
$ jet push prod --stage
$ jet push prod --continue

options.name: All-at-once with rollback
options.detail: Activate every host concurrently, then roll back failures. Fast for homogeneous fleets, but a bad config can hit every machine before proof catches it.
options.code: rollout: .Parallel(on_failure: .RollbackFailed)

options.name: Plan-only until explicit continue
options.detail: Every push computes and uploads generations, then requires a second command to activate. Very cautious, but beginners lose the magic safe default and CI needs extra orchestration.
options.code:
$ jet push prod --stage
$ jet push prod --continue

options.name: Delegate rollout to external orchestrator
options.detail: jetos builds closures and an external deploy tool decides sequencing. This avoids owning rollout semantics but fails the first-party deploy-rs/colmena parity goal.
options.code:
$ jet push prod --emit-plan deploy.json
$ external-rollout deploy.json

comparisons.note: Supports remote activation with rollback-on-failure profile behavior.
Rolling updates default to staged rollout with health gates and stop/rollback controls.
Can deploy to many nodes but the health/proof model is less language-owned.

decisions.title: Desktop option spellings — the one-line swap surface
decisions.gist: The exact user-typeable spellings for choosing a desktop. Everything else derives from these lines, so they are the most-typed jetos options after packages. Under D-JPK-OSNS1=B full-word namespaces.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: B contradicts ratified namespace law (D-JPK-OSNS1=B / D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1 place desktop under services) and spends an amendment on saved keystrokes; C's record value has undefined merge semantics — does setting the record reset unset fields? — vagueness that bites the option-priority engine; D's combinatorial enum explodes on every new session type and has no home for displayManager. A wins but leaves `.Auto` derivation and invalid-combo diagnostics unstated, which is where implementers diverge. One flag for the ratifier: the environment enum has no value for the D-JOS-DESKTOP1=A JetOS-owned Wayland session — reconcile when that frozen surface (D-JETOS-FREEZE1) ships natively.
decisions.story: One line must swap the whole desktop; a second may pin the session type; a third may override the display manager. Enum values are teaching surfaces: unknown values list the valid set.
decisions.inWild:
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.desktop.environment: .Kde        // entire desktop swapped
services.desktop.session: .X11             // wayland is the default
services.desktop.displayManager: .Greetd   // else auto-derived

options.label: services.desktop.{environment, session, displayManager}
options.detail: Nested under the existing services.desktop.* namespace next to autoLogin/profile; enums .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri, .Wayland/.X11, .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd.

options.label: top-level desktop.* namespace
options.detail: desktop.environment / desktop.session / desktop.displayManager as a new top-level namespace — shortest to type, needs a namespace-list amendment to D-JPK-OSNS1.

options.label: single record option
options.detail: services.desktop: Desktop.{ environment: .Kde, session: .Wayland } — one structured value, one line for the common case, record fields for the rest.

options.label: DE value carries session
options.detail: desktop: .KdeWayland / .KdeX11 / .Gnome / .Hyprland — one enum, zero second line; combinatorial values, no invalid combos possible by construction.

options.name: services.desktop.* with lawful .Auto derivation and typed assertions (hybrid)
options.detail: Spellings are Option A's under the ratified full-word tree (D-JPK-OSNS1=B, D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1): `services.desktop.environment: .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri`, `session: .Auto/.Wayland/.X11` defaulting `.Auto`, `displayManager: .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd` defaulting `.Auto` — one line swaps the desktop; the other two exist only as overrides. `.Auto` derivation is law, not vibes: session resolves to the DE's preferred session, displayManager resolves Gnome->.Gdm, Kde->.Sddm, Hyprland/Niri->.Greetd, and `jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager` prints the derivation and winning priority. Invalid combos fail at eval as typed assertions naming both source lines (`.Niri` supports only `.Wayland`/`.Auto`), and an unknown enum value lists the full valid set with a nearest-match suggestion. Combinatorial DE-x-session values (Option D) are rejected forever: every fact keeps exactly one option home, so adding a session type or DM never renames existing configs.
options.code:
services.desktop.environment: .Kde     // one line, whole desktop swaps
services.desktop.session: .X11          // optional; default .Auto -> wayland
// error: .Niri supports only .Wayland — set at services.desktop.session (line 7)
jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager   # .Sddm, derived from .Kde

decisions.title: Baseline profiles — exact visible contents of terminal and graphical installs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos ships a lean modern terminal and a complete no-command-line desktop while keeping every installed part visible in config.jet.
decisions.explainer: Recommended D treats baselines as source templates, not runtime imports. The installer materializes every package, service, option, policy, and low-level component into config.jet; the realized closure must trace every installed root back to one of those source entries. The terminal template stays small but modern. The graphical template adds one complete GNOME path and hardware support, with Studio handling settings, packages, updates, generations, proof, and rollback without requiring a terminal. No duplicate app for the same job, no second package system by default, and no unexplained background service. Experts may remove or replace any layer; jetos reports broken obligations and proof failures but never silently restores a baseline choice.
decisions.story: Maya installs jetos on a small server and wants a useful modern terminal without a desktop. Her father installs it on a laptop and expects Wi-Fi, headphones, printing, updates, files, documents, media, and system settings to work without opening a terminal. Later Maya replaces the kernel and network stack. Both need config.jet to show the whole system, with no hidden profile contents or defaults silently returning after an edit.

options.name: Named profile imports
options.detail: config.jet imports baseline.terminal or baseline.graphical. This keeps the file short, but the installed package and service graph is hidden behind the import until the user follows it elsewhere. Baseline updates can also change a machine without an obvious local source diff.

options.name: Fully materialized minimal profiles
options.detail: Both terminal and graphical installs write their complete contents into config.jet, but the graphical set adds only GNOME, a browser, audio, fonts, Bluetooth, and printing. Auditability is strong; the desktop still leaves common beginner jobs and system administration dependent on package discovery or the terminal.
options.code:
packages: [packages.fish, packages.helix, packages.git, packages.ripgrep]
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.audio.pipewire.enable: true
// Files, updates, documents, archives, disks, and media need later setup.

options.name: One universal batteries-included profile
options.detail: Every install writes the complete graphical tool and service set into config.jet, including headless machines. This is maximally consistent and visible, but a server receives desktop packages and services with no baseline job to perform.

options.name: Two fully materialized, purpose-built baselines (recommended)
options.detail: Terminal and graphical are two source templates, expanded directly into config.jet by init/installer; there is no baseline import and no hidden installed default. Terminal contains the boot/kernel/init/filesystem/user/logging/time/locale/certificate/network/firewall/package-management substrate; standard compatibility utilities; fish, Helix, Git, OpenSSH client, curl, rsync; and the curated modern interactive set ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, fzf, zoxide, jq, and btop. No remote server is enabled by default. Graphical contains all terminal entries plus GNOME on Wayland/GDM; NetworkManager UI; PipeWire/WirePlumber; Bluetooth; printing/scanning; firmware and power management; portals, polkit, keyring, fonts, input, automount, and notifications; jetos Studio; Firefox; Nautilus; GNOME Console, Text Editor, Papers, Loupe, Showtime, File Roller, Calculator, Calendar, Clocks, Disks, Snapshot, Settings, and a Jetpack-backed Software view. One app per baseline job; Flatpak and alternate app stores remain explicit opt-ins. Studio exposes install/remove, settings, updates, generations, proof, and rollback through the same config.jet transactions. Baseline evolution arrives as a reviewable source diff and never applies silently. Removing or replacing a low-level entry is authoritative: jetos shows unmet typed obligations and failed proof, but does not heal or reinsert the old choice.

comparisons.note: NixOS offers deep declarative control, but imports and module defaults can make the effective system larger than configuration.nix shows. D keeps the declarative graph while materializing the chosen baseline into the user's source and requiring source provenance for every installed root.

Arch makes a minimal system and expert choice straightforward, but the user assembles desktop completeness by hand. D preserves a lean terminal target while giving graphical users a complete, maintained starting source.
comparisons.code:
pacstrap /mnt base linux networkmanager
# User chooses and wires every desktop component afterward.

comparisons.note: Fedora provides a cohesive GNOME experience and modern applications, but image manifests and package layering are not a single user-owned declarative system file. D adopts cohesive desktop curation while keeping the whole machine editable as source.
comparisons.code:
rpm-ostree status
# Strong image provenance; baseline contents are not materialized into one local config.

comparisons.note: Guix can describe a whole system in one program and supports generations, but users still commonly compose imported service sets and package lists. D shares the source-owned system model and adds a no-terminal graphical authoring path over the same source.

decisions.title: Cross-platform executable lease security
decisions.gist: Which existing promise changes so executable packages can work safely on macOS and Windows.
decisions.explainer: Jetpack verifies a package, copies its output into a lease snapshot, and must keep every executable name bound to those verified bytes while a child and its descendants run. Linux does this with a private read-only mount. An unprivileged macOS process has no equivalent immutable named PATH view; Windows file handles can block replacement of files but do not alone protect every descendant name lookup. Today the non-Linux backend returns an error for every lease, even data-only outputs; that empty-output bug is ungated and will be fixed. Executable outputs expose a real conflict among three ratified promises: hostile same-user swaps fail before handoff, Linux/macOS/Windows are tier-1 native, and Jetpack uses no root or daemon. No known design keeps all three. The owner must choose which promise changes.
decisions.story: Mira uses one committed lockfile on Linux, macOS, and Windows. She runs a formatter directly and through jet env. Another same-user process swaps the original package path after verification. Jetpack must execute the verified bytes or refuse; it must never follow the replacement. Beginners need one ceremony-free workflow, while experts need exact audit proof of the native protection used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files

# A same-user process renames the verified output and replaces it with a malicious symlink tree.
# Jetpack must execute the leased bytes or refuse, never follow the replacement.

options.name: Protected native lease service
options.detail: Keep tier-1 usability and the hostile-race guarantee by narrowly amending the no-root/no-daemon law. Linux keeps its unprivileged private mount. This option also ratifies new macOS/Windows distribution-installer behavior: official Jet installers register a root-owned macOS LaunchDaemon or Windows LocalSystem service after one explicit admin approval; no new Jet command is added. The service independently re-verifies the locked digest and copies executables into an OS-protected lease directory the caller cannot rewrite. It authenticates the local caller, then impersonates that caller and launches the child under the caller UID/session/token with no root/SYSTEM privileges or inherited service handles. The child PATH puts protected lease bins first, followed by the caller's approved inherited/system PATH; privilege-sensitive service variables and handles are removed, and package executable names can resolve only through protected lease dirs. A jet env lease lives through the shell and all descendants, then deletes after the process tree exits. The service has no network access, never resolves packages, and fails closed if stopped, mismatched, or unverifiable. Ordinary run/env use remains ceremony-free and offline.
options.code:
# During the new official macOS/Windows installer flow ratified by A:
Install protected executable lease service? [yes/no] yes
installed jet-lease-service 1.0.0

$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  protected
service            1.0.0, toolchain-matched
request identity   user, authenticated
child identity     user, no service privileges
handles/env        service authority removed
PATH                protected lease bins, then approved caller/system bins
network             denied
handoff             root-protected verified lease
same-user redirect blocked

$ jet env  # service stopped or version mismatched
error E1292: protected executable lease service is unavailable
fix: repair the Jet installation; no child or shell was started

options.name: Relax the hostile same-user guarantee
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and tier-1 usability, but explicitly weaken the security law on macOS and Windows. Jetpack uses a private snapshot, restrictive native handles where available, and digest validation immediately before launch. This catches corruption and non-racing swaps, but a hostile process running as the same user can race the final validation and a descendant PATH lookup; post-exit detection cannot undo executed code. Doctor and audit output name the weaker guarantee. This option is an intentional safety downgrade, not an equivalent backend.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
warning L1292: this host cannot exclude a same-user executable PATH race
why: macos has no unprivileged immutable named PATH view
fix: audit local same-user processes before running executable packages
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
warning L1292: commands in this environment have the weaker macos lease guarantee
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files  # a hostile same-user final-lookup race is not excluded

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  guarded, weaker than linux
same-user redirect not excluded

options.name: Fail closed for non-Linux executables
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and the full hostile-race guarantee. Fix data-only leases on every platform, but reject leases containing executables on macOS and Windows before any child starts. A new registered diagnostic explains that the platform cannot provide the required immutable handoff. This narrows D-JPK-PLATFORM1: macOS and Windows remain native for data libraries and non-executable package operations, but executable packages are Linux-only until an equally safe unprivileged primitive exists.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
error E1292: executable leases are unavailable on macos
why: Jetpack cannot create an immutable PATH view without a protected service
fix: run this executable package on Linux; mutable cache paths are never used

$ jet env  # project declares formatter executable
error E1292: this environment needs an executable lease unavailable on macos
no shell was started

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  unavailable
policy             fail closed

$ jetpack build data:unicode-tables
completed  # data-only leases still work

comparisons.note: Nix protects immutable store objects through privileged ownership and a daemon. Option A uses the same concrete authority boundary, but scopes it to verified executable handoff: no resolution, builds, cache networking, or general store ownership.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-store --verify --check-contents
# protected store paths remain outside user write authority

comparisons.note: Linux supplies a private read-only mount view inside an unprivileged user namespace. Jetpack already uses it to map stable PATH names to inherited descriptors.
CreateFile sharing flags can prevent replacement or deletion of opened executables, but a complete PATH solution must also protect directory/name resolution and child handoff.

decisions.title: jetos user-data backup and snapshot declaration
decisions.gist: How a jetos system declares backup/snapshot coverage for /home and other user data — generations (#327) only cover the system store, so there's no restore path for a user's own files today.
decisions.story:
Glossary: a generation is an atomic, versioned record of a full system build/switch (jet os generations, jet os rollback). A snapshot is a captured copy of file data at one point in time. A workload (D-JOS-CONTAINER1) is jetos's existing managed-thing mechanism: pick a backend, get shared image/mounts/secrets/health/resources/proof/rollback fields. Retention is how long old backups are kept before they're pruned.

Alex is editing ~/Documents/report.docx, fat-fingers a find-replace, saves over the good version, and closes the laptop. Ten minutes later Alex wants yesterday's copy back — no git repo, no cloud sync, just "give me my file from before." Priya, on the same jetos machine, wants more: her whole home directory backed up weekly to an offsite bucket, encrypted, in case the laptop is stolen or the disk dies — borgbackup-class protection she already runs on her old distro. Today jetos has no declaration surface for either need.

options.name: Fold backup into the existing generation/rollback engine
options.detail: Backup becomes a scoped extension of the system-generation source: a backup { ... } block inside system.<host> or user.<name>, walked by the same jet os generations / jet os rollback engine already ratified in D-JPK-OSGEN1/D-JOS-USERAPPLY1. No new CLI verb. Rejected: generations were designed for atomic whole-system state transitions triggered by jet os build/switch; backups are periodic captures of mutable data on their own clock. Mixing the two in one history list means a system-config rollback and a file-restore look like the same operation when they aren't — a real safety and long-term-correctness problem, not just an ergonomic one: jet os rollback on a mixed timeline risks reverting unrelated system state when the user only meant to recover a file.
options.code:
# config.jet
system.laptop {
  backup {
    hourly: paths(["~/Documents"])
    weekly_offsite: paths(["~"], encrypted: true, remote: "s3://alex-backup/home")
  }
}

$ jet os build && jet os switch
switched to generation 42 (system, 2026-07-10 14:00)
backup scope armed: hourly(~/Documents), weekly_offsite(~, encrypted)

$ jet os generations
  42  2026-07-10 14:00  system   switch (kernel bump)
  41  2026-07-10 13:00  backup   hourly snapshot (~/Documents)
  40  2026-07-10 12:00  backup   hourly snapshot (~/Documents)
  39  2026-07-09 09:00  backup   weekly_offsite snapshot (~, encrypted)
  ...

$ jet os rollback --path ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from generation 17 (2026-07-07 14:00)

options.name: Standalone top-level `backup.<name>` mechanism
options.detail: A new declaration kind, independent of generations and of workload: backup.<name> { source, schedule, backend } with its own backend enum (.LocalSnapshot / .EncryptedRemote) and its own CLI surface (jet os backup snapshot|restore|list|verify|prune). Clean separation of concerns, but it duplicates the exact field spine — secrets, health, proof, rollback, resources — that D-JOS-CONTAINER1 already built for workload. That's a second mechanism doing a job ("declared thing with a backend enum, health checks, and a rollback path") the platform already has one mechanism for, which is the I8 violation the workload precedent exists to prevent: the next managed-thing need after this one faces the same fork (extend workload, or mint backup.<name>-style #3), fragmenting the surface further over time.
options.code:
# config.jet
backup.documents {
  source: paths(["~/Documents"])
  schedule: .Hourly
  backend: .LocalSnapshot
}

backup.home_offsite {
  source: paths(["~"])
  schedule: .Weekly
  backend: .EncryptedRemote {
    remote: "s3://alex-backup/home"
    encryption: .AgeKey(secrets.backup_key)
  }
}

$ jet os backup list documents
  2026-07-10 14:00  snapshot 118
  2026-07-10 13:00  snapshot 117
  2026-07-09 14:03  snapshot  94
  ...

$ jet os backup restore documents --file ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from snapshot 94 (2026-07-07 14:03)

options.name: `workload.<name>`-style backend enum, backup as a managed workload
options.detail: Reuses the exact mechanism D-JOS-CONTAINER1 ratified for Container/MicroVM: one workload.<name> declaration, a backend enum that now also includes .Snapshot and .EncryptedRemote, and the same shared fields — mounts (what to capture), secrets (encryption key), health (did the last capture/restore succeed), resources, proof, and rollback. Restore goes through jet os rollback, the exact verb users already know from generations and other workloads — no new CLI surface to learn, and the proof/health machinery already gating container and microVM workloads (partial-write detection, post-action health check) applies to backups automatically instead of needing its own copy. One declaration shape covers 'run a container,' 'run a microVM,' and 'protect this data' — genuinely the same underlying question (what backend manages this, and how do I roll it back) asked three ways.
options.code:
# config.jet
workload.documents_backup {
  backend: .Snapshot
  source: paths(["~/Documents"])
  schedule: .Hourly
  rollback: .Enabled
}

workload.home_offsite {
  backend: .EncryptedRemote
  source: paths(["~"])
  schedule: .Weekly
  secrets: [secrets.backup_key]
  remote: "s3://alex-backup/home"
}

$ jet os build && jet os switch
switched to generation 42
workload documents_backup: healthy (last capture 14:00, 118 snapshots, 3d retention)
workload home_offsite: healthy (last capture 2026-07-09 09:00, encrypted, verified)

$ jet os rollback --workload documents_backup --path ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from workload documents_backup capture 94 (2026-07-07 14:03)

comparisons.note: Scheduled local snapshots (rsync/btrfs) with a GUI restore browser — the beginner story this ballot must match: no config, click a date, get the file back.
Encrypted, deduplicated, retention-pruned remote backups — the expert story: borg init --encryption=repokey, borg create, cron schedule, borg prune --keep-weekly=4.
comparisons.code:
# borgbackup: borg create repo::'{hostname}-{now}' ~ ; borg prune --keep-weekly=4
# jetos target: workload.home_offsite { backend: .EncryptedRemote, schedule: .Weekly, secrets: [...] }

decisions.title: jetos options search: dedicated verb, extend jet search/info, or Studio-only
decisions.gist: Whether searching/browsing jetos's typed system.* options (search.nixos.org parity) is a new `jet os options <query>` verb, a type-aware extension of the already-ratified `jet search`/`jet info` verbs, or a GUI-only feature in jetos Studio with no CLI at all.
decisions.explainer: B wins on discoverability (a beginner reaches for the one front door they already learned from package search, D-JPK-DISCOVER1, instead of remembering a second jetos-specific command) and on I8 (options become another typed, tagged result kind in the one 'find a named thing' index rather than a second search implementation to keep in sync). A is the runner-up if the owner wants option results to never carry a type tag. C is ruled out by the kill criteria: it strips a working default (option discovery) from every headless/terminal-baseline host, which is jetos's own first-class target.
decisions.story:
Terms used below — typed option: a `system.*` config field jetos already knows the type, default, and doc string for from the schema itself, not scraped from doc comments like NixOS's option pages; provenance: which `config.jet` line last set a value, and why it won over other declarations that touch the same option; offline index: a precomputed local search index, no network needed; front door: the command a user types first when they don't know the exact name yet.
