decisions.title: One generic definition per number family instead of one hand-written type per size
decisions.situation: Jet has whole-number types of fixed sizes, such as U8 and I32, and decimal types such as F32. Each size is hand-written into the compiler in hundreds of places, so the approved 16-bit decimals and 128-bit whole numbers still do not exist. You suggested one definition that builds whichever sizes Jet needs. We recommend one generic library type per family, with the familiar names kept and only the standard sizes allowed.
decisions.gist: Should Jet define each number family once, generically, and keep U8, I32 and F32 as names for its sizes?
decisions.lesson: A number family is a set of types that differ only in size, such as U8, U16, U32 and U64. A generic type takes the size as a build-time number, as in Unsigned<8>. An alias gives one size a short name, so U8 means Unsigned<8>.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing changes. Int stays exact and unlimited. U8{300} is still an error, and errors still say U8.

Expert path: every size behaves the same way because one definition serves them all. The approved overflow policy, conversions and lane types work for every size.

Shared by every option: the approved number rules stay. They cover exact Int by default, checked fixed sizes, lossless widening, the overflow policy and destination-named conversions. The options differ in how the sizes are defined and which sizes exist.
decisions.story: Lena trains a small model and needs 16-bit decimals. Jet approved them months ago, but adding a size means editing hundreds of places in the compiler, so they are still missing.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570: one type with a build-time program that builds whichever sizes Jet needs, instead of ten classes. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, section 6. Depends on D-CORE-BUILTINS1 for storage and D-CORE-ROLE1 for literal and operator roles.

Settled, not balloted. D-TYPE2-NUM1=A says a sized width is Int plus a proven range and a layout. D-INTBIG1=A keeps exact Int as the default. D-WRAP-SCOPE1=A selects overflow behaviour lexically, D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A keeps from_<source> names, and D-FOUND-LITERAL1=A routes literals through a capability. D-LOWFLOAT1=A adds F16, BF16 and two 8-bit storage formats, and D-LANES1=A defines Lanes<T, N>.

Today: types.rs:1100-1125 parses only 8, 16 and 32 bits, plus 64 unsigned and the name I64. BuiltinStatics.jet:210-238 lists nine widths and thirteen conversion sources by hand. Rust code matches Type::IntN at 310 sites and Type::Float32 at 204. F16 and BF16 appear nowhere in crates, Compiler or Core.

Peers: Zig builds any width with std.meta.Int. Carbon declares one generic class Int(N). Rust expands one int_impl! macro per width, Swift one template per width, and Julia generates methods with @eval loops.

Compile time: instances are built when the Core bundle is built and stored in the interface record. A user build adds no compile-time evaluation for numbers, against the speed plan's 0.10 s comptime budget for 300k lines.

options.name: One family, standard sizes
options.detail:
The library defines Signed<bits>, Unsigned<bits> and IEEE<exponent, fraction> once each. U8, I32, I128, F16, BF16, F32 and F64 become one-line aliases. Methods, operators, conversions and literal checks are written once per family.

Only the standard sizes exist: 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 bits for whole numbers, and the four standard decimal formats. A value set between sizes, such as 0 to 127, uses the range types Jet already has.

Errors, hovers and documents always show the alias name, such as U8.
options.technical:
Families wrap builtin.Bits<bits> and builtin.Float<e, f> (D-CORE-BUILTINS1=A). The #Arithmetic policy picks add_checked, add_wrap or add_saturate. One prep loop generates the from_<source> methods, and widening becomes one rule over bits and sign.

Type::IntN and Type::Float32 collapse into ordinary generic application. The remaining width-aware sites are layout, ABI and kernel lowering. numeric_type_from_name and the BuiltinStatics tables are deleted. Instances live in the interface record (SP12).

Odd widths stay ranges because D-TYPE2-NUM1 already models a width as Int plus range plus layout. A second spelling such as Unsigned<7> would violate I8.

options.name: One family, any size
options.detail:
The same generic families, but any whole-number size from 1 to 128 bits is allowed, such as Unsigned<24> or Signed<7>. Standard sizes keep their short names.

Bit-packed formats and odd hardware registers get a native type. A value set such as 0 to 127 can then be written two ways: as a range or as Unsigned<7>.
options.technical: Same as A, plus every width in 1..128 for Bits<n> in the kernel and back ends. LLVM supports arbitrary iN; Jet's own code generator would need widening and masking for odd widths. Two spellings for one value set conflicts with I8 and D-TYPE2-NUM1's grid.
options.code:
alias U8 :: Unsigned<8>
sample :: Unsigned<24>{0x7FFFFF}    // native 24-bit value
small :: Unsigned<7>{100}           // same values as Int(0..127)

options.name: One hand-written type per size, in the library
options.detail: Each size keeps its own type, now written in library source instead of the compiler. A shared template or copy keeps the sizes alike. Adding a size means adding a file and teaching the compiler its name.
options.technical: Rust int_impl! and Swift gyb shape. The compiler keeps per-width knowledge in its type enum and name parser.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: lib/std/meta.zig:942-955 at 0.14.0. One function builds an integer type of any width at build time. This is option B's reach.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: core/prelude/types/int.carbon:15-19. One generic class defines every integer size over a builtin. This is option A's shape.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: library/core/src/num/mod.rs:382-405. One macro call per width generates each type's methods. This is option C's shape.
Primary sources read 2026-10-04: base/boot.jl:280-288 and base/int.jl:87. Each width is a declared primitive type; arithmetic is written once for every bit integer.
comparisons.code:
primitive type Int8    <: Signed   8 end
(+)(x::T, y::T) where {T<:BitInteger} = add_int(x, y)

recommendation.why: A defines each family once, so new sizes are one line and every size behaves alike. Keeping only standard sizes leaves one way to write each value set.
gains: F16, BF16, I128 and U128 arrive as one alias line each.
Every size shares one tested definition of each operation.
User code and error messages keep the familiar names.

losses.loss: Odd sizes such as 24 bits have no native type.
losses.mitigation: A range type with an explicit packed layout covers them; a future battery that needs native odd sizes can reopen this.

losses.loss: Error messages could show Unsigned<8> instead of U8.
losses.mitigation: The alias is the display name in every error, hover and document, and snapshot tests prove it.

whyNot.reason: B gives odd value sets two spellings and adds odd-width work to every code generator.
C keeps eleven near-copies and a compiler change for every new size.

recommendation.tradeoff: Standard sizes only, in exchange for one definition per family and one spelling per value set.

decisions.title: Keep markers independent; make their derivation link explicit
decisions.situation: Jet writes routine code, such as field-by-field equality, for eligible types without asking beginners to add labels. Today a marker and a trait are linked by sharing a name, which hides why they belong together. Markers and traits otherwise do different jobs, so putting one inside the other teaches the wrong relationship. This vote chooses where to write the link; we recommend naming the trait on a separate marker declaration.
decisions.gist: Where should a marker say which trait it implements?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a compile-time label at a code site: a rule records a fact, a code-writing marker adds code, a gate permits a checked exception, and a group names fixed markers. A trait is a type contract: functions a type promises. Neither contains the other. They meet only in derivation, when a code-writing marker writes a trait implementation.
decisions.story: Omar follows #Equatable to its declaration and wants to see which contract its generated code fulfills, without treating every marker as a trait.
decisions.detail:
Owner direction, 2026-10-05: implicit beginner magic, explicit expert control; marker names are PascalCase. Markers and traits are independent, neither a subset of the other. They overlap only where a code-writing marker implements a trait. The nested-marker recommendation is withdrawn. This remains D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 on card #4570, c0s7shwh.

Settled: D-MARKER-LAW1=A merges providers into marker bodies, allows package markers to read/add/reject, and reserves checking changes to trusted built-ins. D-META-BODY1=A supplies a member-list body for an implementation. D-META-NAME1=A requires marker as the declaring word. D-META-FORM1=A and D-MARKER-SITES1=B supply typed parameters and $ facts. D-MARKER-GROUP1=A supplies fixed groups and exclusions; D-MARKER-MODULE1=A supplies pub and qualified library uses. D-CORE-BUILTINS1=A, ratified 2026-10-05, puts compiler-provided markers in jet_builtins and restricts imports. D-CORE-ROLE1=A puts Role(role:) there and restricts its use to Core.

Read-only Tower checks: D-META-AUTO1=A is ratified, automatically derives every structurally eligible trait, and silently leaves ineligible traits absent. D-AUTODERIVE-SYNTAX1=D is ratified: policy: .{ auto_derive: false } disables package defaults; #Equatable requests and #!Equatable refuses automatic generation. A hand-written impl wins over policy and either sign. D-META-AUTO1 also preserves project-wide selection of disabled traits. This ballot neither narrows defaults to four nor adds $auto: false nor changes package controls.

The choice is not settled: D-MARKER-NAME-HYGIENE1=A and D-MARKER-LAW1=A use shared marker/trait names for derivation, without mandating nesting or explicit linkage. B retains that convention; A replaces it with a marker-side clause; C puts selection on the trait. All three keep separate top-level declarations, which can share a file.

Source facts read this session: crates/jet-foundation/src/Generics.rs:9-13 lists standard trait-name constants. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:79-100 lists request rows, including Equatable at 92. Prelude/Derives.jet:13-53 supplies equality for enums, records and numeric bases. Markers.jet:28 supplies Unsafe's signature; :42 supplies Inline independently of traits. Role's declaring signature is grounded in D-CORE-ROLE1; full metadata stays governed by that law. These remnants explain migration, not a reason to retain the old split.

The complete marker-authoring catalog appears once in explainer. Each option shows the same Equatable contract, field-equality body, Point and equal_origin function. Only the link changes.

options.name: Marker names the trait
options.detail: Every marker is an independent top-level marker declaration. A code-writing marker that implements a trait writes derives Trait on its own header. The trait remains only its function contract. Both declarations may sit together in one file, but neither is nested in the other. The explicit link, not a matching name, identifies the generated implementation.
options.technical:
New surface: pub marker Equatable($sites: [.Type]) derives Equatable { member-list }. derives resolves a trait; Self is the marked type. It supplies the association and implied impl header under D-META-BODY1=A. Ordinary code-writing markers without derives retain their ordinary added-item bodies. A marker can use a different name from its trait. Trait references use ordinary resolution; library marker uses follow D-MARKER-MODULE1=A.

One deriving marker names one trait; existing groups combine derivations. Matching names without derives do not invent a link. The explicit clause replaces inferred registration, leaving eligibility, automatic defaults, signed requests/refusals and hand-written precedence unchanged. The marker declaration is the sole registry row, never a row generated from the trait.

Amends name-inferred derivation pairing in D-MARKER-NAME-HYGIENE1 and makes the member-body trait context explicit under D-MARKER-LAW1. Unrelated naming, marker kinds and tiers stay settled. derives is a linking clause, not the removed derive-provider form. Migrate every provider body and redundant request row together, preserving enum and numeric behavior. Diagnostics identify an unknown/non-trait derives target, invalid site or generated members failing the contract, with declaration and use locations.

options.name: Shared name beside the trait
options.detail: Keep today's approved name-pairing law. Declare the pure trait and a separate marker beside it in the same file. The marker is linked to the trait solely because both are named Equatable; there is no link clause. Readers see the code together and write no new linking word, but must know the name-pairing rule.
options.technical: Retains D-MARKER-LAW1=A and the derivation name-pairing convention in D-MARKER-NAME-HYGIENE1=A. The matched trait name supplies the implied implementation context for the D-META-BODY1=A member list; Self is the marked type. Colocation helps reading, but no nesting, trait-owned marker or extra derives/derive clause is introduced. Other marker kinds, the registry, eligibility and automatic/refusal/manual precedence are the shared laws. A rename must keep the pair's spellings synchronized.

options.name: Trait names the marker
options.detail: The trait header writes derive #Equatable to select a separately declared marker. That marker still has its own top-level marker declaration and code-writing body; no hidden marker is created. Readers discover the generator from the contract, while the contract now includes a generation choice beyond the functions it promises.
options.technical:
New header: pub trait Equatable derive #Equatable { contract-members }. Resolve one separately declared code-writing marker, using normal library qualification. The association supplies the D-META-BODY1=A implementation context; Self is the marked type. The trait body contains only contract members. No nested marker, implied declaration or old provider body is introduced. Explicit linkage replaces name-inferred pairing; renaming updates the reference.

The selected marker must accept type sites and generate members satisfying the contract. Resolve declarations independently of file order. The marker declaration remains the sole registry row; the trait reference supplies only the association. Eligibility, signed uses, defaults, manual precedence, origin restrictions and groups stay unchanged. Diagnostics name an unknown/non-code-writing marker or generated members failing the contract.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-05: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html, proc_macro_derive section. A named derive macro is declared separately, receives the marked type and appends items. This demonstrates independent code generation, not Jet's proposed derives syntax or its automatic defaults.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(PartialEq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

recommendation.why: A writes the relationship where the generated code is built, while keeping traits pure and markers independent. Beginners keep automatic code; experts can read and control the link.
gains: The generating marker explicitly names its contract.
Traits stay pure contracts, not marker containers.
Every marker has a visible top-level declaration.

losses.loss: Deriving marker headers gain one short clause.
losses.mitigation: Write it only when authoring a generator; automatic derivation and existing request/refusal sites stay unchanged.

whyNot.reason: B is familiar and concise, but the link remains an unwritten name-pairing convention.
C makes the generator discoverable from the trait, but mixes generation choice into its contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: A short generator-side clause buys an explicit link without nesting either concept.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Validate offline with node $JET_STATE_ROOT/ballots/READY/validate.mjs $JET_STATE_ROOT/ballots/READY/D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1.json and require exit 0. The validator mutates only a detached in-memory snapshot. No Tower writes or commits are authorized. Compiler, test and performance runs are outside this rewrite.

Owner acceptance: A keeps every marker independent at top level and explicitly writes derives Equatable beside a pure trait contract. B retains same-file name pairing; C writes derive #Equatable on a trait with the marker still separate. All panes show the same six-line Point/equal_origin program. Teach rule/code-writing/gate/group markers, pure traits and derivation as their only link. Show the complete creation catalog once, including pub library markers and jet_builtins. Do not add $auto: false or weaken automatic eligibility defaults.

After ratification, Main should plan one clean cutover in both compiler paths and the registry. Migrate every provider, redundant request row and affected docs/examples/tests; remove obsolete forms and inferred pairing if A or C wins. Preserve full enum/numeric bodies, eligibility, signed uses and manual precedence.

Implementation checks: automatic Point equality, package-off plus positive request, refusal without generated equality, manual equality winning over signs and policy, and silent absence for ineligible fields. Also check qualified pub/private library markers, group exclusions, restricted jet_builtins imports and Core-only Role use. For A, cover a differently named marker deriving Equatable and a same-name marker without derives. These are future implementation checks, not verification exercised by this rewrite.

surface.gist: Where should a marker say which trait it implements?
surface.lesson: A marker is a compile-time label at a code site: a rule records facts, a code-writing marker adds code. A gate permits a checked exception; a group names fixed markers. A trait is a type contract: promised functions. Neither contains the other. Their link is derivation: a code-writing marker implements a trait.

current.note: Today's approved rule links separate declarations by their shared name.

wild.note: Rust declares a derive macro separately; users request it on types.
wild.code:
#[derive(PartialEq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

options.name: Marker names the trait
options.gist: The independent marker explicitly names the contract it implements.
gains: Pure trait; explicit link.
losses: One clause when authoring a generator.

options.name: Shared name beside the trait
options.gist: Separate declarations share a name, with no written link.
gains: Keep today's convention.
losses: The relationship is implicit.

options.name: Trait names the marker
options.gist: The trait selects a separately declared deriving marker.
gains: Find the generator from the contract.
losses: The contract includes generation choice.

recommendation.why: A keeps contracts pure and writes the link on the generator. Beginners still get every eligible derivable trait automatically unless refused.
gains: Independent concepts; explicit derivation.

losses.loss: One generator-header clause.
losses.mitigation: Only generator authors write it; automatic code, #Equatable and #!Equatable keep their behavior.

whyNot.reason: B is concise, but relies on matching names.
C is discoverable, but adds generation choice to the contract.

designAway.loss: Nesting markers in traits would teach that one concept contains the other.
attempts: Use a nested marker to colocate code; rejected by the owner's independent-concepts direction.
Keep separate top-level declarations beside each other, with an explicit marker-side link; kept.

decisions.title: One way to choose who implements a library service, in builds, scopes and tests
decisions.situation: Library services such as the clock, files, network and memory need an implementation, and sometimes a program wants a different one. Today there are four ways to pick it: a board's build profile, a scope marker with a fixed menu, a test marker for injected failures, and separate fake-maker functions. All four answer one question in four different shapes. This vote decides whether they become one mechanism, and we recommend one interface per service that all four places use.
decisions.gist: Should board profiles, scoped replacements and tests all pick a service implementation the same way?
decisions.lesson: A service is something the library does for you through the system, such as telling the time or writing files. A provider is the code that implements it. A test can install a fake provider, and a small board can install its own hardware provider.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing changes. Programs use the real clock and files; tests stay short.

Expert path: each service has one interface in the library, such as Clock. A board profile, a #Context block and a test all name a value of that interface. Writing a fake for tests and a driver for a board is the same work.

Shared by every option: effects keep saying what a function may use, and providers say which code does it. The approved scope marker and board profile keep their names.
decisions.story: Dev writes a fake clock for his tests, then needs a hardware clock for a small board. Today the test fake, the board clock and the scoped replacement each use a different shape.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570: one uniform way to mark effects, abilities, requirements and features where meanings coincide. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, sections 7.1 and 8.

Today: target profiles name providers per fact (D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A; Prelude/Facts.jet:54-67). #Context replaces a Core service per scope (D-EFFECT-HANDLE1=A). Its registry row still lists only allocator, logger and deadline (Prelude/Markers.jet:177).

Tests inject failures with #Test(faults: [Effect]) (D-TESTFAULT1=A; Markers.jet:187). Fakes are separate calls such as testing.fake_clock and testing.fake_rng (Prelude/Core.jet:415-417).

The four answer one question, which implementation runs, so I8 asks for one mechanism. Effects stay separate: an effect is permission, a provider is implementation. D-FREESTAND-FACTS1 keeps machine provision apart from permission planes, and so does this proposal.

options.name: One interface per service; short test faults stay
options.detail:
Each replaceable service is one library trait, such as Clock, Files, Transport, Allocator or LogSink. A board profile, a #Context block and a test all name a value of that trait, with the same key names in each place.

The fake makers become ordinary provider types, such as testing.FixedClock. #Test(faults: [.FS]) stays as the short way to inject failures and is defined as a failing provider over the same trait.
options.technical:
One generated list of service keys feeds both the target-profile fact keys and the #Context marker signature (D-OPENTABLE1). The Markers.jet row's fixed allocator, logger and deadline menu is replaced by that list.

testing.fake_clock and testing.fake_rng dispatcher rows retire into provider types. #Test(faults:) keeps its D-TESTFAULT1 spelling and lowers to a Failing provider. Target-profile providers bind at link time; scope providers reuse D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's context read.

options.name: One interface per service; test faults retire
options.detail: The same single interface per service as A, but #Test(faults:) retires. A test that injects failures installs a failing provider with #Context, the same way as any other replacement. There is exactly one spelling, at the cost of longer tests.
options.technical: As A, plus retirement of D-TESTFAULT1's faults parameter with a teaching diagnostic pointing at #Context(fs: testing.Failing(...)).

options.name: Keep four ways
options.detail: Board profiles, #Context, test faults and fake makers stay separate mechanisms with their own names and shapes.
options.technical: Status quo; implement D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's providers in #Context without sharing them with target profiles or tests.

comparisons.note: D-EFFECT-HANDLE1=A, read 2026-10-04: Core defines one trait per replaceable service, and #Context replaces it for a scope. Option A extends the same trait to board profiles and tests.
[INFERENCE, not re-read this session] Odin's implicit context carries the allocator and logger, which a scope may replace for the code it calls.
comparisons.code:
context.allocator = my_arena_allocator()
process_input()   // allocations inside use the arena

recommendation.why: A gives every service one interface that boards, scopes and tests share, while keeping the short test spelling programmers already use.
gains: A fake for tests and a driver for a board are the same kind of code.
The scope marker accepts every service, not a fixed three.
Fake makers become ordinary library types.

losses.loss: Test faults keep a second, shorter spelling.
losses.mitigation: It is defined as a failing provider over the same interface, so there is one mechanism with a short form.

whyNot.reason: B makes the common failure test longer for no gain in meaning.
C keeps four shapes for one question.

recommendation.tradeoff: One interface per service, with the short test-fault form kept as a spelling over it.

decisions.title: Chip features: automatic by default, explicit control for experts
decisions.situation: Some fast code uses instructions that only newer processors have, such as the wide math of recent Intel chips. Today such code must sit inside a copy built for that chip level, so a helper deep inside a library can stop a beginner's build. You asked why the safe choice is not automatic, with explicit control for experts. This vote decides that, and we recommend that Jet builds the chip copies itself, picks one when the program starts, and keeps the existing marks for experts.
decisions.gist: Should Jet handle chip-specific instructions automatically, with marks only for experts who want control?
decisions.lesson: A chip feature is a group of instructions only some processors have, such as AVX-512 wide math. A chip copy is a version of a function Jet builds for one processor generation. Jet checks the processor once at start and uses the best copy. Every instruction also has a plain version that gives the same answer on any chip.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write nothing. When code uses a chip feature, directly or through a library, Jet builds a fast copy and a plain copy, checks the chip once at start, and runs the best one. Answers are identical on every chip.

Expert path: #Multiversion picks the chip levels and where the switch sits. prep if $build.cpu.has(.AVX512F) writes a branch by hand. jet build --cpu fixes the chip for the whole program. #!Multiversion on a function refuses automatic copies, so its callers must supply the feature.

Shared by every option: chip copies, the start-up chip check, build-time feature tests and instructions with plain meanings are already approved. Nothing here rebuilds code while the program runs; that stays the separate opt-in optimizer.
decisions.story: Mia calls a package's dot function, which uses AVX-512 inside a small helper. Her laptop lacks AVX-512 and her server has it. She should get a correct program on both, and the fast path on the server, without learning any of this.
decisions.detail:
Owner question, 2026-10-05, on this ballot: "why not implicit magic default, explicit expert option." Owner direction the same night: implicit beginner magic, explicit expert control. Card #4570. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, sections 7.2 and 8.

Settled, not balloted. D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A builds #Multiversion copies and binds the best one at start. D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A already dispatches Core's measured kernels automatically, even in a portable build, and gives forced-level tests and JET_CPU_MAX. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A gives every instruction entry a plain Jet body that tests compare with the chip.

What A changes. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A and D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A make an entry used outside a matching copy a build error. A narrows that error to the two cases where an expert's explicit mark conflicts, listed in option A. Everywhere else Jet adds the copies itself, extending D-SIMD-NATIVE1's Core-kernel default to all code.

Not adaptive. Copies are built ahead of time and chosen by the existing start-up probe. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B, which rebuilds code inside a running program, stays opt-in as the owner ruled. Features stay a separate plane from effects: an effect is permission, a feature is machine provision (D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A).

options.name: Automatic copies, with expert marks to steer or refuse
options.detail:
Jet works out which chip features each function needs, across calls, as it does for effects. Where code that needs a feature is reached from code that lacks it, Jet adds the switch itself. It builds a copy for the chip level that adds the feature and a plain copy, and the start-up check picks one. Hover, documents and jet inspect show every automatic switch and its copies.

Experts take control with marks Jet already has. #Multiversion(levels) sets the switch point and levels. prep if $build.cpu.has(.X) branches by hand. jet build --cpu or --features fixes the chip for the whole program, so no copies are needed. #!Multiversion refuses an automatic switch on one function.

The build stops only where explicit intent conflicts. One case is an instruction written directly in a #Multiversion copy whose level lacks it, outside a feature check. The other is a #!Multiversion function called where no copy, check or --cpu supplies its feature. Both errors name the call chain.
options.technical:
Feature needs are an inferred plane solved over the existing per-function summaries, separate from the effect row. An automatic switch goes on the outermost needing function in the module where the need arises: the first function on the chain called from another module or from code without the need. Calls inside the copies stay direct and inlinable, under D-CPU-DISPATCH1's same-level rule.

The copy set is the baseline plus the lowest target level that adds each needed feature, such as x86_64_v4 for AVX512F. On a target with no such level, the one copy uses the plain bodies. Plain bodies are tested bit-equal to the instruction (D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A), and D-SIMD-NATIVE1's result law binds every copy, so no FMA or approximate instruction is introduced. The interpreter and JIT run the baseline copy (I9). JET_CPU_MAX caps the choice.

An exported function with an automatic switch records it in the package interface, so callers see no unmet need. A #!Multiversion function exports its need instead. #!Multiversion reuses the ratified refusal sign (D-AUTODERIVE-SYNTAX1=D) on the existing marker: one registry change under I7. Cost: one bit set per function in the summary solve, inside the speed plan's 0.05 s budget, plus one copy per extra level of each switched function.

options.name: Inferred, but an unmet need is a build error
options.detail: Jet works out each function's needs the same way and shows them, but builds no copies on its own. Calling code that needs a feature from code without it is a build error that names the chain. The fix is to add #Multiversion or a feature check. Nothing is built that the author did not ask for.
options.technical: Same inferred plane as A, with no automatic switch. Exported needs are recorded in the package interface. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A's error stands as ratified and extends to helpers.

options.name: Written on every function in the chain
options.detail: A function that uses a feature says so with a marker, #Requires(.AVX512F), and so does every caller up to a chip copy. Needs are visible in source, and nothing happens automatically.
options.technical: New marker #Requires(features...), registered under I7. This is the shape of Rust's target_feature and Odin's enable_target_feature.

comparisons.note: Primary sources read 2026-10-04: base/intrinsics/intrinsics.odin:386-391 and 410-411. A feature is required by an attribute on each procedure and tested with has_target_feature. This is option C's shape.
comparisons.code:
@(require_target_feature="atomics")
wasm_memory_atomic_wait32 :: proc(ptr: ^u32, expected: u32, timeout_ns: i64) -> u32 ---

comparisons.note: D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A, read 2026-10-05: Core's measured kernels already use the best chip level the running chip has, with no user mark. Option A extends that default to all code.
comparisons.code:
values :: [F64]{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}
print(values.sum())   // Core's kernel may use AVX2 here; same answer everywhere

recommendation.why: A gives beginners fast, correct code on every chip with nothing to write. Experts keep exact control through marks Jet already has, plus one refusal.
gains: A library's chip-specific speedups need no marks and never break a beginner's build.
Answers are identical on every chip, checked by the existing forced-level tests.
Experts steer with #Multiversion, feature checks or --cpu, or refuse with #!Multiversion.

losses.loss: Automatic copies make the program larger.
losses.mitigation: Copies are made only for code that uses a feature, one per extra chip level. jet inspect lists every switch and its size.

losses.loss: A call into a switched function costs one indirect jump.
losses.mitigation: Calls inside a copy stay direct and inlinable. An expert moves the switch outward with #Multiversion.

whyNot.reason: B stops a beginner's build over a chip detail that a library chose.
C repeats the same mark on every function in a chain and is never automatic.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds chip copies by itself, in exchange for no chip marks and no chip errors on the beginner path.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, Main confirms this update is linked to card #4570 (c0s7shwh) and runs Tower's ballot validator. The reviser ran validate.mjs offline only. No Jet compiler, test or performance run was made. Decide after D-CORE-BUILTINS1, because instruction entries are declared through it.

Owner acceptance: confirm that automatic copies are the default and that #!Multiversion is the one new spelling. Also confirm that A narrows the instruction-outside-a-copy error of D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A and D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A to the two explicit-conflict cases.

After ratification, one card: the need plane in the summary solve, automatic switch placement, the refusal row, and interface records, once #Multiversion lands (#4167, #4168). Proofs: forced-level bit tests per level on an automatically switched function, UI snapshots for both conflict diagnostics, and a size report for one switched Core kernel.

surface.lesson: A chip feature is a group of instructions only some processors have. A chip copy is a version of a function built for one processor generation. Jet checks the processor once at start and runs the best copy.

current.note: Today a helper that uses AVX-512 has no rule, and a direct use outside a chip copy stops the build.

fn dot16(a: [F32], b: [F32]) -> F32 { ... }   // uses AVX-512: no rule today

options.name: Automatic, with expert marks
options.gist: Jet builds fast and plain copies itself; experts steer or refuse with marks.
gains: Beginners write nothing and never hit chip errors.
Experts keep full control with existing marks.
losses: Programs grow by one copy per extra chip level.

options.name: Inferred, errors when unmet
options.gist: Jet works out each need but builds nothing on its own.
gains: Nothing is built that the author did not ask for.
losses: A library helper can stop a beginner's build.

options.name: Written on every function
options.gist: Each function in the chain carries a marker naming its features.
gains: Needs are visible in source.
losses: Every function in a chain repeats the mark.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners fast, correct code on every chip with nothing to write, and experts keep exact control.
gains: No chip marks or chip errors for beginners.
Same answers on every chip.
Experts steer or refuse with marks.

losses.loss: Programs grow by automatic copies.
losses.mitigation: Copies exist only for code that uses a feature, and an inspect command lists each one with its size.

losses.loss: A switched call costs one indirect jump.
losses.mitigation: Calls inside a copy stay direct, and experts can move the switch outward.

whyNot.reason: B stops beginners' builds over a library's chip choice.
C repeats marks along every chain and is never automatic.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds copies by itself, for no chip marks or errors on the beginner path.

designAway.loss: Automatic copies could grow programs without the author knowing.
attempts: Copy the whole program per chip level; rejected because size doubles for code that never uses a feature.
Copy only switched functions and their same-module callees, one extra level each, listed by jet inspect; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation.

designAway.loss: A switch placed at the innermost helper would put an indirect call inside hot loops.
attempts: Switch at the function that uses the instruction; rejected for that reason.
Switch at the outermost needing function of the module, so loops inside stay direct, and let experts move it with #Multiversion; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation.

designAway.loss: Automatic copies could change answers between chips.
attempts: Trust each instruction's documentation; rejected.
Use only instructions whose plain body is tested bit-equal, under the existing result law; kept.
designAway.result: Removed.

decisions.title: Learning from real runs: rebuild with a record, and optionally re-optimize while running
decisions.situation: A built Jet program is fully compiled before it ships, so it never learns how it is really used. Java, C# and JavaScript engines watch a running program and rebuild its busiest code, which helps long-running servers. This vote decides whether Jet uses recorded runs when building, also lets long-running programs re-optimize themselves, or stays fully static.
decisions.gist: Should Jet use recorded runs to build faster programs, and may a long-running program re-optimize itself?
decisions.lesson: A record is a file listing what a run used most: busy functions, which way decisions usually went, and which functions a call usually reached. Building with a record changes speed only, never results. An in-program optimizer is a part of the program that recompiles its busiest functions while it runs, using Jet's own code generator. Phones, game consoles and browsers forbid programs from making new machine code while running.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing new to learn. If a package contains a record, release builds use it and say which record they used. Without one, builds work as today.

Expert path: record a real workload with Jet's existing performance tools, keep the record with the source, and rebuild. Under option B, add one build flag to a long-running server to let it keep improving while it runs.

Shared by every option: chip-level copies, build-time code and Jet's own code generator stay as already approved. Recording already follows approved rules: it samples by default and counts exactly on request. Nothing is ever sent off the machine.

The options differ in one thing. A uses recorded runs when building. B does that and also lets long-running programs re-optimize themselves. C uses neither.
decisions.story: Lena runs a Jet web service for months. Her traffic changes with the seasons, and she wants every bit of speed without hand-tuning.
decisions.inWild:
# Go profile-guided optimization (go.dev/doc/pgo)
$ curl -o cpu.pprof "http://localhost:8080/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30"
$ mv cpu.pprof default.pgo     # in the main package directory, committed with the source
$ go build                     # -pgo=auto uses default.pgo; Go 1.22 measured about 2-14% faster
decisions.detail:
Owner questions, 2026-10-04, card #4571. Can a JIT beat AOT? Does a hybrid JIT help when every scenario must be as fast as possible? Could a JIT report hot paths to an AOT build, or could an AOT binary carry an onboard optimizer? Research: Docs/research/adaptive-runtime-specialization-2026-10-04.md.

Settled, not balloted. The Cranelift jet-jit crate is not ported (D-EXEC1=A, ruling of 2026-10-04). Recording is local and never sent (D-TELEMETRY1=A, Docs/spec/reference/network-policy.md:3-4). The record is the existing .jettrace artifact (D-PERFSESSION1=D, D-ARTIFACT-EXT1=A, Docs/spec/observability.md:23,36-52). Sampling by default with explicit counting (D-PROFILE-METHOD1=A), and source records with function totals (D-PROFILE-DETAIL1=A), are law. The compiler never adds CPU copies on its own, because D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A rejected compiler-chosen clones (its option D).

Evidence that runtime tiers beat AOT, and by how much.
- The big factors compare a JIT with an interpreter of a dynamic language: TurboFan 4.35x on JetStream (v8.dev/blog/maglev) and PyPy about 4x CPython 3.11 (pypy.org).
- Jet's static types already capture most of that.
- Over compiled code, gains are 2-20%: .NET dynamic PGO up to 20% (Announcing .NET 8) and JEP 515 training profiles 19% faster warm-up.

JEP 544 (JDK 28) says profile-guided static code "can even be competitive with HotSpot". It keeps a JIT for three reasons: workload change, exact hardware and dynamic loading. .NET documents that ReadyToRun code "is not as highly optimized as code produced by the JIT", so tiering replaces hot methods.

Evidence for recorded runs into AOT.
- Go PGO is about 2-14% faster and recommends committing default.pgo for reproducible builds.
- AutoFDO reaches a 10.5% geomean, which is 85% of instrumented FDO (CGO 2016).
- BOLT adds up to 8.0% on top of PGO and LTO for data-center services, and 20.4% for GCC and Clang (arXiv:1807.06735).
- Propeller adds 1.1-8% beyond PGO and ThinLTO (ASPLOS 2023).
- Android Baseline Profiles make code about 30% faster from the first launch.

Evidence for AOT and against always-on JITs.
- JEP 544 cuts startup 65-80% with AOT code.
- Julia 1.9 cut CSV.jl's time to first run from 11.66 s to 0.08 s.
- About 45% of V8 CVEs since 2019 were JIT bugs, and the JIT kept CET and ACG off (Edge security blog).
- iOS guideline 2.5.2 forbids running new code.
- V8 names iOS, smart TVs and consoles as platforms that forbid writable executable memory, and macOS needs the allow-jit entitlement.

Jet pieces reused.
- One lowering and one runtime (D-TIER-ONEIR1=A, D-TIER-FORM1=A, D-EXEC1=A).
- Slot-table recompilation is already designed: Docs/research/jet-backend-design-2026-10-01.md:513-541, with x64_rebind_slot exercised on an import slot.
- The W^X loader is at :346-352.
- #Multiversion's bit-identical result law (D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A).

Gaps today.
- .jettrace profile rows attribute only to fn run, with no stack samples (observability.md:50-52).
- Release builds still go through rustc (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:166).
- The word --profile already names build profiles (cli.md:166, D-BUILDPROFILE1), so the record flag needs another word.

Performance law: AGENTS.md:165-168 requires a paired two-program cell. A surface's ratification waits until it strictly beats the plain form. This ballot sets the direction, and the measurement plan in the research report section 4.6 gates each surface.

options.name: Learn from recorded runs
options.detail:
A release build reads a record of real runs and uses it to lay out busy code together and put likely branches first. It also inlines calls the record shows are common, guards and calls the usual target of a closure or trait call directly, and presizes buffers where the record shows typical sizes.

A record kept in the package is used automatically. An explicit flag picks another record or turns recording off. The build receipt names the record and how much of it still matched the code.

Records come from Jet's existing performance tools. You can attach to a live server, which samples it, or run a representative workload with exact counting. Results never change; only speed does.

The same source, the same record and the same toolchain always give a byte-identical program. A record from older code still applies to the functions that did not change, and the rest are skipped.
options.technical:
The record is a canonical profile record inside .jettrace. It is keyed by stable function symbol plus MIR body digest, sorted, and its counts are quantized to log2 buckets of the run total, so re-recording noise gives the same bytes.

The record is a hashed build input in the action key (D-BUILDCACHE1=A). It never reaches comptime, prep if or $build facts. Counts are taken on MIR blocks, the one lowering, so a counting run at O0 equals one at O2.

O1, the Jet backend, uses the record in four ways. Branch weights drive LIR block layout and hot/cold splitting. A hotness-weighted inline budget and guarded devirtualization run inside the bounded O1 passes (#4135, SP20). Value-specialization clones get entry guards. The in-process linker orders functions by hotness (SP19), the Propeller relink approach with no binary rewriting.

O2: when O2 emits LLVM IR, the record becomes !prof branch weights, function entry counts and VP metadata. The rustc bridge is not fed -Cprofile-use, because the emitter retires and its symbols churn. O0 ignores the record.

CPU level: the record reports which level ran, and jet explain suggests a #Multiversion level instead of adding copies on its own.

Needed first: a real PC and stack sampler in the shared runtime, plus function identity and body digest in the source map. Proofs come in three parts. Artifacts with a record are byte-identical at 1 job and N jobs. Goldens are identical with and without a record. A paired run-time cell is measured on a workload different from the recorded one.

options.name: Recorded runs, plus an opt-in in-program optimizer
options.detail:
Everything in A, and one more build flag for long-running programs such as servers. With it, the program starts on its normal prebuilt code. After warm-up it watches itself at a low rate and recompiles its busiest functions in memory.

It does so in three cases. Traffic has moved away from the build's record. A value fixed after startup, such as a route table or a setting, can be built into the code. Or the machine's chip allows more than the build assumed, under the same exact-result rule.

The new code comes from the same program description, through the same Jet code generator, calling the same runtime, so answers are identical. When the program exits it writes a record, so the next build learns too.

The optimizer is off unless you ask for it. It has caps on CPU share and code memory. The build refuses the flag for phones, consoles, browsers and bare-metal targets, and names the reason. On macOS the package must declare the permission to make code. A switch at launch turns the optimizer off, and the program then runs the identical prebuilt code.
options.technical:
Under --adaptive (spelling illustrative), eligible functions call through the slot table: the record's hot functions, or all non-inlined functions if there is no record. Today static images keep rel32 (jet-backend-design:541). The binary carries a compact MIR slice for those functions (D-TIER-FORM1, no second IR). It also carries the Jet O1 pipeline and x86-64 code generator, linked as a library from the same Jet source, plus a sampler thread and Image/Loader.jet.

Compiles run on one background thread. They map RW, copy, mprotect to RX and rebind the slot (:528-533). Thresholds rise as the code cap fills, as JSC does.

Specializations guard at function entry only, and a failed guard calls the kept prebuilt copy. There is no on-stack replacement and there are no frame-state maps; running frames finish in the old body. Jet's immutability facts make folding run-time constants safe with an identity guard only.

I9: a forced test mode compiles every eligible function immediately with synthetic profiles and guards taken both ways, and it runs the goldens (the HotSpot -Xcomp analogue). D-CPU-DISPATCH1's bit-identical rule binds every runtime copy.

Platforms: the build refuses iOS, consoles, wasm and freestanding targets. It checks the macOS allow-jit entitlement and adds a MAP_JIT loader. Windows needs a VirtualProtect loader. Today the OS layer is Linux only.

This is not the Cranelift engine, has no interpreter, and adds no user API. It extends D-EXEC1: shipped binaries may carry the O1 generator, but only under this flag.

Shipping gate: a long-running service whose traffic mix shifts mid-run, plus one run-time-constant workload, must strictly beat A's prebuilt binary, with warm-up and steady state reported separately. Peers are HotSpot with JEP 544 and .NET with ReadyToRun plus dynamic PGO.

options.name: Fully static
options.detail:
Builds never read records, and programs never re-optimize while running. Speed comes from what is known when building: chip-level copies chosen at start, build-time code, and the code generator's own guesses about which branches are likely.

The performance tools still record runs for people to read, but builds ignore those records.
options.technical: No change beyond the ratified #Multiversion and comptime. This gives up the measured profile gains: Go 2-14%, AutoFDO 10.5% geomean, BOLT and Propeller 1-8% on large binaries. It also gives up any response to workload drift or run-time constants. It matches what a Rust user gets without the manual -Cprofile-generate and -Cprofile-use steps.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: go.dev/doc/pgo. A committed CPU profile named default.pgo is used automatically, and Go 1.22 measured about 2-14%. Option A follows this shape.
comparisons.code:
$ mv cpu.pprof default.pgo     # main package directory
$ go build                     # -pgo=auto
$ go build -pgo=off            # opt out

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: openjdk.org/jeps/544. A training run stores AOT code and profiles. Production starts on them, and the JIT re-optimizes if the workload changes. This is the hybrid of option B; startup falls 65-80%.
comparisons.code:
$ java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App ...   # training run
$ java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App ...         # production

comparisons.note: Primary sources read 2026-10-04: learn.microsoft.com ready-to-run and runtime-config/compilation, and the .NET 8 announcement. Prebuilt ReadyToRun code starts fast. The tiered JIT with dynamic PGO replaces hot methods, which helps by up to 20%.
comparisons.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>  <!-- prebuilt code at start -->
  <TieredPGO>true</TieredPGO>                  <!-- hot methods re-JITted with live profiles -->
</PropertyGroup>

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: clang.llvm.org/docs/UsersManual.html. An instrumented build is run, the profile is merged, and the program is rebuilt. Instrumented counts are reproducible; sampling has very low overhead.
comparisons.code:
$ clang++ -O2 -fprofile-instr-generate code.cc -o code
$ ./code typical-input
$ llvm-profdata merge -output=code.profdata default.profraw
$ clang++ -O2 -fprofile-instr-use=code.profdata code.cc -o code

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: developer.android.com/topic/performance/baselineprofiles/overview. A recorded user journey is compiled ahead of time at install, making it about 30% faster from the first launch.

recommendation.why: B gives every release build the measured speed-up of recorded runs, and lets long-running programs keep improving where the platform allows it. It uses Jet's one code generator, one runtime and the function-swap mechanism already designed, so answers stay identical.
gains: Every release build can use recorded runs, typically 2-20% faster in peers' measurements.
Long-running servers can follow traffic changes and settings fixed at startup, as Java and .NET do.
No second engine: the same program description, code generator and runtime serve every path.

losses.loss: A program built with the optimizer is bigger and spends some CPU and memory while warming up.
losses.mitigation: It is off unless a build asks for it, with fixed caps on CPU share and code memory. It ships only after a paired benchmark shows it beating A's prebuilt program on a long-running workload.

losses.loss: It makes new machine code while running, which phones, consoles and browsers forbid and some security reviews reject.
losses.mitigation: The build refuses the flag for those targets and names the reason. Elsewhere, memory is never writable and runnable at once, and a launch switch runs the identical prebuilt code.

whyNot.reason: A cannot follow traffic that changes after the build or use settings fixed at startup, which is what you asked a runtime tier for.
C leaves measured 2-20% speed-ups unused, against your goal of maximum speed in every scenario.

recommendation.tradeoff: An opt-in, bigger program for long-running servers buys the speed only a running program can find; every other build gets recorded-run speed at no cost while running.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, Main confirms that this draft is linked to card #4571 (c0nxupyn). Main then runs Tower's ballot validator. The drafter ran the store's ballotGaps check offline only. This is a short ballot with three options; independent full-profile reviews are not claimed. No Jet compiler, test or performance run was made for this draft. Every number is cited from primary sources in the research report.

Owner acceptance has five points.
1. A record kept in the package is used by release builds automatically, Go-style, with an explicit override and opt-out. The flag spelling settles when its CLI row lands; it cannot be --profile, which names build profiles.
2. The in-program optimizer is opt-in for long-running programs and refused for targets that forbid run-time code. This extends D-EXEC1: shipped binaries may carry the O1 code generator, but only under that flag.

3. Under AGENTS.md:165-168, each surface's ratification waits for its paired cell. This ballot decides the direction and the order of work.
4. The in-program optimizer is the one Jet backend linked as a library, never the retired Cranelift engine.
5. A forced-compile test mode joins the I9 differential matrix.

After ratification, Main plans cards in this order.
1. A runtime PC and stack sampler, with function identity and MIR body digest in source maps.
2. The canonical profile record in .jettrace, and O1 consumption: layout, hot/cold splitting, the inline budget, guarded devirtualization, value clones and linker ordering.
3. Counting mode.
4. O2 metadata once O2 emits LLVM IR.

5. A's paired cells.
6. For B: slot calls in static images, the MIR slice, the backend as a runtime library, the sampler policy and caps, the macOS and Windows loaders, and the forced test mode.
7. B's paired cell against A and against HotSpot JEP 544 and .NET ReadyToRun plus dynamic PGO.

Proofs come in four parts. Artifacts with a record are byte-identical at 1 job and N jobs. Goldens are identical with and without a record and under the forced adaptive mode. Forbidding targets get refusal diagnostics. An strace shows no mapping that is writable and executable at once.

surface.gist: Should Jet use recorded runs to build faster programs, and may a long-running program re-optimize itself?
surface.lesson: A record lists what a run used most: busy functions, usual branch directions and usual call targets. Building with it changes speed, never results. An in-program optimizer recompiles a running program's busiest functions with Jet's own code generator. Phones, consoles and browsers forbid making new machine code while running.

current.note: Today Jet can record where a run spent time, but builds never use the record.
current.code:
$ jet perf run server.jet --out server.jettrace   # records where time went
$ jet perf view server.jettrace                     # you can read it...
$ jet build --release server.jet                    # ...but the build never uses it

wild.note: Go builds automatically use a committed CPU record from production, for about 2-14% more speed.
wild.code:
$ curl -o cpu.pprof "http://localhost:8080/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30"
$ mv cpu.pprof default.pgo     # main package directory
$ go build                     # uses default.pgo automatically

options.name: Learn from recorded runs
options.gist: Record what real work used most; the next build uses it.
gains: Typically 2-14% faster in Go's measurements, at no cost while running.
The same source and record always give the same program.
losses: Someone must record real work and refresh it.
Cannot follow traffic that changes after the build.

options.name: Recorded runs, plus an opt-in in-program optimizer
options.gist: A, and long-running programs may recompile their busiest functions while running.
gains: Follows traffic changes without rebuilding.
Can build settings fixed at startup into the code.
losses: A bigger program that uses some CPU and memory while warming up.
Not allowed on phones, consoles or browsers.

options.name: Fully static
options.gist: No records and no optimizer while running; only what is known when building.
gains: Nothing to record, refresh or ship.
losses: Leaves the measured 2-20% gains of recorded runs unused.
No response to changing traffic.

recommendation.why: Every release build gains from recorded runs, and long-running programs keep improving where allowed, with one code generator and identical answers.
gains: Recorded-run speed for every release build.
Long-running servers follow changing traffic.

losses.loss: With the optimizer, the program is bigger and warms up in the background.
losses.mitigation: Off unless asked for, capped, and shipped only after a benchmark beats A.

losses.loss: It makes new machine code while running, which some platforms forbid.
losses.mitigation: The build refuses it there; elsewhere a launch switch runs identical prebuilt code.

whyNot.reason: A cannot follow traffic that changes after the build.
C leaves measured speed-ups unused.

recommendation.tradeoff: An opt-in, bigger program for long-running servers; every other build gets recorded-run speed for free.

designAway.loss: A record could make builds unreproducible.
attempts: Pick up the latest record from a cache or the environment automatically; rejected because the output would depend on hidden machine state.
Make the record an explicit hashed build input, in a canonical sorted form with counts quantized so noise does not change bytes; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: the same source, record and toolchain give a byte-identical program.

designAway.loss: An old record could slow or break a build after the code changes.
attempts: Require a fresh record for every build; rejected as too much ceremony.
Match records by function name and body fingerprint, skip mismatches, and report the matched share; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: stale parts are ignored, and the build says how much still matched.

designAway.loss: A record could change what a program computes.
attempts: Let recorded values feed build-time code; rejected.
Let the record only choose among lowerings the compiler already proves equal, keep it away from build-time code, and test goldens with and without it; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: the record changes speed only.

designAway.loss: Recorded values could capture private data.
attempts: Record any argument value; rejected.
Record counts, call targets and opt-in small scalar values only, never text or collections, and keep the file local; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: records hold no user text and never leave the machine.

designAway.loss: An in-program optimizer could be a second engine that disagrees with the normal build.
attempts: Port the retired Cranelift engine; rejected by the 2026-10-04 ruling.
Link the one Jet code generator as a library, compile from the same program description, call the same runtime, and run all goldens in a forced-compile test mode; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: one code generator and one runtime serve every path.

designAway.loss: Undoing a wrong guess in the middle of a running function is complex and error-prone.
attempts: Copy JavaScript engines' mid-function bail-out with saved frame maps; rejected.
Guard only at function entry, keep the prebuilt copy for every miss, and let running calls finish in the old code; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: no mid-function bail-out exists.

designAway.loss: The optimizer makes programs bigger and uses CPU and memory while warming up.
attempts: Turn it on for every build; rejected.
Make it opt-in with CPU and code-memory caps, and ship it only after a paired benchmark beats the prebuilt program; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: only programs that ask for it pay.

designAway.loss: Some platforms forbid making machine code while running, and it widens what an attacker can target.
attempts: Turn it off silently at run time on such platforms; rejected because the program would behave unexpectedly.

Refuse the flag at build time with a named reason, never map memory writable and runnable at once, compile only the program's own checked code, and offer a launch switch to run the prebuilt code; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: forbidden targets fail early and clearly.

designAway.loss: The natural flag word, profile, already names build profiles.
attempts: Reuse --profile; rejected because it collides with --profile release.
Use a different word, settled when the command-line row lands; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: no meaning collision.

decisions.title: Jet's user files: disposable cache and protected identity
decisions.situation: Jet spreads downloaded packages, settings, signing keys and remembered trust across two user folders. You asked to keep only the cache folders, but deleting a cache must not also destroy your identity. This vote decides what moves and where the irreplaceable files stay. No files are moved or deleted by this vote.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet keep files that a cache cleanup must not erase?
decisions.lesson: A cache holds replaceable downloaded or built files. A signing key identifies you; a decrypting key unlocks secrets. Trust records remember which projects and publishers you allowed. Those files and your settings need backup, not cache cleanup.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: keep running the same Jet and Jetpack commands; the default locations change, not project syntax. Expert path: use the existing explicit store and key-folder overrides and standard Linux directory settings; no new override or migration command is proposed.

Both options preserve keys, settings, trust, installed-tool declarations and retention records. Retention records say which package objects an installed tool, project or running process still needs. Project-local .jet files are a separate matter and do not move. Developer scratch remains separate from product files.
decisions.story: Ana wants to reclaim downloaded package space without losing her ability to decrypt a project's secrets or changing which publishers she trusts.
decisions.inWild:
# Linux separates settings from disposable cache.
~/.config/app/
~/.cache/app/
decisions.detail:
Source: $JET_STATE_ROOT/burndown/JET-HOME-QUESTION.md:3-5 records owner prompt 2782 asking about ~/.jet. Item 101/SEED 7 says only ~/.cache/jet and $JET_STATE_ROOT may remain. Its inventory reports ~/.jet at 819 MB and ~/.local/share/jet at 7.0 GB. These are supplied sizes, not fresh measurements.

The inventory lists keys, trust, store, tools, registry content and Git downloads in ~/.jet. The data home contains hangar, leases, lease-service, config, source-kinds and locks. Folder names do not prove every byte is disposable.

The decision list has no general user-home consolidation ballot. Archived D-ECO-HANGARPATH1=A specifies native per-user data paths. Linux uses $XDG_DATA_HOME/jet/hangar or ~/.local/share/jet/hangar. macOS uses Application Support; Windows uses LOCALAPPDATA. Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Store/HangarRoots.jet:111-146 cites that rule and resolves JETPACK_ROOT or platform data. Only absolute XDG_DATA_HOME values are honored. Archival is not a contrary ruling. D-GENERATED-STORAGE2 concerns project files, not user-global homes.

D-CORE-SECRETSTORE1=A places secrets.identity at ~/.jet/keys with mode 0600. JET_KEYS_DIR overrides its folder. Jetpack/Trust/Source/Secrets/RepoSecrets.jet:51-61 does the same. crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:14-18 documents ~/.jet/trust. Jetpack/Nix/Source/Index/IndexClient.jet:50-63 reads public-key and endpoint configuration under the Hangar root. Jetpack/Store/Source/ArtifactStore/StoreConfig.jet:103-105 already uses ~/.cache/jet/store for artifacts. Consolidation changes public default paths, not just leftover folders. Migrate these readers and writers together.

A requests a narrow protected-identity exception to the owner's cache-only instruction. It amends the Linux path in D-ECO-HANGARPATH1 and identity default in D-CORE-SECRETSTORE1. B revises the instruction by preserving the data home and consolidating identity there. Neither elevates the older ruling over the newer owner instruction.

Neither option puts private keys in disposable cache. Moving everything into ~/.cache/jet is not offered as a safe third choice. External cache cleanup can erase it regardless of Jet's own rules.

Scope: Linux default user-global homes only. macOS/Windows defaults and administrator-owned shared stores stay unchanged. Existing JETPACK_ROOT and JET_KEYS_DIR remain expert controls; their owners choose the locations. Honor absolute, nonempty XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME, plus XDG_DATA_HOME under B. Otherwise use standard Linux fallbacks. Empty or relative values do not select another home. $JET_STATE_ROOT remains developer-only scratch/proofs, never product keys or settings.

Migration: inventory actual contents before deleting anything. Preserve key bytes and restrictive permissions, public trust roots, trust decisions and user configuration. Preserve native recipes/source registrations, installed-tool declarations, registry identity and retention/lease metadata. Only replaceable package/artifact payloads and fetched Git/index content are cache. Do not assume local or unreproducible objects can be fetched again. Preserve irreplaceable objects and exact receipts before relocation or cleanup.

Stop relevant processes before relocating live leases or sockets. Recreate transient sockets and locks rather than copy stale ones. Verify the complete destination first. Detect conflicting identities/settings instead of overwriting. Remove only accounted-for old contents after successful cutover. Unknown files block removal of their folder and get reported. This ballot task deletes no user files.

After cutover, one resolver serves all affected readers and writers. No persistent old-path fallback, symlink home, dual writes or migration alias remains. Update commands, examples, tests and documentation together. Keys must decrypt the same ciphertext; trust must authorize exactly the same identities. A path change grants no new trust. Cache removal may require reacquisition or a confirmed rebuild, but never regeneration of signing identity. Existing retention rules protect live objects. This vote does not authorize blanket automatic deletion.

options.name: Separate disposable files from identity
options.detail: Move replaceable package and build payloads to the cache home. Keep keys, trust, settings, tool declarations and durable retention metadata in one protected configuration home. Remove the old hidden home and old data home after the verified migration. Ordinary commands need no change; experts keep existing path overrides.
options.technical:
Cache root: $XDG_CACHE_HOME/jet, falling back to ~/.cache/jet. Hangar payloads use <cache>/hangar; artifacts retain <cache>/store. Protected root: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jet, falling back to ~/.config/jet. The identity becomes <config>/keys/secrets.identity; trust becomes <config>/trust.

Move public publisher keys, catalog/cache settings, user settings, native recipes/source registrations and tool/retention records under the protected root. Preserve existing relative names where unambiguous. Recreate process sockets/locks on restart beside their owning storage. Durable lease/root facts must survive cache cleanup.

Introduce no public spelling. Amend the cited default-path contracts explicitly. Remove ~/.jet and ~/.local/share/jet only after accounting for every old file. Preserve nonreplaceable store payloads; never delete them automatically. Linux expert overrides remain unchanged.
options.code:
# Before: identity and packages are mixed in two homes.
# After: the same commands use these Linux defaults.
~/.config/jet/keys/secrets.identity  # keep and back up
~/.config/jet/trust                  # keep
~/.cache/jet/hangar/                 # package payloads
$JET_STATE_ROOT/                    # developer scratch only

options.name: One backed-up user-data home
options.detail: Consolidate keys, trust, settings, package storage and durable retention metadata in the established user-data home. Remove the old hidden home. Existing build cache and developer scratch remain caches. Beginners have one product-data folder to back up; experts keep the current data-home and explicit overrides.
options.technical:
Durable root: $XDG_DATA_HOME/jet, falling back to ~/.local/share/jet. Preserve <data>/hangar under D-ECO-HANGARPATH1. Move keys to <data>/keys and trust to <data>/trust. Move user configuration/declarations under this root with unambiguous existing names. Amend D-CORE-SECRETSTORE1's identity default and explicitly revise the owner's cache-only instruction.

Keep ~/.cache/jet build/artifact cache and $JET_STATE_ROOT scratch separate. Do not move all caches into durable data or claim the 7 GB disappears. Existing Hangar retention/cleanup reclaims unneeded objects but excludes identities/settings. Remove ~/.jet after verified cutover, without old-path fallback.
options.code:
# Before: identity is separate from the package store.
# After: the same commands use one Linux data home.
~/.local/share/jet/keys/secrets.identity  # back up
~/.local/share/jet/trust                  # keep
~/.local/share/jet/hangar/                # package payloads
~/.cache/jet/                            # build cache stays

comparisons.note: Configuration and user data are not disposable cache. Existing Jet code already uses XDG_DATA_HOME; this ballot chooses the Linux classification of Jet's own files, not a new cross-platform directory standard.

recommendation.why: A removes both old homes while keeping identity and trust out of disposable cache. The only exception is one small protected folder.
gains: Cache cleanup cannot erase identity or trust.
Both old default homes disappear after safe migration.

losses.loss: One protected folder remains beyond the requested cache folders.
losses.mitigation: Limit it to identity, settings and durable declarations; put replaceable large payloads in cache and document exactly what needs backup.

whyNot.reason: B is safe and simpler to back up, but keeps the large user-data home you asked to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Make one explicit protected-data exception rather than risk losing secrets during cache cleanup.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Linked to card #4573 (c0ake1k7). Main runs Tower's validator before decision add --file. Confirm the Linux-only scope and explicit exception/revision of the newer cache-only instruction. This drafter ran the ballot validator only. No files were migrated or deleted; no compiler programs or tests were run.

After ratification and the stage-2 gate, test HOME and absolute/empty/relative XDG settings. Test existing JETPACK_ROOT/JET_KEYS_DIR controls, key bytes/modes, decryption and identical trust decisions. Test live retention, conflicting destinations, unknown files and interrupted migration. Remove all old default-path callers/fallbacks together. Inventory local-only objects before permitting cache relocation or cleanup.

surface.lesson: Caches are replaceable files. Keys unlock secrets or identify you; trust records remember your permissions. Those and settings need backup.

current.note: Supplied inventory; these are not all disposable bytes.
current.code:
~/.jet/              # 819 MB: keys, trust, store, downloads
~/.local/share/jet/   # 7 GB: package storage and runtime state

wild.note: Settings and disposable cache have separate homes.
wild.code:
~/.config/app/
~/.cache/app/

options.gist: Move large replaceable files to cache; keep one small protected home.
gains: Both old homes disappear.
Identity survives cache cleanup.
losses: One protected folder remains; limit it to files needing backup.

proposed.code:
# Before: two mixed homes. After:
~/.config/jet/keys/secrets.identity
~/.config/jet/trust
~/.cache/jet/hangar/
$JET_STATE_ROOT/

options.name: One backed-up user-data home
options.gist: Move identity beside the established package store; keep that data home.
gains: One product-data backup location.
losses: The large data home remains.

proposed.code:
# Before: identity is separate. After:
~/.local/share/jet/keys/secrets.identity
~/.local/share/jet/trust
~/.local/share/jet/hangar/
~/.cache/jet/

recommendation.why: Remove both old homes without putting identity in disposable cache.
gains: Identity and trust survive cache cleanup.

losses.loss: One protected folder remains beyond cache.
losses.mitigation: Limit it to identity, settings and durable declarations; document its backup contents.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the large user-data home you asked to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: One protected-data exception avoids losing secrets.

designAway.loss: A blanket move into cache could destroy keys during an external cache wipe.
attempts: Give cache subfolders protected names; rejected because external cleanup ignores Jet's names.
Keep identity and durable declarations outside cache; retained.
designAway.result: Removed: neither option puts default private keys in disposable cache.

designAway.loss: Migration could overwrite a different identity or lose local-only package bytes.
attempts: Verify contents and conflicts before deleting old files; preserve irreplaceable objects and exact receipts.
designAway.result: Removed from the contract: unknown/conflicting contents block removal, not silently overwrite.

decisions.title: Rule tests written inside a trait, run against every type that implements it
decisions.situation: A trait such as Equatable comes with rules every implementation should keep, such as "a value equals itself". Today nothing writes those rules down, so a wrong == on your own type is found only when something else breaks. Jet already has property tests: a test that takes parameters runs on about 200 generated inputs. This vote decides whether a trait may carry such rule tests, run automatically for every type that implements it.
decisions.gist: Should a trait carry rule tests that jet test runs, without being asked, for every type that implements it?
decisions.lesson: A law is a rule every implementation of a trait must keep, such as "a == a" for Equatable. A property test is a test with parameters; jet test fills them with many generated values and shrinks a failure to the smallest example.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write nothing. When your type implements Equatable or Comparable, by hand or automatically, jet test also checks the trait's laws on generated values of your type and names the smallest value that breaks one.

Expert path: write laws in your own traits as #Test functions inside the trait body. A type that breaks a law on purpose says so with #Waive and a reason, and team policy can forbid waivers.

Shared by every option: the standard traits get Jet declarations in the built-in library, as already approved. The options differ only in whether laws are written, and whether they run.
decisions.story: Mia's Fraction type compares by cross-multiplying, so 1/2 and 2/4 sort as equal, but her equal compares the fields, so they are not equal. Removing duplicates from a sorted list of fractions gives wrong answers weeks later, and nothing pointed at the mismatch.
decisions.inWild:
-- Scala Cats with Discipline: law tests are run per type, by hand
checkAll("Int", MonoidTests[Int].monoid)

-- Haskell base: Monoid laws are written only in the documentation
