decisions.title: Web-style names: camelCase for functions, fields and variables
decisions.situation: Today Jet writes function, field and variable names in lowercase with underscores, such as fetch_user_profile and user_id. You asked for the most practical defaults across fields of work, leaning toward web development, where JavaScript, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift and Go write these names in camelCase. You already decided that type names keep capital acronyms, such as TaskID, and that camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, such as userId. This vote decides how values are spelled in code. We recommend camelCase with acronyms in capitals, userID, so every Jet name follows one acronym rule while web data still reads userId.
decisions.gist: Should Jet values use camelCase, and should acronyms inside them read userID or userId?
decisions.lesson: camelCase capitalizes each word after the first: fetchUserProfile. snake_case joins lowercase words with underscores: fetch_user_profile. An acronym is a word of initials, such as ID or URL. Types keep capital acronyms under every option: HTTPClient, TaskID. camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, userId, as you already decided. The choice is how values look in code.
decisions.explainer:
Every option shows the same small program: one record type, one choice type, one constant and two functions. Types, markers, effects and enum cases stay PascalCase with capital acronyms in every option, as already ratified. Constants stay in full capitals. Shared work for A or B: one casing section in the spec, compiler checks with automatic fixes, and one rename of Jet's own code.

Under A, an acronym looks the same in every Jet name: TaskID the type, taskID the field, parseURL the function. Only a leading acronym is lowercase, as in urlText and httpClient, the Swift and Go rule. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL, like HTTP_API.

JSON keys are computed, not copied. Under A, the field userID sends and reads the key userId, the web's usual spelling, because you ratified word-cased acronyms in data keys. A key spelled userID gets an error naming userId, and jet inspect shapes prints every outside name.

Under B, acronyms in values are written as words: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl. A field then matches its JSON key letter for letter. But a value and its type spell the acronym differently, taskId: TaskID, which is a second acronym rule. It also reverses your ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.

Under C, values keep underscores, and JSON keys default to snake_case unless a package asks for camelCase.
decisions.story: Kai builds a web service in Jet and its browser front end in TypeScript. The same record travels between them as JSON. He wants Jet names that read like the rest of his web code, one acronym rule to learn, and JSON keys his front end already expects.
decisions.detail:
Revision, 2026-10-10, by BallotPolishA. The owner ratified D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A at 2026-10-07T20:23, about two hours after this ballot was posted. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A recommends "writing userId in data keys while Jet code keeps userID". Its option text says "Inside Jet code, acronyms stay fully capitalized." D-WIRE-CASE1=A's examples use camelCase fields with capital acronyms.

The posted A word-cased value acronyms and withdrew D-WIRE-ACRONYM1. That contradicts law ratified since, so the capital-acronym option now leads. Mapping: new A is the posted B; new B is the posted A; C is unchanged. Its detail now states that companion keys are computed under A, so A no longer carries the posted B's loss that a field "differs from common JSON keys" without a remedy.

Replaces D-CASE-LAW2 (OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07). D-CASE-LAW2's C, which also word-cased acronyms in types (HttpClient, Url), stays withdrawn: it reverses the owner's type rule.

Why A leads. D-ACRO-CASE1=A and the owner rule of 2026-09-30 (spec S66) put capital acronyms in every word of every type-like name. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A then decided camelCase data keys word-case acronyms while Jet code keeps userID. A completes that pair: one acronym rule for every Jet name, and computed keys for web data. B would give values a second acronym rule and reverse the ratified note.

Irreducible part. Given the owner's type rule and the web's word-cased keys, some pair must differ: either field and key (A) or field and type (B). A keeps Jet code on one rule and lets the ratified projection convert the 1.9% of fields that hold an acronym. The projection is exact in both directions, and a near-miss key names the expected one.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner direction, 2026-10-05, given after D-CASE-LAW1=A was ratified the same day. The owner has personal style preferences but ranks pragmatism higher: the best defaults and rules for the most domains at the greatest criticality. The owner added that naming seems most important in web development, so Jet should likely lean toward web conventions. D-CASE-LAW1 is ratified and immutable, so the re-vote is a new decision. Choosing C re-affirms D-CASE-LAW1=A unchanged.

This ballot changes only the case of value-like names. PascalCase stays for types, traits, enum variants, markers including their library part (#Server.Get), effects, unit families and generic type parameters. SCREAMING_SNAKE stays for module-level immutable bindings and compile-time number parameters. The closed acronym lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) and full-capital acronyms in type-like names (D-ACRO-CASE1=A) stand under every option. Foreign names stay verbatim inside binding modules (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A), so browser names such as innerHTML keep their spelling.

COMPANIONS

D-PATH-CASE2=A, D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A are ratified and work unchanged under A. The path word key already reads userID, user_id and userId alike. Under B, D-WIRE-ACRONYM1's note that Jet code keeps userID would need an amendment. Under C, keys default to snake_case words per D-WIRE-CASE1's detail.

WHAT OPTION A SPELLS

camelCase covers functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases and module path segments. Most module segments are one lowercase word, so core.text.fmt is unchanged. Manifest keys in package.jet are fields, so they become camelCase, as in npm's package.json (devDependencies). Acronyms follow the Swift and Go rule. Inside a name they are fully capitalized: userID, avatarURL, parseURL. At the start they are fully lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore: parseHTTP_URL. Jet's own code has 43 such functions.

WHAT OPTION B SPELLS

Every word of a value, an acronym included, is capitalized like a word: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl, httpClient, utf8Bytes. No acronym list is consulted for values, and touching acronyms need no underscore. A value and its type then differ: taskId: TaskID.

RESEARCH: WHAT EACH ECOSYSTEM WRITES

TypeScript and JavaScript use camelCase functions, variables, properties and parameters, and PascalCase classes, types and components. Acronyms are split. The browser platform writes innerHTML, URLSearchParams and toISOString, but also getElementById and XMLHttpRequest. Airbnb 23.9 says acronyms are all upper or all lower case. Google's TypeScript guide word-cases them (loadHttpUrl) unless a platform name says otherwise.

JSON keys are camelCase in Google's JSON style guide, JSON:API's recommendation, Microsoft Graph and protobuf's JSON mapping, and those sources write acronyms as words: userId, webUrl. GitHub's GraphQL API sends avatarUrl and databaseId. Stripe, GitHub REST and Slack use snake_case.

Swift and Go write capital acronyms in values: userSMTPServer, appID. Kotlin and Google Java style word-case them: newCustomerId. C# and .NET write Id and Url. Dart word-cases acronyms longer than two letters.

snake_case values: Python (PEP 8), Rust (RFC 430), Ruby, Elixir, the C standard library, SQL by habit, Odin and Jai. Python keeps capital acronyms in class names and lowercase words in values, the same split option A keeps.

Swift's API Design Guidelines say acronyms that are all capitals in English are "uniformly up- or down-cased according to case conventions": utf8Bytes, isRepresentableAsASCII, userSMTPServer. Go's code review comments ask for capital initialisms such as appID and ServeHTTP, and its linters (golint, staticcheck ST1003) report userId.

POPULATION

Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024: JavaScript has been the most used language every year except 2013 and 2014. [INFERENCE: chart values recalled, not re-read] All respondents: JavaScript about 62%, Python 51%, SQL 51%, TypeScript 38%, Java 30%, C# 27%. Go and Rust are about 13% each, Kotlin 9%, Dart 6% and Swift 5%.

READING STUDIES

Binkley et al., ICPC 2009, 135 subjects: camelCase had 51.5% higher odds of a correct answer and took 13.5% longer. Sharif and Maletic, ICPC 2010, eye tracking, 15 subjects: no accuracy difference, and underscores about 20% faster. Binkley et al., Empirical Software Engineering 2013, 150 subjects: experience shrinks the effect. No study shows a large stable winner; practice dominates.

CENSUS, 7,409 tracked .jet files at 1e300d0af

22,276 function declarations have multi-word names. About 302,000 occurrences of 43,051 distinct snake_case spellings exist, counting call sites, fields, locals and comments. Fields: 13,571 declarations averaging 1.55 words, so most fields are one word and do not change. About 1.9% of fields contain an acronym. Type declarations: 5,396, unchanged under every option.

MIGRATION

Under A or B, one jet fix pass renames multi-word values and every use in one atomic commit between merge waves. A's rename reads each name's words with the shared splitter and lexicon that D-PATH-CASE2 and D-WIRE-CASE1 already use, so it is deterministic. An in-flight branch rebases and re-runs the same pass. The rename commit goes in a .git-blame-ignore-revs file, which git blame and GitHub both honor, so line history skips it.

options.name: camelCase values, acronyms in capitals
options.detail: Functions, methods, fields, parameters, variables and import names use camelCase, as in JavaScript, TypeScript, Swift and Go. An acronym is written in capitals in every Jet name: userID, avatarURL, parseURL, the same as in type names such as TaskID. A leading acronym is lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL. JSON keys come out userId, as already ratified. Compiler errors offer the exact fix.
options.technical:
Amends D-CASE-LAW1=A for value-like names only. Functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases, module path segments and manifest keys become lowerCamelCase. E0357 checks the new case. E0358 and the closed lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) extend from type-like names to values: lexicon acronyms in capitals inside a name, lowercase when leading. Touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore. Digits attach to the word before (utf8Bytes). Plural acronyms: userIDs, or urls when leading.

Data keys follow D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A unchanged: userID encodes and decodes as userId, and a near miss names the expected key. Migration: one jet fix pass in one atomic commit, listed in .git-blame-ignore-revs. Foreign names in binding modules stay verbatim (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A).

options.name: camelCase values, acronyms written as words
options.detail: Values use camelCase as in A, but an acronym inside a value is an ordinary word: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl. Types keep capital acronyms, so a value and its type differ: taskId: TaskID. A field and its JSON key are always the same word. This reverses the ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.
options.technical: Amends D-CASE-LAW1=A for value-like names only, as in A. E0357 rejects a capital run in a value name with a fix (userID to userId). E0358 and the lexicon keep their role for type-like names only. Data keys then equal field names. Amends D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A's statement that acronyms stay fully capitalized inside Jet code. Migration as in A, without lexicon lookups.

options.name: Keep underscores for values
options.detail: Jet keeps the rule confirmed on 2026-10-05: functions, fields and variables in lowercase with underscores, like Python and Rust. Types, constants and acronyms in types are as in A. Nothing is renamed. Code shared with a JavaScript or Swift front end spells every multi-word field differently on each side, while outside names are still computed from words.
options.technical: D-CASE-LAW1=A stands unchanged. No migration. JSON keys copy snake_case field names unless a package or type asks for camelCase (D-WIRE-CASE1). Interop with Python, Rust and SQL needs no projection.

decisions.title: Which ratified ceiling governs metaprogramming: the opt-in advanced mode or the older refusal lists
decisions.situation: Metaprogramming is code that writes or changes code while Jet compiles your program. Jet's ratified rules disagree about how far it may go. Rulings from July to mid-September refuse rewriting written code and splicing code into callers during compilation. Two rulings of September 21 allow those powers behind an approved opt-in, as you asked that day. This vote proposes no new powers and only decides which ratified texts govern; we recommend keeping the September 21 contract, with the older refusals binding projects that do not opt in.
decisions.gist: Which ratified metaprogramming ceiling governs: the September 21 opt-in advanced mode, or the older refusal lists?
decisions.lesson: Standard mode is what every program gets: reading compiler facts, adding new generated code, and type recipes such as prep fn Pair(T: Type). A recipe takes a type and returns a new type. Advanced mode is what an approved root package unlocks with metaprogramming: unrestricted. Today's ratified texts both grant and refuse advanced powers. This vote proposes no new powers, and every change is checked like hand-written code.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A ceiling is the most a metaprogram may do. Standard mode needs no setting. Advanced mode needs metaprogramming: unrestricted in the root package, the package being built, and project trust must approve that root and each provider. A provider is a function the root registers to run in advanced mode for chosen targets. A change set is a checked list of edits that the compiler rechecks as a whole before accepting any of them. A receipt records what changed and the recheck result.

This vote proposes no new metaprogramming powers. Programs still generate new code under the powers already ratified; the vote only decides which ratified texts govern the advanced ones.

The conflict. Older rulings refuse rewriting written code and splicing into callers during compilation. The September 21 rulings allow them behind the approved opt-in. Both are ratified, and the spec prints both. The newer ruling governs today; this vote keeps it (A), withdraws it (B), or withdraws part of it (C).

What every option keeps. No mutable handle into the compiler's internal syntax trees. No forged facts about the program. Every change rechecked by ordinary checking. Generated code keeps a record of where it came from. Host permissions stay separate from metaprogramming.

The grammar stays closed: no token macros and no custom syntax. Advanced parsing reads ordinary Jet with the real parser into checked pieces; it never adds syntax. Type recipes stay in standard mode under every option.

Beginner path: unaffected under every option; standard mode is the same. Expert path: A gives the full checked toolkit behind an approved root and provider; B gives standard mode only; C gives the toolkit without edits to written code. Nothing here proves the advanced API runs; it is unbuilt (card #3520).
decisions.story: Mara's team builds a tracing library that wraps every function in a package with timing code. The spec's advanced API section says a root package can opt in and rewrite those bodies in a checked change set. Three other spec sections say rewriting existing code is rejected forever. She cannot tell whether her design is legal.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision, repaired by SuiteRepair1 after the SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2 passes, 2026-10-07. Quotations below are verbatim, with line breaks and bold flattened; each names whether it is spec text or Tower option text.

Source. Owner directive 23 (2026-10-07) allows reconciliation ballots that resolve a conflict between existing ratified decisions, naming this conflict: S26, D-METAMUTATE1 and D-META-GATE1 against D-META-CONTROL2, D-META-OPTIN2 and D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. It forbids acting on new proposals from the AST research report. So every option is a precedence or a withdrawal among ratified texts, and none adds an API, operation, mode or capability name.

AstResearch1's draft question also asked to name new deniable capabilities (Meta.Rewrite, Meta.Expand, Meta.Types); that is a new proposal and is not offered.

Why the owner decides. Under the project rule, a newer ratified ruling wins, so the September 21 contract governs today; A records that and aligns the older prose. B withdraws that contract and C withdraws part of it, which only the owner can do. None of this shows the advanced API runs: its contract is unbuilt, on card #3520.

THE REFUSING TEXTS

S26 (spec text, syntax-decisions.md:2913-2920). It says: "comptime never creates, parameterizes, or selects a type, and never affects dispatch — polymorphism is traits-only." Also: "Rejected forever: token/AST/attribute macros, custom syntax, comptime types, const generics in v1."

D-FRONTENDAPI1=A (2026-07-06; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:5216-5219). core.compiler exposes read-only lexer and parser APIs for tools, and "no AST mutation enters compilation." It refuses mutation within compilation, not parsing as such.

D-METAMUTATE1=A (2026-07-06; spec summary, syntax-decisions.md:5222-5225). It says: "Jai-style AST mutation/message loop/user macros are rejected." It also grants a non-mutating power surface: additive generated modules, registered targets and actions, read-only enforcement, DSL blocks and front-end APIs.

D-METADEPTH1/2 (spec text, syntax-decisions.md:2998-3003): read-only reflection plus derives; "No mutation, no AST injection, no macros"; "libraries can never mutate grammar". Tower records a later August amendment letting user rules record facts and add code, without mutating existing code.

D-META-GATE1=A (2026-09-19; Tower option text): "Refused: splice into existing code, token or tree macros, use-site type factories, in-place rewrite, a type with no file, running the program inside the compiler. Rewrite and Tokens are never named." Its example adds: "refused, not one flag away."

Docs/spec/reference/metaprogramming.md:304-307, an explanatory page rather than a ratification, rejects "arbitrary message-loop mutation" and says to "generate checked items additively".

THE GRANTING TEXTS

D-META-CONTROL2=A (2026-09-21; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:3093-3098). It says: "type construction, code parsing/capture/insertion, specialization, workspace/build control, and existing-program rewrites use an authorized compiler.advanced session". Its Tower text adds that changes are atomic, checked against affected callers and receipted, and never expose compiler nodes. It also says: "This does not promise equivalence with the original application."

D-META-OPTIN2=A (2026-09-21; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:3100-3105): advanced providers require "metaprogramming: unrestricted" in the approved root package and explicit target registration from root preparation. Its Tower text records the owner's request: "full Jai-level capabilities with powers above level 5 gated by metaprogramming opt-in."

OPTIN2's Tower text also requires project trust and enterprise policy to approve the root and provider. "A previously unapproved or changed privileged provider cannot silently run". Noninteractive runs fail closed, and "Revoking authorization invalidates affected preparation artifacts". Registration "uses compiler-issued DeclarationHandles, not unqualified strings", and dependency targets need exact metaprogramming_targets grants.

D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A (2026-10-02): types are made by prep fn recipes in standard mode, amending S26 and D-META-GATE1's use-site type-factory refusal. Its Tower text: "Building types from reflection or editing other declarations stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A." D-CONSTGEN1=A already replaced S26's const-generics refusal. Both stay under every option.

UNIVERSAL LIMITS, KEPT IN BOTH MODES UNDER EVERY OPTION

These come from specific clauses and never become standard-only. No token, tree or attribute macros and no custom syntax (S26, D-META-GATE1, D-METADEPTH2). No message loop and no user macros (D-METAMUTATE1). No mutable compiler nodes and no forged facts (D-META-CONTROL2). Host permissions stay separate (D-META-OPTIN2), and no AST mutation enters compilation (D-FRONTENDAPI1).

Advanced parsing runs the real Jet lexer and parser into checked fragments; it is not a token or tree macro, so the closed grammar holds in both modes.

OPTION A: CLAUSE MAP

A keeps D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 in full: approval, changed-provider refusal, revocation, handles, dependency grants and the non-equivalence rule included. The older texts are amended clause by clause, not whole paragraphs. S26: the type clause points to D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, and the dispatch clause binds standard mode, while advanced specialization follows D-META-CONTROL2. Its macro and syntax ban stays universal.

D-METAMUTATE1: the message-loop and user-macro ban stays universal; its refusal of rewriting written code binds standard mode, with advanced rewrites only as D-META-CONTROL2 change sets. D-METADEPTH1/2: "no macros" and the grammar ban stay universal; "No mutation, no AST injection" binds standard mode.

D-META-GATE1: token or tree macros stay refused everywhere. Splice into existing code, in-place rewrite, a type with no file and running the program inside the compiler bind standard mode; advanced mode has them only through D-META-CONTROL2. "Rewrite and Tokens are never named" stays, since there is no capability name. The example's "not one flag away" is amended: the approved root opt-in is that gate.

OPTION B: CLAUSE MAP

The older refusals govern. D-META-CONTROL2's compiler.advanced operations are withdrawn, and the compiler.advanced rows leave the syntax table. D-META-OPTIN2 keeps its manifest member with one value: omitted or metaprogramming: standard. The unrestricted value and metaprogramming_targets are withdrawn, so writing them is an unknown-value error.

Standard mode keeps D-META-REFLECT2 facts, D-META-PUBLISH2 additive generation, type recipes and const generics. In D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, "stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A" becomes stays refused.

OPTION C: CLAUSE MAP

C keeps D-META-OPTIN2 in full and keeps every D-META-CONTROL2 clause that only adds. Kept: the ChangeSet add operation, the types service, parsing into new items, specialization, and workspaces with build control and run_prepared. For those, D-META-GATE1's "a type with no file" and "running the program inside the compiler", and S26's dispatch clause, are amended for advanced mode.

C withdraws every D-META-CONTROL2 clause that edits written code: the ChangeSet operations remove, replace_body, replace_signature, replace_type and insert, and register_expansion's caller expansion. For those, D-METAMUTATE1 and D-META-GATE1's "splice into existing code" and "in-place rewrite" prevail in every mode. C only withdraws named existing clauses; it adds no operation or gate.

THE STORY UNDER EACH OPTION

Mara's tracing library needs to change existing function bodies. Under A, an approved root and approved provider can replace them in a checked change set. Under B and C it cannot; the library can only generate new wrapper functions that callers call explicitly. Those wrappers are not transparent rewrites.

WHAT B AND C OFFER

B keeps the meaning of written code in the file itself. A reader and the editor never apply a transformation to know what code does, the benefit D-METADEPTH2 and D-METAMUTATE1 argued for. B also has the smallest authority surface. C keeps the advanced additions while written bodies never change, the clearest audit story of the three.

Precedent, as illustration only. Swift macros add declarations and expand marked uses but never edit other written code; C also refuses call expansion. Rust procedural macros rewrite only the item they are attached to. Jai's message loop may rewrite code. Zig builds types at compile time with no syntax access, which matches Jet's standard mode.

INTERPLAY

Vote this ballot before D-HOOK-STAGES1. That open ballot's change-set rule defers to D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 as this vote leaves them. Under A, approved providers may return change sets; under C, only additions; under B, findings and Generated items only. This ballot adds no hook API. Card #3520 holds the advanced contract.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2, 2026-10-07). Examples now copy the ratified handle-based registration. A keeps OPTIN2's approval, revocation and dependency rules in full. Every option has a clause-level map, with universal limits kept in both modes, and C is defined only by withdrawing named clauses.

B's manifest change is exact. The non-equivalence of rewrites, provider granularity, the tracing story under each option and the strengths of B and C are stated. Quotation sources are labeled.

decisions.title: What a REPL step that fails while running does to earlier variables
decisions.situation: A REPL is the prompt where you type Jet one line at a time and keep variables between lines; notebooks work the same way. Sometimes a line fails while it runs, after it already changed a variable. Today the Jet-written REPL then forgets every variable, while the older Rust REPL keeps them. The vote decides what survives a failed line; we recommend keeping everything that already ran, as Python and Jupyter do.
decisions.gist: When a REPL or notebook step fails while running, what happens to variables from earlier steps?
decisions.lesson: A REPL runs one step at a time and keeps variables between steps. A step can fail while it runs, after it already changed some of them. Jet's Rust REPL keeps earlier variables. The Jet-written REPL currently drops them all. Whichever option wins, a crash of the running program still loses everything.
decisions.story: Mia loads a large data set in a notebook, then spends an hour cleaning it. One cell indexes past the end of a list. She needs to know whether her cleaned data is still there.

decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. Drafted by ExecHost4 and folded into the suite by BallotSuite1. Checked against the ratified execution and session decisions. D-EXEC3=A runs every level with one meaning, so a REPL turn runs at the quick level and fails with the same report as jet run. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A makes stack and memory exhaustion a stop; option A now says that such a stop restarts the session.

Notebooks. D-DX-CELLS1=A makes Jet notebooks reactive: pure descendants rerun and effectful cells wait for confirmation. Under option A a failed cell publishes no new names, its descendants are marked stale rather than rerun, and earlier cells keep their values. Under C every cell would need rerunning after any failure, which D-DX-CELLS1's bounded live state was meant to avoid. No other open ballot touches the REPL.

Card #4719. Rust REPL (crates/jet-repl) clones pure comptime values per trial step, so a failed step keeps all prior bindings. The Jet REPL port (port/solseams2 a5be604c4, Main-approved 2026-10-06) retires the evaluator machine on a run-time failure and reports that runtime bindings were reset. It does so because owned host handles and shared cells cannot be copied.

Under D-EXEC1/D-EXEC2 the REPL moves to the native session host (#4720): bindings live in typed session slots in one persistent child. A recoverable failure (an error value, cancellation, deadline) returns through MIR cleanup; published slots survive. A panic or trap invalidates the child; the host restarts it with a fresh session and never replays earlier steps.

Static check failures already roll back exactly and are not part of this choice. External side effects are never rolled back under any option.

options.name: Keep what ran
options.detail: Earlier bindings stay after a run-time failure, and changes the failed step made before failing stay. A panic or trap still restarts the session and says which bindings were lost.
options.technical:
Session slots published by earlier turns are untouched; the failed turn's unpublished slots are released without glue (CAbiSession end). Fatal invalidation restarts the child with a fresh session.

Resource stops follow D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A. A stack overflow (E3012), a #MaxDepth limit or running out of memory is a stop, so it counts as a fatal invalidation: the session restarts and says which bindings were lost. Output printed before the stop stays on screen, as the prefix rule requires. A failed turn prints the same registered report as jet run, per D-RTFAIL1 and D-EXEC3.
options.code:
>> items.push(4); items[10]
error: index 10 is out of range (length 4)
>> items
[1, 2, 3, 4]

options.name: Undo the step
options.detail: Before each step, copy every binding the step may change; restore the copies if it fails. A step that may change an uncopyable binding (file, socket, shared cell) cannot be undone.
options.technical: Per-turn snapshot of written slots via Clone glue; uncopyable slot types either refuse the turn or are excluded from rollback.
options.code:
>> items.push(4); items[10]
error: index 10 is out of range (length 4)
>> items
[1, 2, 3]

options.name: Start over
options.detail: Any run-time failure resets every binding, as the Jet REPL port does today.
options.technical: The failed turn retires the whole session; the next step starts empty.
options.code:
>> items
error: unknown name `items`

comparisons.note: Interactive mode keeps all variables after an exception; partial changes stay. https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html
comparisons.code:

>>> items

comparisons.note: A cell that raises leaves the kernel's earlier variables and any changes made before the error. https://docs.jupyter.org/en/latest/projects/kernels.html
comparisons.code:
In [2]: items.append(4); items[10]
IndexError
In [3]: items
Out[3]: [1, 2, 3, 4]

recommendation.why: Keeping what ran costs nothing per step, keeps files and connections usable, and matches what people expect from Python and notebooks.
gains: A mistake never costs the session's earlier work.

losses.loss: A half-finished step can leave a variable partly changed.
losses.mitigation: The error names the step that failed; printing the variable shows its current value.

whyNot.reason: Undo copies data every step and still cannot undo files, sockets or printed output.
Starting over throws away a whole session for one mistake.

recommendation.tradeoff: A failed step may leave partial changes, which the user can see and fix.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by ExecHost4; suite edits by BallotSuite1. Validated offline with OwnerNotes1/validate.mjs; no Tower write. Short profile: one policy choice, no syntax or invariant change.

Owner acceptance for A, once the native session host lands (#4720). After items := [1, 2, 3], the step items.push(4); items[10] reports the out-of-range error, and items then prints [1, 2, 3, 4]. A name first bound in a failed step is unknown afterwards. A runaway recursion in a step prints E3012, restarts the session and lists the lost names. A notebook cell that fails marks its descendants stale and leaves earlier cells unchanged.

surface.gist: When a REPL or notebook step fails while running, what happens to variables from earlier steps?
surface.lesson: A REPL runs one step at a time and keeps variables between steps. A step can fail while it runs, after it already changed some of them. Jet's Rust REPL keeps earlier variables. The Jet-written REPL currently drops them all. Whichever option wins, a crash of the running program still loses everything.

decisions.title: Restoring database developer commands
decisions.situation: Database developer commands let people inspect and query data from the terminal, but their original implementation never compiled and was removed during the self-host repair. Restoring them needs CSV and JSON readers with real input limits, plus a quiet output mode for scripted use. Without those limits, inspecting a large file could use excessive memory instead of failing clearly. You choose to restore the feature through those APIs, defer it, or remove it permanently; we recommend designing the safe APIs and restoring it.
decisions.gist: Should Jet restore its database developer commands with bounded input?
decisions.lesson: These terminal commands depend on safe CSV and JSON input and a quiet output mode. Those APIs must be designed before restoration. A does that work and restores the feature, B keeps it planned but unavailable, and C removes it permanently. A does not authorize unbounded readers.
decisions.explainer: The feature is not restored merely by retaining its files. Input size and nesting limits must be enforced before the commands become available. Quiet output is part of their usable scripting behavior.
decisions.story: Bea inspects a table from the terminal. She needs a large or deeply nested input to fail at a known limit rather than fill memory or overwhelm her script's output.
decisions.inWild:
# SQLite ships a developer CLI for queries and importing CSV data.
# https://www.sqlite.org/cli.html
sqlite3 data.db 'SELECT * FROM items LIMIT 10;'
# SQLite also exposes resource limits, including expression depth and length.
# https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html
# These precedents do not supply Jet's proposed CSV/JSON reader limits.
decisions.detail: The source ballot links restoration to the ratified SQL safety plan. Its proposed CLI input defaults are 32 MiB and 64 nesting levels. The exact bounded-reader and quiet-mode APIs remain subject to design and ratification; the example below specifies behavior without inventing a current Core function.

options.name: Design safe APIs and restore commands
options.detail: Design bounded CSV and JSON readers and a quiet output mode, then restore the commands using them. Enforce the agreed limits rather than reviving code that never compiled.
options.technical: Bounded readers use size limits and JSON nesting limits. Proposed CLI defaults are 33,554,432 bytes and depth 64; the output-mode type includes quiet.
options.code:
# After API design and command restoration:
jet db --help
# Database commands documented with bounded CSV/JSON input
# and a quiet output mode; exact flags come from that design.

options.name: Keep the feature planned for later
options.detail: Retain the feature as future work but keep it outside this CLI release. Restore nothing until the dependencies are designed and ratified later.
options.technical: No database developer commands are exposed in this release.
options.code:
# This release has no database developer commands.
# Restoration remains planned.

options.name: Drop the feature permanently
options.detail: Remove the developer command implementation and its feature-specific tests. The CLI no longer promises this feature.
options.technical: Delete the feature's command files and tests from the current tree, without deleting unrelated database APIs.
options.code:
# Database developer commands are removed from the product.
# No restoration is promised.

recommendation.why: A retains a feature already named by the SQL safety plan and restores it only after the input limits are real.
gains: Developers regain database commands with bounded input and usable scripted output.

losses.loss: Restoration waits for API design and ratification.
losses.mitigation: Complete bounded readers first, then restore commands against their approved limits rather than shipping unsafe interim input handling.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the feature promised but leaves its return unspecified.
C permanently removes a feature already named by the safety plan.

recommendation.tradeoff: Do the safe-input API work before restoration rather than defer indefinitely or abandon the planned feature.

decisions.checkInstructions: After API ratification, exercise 32 MiB input limits and JSON depth 64, including refusal just beyond each limit. Verify quiet mode and restored developer commands compile and run against approved bounded readers.

surface.gist: Should Jet restore database developer commands with safe input limits?
surface.lesson: The old commands never compiled and were removed. They need bounded CSV and JSON reading and quiet output. A designs those APIs and restores the commands, B delays the feature, and C drops it. Restoration must not use unbounded interim readers.

gains: Restored commands with enforced limits.

losses.loss: Restoration waits for API approval.
losses.mitigation: Finish bounded readers first and restore commands against their approved behavior.

whyNot.reason: B leaves restoration at an unspecified later time.
C abandons a feature already named by the safety plan.

recommendation.tradeoff: Design safe input first instead of restoring unsafe commands or abandoning the feature.

decisions.title: Whether Jet adds 128-bit integer types
decisions.situation: Integer types set the sizes of whole numbers a program can represent, and Jet's specified fixed-width list currently stops at 64 bits. Compiler code introduced 128-bit names without making them part of that language contract, leaving users unable to rely on consistent support. Adding them would require overflow and conversion rules rather than just keeping two names in one file. You choose the existing list or complete 128-bit support; we recommend the existing list until a real program needs the larger types.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add signed and unsigned 128-bit integer types?
decisions.lesson: Fixed-width integers have a maximum range and rules for overflow. Jet's current list stops at 64 bits. A removes unapproved 128-bit names; B adds both types with full conversion and overflow rules. A leaves larger-number needs to a library or a later language decision.
decisions.explainer: A compiler's internal name is not automatically a supported language type. Adding I128 and U128 requires a consistent contract across checking, execution and conversions.
decisions.story: Hank sees a 128-bit name in compiler code while writing a large-number hash. He needs to know whether that type is truly supported or merely an unapproved implementation detail.
decisions.detail: The source ballot says the integer-kinds module introduced I128 and U128 outside the spec, and its one 128-bit use had already moved to Int. Option B is a proposed language addition, not a claim that these types work today.

options.name: Keep the specified integer list
options.detail: Remove the unapproved I128 and U128 names. Retain the specified types at 64 bits or less rather than creating a language addition without a demonstrated caller.
options.technical: Integer kinds and exposed numeric names must agree with the current specification; the one reported use remains Int.
options.code:
count := Int{0}
// The supported list remains at 64 bits or less.

options.name: Add complete 128-bit support
options.detail: Make I128 and U128 supported fixed-width language types. Specify overflow traps and conversions, and implement them consistently rather than preserving unsupported names.
options.technical: Add signed and unsigned 128-bit types to the numeric menu with overflow trapping consistent with other fixed-width integers.
options.code:
// Proposed type, available only if B is implemented:
count := I128{0}

recommendation.why: A keeps the implementation aligned with the current spec and avoids adding types without a demonstrated program need.
gains: One consistent, specified list of integer types.

losses.loss: Programs needing more than 64 bits cannot use these built-in types.
losses.mitigation: State the limit clearly and revisit complete wider-type support when a real program demonstrates the need.

whyNot.reason: B is a full language addition with overflow and conversion rules, while the source ballot identifies no current program requiring it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the specified type list now while acknowledging that wider built-in arithmetic requires a later explicit decision.

decisions.checkInstructions: Under A, check numeric names and integer kinds contain no unapproved 128-bit types and the reported caller uses Int. Under B, require consistent overflow, conversion and execution tests before claiming support.

surface.gist: Should Jet add 128-bit integer types?
surface.lesson: Fixed-width integers have a maximum range. Jet's specified list stops at 64 bits. A keeps that list and removes unapproved names. B adds signed and unsigned 128-bit types with overflow and conversion rules. Bigger built-in numbers are not delivered by keeping names alone.

current.note: 128-bit names appeared outside the specified language contract.
current.code:
// I128 and U128 are not approved public types.
count := Int{0}

wild.note: Rust explicitly supports both 128-bit primitives; sources are in the long form.
wild.code:
let signed: i128 = 0;
let unsigned: u128 = 0;

options.name: Stay at 64 bits
options.gist: Keep the current list and remove unapproved names.
gains: Implementation matches the existing specification.
losses: No built-in fixed-width arithmetic beyond 64 bits.

proposed.code: count := Int{0}

options.name: Add 128-bit types
options.gist: Add both types with complete overflow and conversion behavior.
gains: Larger fixed-width numbers become built in.
losses: Two additional types and their rules to learn.

proposed.code:
// Proposed type after implementation:
count := I128{0}

recommendation.why: A keeps the existing specification consistent; no current program in the source ballot needs the larger types.
gains: One specified integer menu.

losses.loss: No larger built-in fixed-width integers.
losses.mitigation: State the limit and revisit wider types when a real program demonstrates the need.

whyNot.reason: B adds language rules without a demonstrated current caller.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the existing list while making the larger-number limitation explicit.

decisions.title: Replacing a borrowed field while returning its old value
decisions.situation: A reusable reader stores the current row in a field, then needs to hand that row to its caller and begin the next one. Jet forbids moving a value out of a borrowed field, so today's workaround copies the row and resets the field, adding an allocation each time. A replace operation would put a new value in immediately while returning the old one without that copy. You choose standard replacement, continued copying, or consuming the whole reader; we recommend one standard replacement operation.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add a standard operation to replace a field and return its old value?
decisions.lesson: Borrowing permits access without taking ownership. Moving a field out would leave a borrowed object incomplete. Replacement fills the field while returning its old value. A adds that operation, B copies and resets, and C consumes the whole object. A lets a reader continue without a row copy.
decisions.explainer: The desired operation does not weaken the rule against leaving a borrowed field empty. The replacement is already present before the old value is returned. Consuming an entire object works for final results but not for a reader that must produce another row.
decisions.story: Priya's file reader emits thousands of rows. She wants each finished row handed to its caller without copying its values or giving up the reader she needs for the next row.
decisions.detail: The source ballot identifies an extra allocation per emitted row from copying before reset. mem.replace is proposed Jet API, not an existing function in core.mem. The syntax below uses current Jet borrowing and collection construction; A requires adding the operation's checked move semantics.

options.name: Add standard replacement
options.detail: Add one operation that installs a new value in a writable place and returns the old one. Use it for row handoff instead of copying, without ever leaving the borrowed object incomplete.
options.technical: Proposed mem.replace(&place, new) returns the old value. The write borrow ends before the following statement, and the old value is moved rather than copied.

options.name: Keep copying and resetting
options.detail: Keep the current borrowed-field move rule and add no replacement operation. Reusable readers copy the finished row and reset their field, retaining an allocation for every row.
options.technical: No new Core operation or special field extraction. The copy remains an ordinary allocation.

options.name: Consume the object for its final result
options.detail: Give types a finishing method that consumes the whole object and returns its result. Avoid a general replacement operation, but the object cannot continue producing rows afterward.
options.technical: A consuming finish method moves its payload out and ends the object's use. This fits terminal results such as a hash digest, not repeated handoff from a reusable reader.

recommendation.why: A preserves the borrowed-field rule while giving reusable readers an allocation-free handoff instead of copying each row.
gains: Reusable readers hand off old values without an extra copy allocation.

losses.loss: Users must learn one additional operation and its ownership rule.
losses.mitigation: Document replacement next to existing cell swapping, with one reader example showing the new value remains installed.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a copy allocation on every row even though replacement can preserve the ownership rule.
C fits a final result but consumes the reader needed to produce the next row.

recommendation.tradeoff: Add one explicit ownership-preserving operation rather than pay per-row copies or restrict handoff to final results.

decisions.checkInstructions: Test that replacement returns the old value, leaves the new value installed and ends its write borrow before the next statement. Exercise repeated reader handoff without a copy allocation and verify consuming finish still forbids reuse.

surface.gist: Should a standard replacement operation return a field's old value without copying?
surface.lesson: Moving out of a borrowed field is forbidden. Today the reader copies its row and resets the field. A replaces the field and returns its old value, B keeps copying, and C consumes the whole object. Only A avoids copies while letting the same reader continue.

current.note: Each row is copied before the reader resets its field.
current.code:
row := ~self.fields
self.fields = [String]{}

wild.note: Replacement preserves a complete object without cloning the payload; source is in the long form.
wild.code: let row = std::mem::replace(&mut reader.fields, Vec::new());

options.name: Standard replacement
options.gist: Install a new field value and return the old one.
gains: No row-copy allocation.
Reader can keep producing rows.
losses: One operation and ownership rule to learn.

proposed.code:
// Proposed Jet operation:
row :: mem.replace(&self.fields, [String]{})

options.name: Copy and reset
options.gist: Keep the current workaround and ownership rules.
gains: No new operation.
losses: An extra copy allocation per row.

proposed.code:
row := ~self.fields
self.fields = [String]{}

options.name: Consume at the end
options.gist: A finishing method returns the payload and consumes its object.
gains: No general replacement operation.
No copy for terminal results.
losses: The consumed reader cannot produce another row.

proposed.code:
row :: reader.finish()
// Reader is consumed.

recommendation.why: A avoids the row copy while preserving a complete borrowed object and allowing the reader to continue.
gains: Allocation-free row handoff.

losses.loss: One more ownership operation.
losses.mitigation: Document it beside cell swapping with an example showing the installed replacement.

whyNot.reason: B pays a copy allocation on every row.
C ends the reader instead of letting it produce more rows.

recommendation.tradeoff: Learn one replacement operation to avoid repeated copies without weakening ownership rules.

decisions.title: User Rust libraries in native Jet programs
decisions.situation: A Jet program can call a Rust library supplied by its author, with Cargo building a helper outside Jet's own runtime. Native support is already ported, but the owner must choose whether helpers use a static musl build, disappear, or link dynamically against glibc. Static musl avoids a target glibc dependency but currently needs an opt-in toolchain limited to x86_64 Linux. We recommend retaining user Rust support through that static helper, with the platform limit stated clearly.
decisions.gist: Should native Jet retain user Rust libraries through a static musl helper?
decisions.lesson: User-written Rust is separate from Jet's runtime. Cargo can remain the user's external build tool. A keeps static helpers on x86_64 Linux with an opt-in musl toolchain, B removes Rust support, and C uses dynamic glibc helpers. Dynamic output needs compatible libraries on the target machine.
decisions.explainer: Removing Rust from Jet itself does not necessarily remove a user's choice to call Rust. This vote concerns authorized user helpers, not permission to run Cargo or LLVM by default. Static libraries still need their native dependencies accounted for.
decisions.story: Hank calls his team's Rust hashing library from Jet. He wants to build the helper once and run the result without installing Rust or depending on a target glibc version.
decisions.inWild:
# Rust supports staticlib for linking Rust into a non-Rust application.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html
rustc --crate-type=staticlib helper.rs
# The x86_64 Linux musl target defaults to a static C runtime.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html#static-and-dynamic-c-runtimes
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# A cdylib is a dynamic library for loading from another language.
rustc --crate-type=cdylib helper.rs
decisions.detail: The source ballot reports native RustForeign.jet support in 00f3b5bb5 and an opt-in musl toolchain in ce42a475a. JET_RUST_MUSL_TOOLCHAIN selects it; normal compiles retain the default nixpkgs toolchain. Docs/spec/reference/jetpack-epoch5.md permits only committed, source-proved foreign crate cases and denies Rust/LLVM execution by default. Card #4948 separately decides the cargo-metadata environment-forwarding gap. The static option currently covers x86_64 Linux only.

options.name: Retain static musl Rust helpers
options.detail: Keep Cargo as the user's external tool. Build authorized user helpers as musl static libraries with the opt-in toolchain. Avoid a glibc dependency while clearly limiting this path to supported x86_64 Linux builds.
options.technical: Use JET_RUST_MUSL_TOOLCHAIN, JET_RUST_MUSL_LINKER and JET_RUST_MUSL_AR. Preserve source-proof authorization. Cargo environment forwarding is decided separately.
options.code:
# Generated helper crate uses crate-type = ["staticlib"].
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# Jet links the resulting authorized helper archive.

options.name: Remove user Rust support
options.detail: Remove native user Rust helpers and their toolchain integration. Users must expose their library through the C interface or rewrite it; direct Rust support no longer exists.
options.technical: Remove RustForeign.jet, its fixtures and ABI test, the musl toolchain exposure and the spec permission for foreign crate builds.
options.code:
# Native Jet no longer builds a user Rust helper.
# Use an explicitly supplied C interface instead.

options.name: Use dynamic glibc helpers
options.detail: Build helpers with the default Rust toolchain as dynamic libraries against glibc. Avoid the special musl toolchain, but require compatible glibc and the helper library on the target machine.
options.technical: Use the default nixpkgs Rust target for helpers. Remove musl toolchain exposure and document dynamic linking for these FFI programs.
options.code:
# Generated helper crate uses crate-type = ["cdylib"].
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# Target deployment includes the helper and compatible glibc.

recommendation.why: A keeps authorized user Rust libraries working without making the resulting program depend on the target's glibc version.
gains: User Rust support remains available without a target glibc dependency.

losses.loss: The opt-in static helper path currently supports only x86_64 Linux.
losses.mitigation: Document the supported target and required toolchain, refuse unsupported builds clearly, and keep the environment-forwarding gap separately tracked.

whyNot.reason: B removes a working user feature already admitted under the source-proof authorization rule.
C introduces target glibc and dynamic-helper deployment dependencies that the static option avoids.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep static user Rust helpers on the explicitly supported target, with an opt-in toolchain rather than dynamic deployment dependencies.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the committed foreign-helper fixtures and ABI test on x86_64 Linux. Verify static native linkage and the absence of a glibc dependency. Confirm unsupported targets are refused clearly and default builds do not execute unauthorized Rust tools.

surface.gist: Should native Jet keep static user Rust helpers?
surface.lesson: A user's Rust library is separate from Jet's runtime. A builds static musl helpers with an opt-in x86_64 Linux toolchain. B removes direct Rust support. C uses ordinary dynamic glibc helpers and requires compatible libraries at deployment. Authorization remains unchanged.

current.note: The native static helper path exists provisionally on x86_64 Linux.
current.code:
# Authorized generated helper crate:
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# Requires the opt-in musl toolchain.

wild.note: Static libraries can link into non-Rust applications; source is in the long form.
wild.code: rustc --crate-type=staticlib helper.rs

options.name: Static musl helpers
options.gist: Retain user Rust through the opt-in static helper path.
gains: User Rust code remains supported.
No target glibc dependency.
losses: Opt-in toolchain; x86_64 Linux only today.

proposed.code:
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# Generated staticlib helper linked into Jet output.

options.name: Remove direct Rust support
options.gist: Users expose a C interface or rewrite their library.
gains: No Cargo helper or musl integration.
losses: Existing direct Rust use stops working.

proposed.code:
# Rust helper build removed.
# A supplied C interface is required instead.

options.name: Dynamic glibc helpers
options.gist: Use the ordinary toolchain and deploy a dynamic helper.
gains: No opt-in musl toolchain.
losses: Target needs compatible glibc and the helper library.

decisions.title: What happens when a native runtime feature is missing
decisions.situation: A native build uses Jet's replacement runtime, but some existing features still have no native implementation. Today a UDP program can reach the linker before a missing-provider error names an internal symbol instead of explaining the unavailable feature. This leaves application authors unsure whether their code is wrong or the runtime is incomplete. You choose clear compiler refusals, today's linker errors, or delaying the entire cutover; we recommend clear refusals for each missing feature.
decisions.gist: Should missing native features be rejected clearly before linking?
decisions.lesson: A compiler checks code before the linker assembles the executable. Some native runtime features are still missing. A explains each missing feature at compile time, B keeps the generic linker error, and C waits for every feature before cutover. No option may pretend missing features work.
decisions.explainer: This vote chooses how unavailable features are reported and whether they block the whole cutover. It does not authorize reducing any feature's behavior or decide which implementation to port first.
decisions.story: Nora receives a UDP packet in her program. Today her native build fails with a missing symbol; she needs an error that explains the unavailable feature and her next step.
decisions.detail: The source ballot lists service authority, workflows, HTTP server, WebSocket, UI host, browser, Raylib, devtools, process pipelines, sandboxed launches and UDP as incomplete. TLS is decided separately in D-NATIVE-TLS1. Today's missing-provider linker diagnostic is E2104. New per-family codes must enter the diagnostic catalog and documentation.

options.name: Clear compiler refusal for each feature
options.detail: Reject each unavailable runtime family at compile time. Name the family, explain why this build lacks it, and give the fallback or next step. Register and document every new diagnostic code.
options.technical: One availability list drives both the native checker and runtime pack. Each excluded family has one canonical diagnostic.

options.name: Keep the generic linker error
options.detail: Keep today's behavior. Linking fails with the generic missing-provider error and an internal symbol name. No new compiler refusal is added.
options.technical: The existing native link path reports E2104. No fake provider is introduced.

options.name: Wait for every native feature
options.detail: Block the cutover until every listed runtime family is implemented natively. Programs retain the full feature set at cutover, but complete features cannot ship ahead of unfinished ones.
options.technical: The native runtime pack's exclusion list must be empty before cutover.

recommendation.why: A explains missing features before linking and lets completed native work ship without pretending the rest works.
gains: Users learn which feature is missing and what to do next.

losses.loss: New diagnostic codes must remain correct and documented.
losses.mitigation: Drive compiler refusals and the runtime pack from one availability list, and register each code in the catalog.

whyNot.reason: B gives users an internal symbol name late in the build instead of an actionable explanation.
C holds the entire cutover behind every remaining feature even when unrelated native programs already work.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep a small set of documented refusals rather than delay all completed native functionality.

decisions.checkInstructions: For each excluded family, verify one canonical compiler diagnostic and its documented next step. Confirm the checker and runtime pack read the same availability list and that implemented families are not refused.

decisions.title: Process pipelines and sandboxed launches on the native runtime
decisions.situation: A process pipeline connects commands while sharing time and output limits, and a sandbox restricts what a launched command can access. Both still depend on Rust, so native build scripts using pipelines fail before their commands start and sandboxed launches remain refused. Running commands one by one or silently removing a sandbox would change promised behavior. You choose a complete port, continued exclusion, or pipelines first; we recommend faithful pipelines first and a separate security-reviewed sandbox port.
decisions.gist: Should native Jet restore process pipelines before sandboxed launches?
decisions.lesson: Pipelines connect running commands and share limits, cleanup and cancellation. A sandbox is a security boundary. A ports both, B leaves both unavailable, and C restores pipelines first. A missing sandbox must always refuse the launch, never run the command without protection.
decisions.explainer: Plain run, spawn and capture are separate from this vote. The pipeline port must preserve direct pipes, bounded relays, shared budgets and process-group cleanup. Serial execution is not equivalent.
decisions.story: Sam's build script pipes generated source through two tools with a timeout. Native linking currently fails before any stage runs, and he needs the same cancellation and cleanup guarantees back.

# https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/utilities/V3_chap02.html#tag_19_09_02
printf 'hello\n' | wc -c
# Bubblewrap provides Linux sandboxing as a separate process tool.
# https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap
bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-net /bin/true
decisions.detail: The source ballot identifies Process.rs around lines 2051-2455, about 405 lines, and ProcessSandbox.rs at about 1,059 lines. Plain run, spawn and capture were being ported separately for the native CLI. Restore pipeline lifecycle and timeout cases. These sizes describe reference Rust code, not a measured Jet implementation.

options.technical: Port direct-pipe versus bounded-relay behavior, per-stage process groups, bubblewrap probing, profiles and secure output directories. Preserve existing error codes.

options.name: Keep both unavailable
options.detail: Keep pipeline and sandbox-bound launches outside the native pack. Plain run, spawn and capture are unaffected. Refuse missing behavior rather than substituting serial execution or an unsandboxed launch.
options.technical: Private pipeline launch and sandbox-bound ProcessSpec remain unbound. The source wrapper remains in Jet; missing pipeline providers report E2104.

options.name: Port pipelines first

recommendation.why: C restores pipelines without tying them to the separate security review required for sandboxed launches.
gains: Native pipelines retain shared limits, cancellation and cleanup.

losses.loss: Sandbox-bound launches remain unavailable natively.
losses.mitigation: Refuse every sandbox-bound request and track its separate port with the security review, never running it unsandboxed.

whyNot.reason: A makes pipeline availability wait for sandbox profiles and their security review.
B leaves the pipeline path unavailable even though it can be ported independently.

recommendation.tradeoff: Restore pipelines separately while retaining a strict refusal for every unavailable sandboxed launch.

Wiring them would bring roughly 170 additional files into the build and deliberately expand its agreed boundary. decisions.title: Expert metaprogramming as nested effects you can block as a family or one at a time
decisions.situation: Jai, the game language Jet is matching, trusts the programmer completely: build code can rewrite your program, run any tool while compiling, and switch off array checks for a whole build. Jet already has one way to say what code may do: effects such as Net or FS.Read, which nest, so denying FS also denies FS.Read. The earlier draft of this ballot added a separate list of powers beside effects, a second way to give permission. The vote decides how Jet's strong metaprogramming becomes a family of nested effects that a team can block whole or one at a time, and where whole-build check removal belongs. We recommend a Meta effect family, with check removal kept on the existing safety-gate rules.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's strong metaprogramming be nested effects a team can block whole or one at a time, and where does check removal go?
decisions.lesson: An effect names something code may do, such as Net. Effects nest: denying FS also denies FS.Read. A package's authority block lists effects it holds (may use) and denies. Expert effects are strong ones, such as rewriting code while compiling; nobody holds them until the main package names them. A safety gate, such as `#Unsafe`, is a written, audited place where a safety check is waived. A bounds check stops a read past the end of a list; without it, a bad index can corrupt memory.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a Jai game to Jet. His build runs the level editor while compiling, one library rewrites functions marked as game systems into faster code, and release builds run without array checks. His security lead wants one line for a sister project: generated code and macros yes, anything stronger no. Both want to use the effects and safety rules they already know, not a second list of switches.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q2d1w7aw: the earlier powers list deviated from effects. Powers should be nested effects, so a team can block all stronger metaprogramming or one thing. The old syntax was not idiomatic. Jet is the language being designed; Jai is Jonathan Blow's game language that Jet is reaching parity with (Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md). Spellings use `comptime` (D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A) and the arrow form `-[ ]>` (D-EFFECT-ROW2).

Ratified ground for effects: D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1=A (one rights tree), D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1=A (nested roots; `!FFI` denies every leaf), D-EFFTREE1 (holding a parent covers its children). Also D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A (the `authority` block; `policy:` keeps floors and unsafe mode). Also D-EFFECT-DECL1=A (`effect` declarations) and D-META-EFFECT1=A (one effect model at both stages).

For metaprogramming: D-META-GATE1=A (`Meta.Generate`, `Meta.Include`), D-META-OPTIN2=A, D-META-CONTROL2=A and D-META-RECONCILE1=A (the opt-in advanced mode governs; older refusals bind projects that do not opt in). Also D-JAI-CODE1=A (everyone gets code values, pasting and macros; text-to-code is expert). For safety gates: D-ONCE-GATE1=A and D-GATE-LAW1=A.

THE META FAMILY UNDER A. Effects.jet gains these declarations. `$expert` is a new value in the attribute slot that already holds `$irreversible`.

```jet
effect Meta                        // compile-time code acting on the program
effect Meta.Generate               // add generated files: b.generate, derives
effect Meta.Include                // run a dependency's build inside yours
effect Meta.Paste                  // code values and #Expand macros pasted at a call
effect Meta.Code $expert           // change the program beyond adding and pasting
effect Meta.Code.Raw $expert       //   parse(text) to code, and macros with uses: *
effect Meta.Code.Types $expert     //   build types from facts, with no source file
effect Meta.Code.Rewrite $expert   //   change written code through checked change sets
effect Meta.Host $expert           // reach the build machine while compiling
```

HOLDING. Every Meta leaf is checked against the package's authority block, as Net is. Deny always wins, and denying a parent denies every child: `deny: [Meta]` blocks the whole family. Held means the package may use it. Non-expert leaves are held unless denied, so beginners write nothing. An `$expert` leaf is never held by default, and holding a parent never covers it: it must be named.

`allow: [Meta]` holds Generate, Include and Paste only; a note names the expert leaves it left out. `allow: [Meta.Code]` names an expert node, so it holds all three of its children. Only the main package, the one you build, may hold an expert leaf. It may pass one to a named dependency with `grants:`; a dependency cannot hold one by itself.

This follows existing precedent: effect declarations already carry an attribute, and the Mem and Panic roots already have their own holding rule (deny-only, E0751). There is one rights tree and one attribute table.

APPROVAL. Adding an expert leaf to the main package is a project-policy edit. The trust prompt's Update project policy choice shows the diff (D-TRUST-LAUNCH1=A). Expert leaves are never approved by Trust once, `--trust`, `-T` or `--allow`. CI never prompts; it fails with the exact `authority` line to add. Removing a leaf needs no approval. An organization file may deny any Meta leaf, and the outermost refusal wins.

WHERE META LEAVES APPEAR. Meta leaves describe compile-time work, so they appear only in rows of compile-time code: `fn build`, providers, hooks and `comptime fn`. A run-time function that calls a macro keeps its own row; the package's hold of `Meta.Paste` governs the paste. So `fn build(b: BuildContext) -[!Meta.Generate]> BuildPlan` makes `b.generate` an error there. Holding is the package's permission; a build entry's row still lists the Meta leaves it uses, as D-META-GATE1=A requires.

WHAT EACH OLD POWER BECOMES. `metaprogramming: unrestricted` (D-META-OPTIN2) becomes holding `Meta.Code`; its registration, target and approval rules stay. raw_code (D-JAI-CODE1) becomes `Meta.Code.Raw`. comptime_host becomes `Meta.Host`: compile-time code that runs programs, uses unpinned network, loads foreign libraries or opens windows needs `Meta.Host` held.

The site still writes `#Impure("reason")`, and the function row still lists the ordinary effect, such as Exec. That is the same shape as run-time code. unlimited_steps is dropped: the step limit is a budget, not an effect, and `#StepLimit(n)` (D-PREP-FUEL1=A, ratified, not yet built) covers long work. open_generics is dropped with the D-JAI-GENERIC1 revision.

CHECK REMOVAL UNDER A. Removing run-time checks is not something code does, so it is not an effect. It is an audited safety waiver, like `#Unsafe`, and uses the existing gate rules. A new gate kind, `check_removal`, joins the D-GATE-LAW1 list. Its written gate is a check field set to `off` in the main package's build settings (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1), such as `bounds: off`, or `#Unchecked(bounds)` inside `#Unsafe("reason")`.

The default `.GateOnly` allows it and lists it in `jet inspect gates` and the build receipt. A package whose policy says `check_removal: .Forbid` is always compiled with its checks, even in an unchecked build, and the receipt says so. An organization `.Forbid` refuses the build. Generic and inlined code takes the setting of the package that wrote it.

I1 AMENDMENT. Today I1 reads: 'The expert escape hatch is a user-written, audited `#Unsafe("reason") { … }` block or `#Unsafe("reason") fn`. Generated Rust `unsafe` appears only there or in vetted standard-library and memory internals.'

Under A and B, the code generator leaves out the named check at each site in packages built with the gate. On the Rust tier that site becomes an unchecked access inside a generated `unsafe` block. The receipt lists the gate and every package built without the check. I1 adds this text: 'or a check field set to off in the main package's build settings, an audited gate listed in every receipt.'

Under C, I1 is unchanged.

AMENDS. D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 (root list gains Meta). D-META-GATE1: the Meta family replaces its names. Its refusals ('in-place rewrite, a type with no file, running the program inside the compiler') were already lifted for opted-in projects by D-META-RECONCILE1=A.

Under A, opted in means holding `Meta.Code` or `Meta.Host`. Also `Meta.Reflect` and `Meta.Const` are not declared, since reflection is pure and compile-time parameters are ordinary generics. D-META-OPTIN2: the manifest member becomes holding `Meta.Code`. Its standard mode 'forbids … caller-code insertion'; pasting is now allowed there, as D-JAI-CODE1=A already ruled.

Also D-CTEFFECT1 and D-ONCE-GATE1: at compile time `Meta.Host` replaces the per-run `--gate impure=allow`, and E3410, E3411 and E1343 change their fix text. Run-time `#Impure` keeps its gate. D-TRUST-LAUNCH1: expert leaves are excluded from one-run approval. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1: `off` needs the `check_removal` gate instead of a power. D-GATE-LAW1: the gate list gains `check_removal`.

MIGRATION. One cutover with machine-applicable `jet fix` rewrites: `metaprogramming: unrestricted` becomes `authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code] } }`, and a compile-time `--gate impure=allow` becomes an `allow: [Meta.Host]` line. No aliases remain. New names get Syntax.rs and Effects.jet rows (I7); every refusal has a registered code and UI snapshot (I4).

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. A beginner writes nothing: generated code, includes and macros work, and every expert effect and every check stays on. An expert names expert leaves in the main package's allow list, or sets `bounds: off` in a release profile. A careful team writes `deny: [Meta.Code, Meta.Host]` and `check_removal: .Forbid`.

WHY NOT B. B makes check removal an `Unchecked` effect family too. A held effect does nothing by itself, and an effect row cannot see how another package was compiled, so `-[!Unchecked]>` could not be checked by the call graph. WHY NOT C. C keeps every Meta effect but offers no whole-build check removal; experts waive checks only per scope.

OPEN DEPENDENCIES. D-META-HASH1 (open) may respell `$` attributes mechanically. D-LSP-BUILDSAVE1 (open) says a check never uses `Meta.Host`.

EVIDENCE. Jai: #run opens windows and calls DLLs while compiling (Blow UTqZNujQOlA 00:44:04-00:53:31). Jai build options turn checks off (The Way to Jai examples/30/30.4_build_options.jai:50-123). Rust: `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` lets a crate refuse a power at its root. Zig: build-wide safety modes plus per-scope `@setRuntimeSafety`.
