decisions.title: What the editor runs on save, and what a check may touch
decisions.situation: While you type, Jet's editor support checks your code and shows errors. Checking already runs some compile-time code, and the project's build file adds more: its fn build plan, its compile-time code and its hooks. Some of that code can start programs, use the network or write files. Running it on every save could do things the user never asked for, silently. Today, mistakes in the plan show up only when someone runs jet build. The vote decides when the plan runs and what any check may touch. We recommend that a check never touches the outside world, that a check command runs the plan, and that running it on save is opt-in.
decisions.gist: When should the editor run the project's build plan, and may any check run code that touches files, the network or programs?
decisions.lesson: Checking finds type and ownership errors, and it already runs the compile-time code that types depend on. The build plan is the `fn build` function in build.jet; running it runs more compile-time code and hooks. Some compile-time code reads files, downloads, starts programs or writes files. A full build also links and writes the program.
decisions.story: Ken saves build.jet with a bad `b.add_executable` call and wants to see the error before he runs a build. His teammate Mia's plan downloads textures and runs a converter program. She does not want a download and a converter run every time she presses save. Both want the editor to show plan mistakes without doing anything behind their backs.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 1.3 (ZLS build-on-save), section 2.5 rule 5 and section 5, ballot 7. Owner question q0d271iq asked for a check command or an opt-in save step, because compile-time code can act silently. Ratified context: D-LSP1=C (one compiler service), D-HOOK-STAGES1=A, D-CTEFFECT1=A (compile-time effect tiers), D-BUILD-IO1=A, D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A (checks run comptime tries) and D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1=A (one tighten rule).

ONE RULE FOR EVERY CHECK. Under A, a check is side-effect free wherever it starts: `jet check`, the editor while typing, the plan check and an attached session request. Compile-time code in a check may compute and may read files inside the workspace. It may also use values already in Jet's cache, such as an earlier pinned download.

A check never starts a program, uses the network, writes a project file, calls a foreign library or runs an `#Impure` block. It never asks for trust. Generated code and lock entries a check computes stay in the session's memory and cache. Only build, run, test and dev write `.jet/generated` and `.jet/lock`.

HOW IT IS ENFORCED. The session runs a check request under a read-only ceiling: the package's held rights narrowed to reading the workspace. This is the existing tighten rule of the one authority model, not a second checker. Compile-time effects in a check meet the same rights tree as everywhere else. Metaprogramming that only changes the program being checked keeps working when the package holds it. Compile-time host access never runs in a check.

THE PLAN CHECK. `jet check --plan` and the editor command Jet: Check build plan both send the session request check{plan: true}. It runs the `fn build` plan, its compile-time code and its hooks under the same ceiling. Nothing is linked or written. Plan results are cached by key, so an unchanged plan costs nothing.

The editor setting `"jet.checkPlanOnSave": true` sends the same request on each save. Its default is false. No setting gives a check more rights; outside work runs only in build, run, test and dev.

EDGE CASES. A pinned `fetch` whose bytes are not cached yet is reported as not downloaded yet. Errors that depend on it are held back, not shown as false errors. An `#Impure` block, a `b.action` step or a process probe is listed by name as not run in a check, with its site. Today an `#Impure` block without the gate flag is error E3411; in a check under A it is a note.

Dependency build entries stay checked but not run, as today. The plan check uses the current snapshot, including unsaved editor text. Cancellation and caching follow section 2.5 of the session design.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. A beginner configures nothing: errors appear while typing, and saving does nothing extra. To see plan errors early they run `jet check --plan` or the editor command. An expert turns on the save setting, or runs `jet build` when outside work must run.

WHY NOT B AND C. B runs the whole plan on every save even when nobody asked. That is safe but costs time on large plans, and it is not what the owner asked for. C is what Zig's and Rust's editors do. Once opted in, every save starts programs and downloads with the project's rights, the silent behavior this revision removes.

options.name: Checks touch nothing outside; plan check on request
options.detail: Every check runs compile-time code under a read-only ceiling: it may compute and read workspace files, and nothing else. `jet check --plan` and an editor command run the build plan under that ceiling. An editor setting runs it on save too; it is off by default. Outside work runs only in build, run, test and dev.
options.technical: Session request check{selection, plan: Bool}. The ceiling is the package's holds narrowed to FS.Read of the workspace plus cached recorded inputs, by the D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1 tighten rule. Tier 2 and `b.action` sites become typed not-run notes. Setting key `jet.checkPlanOnSave`, default false. New CLI flag `--plan` on `jet check`, registered under this decision.
options.code:
$ jet check --plan
error: unknown source `run.jt` in add_executable
  --> build.jet:2:40
note: not run in a check: action `convert_textures` (Exec)
  --> build.jet:5:9  runs at `jet build`
// editor settings, off by default:
"jet.checkPlanOnSave": true

options.detail: As A, but saving always runs the plan check. No setting is needed to see plan errors. Every save of a changed plan pays one plan run.
options.technical: As A, with check{plan: true} sent on every didSave. The setting turns it off instead of on.

options.detail: Checks while typing stay as in A. An editor setting makes each save run the plan with the same rights as `jet build`, including approved downloads, programs and gated blocks. This matches Zig's and Rust's editors.

comparisons.note: ZLS runs the build's check step on save through Zig's build-system protocol. That step runs build.zig with its full rights.

gains: No check ever starts programs, downloads or writes files.

losses.mitigation: The check names each step it did not run and where, so nothing is hidden.

whyNot.reason: B is just as safe but spends a plan run on every save, even when nobody asked for one.
C lets an opted-in save start programs and downloads silently, the risk this revision removes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Plan errors on request instead of on every save, so no check can act on the outside world.

decisions.title: How a program starts a compiler session it talks to
decisions.situation: A compiler session is one running Jet compiler that tools can send requests to. People already have a public way to share one: `jet dev --serve` opens a socket, and `jet build` can attach to it. A parent program such as Jetpack, an editor build task or a test harness also needs to start its own private session on standard input and output. This vote picks that entry point. We recommend a hidden internal command, `jet __session`, which replaces today's hidden `jet __jetpack` instead of adding public surface.
decisions.gist: How should a parent program such as Jetpack start a private compiler session that it talks to over standard input and output?
decisions.lesson: A parent program can start `jet` as a child and send it requests on standard input. Today Jetpack does this with a hidden command, `jet __jetpack`, once per value. The session needs one such entry point for every first-party client. It can stay hidden, become a flag value on `jet dev`, or become a flag on every runnable command, as Zig does.
decisions.story: Ken runs `jetpack env` on his game. Jetpack needs the compiler to evaluate 40 computed values in `env.jet`. It should start one `jet` child, send 40 evaluate lines and read the answers. Ken never types this command; he only sees that `jetpack env` got faster.
decisions.inWild:
# ZLS starts Zig's build runner as a child and talks over stdio:
zig build --listen=-
# Zig's compiler server works the same way on every build verb:
zig build-exe main.zig --listen=-
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.7 and section 5, ballot 2. Ratified today: `jet dev --serve` (socket) and `--session=auto|off|required` on `jet build`, `jet run` and `jet test` (D-BUILD-SESSION1=A).

Under A, `jet __session` speaks the session protocol on stdio (wire format per D-SESSION-WIRE1). Like `__jetpack` today it is absent from help and answers a malformed request with E2104. It replaces `__jetpack` and its two operations in the same cutover (see D-JETPACK-SERVICE1).

Under B, `jet dev` gains a non-interactive mode that runs nothing, which is new behavior for a command whose job is running the program. Under C, check, build, test, run and dev each gain `--listen=-`, and each must define what an update request means for that verb.

B is the upgrade path if the owner later wants third-party build tools to drive sessions. A hidden verb is still a command, but it is the same kind of surface `__jetpack` already is.

options.name: Hidden internal command `jet __session`
options.detail: One hidden verb serves every first-party parent. It is not in help and adds no public surface; it replaces `jet __jetpack`. Third-party tools are not supported; they use the CLI or attach to `jet dev --serve`.
options.code:
# Jetpack, once per jetpack command:
$ jet __session
> {"kind":"request","id":1,"op":"evaluate","program":"env.jet#port"}
< {"kind":"response","id":1,"status":"ok","value":8080}
> not json
< E2104 report (malformed request), as `__jetpack` answers today
$ jet help    # __session is not listed

options.name: `jet dev --listen=-`
options.detail: One documented flag value on `jet dev` serves the session on stdio. Third-party tools get a supported entry. `jet dev` must gain a mode that starts nothing, so Ken's game must not launch when Jetpack uses it.
options.code:
$ jet dev --listen=-      # serves stdio; does not start the game
> {"kind":"request","id":1,"op":"evaluate",...}

options.name: `--listen=-` on every runnable command
options.detail: Check, build, test, run and dev each accept `--listen=-`, matching Zig. Third-party tools are fully supported, but five commands gain a documented flag and each must define what an update means.
options.code:
$ jet check --listen=-
$ jet build --listen=-
$ jet test --listen=-

comparisons.note: Every Zig build command accepts --listen=- and serves its binary protocol on stdio; ZLS uses `zig build --listen=-`.

recommendation.why: Every current client is first-party, and people already have a public spelling in `jet dev --serve`. A replaces the existing hidden `__jetpack` command instead of adding a second surface.
recommendation.tradeoff: Third-party build tools cannot start their own session; they attach to `jet dev --serve` or use the CLI.

whyNot.reason: It gives `jet dev` a second mode that runs nothing, with no current client that needs it.
It adds a documented flag to five commands for clients that do not exist yet.

losses.loss: Third-party tools have no stdio entry.
losses.mitigation: They attach to the public `jet dev --serve` socket; B stays available if the owner wants more.

surface.gist: How should a parent program like Jetpack start a private compiler session it talks to?
surface.lesson: A parent program can start `jet` as a child and send it requests. Jetpack does this today with a hidden command, once per value. People already have a public shared session, `jet dev --serve`. This vote picks the entry point for private child sessions.

$ jet __jetpack comptime-evaluate env.jet#host
# ... 40 processes for 40 values

wild.code: zig build --listen=-

gains: No new public surface.
One child per Jetpack command.
losses: Third-party tools have no stdio entry.

options.name: `jet dev --listen=-`
options.gist: A documented flag value on `jet dev`.
gains: Third-party tools get a supported entry.
losses: `jet dev` needs a mode that runs nothing.

proposed.code: $ jet dev --listen=-   # does not start the game

gains: No new public flags.
Jetpack drops from 40 processes to one.

losses.loss: No stdio entry for outside tools.
losses.mitigation: They attach to `jet dev --serve`; B remains the upgrade path.

whyNot.reason: It adds a run-nothing mode no client needs today.
It adds five public flags for clients that do not exist.

recommendation.tradeoff: Outside tools wait for a later vote; first-party clients get one entry.

decisions.title: Where the MCP methods on today's editor channel go
decisions.situation: Jet's language server is the background program editors talk to. Today's Rust version also answers a few methods from MCP, the protocol AI agents use to read resources. It mixes them into the editor protocol and advertises MCP fields in its start-up reply. The Jet language server card requires advertising only editor-protocol features. This vote decides where those agent methods go in the Jet port. We recommend moving them to a separate MCP adapter over the compiler session, using the MCP surface Jet already ratified.
decisions.gist: Should the MCP methods that today's language server answers move to a separate MCP adapter, be ported as they are, or be dropped?
decisions.lesson: LSP is the protocol editors speak; MCP is the protocol AI agents speak. Today's Rust language server answers MCP's resources/list, resources/read and ping on the editor channel, and puts MCP's protocol version into its LSP start-up reply. Editors ignore the extra fields, but the server is no longer a clean LSP server. Jet already ratified a typed MCP surface for agents.
decisions.story: An agent helping Ken wants to read his `env.jet` environment resource. Today it must connect to the editor's language server and speak MCP on a channel built for LSP. Ken's editor, meanwhile, receives start-up fields it does not understand.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 5 ballot 6, and finding F2. The Rust server mixes MCP into LSP at Server.rs lines 364-369, 512-513, 567 and 624-627. Ratified: D-MCP-SURFACE1=A (first-party MCP surface: a layered typed SDK over one protocol core, with its own versioning and authorization).

Card #3410 criteria c2 and c5 require truthful capabilities and forbid canned responses. Under A, the LSP advertises only LSP capabilities. The environment resources move to an MCP adapter that is a client of the compiler session, built on the D-MCP-SURFACE1 SDK.

The adapter's command spelling (the proposal suggests `jet self mcp`) is a separate future vote, not decided here.

Under B, the Jet port copies the mixing, so its start-up reply carries foreign fields. Under C, agents lose the environment resource until someone builds it elsewhere.

options.name: Move them to an MCP adapter over the session
options.detail: The language server speaks only LSP. A separate MCP adapter, built on the ratified MCP SDK and attached to the same compiler session, serves the environment resources with MCP's own versioning and authorization. Its command spelling is voted separately.

options.name: Port them into the Jet language server as they are
options.detail: Copy today's behavior: the language server answers the MCP methods and adds MCP fields to its LSP start-up reply. Agents keep their current connection, but the server breaks the card's rule of advertising only real LSP capabilities.
options.code:
// jet self lsp initialize result
{"capabilities":{...,"resources":{...}},"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25"}

options.name: Drop them
options.detail: The Jet language server answers only LSP, and no MCP adapter is built now. Agents cannot read the environment resource until a later card adds it.
options.code: // agent: resources/read -> no server offers it

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer speaks only LSP plus documented rust-analyzer/ extension methods; agent protocols live in separate tools.

recommendation.why: The editor channel then advertises only LSP, as the language server card requires. Agents keep the environment resource through the MCP surface Jet built for them.
recommendation.tradeoff: Agents connect to a second endpoint instead of the editor's; the adapter shares the same session, so answers match.

whyNot.reason: The start-up reply would carry foreign fields, breaking the card's truthful-capability rule.
Agents would lose a working feature with no replacement.

losses.loss: Agents must connect to a separate adapter.
losses.mitigation: The adapter attaches to the same session, so its answers match the editor's exactly.

decisions.title: Which processes may own the shared workspace session
decisions.situation: A workspace session is one warm Jet compiler that other commands in the same project can attach to, so they reuse its work. Today only `jet dev --serve` may open that shared endpoint. When an editor is open, its language server already holds a warm compiler for the same project. If it cannot share, the editor and `jet dev` check every edit twice with two caches. We recommend letting the language server own the endpoint too, when started with `jet self lsp --serve`.
decisions.gist: Which long-lived processes may open the one shared session endpoint for a workspace: `jet dev --serve` only, the language server too, or any session automatically?
decisions.lesson: A workspace has at most one shared session, guarded by a lock. Other commands attach to it and reuse its checked results. The ratified rule lets only `jet dev --serve` own it. The editor's language server is also a long-lived compiler session for the same files. This vote decides whether it may own the shared endpoint, so one warm brain serves the whole workspace.
decisions.story: Ken edits his game in VS Code, saves, then runs `jet build` in a terminal. The editor has already checked every file. He expects the build to reuse that work instead of checking everything again. When he also runs `jet dev --serve`, he expects the editor and the dev server to share one cache, not keep two.
decisions.inWild:
# TypeScript: the editor's tsserver and tsc --watch share the same Program model
tsc --watch
# Gradle: one build daemon per workspace serves the IDE and the terminal
./gradlew build
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.7 and section 5, ballot 3. Ratified: D-LSP1=C (one incremental compiler service, all tools are its clients), D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (only `jet dev --serve` opens a socket; `--session=auto|off|required`), D-JPK-NODAEMON1=A (no resident background daemon).

Under A, `jet self lsp --serve` is opt-in. The first owner holds the workspace lock; a later LSP attaches to it as a client. When the editor closes, the endpoint disappears and a CLI run falls back to a fresh process, saying why under --verbose. The editor-owned session is a foreground process, so D-JPK-NODAEMON1 still holds.

Endpoint security is as ratified: a 0700 per-user directory, symlinks rejected, peer credentials checked, a nonce from .jet/session, and one owner per workspace by lock.

Under C, an editor-started server would listen without any flag. That widens D-BUILD-SESSION1's opt-in rule.

options.name: `jet dev --serve` and `jet self lsp --serve`
options.detail: Either long-lived process may own the workspace endpoint when started with --serve. The first owner holds the lock and the other attaches as a client. A build after editing is faster while the editor is open, and every edit is checked once.

$ jet build              # attaches to the editor's warm session
$ jet dev --serve        # lock held by the LSP: dev attaches as a client
# editor closes -> endpoint gone
$ jet build --verbose
note: no workspace session; running a fresh compiler

options.name: Only `jet dev --serve`, as ratified
options.detail: Keep today's rule. Without `jet dev --serve`, a build runs fresh even while the editor is open. With both running, the language server keeps its own engine beside `jet dev`, so there are two warm caches and every edit is checked twice.
options.code:

$ jet build              # fresh compile; editor's work not reused
$ jet dev --serve        # second warm cache beside the editor's

options.name: Any long-lived session, automatically
options.detail: Every long-lived session opens the endpoint with no flag. Attaching is automatic, but an editor-started process would listen on a socket the user never asked for, which widens the ratified opt-in rule.

$ jet build              # attaches with no flag

One build daemon serves both the IDE and terminal builds, but it lives in the background, which Jet ruled out.

recommendation.why: One warm brain per workspace is the point of the ratified editor engine decision. Under B, an open editor and `jet dev` keep two caches and check every edit twice.
recommendation.tradeoff: The editor process may hold the workspace lock; `--session=off` always forces a fresh, independent compile.

whyNot.reason: It keeps two warm caches and checks every edit twice whenever the editor and `jet dev` both run.
It opens a socket without the user's opt-in, widening the ratified session rule.

losses.mitigation: Attached and fresh builds must be byte-identical, and `--session=off` always forces a fresh compile.

surface.gist: Should the editor's language server, as well as `jet dev`, be allowed to own a workspace's shared session?
surface.lesson: A workspace has at most one shared session; other commands attach and reuse its work. Today only `jet dev --serve` may own it. The editor's language server is also a warm compiler for the same files. Letting it own the session means one warm cache per workspace.

options.gist: Keep the ratified rule.

gains: Attaching needs no setup.
losses: Opens a socket nobody asked for.

Faster builds while editing.

decisions.title: The session protocol's wire format
decisions.situation: A compiler session is one running Jet compiler that several tools can talk to: the editor, a build in a terminal, and Jetpack. When a tool attaches from another process, the two sides need a shared message format on the wire. Jet's error reports and build events already have one ratified JSON shape, one object per line. This vote picks the wire format for everything else the session sends. We recommend newline-delimited JSON, so the wire reuses that shape and an attached build prints exactly what a fresh one prints.
decisions.gist: Which message format should Jet's compiler session use between processes: JSON lines, binary frames, or JSON-RPC with editor-protocol framing?
decisions.lesson: When `jet build` attaches to a running session, the two processes exchange requests, events and error reports. Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON form, one object per line. The wire carries no syntax trees or compiled files, only these control messages, so its speed matters little. The choice is mostly about reuse, debugging and keeping one shape per message.
decisions.story: Ken runs `jet dev --serve` for his game, then `jet build --session=required` in a second terminal. When the build fails, he wants the attached build to print exactly what a fresh build prints. When something goes wrong between the two processes, he wants to read the messages with a pipe and `jq`, not a decoder.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 3 (transports) and section 5, ballot 1. Builds on D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (versioned protocol, request envelope), D-REPORT-MACHINE1=A (one JSON report per line) and D-BUILD-UI1=A (--json streams NDJSON events).

Under A, the first line is hello with the toolchain identity. A mismatch refuses the attach and the CLI falls back to a fresh process, saying why under --verbose. Jetpack reports E1227 as the engine handshake does. There is no negotiation and no compatibility branch.

Reports are the D-REPORT-MACHINE1 object unchanged, and build events are the D-BUILD-UI1 events unchanged. Artifacts never cross the wire; events carry store identities and paths. A line is capped at 1 MiB, as jet.devtools.v1 caps envelopes, and JSON escapes newlines inside reports.

Reuse: CompilerService.jet's tagged-value and CtValue codecs become the JSON codec, and its narrow diagnostic codec is replaced by the report writer. The proposal sets a revisit trigger: a paired measurement if protocol cost passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time on the corpus.

options.name: Newline-delimited JSON
options.detail: One JSON message per line, UTF-8. Reports and build events reuse their ratified shapes byte for byte. Any JSON tool can read the stream. Encoding JSON costs a little on a channel that carries only control messages.

options.name: Binary frames
options.detail: Each message is a fixed header with a tag, a length and a request number, then a binary body in Jet's record codec, as Zig's compiler server does. It is the cheapest to encode. Reports would need a second, binary encoding beside their JSON form, and reading the stream needs a decoder.

options.name: JSON-RPC 2.0 with the editor protocol's framing
options.detail: Each message has a Content-Length header and a JSON-RPC body, as LSP and BSP use. It reuses JSON-RPC ids and error codes. Events become notifications, and request ids reused after a cancel must be handled as in LSP.
options.code:
Content-Length: 88

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"build","params":{"targets":["game"]}}

comparisons.note: Zig's compiler server uses binary frames with a tag and a length, and checks only an exact version string.
comparisons.code: Header{tag: u32 LE, bytes_len: u32 LE} + body

comparisons.note: The Build Server Protocol used by IntelliJ and Metals is JSON-RPC 2.0 with LSP framing.

recommendation.why: Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON home, so A adds no second shape for them. The wire carries no syntax trees or artifact bytes, so binary frames would save little.
recommendation.tradeoff: JSON encoding costs a little; the proposal re-measures if protocol cost ever passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time.

whyNot.reason: It needs a second encoding of every report, and version skew becomes silent corruption unless separately checked.
It adds framing and request-id rules that a line-based stream does not need, for no gain on this channel.

losses.loss: JSON is slower to encode than binary frames.
losses.mitigation: Only control messages cross the wire; a paired measurement is required if cost passes 5 percent.

surface.gist: Which message format should Jet's compiler session use between processes?
surface.lesson: When a build attaches to a running session, the processes exchange requests, events and error reports. Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON form, one object per line. Only these small control messages cross the wire, so speed matters little. The choice is about reuse and debugging.

current.note: Error reports and build events already stream as JSON lines.

wild.note: Zig's compiler server sends binary frames: a tag, a length, then bytes.
wild.code: Header{tag: u32 LE, bytes_len: u32 LE} + body

options.name: JSON lines
options.gist: One JSON message per line, reusing the report shape.
gains: Attached output equals fresh output byte for byte.
Readable with any JSON tool.
losses: Slightly slower than binary.

options.name: Binary frames
options.gist: Tagged binary messages, like Zig's server.
gains: Cheapest to encode.
losses: A second encoding of every report.
Needs a decoder to debug.

proposed.code:
header {tag: u32, len: u32, request: u64}
body   binary record bytes

options.name: JSON-RPC with editor framing
options.gist: Content-Length headers and JSON-RPC bodies, like LSP.
gains: Reuses JSON-RPC ids and error codes.
losses: Extra framing and id rules for no gain here.

proposed.code:
Content-Length: 88

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"build",...}

recommendation.why: Reports and events already have one JSON form, so JSON lines add no second shape. The wire carries only small messages.
gains: One shape per message everywhere.

losses.loss: A little encoding cost.
losses.mitigation: Re-measure if it passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time.

whyNot.reason: It duplicates the report shape and hides version mistakes.
Its framing adds rules this channel does not need.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small encoding cost for one readable shape.

decisions.title: What an update request means for each command that serves the session on stdio
decisions.situation: A tool such as Jetpack or a third-party build tool can start a Jet command with --listen=- and talk to the compiler over standard input and output. The owner chose that every runnable command gets this flag: check, build, test, run and dev. Zig's build tool works the same way, and its main message, update, means do the work again on the newest files. Jet has not said what update means for each command, or whether a stdio session shares the warm compiler that an open editor already runs. The vote decides both. We recommend that update redoes the command's own work, and that a stdio session joins the workspace's running session when there is one.
decisions.gist: What should an update request do on each command started with --listen=-, and should it share a running session?
decisions.lesson: With `--listen=-`, a command reads requests from standard input and writes answers to standard output instead of to the terminal. `update` is the short request that says: do this command's work again on the newest files. A workspace session is a warm compiler run by `jet dev --serve` or `jet self lsp --serve`; other commands can join it.
decisions.story: Lena writes a build-tool plugin for her team's editor. It starts `jet build --listen=-`, sends update after each save and shows the errors. Her teammate's editor already runs `jet self lsp --serve`, a warm compiler for the same folder. Lena wants to know what update does for build, test and run, and whether her plugin checks every file a second time.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, sections 2.4 and 2.7, and BallotFollowThrough's FOLLOWTHROUGH.md sections 4-9. Ratified: D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C (`--listen=-` on check, build, test, run and dev; each verb must define what an update means). Also D-SESSION-WIRE1=A (NDJSON), D-SESSION-OWNER1=A (`jet dev --serve` and `jet self lsp --serve` may own the workspace endpoint), D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (`--session=auto|off|required`).

WHAT EVERY OPTION SHARES. A `--listen=-` session first sends `hello` with the toolchain identity, then does nothing until asked. It accepts the full request set of section 2.4, such as `check`, `build`, `test`, `query` and `cancel`.

`exit`, or end of input, cancels in-flight work and exits with status 0. A malformed line gets an E2104 report line and the session continues. `--listen=<address>` with anything but `-` is refused with E2104, because sockets stay `--serve` only. `--listen=-` with `--watch` is refused, because `watch{}` is a request. `--listen=-` with `--serve` is refused: one process has one endpoint.

THE UPDATE TABLE (options A and B). `jet check --listen=-`: update is `check{selection}` on the newest revision, for the files or package named on the command line. It returns reports and writes no artifacts. `jet build --listen=-`: update is `build{targets, profile}` from the command line. It returns events and artifact paths; bytes never cross the wire.

`jet test --listen=-`: update is `test{filter}` from the command line. Test output is captured into `test.*` events. `jet run --listen=-`: update builds, then runs the target once with the program arguments. The program's output becomes `run.output` events and never reaches the terminal, and its standard input is empty. An update while the program runs cancels it and starts again.

`jet dev --listen=-`: update is `dev.update{mode: auto}`, a swap or restart under the D-LIVE1 rules. The first update builds and starts the program. Program output becomes `run.output` events.

JOINING A RUNNING SESSION. Under A, a stdio session for check, build, test or run follows the `--session=auto|off|required` rule of D-BUILD-SESSION1. `jet check` gains that flag for this purpose. With the default `auto`, it forwards its requests to the workspace session when one runs, so the editor and the tool share one warm compiler. `off` keeps a private compiler. `required` fails at start with no workspace session.

If the workspace session ends mid-stream, in-flight requests end with a cancelled response. Later requests run on a private compiler, and a `session.detached` note says so. `jet dev --listen=-` never joins, because dev itself may own a session; it keeps its own compiler.

Under B, `--listen=-` with any `--session` value is refused with E2102, and a stdio session always runs its own compiler. Jetpack still attaches to a `--serve` socket directly when one runs, as D-JETPACK-SERVICE1=A says.

OPTION C. There is no `update` request. The command word only sets the default selection, and a client always sends the typed request: `check{}`, `build{}`, `test{}`, `run{}` or `dev.update{}`.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. Beginners never type `--listen=-`; tools do. A tool author sends update after each change, as with Zig. An expert sends typed requests with explicit selections, and chooses `--session=off` for an isolated compiler.

Why A over B: B gives a second warm compiler beside the editor's, so every edit is checked twice, which D-SESSION-OWNER1=A was ratified to avoid. Why A over C: C drops the one request D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C's option text assumed, and Zig-style tools would need per-verb logic.

New diagnostics and the `session.detached` event get registry rows with UI snapshots (I4). Implementation lands on #5050.

options.name: Update redoes the command's work; join a running session
options.detail: Update redoes each command's own work on the newest files, as in the table in the detail. Check, build, test and run started with --listen=- join the workspace session when one runs, under the same --session rule as the plain command. Dev keeps its own compiler.
options.technical: Per-verb update mapping as in the detail. `--session=auto` default forwards requests to the D-SESSION-OWNER1 endpoint; `off` keeps a private compiler; `required` fails at hello. Owner loss mid-stream: in-flight requests end `cancelled`, then a `session.detached` event, then local execution.

options.name: The same update table; a stdio session never joins
options.detail: The same update table as A. A --listen=- session always runs its own compiler, and --listen=- with --session is refused. This is the draft in the follow-through notes.
options.technical: As A for update. `--listen=-` plus any `--session=` value is E2102.
options.code:
$ jet build --listen=- --session=auto
error[E2102]: a --listen=- session runs its own compiler; drop --session
$ jet build --listen=-          # private compiler, even with the editor open

options.name: No update request; typed requests only
options.detail: There is no update request. The command word only sets the default selection, and a client always sends the typed request for the work it wants. Joining follows A.
options.technical: Remove `update` from the request set; the verb seeds default selection, targets, profile and filter for the typed requests.

comparisons.note: zig build --listen=- rebuilds on each update message and replies with an error bundle and output paths.
comparisons.code: $ zig build --listen=-   # client sends update after each change

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer runs cargo check as a separate process, so the editor and cargo keep two caches and check edits twice.

recommendation.why: Update means the obvious thing on every command, as tools expect from Zig, and joining the running session keeps one warm compiler per folder. That is the reason the editor session exists.
gains: One short request works on all five commands.
Tools and editors share one warm compiler.

losses.loss: If the editor closes mid-stream, some requests are cancelled.
losses.mitigation: The session says so with a detached note and continues on its own compiler.

whyNot.reason: B checks every edit twice while an editor session runs, the waste the shared session was ratified to remove.
C drops the request the ratified flag decision assumed, so Zig-style tools need per-command logic.

recommendation.tradeoff: One forwarding hop to the shared session, for one warm compiler per folder.

surface.gist: What should update do on each command started with --listen=-, and should it share a running session?
surface.lesson: With `--listen=-`, a command takes requests on standard input and answers on standard output. `update` is the short request that means: do this command's work again on the newest files. A workspace session is a warm compiler that an editor or `jet dev` runs for the folder.

current.note: The flag is approved, but update has no meaning yet on any command.

wild.note: zig build --listen=- rebuilds on each update message (Zig build-system protocol).
wild.code:
$ zig build --listen=-
// client: update -> server: error_bundle, emit_digest

options.name: Redo the work; join the session
options.gist: Update redoes the command's work; the tool joins the editor's warm compiler.
gains: Update works the same way on all five commands.
One warm compiler per folder.
losses: Editor closing cancels in-flight requests.

options.name: Redo the work; never join
options.gist: Same update meaning; each stdio session keeps its own compiler.
gains: Simplest: no forwarding.
losses: Edits are checked twice while an editor runs.

proposed.code:
$ jet build --listen=-    // private compiler
$ jet build --listen=- --session=auto
error[E2102]: drop --session

options.name: Typed requests only
options.gist: No update; clients always name the work they want.
gains: No command-specific meaning.
losses: Zig-style tools need per-command logic.

proposed.code: > {"kind":"request","id":1,"op":"test","filter":"physics"}

recommendation.why: Update means the obvious thing on every command, as Zig tools expect, and joining the running session keeps one warm compiler per folder.
gains: One request, one warm compiler.

losses.loss: Editor closing cancels in-flight requests.
losses.mitigation: A detached note says so, and later requests run on a private compiler.

whyNot.reason: Checks every edit twice while an editor runs.
Tools need per-command logic for basic work.

recommendation.tradeoff: One forwarding hop, for one warm compiler per folder.

decisions.title: Compiler pipeline: one non-SSA slot IR between the AST and machine code
decisions.situation: The compiler copies every program through five forms on the way to machine code: the syntax tree, a typed tree, two SSA graphs, and a machine instruction list. Each copy costs allocation, lookups and a separate validation walk, and together they hold most of the 105 second self-compile. The vote picks the shape we build next; we recommend one flat, slot-based IR that keeps loops and branches structured, with SSA built only where a pass proves it needs it.
decisions.gist: Which intermediate form should sit between the syntax tree and machine code?
decisions.lesson: An intermediate representation is the program as the compiler works on it after parsing. Fewer forms means fewer full copies of the program, which is where much of compile time goes.
decisions.story: Jet compiles itself in 105 seconds today; the goal is 30 seconds now and a million lines per second later. Parsing to machine code passes through AST, TIR, MIR, LIR and an x64 list.
decisions.inWild:
Jai: one linear bytecode, interpreted at compile time and translated to machine code.
Wasm: structured blocks and local slots, no SSA.
decisions.detail:
Measured phases on a quiet run: front end about 45 s, MIR lowering 8 s, optimizer 7 s, native lowering 14 s, object emission 23 s. Half of all LIR instructions were back-edge copies created by SSA block parameters. Option A with a data-oriented front end is the route to 30 s; the IR change alone reaches about 60 to 70 s.

Card #5073 maps every current consumer and the migration. Consumers include the comptime evaluator, web emit, O1 and O2 passes, debug info, hot reload, LSP and the package store. Each cutover is proven by identical program behavior on the old and new paths.

options.name: One slot IR
options.detail: AST plus sema facts in node-id tables, then one linear slot-based IR per function with structured blocks, loops and branches, then machine code. Ownership is explicit move/copy/drop instructions. A pass that needs SSA builds a per-function SSA view and discards it, so debug builds never pay for SSA.
options.technical: IR: flat arena per function, integer ids, content-hashable. Machine layer: linear-scan allocation over slot live ranges. Migration: spike on Core plus examples first (go/no-go on speed and identical output), then front end, then IR, each cutover proven by identical program behavior on old and new paths.
options.code: source -> AST (+ facts by node id) -> IR (slots, structured control) -> machine code

options.name: Keep SSA, flatten
options.detail: Keep AST, TIR, MIR and LIR, but store each in flat arrays with integer ids and interned names.
options.technical: Data-oriented internals only; structure unchanged.
options.code: source -> AST -> TIR -> MIR (SSA) -> LIR (SSA) -> machine code, all flat

options.name: One SSA IR
options.detail: Drop TIR for facts tables and lower one SSA graph in place from semantic to layout level.
options.technical: MLIR-style progressive lowering inside one SSA form.
options.code: source -> AST (+ facts) -> IR (SSA, lowered in place) -> machine code

recommendation.why: Jet owns both ends, so SSA is not needed as an exchange format; one slot IR removes the most copies.
gains: Fewest full program copies; debug builds skip SSA entirely.

losses.loss: SSA-based optimizer passes must be rewritten.
losses.mitigation: Passes that truly need SSA build a per-function SSA view on demand; the spike measures this before any cutover.

whyNot.reason: B keeps every copy and the SSA overhead, so it cannot reach the speed goals.
C still pays SSA construction on every build and does not map onto Wasm structured control.

recommendation.tradeoff: More rewrite now in exchange for the fewest copies and one meaning across comptime, native and web.

surface.gist: Which intermediate form should sit between the syntax tree and machine code?
surface.lesson: An intermediate representation is the program as the compiler works on it after parsing. Fewer forms means fewer full copies of the program, which is where much of compile time goes.

current.note: Today a ten-line program becomes this SSA graph (MIR), then a second SSA graph (LIR), then x64 instructions.
current.code:
fn run() -> Unit<>
  local l0 mut fuel: Int [copy] at p0
  local l1 n: Int [copy] at p1
  place p0 = l0: Int
  place p1 = l1: Int
  b0:
    v2: Int [copy] = read p0
    v19: Int [copy] = const 0
    v11: Bool [copy] = gt v2, v19
    branch v11, b5, b4
  b1:
    loop-range-advance v7
    jump b3
  b2:
    v1: Int [copy] = const 3
    write p0 <- v1
    jump b0
  b3:
    v6: Bool [copy] = loop-range-has-next v7
    branch v6, b6, b2
  b4:
    v12: String [owned] = string ["liftoff"]
    v15: Unit<> [copy] = semantic Print [v12]
    return
  b5:
    v4: Int [copy] = read p0
    v10: String [owned] = string ["t-minus ", v4]
    v14: Unit<> [copy] = semantic Print [v10]
    v3: Int [copy] = const 1
    v8: Int [copy] = read p0
    v9: Int [copy] = sub v8, v3
    write p0 <- v9
    jump b0
  b6:
    v5: Int [copy] = loop-range-value v7
    write p1 <- v5
    v0: Int [copy] = read p1
    v18: String [owned] = call label(v0)
    v13: Unit<> [copy] = semantic Print [v18]
    jump b1
  b7 (entry):
    v16: Int [copy] = const 1
    v17: Int [copy] = const 15
    v7: RangeCursor<> [owned] = loop-range v16..v17
    jump b3
fn label(n: Int) -> String
  local l0 n: Int [read-borrow] at p0
  place p0 = param v20: Int
  b0 (entry):
    v20: Int [read-borrow] = param 0 n
    v12: Int [copy] = read p0
    v2: Int [copy] = const 15
    v14: Int [copy] = mod v12, v2
    v13: Int [copy] = const 0
    v21: Bool [copy] = eq v14, v13
    branch v21, b2, b1
  b1:
    v1: Int [copy] = read p0
    v7: Int [copy] = const 3
    v5: Int [copy] = mod v1, v7
    v4: Int [copy] = const 0
    v10: Bool [copy] = eq v5, v4
    branch v10, b4, b7
  b2:
    v0: String [owned] = string ["FizzBuzz"]
    jump b3
  b3:
    v6: String [owned] = phi [b2: v0, b4: v18, b5: v9, b6: v19]
    return v6
  b4:
    v18: String [owned] = string ["Fizz"]
    jump b3
  b5:
    v9: String [owned] = string ["Buzz"]
    jump b3
  b6:
    v11: Int [copy] = read p0
    v19: String [owned] = string [v11]
    jump b3
  b7:
    v3: Int [copy] = read p0
    v16: Int [copy] = const 5
    v8: Int [copy] = mod v3, v16
    v17: Int [copy] = const 0
    v15: Bool [copy] = eq v8, v17
    branch v15, b5, b6

wild.note: Jai compiles through one linear bytecode that it both interprets at compile time and translates to machine code. Wasm uses structured blocks and local slots instead of SSA, so a slot IR with structured control maps onto it one-to-one.

block $exit
  loop $top
    local.get $n
    br_if $exit
    br $top
  end
end

gains: One graph instead of two; optimizer passes keep their SSA form.
losses: SSA construction and destruction stay on every build, including debug.

gains: Fewest full program copies; debug builds skip SSA entirely.

losses.mitigation: Passes that truly need SSA build a per-function SSA view on demand; the spike measures this before any cutover.

decisions.title: Jetpack: delete the two legacy migrations
decisions.situation: Jetpack still carries two migrations from older layouts. One command folds old role files such as pkg.jet and config.jet into package.jet, and every write command first converts an old on-disk store layout. Both keep retired file names alive in the code after everything else moved to package.jet. The vote decides whether they go now; we recommend deleting both, with env.jet and workspace.jet staying canonical.
decisions.gist: Should Jetpack keep its migrations from retired file layouts?
decisions.lesson: A migration rewrites old files or stores into the current layout. Keeping one means the old names stay understood forever; deleting it means old layouts become plain errors.
decisions.story: Every other retired spelling was removed on 2026-10-20. These two migrations are the last code that still reads pkg.jet and the old store layout.
decisions.inWild: Cargo reads only Cargo.toml; a directory without it is an error, not a migration.
decisions.detail:
TransitionPlan.jet holds env_transition_legacy_plan. It reads pkg.jet, env.jet, workspace.jet and config.jet, then writes package.jet. Jetpack Foundation still defines PAYLOAD_FILE (pkg.jet) only for it and marks CONFIG_FILE retired.

store_migrate_legacy_hangar runs before every jetpack command that writes. env.jet and workspace.jet are still current files that the devserver and env model read.

options.name: Delete both now
options.detail: Delete env_transition_legacy_plan, PAYLOAD_FILE, the retired CONFIG_FILE handling and store_migrate_legacy_hangar in one cutover. env.jet and workspace.jet stay canonical.
options.technical: One commit; tests that exercise the migrations are deleted with them.
options.code:
# after
jetpack env   # a pkg.jet-only project reports: no package.jet found

options.name: Keep, then delete
options.detail: Leave both migrations in place, delete them in a later cutover.
options.technical: No change now.
options.code:
# unchanged
jetpack transition

recommendation.why: Greenfield policy removes retired forms; no in-repo project uses the old layouts.
gains: Jetpack stops reading retired file names.

losses.loss: A stray old project on disk would need a manual rename.
losses.mitigation: The error names package.jet, and the rename is one file.

whyNot.reason: B keeps retired names alive with no in-repo user.

recommendation.tradeoff: Old local layouts need a manual rename in exchange for no legacy readers.

surface.gist: Should Jetpack keep its migrations from retired file layouts?
surface.lesson: A migration rewrites old files or stores into the current layout. Keeping one means the old names stay understood forever; deleting it means old layouts become plain errors.

decisions.title: Command entry functions take one context named after the command
decisions.situation: A Jet package can replace what a command does by writing a function named after it, such as fn build or fn test. Today each one takes a differently named context: BuildContext for build, TestSuite for test, and nothing at all for dev. The compiler build is about to become the first large fn build, so the shape should be settled first. We recommend one rule where every entry takes a context named after its command.
decisions.gist: What parameter should each command entry function take?
decisions.lesson: A command entry is a function the toolchain calls for a command, like fn build for jet build. Its parameter is the handle it uses to do the work.
decisions.story: The Jet compiler will build itself with jet build Compiler/, which runs fn build in the compiler workspace instead of a separate script.
decisions.inWild: Zig: `pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void` takes a handle named after the command.
decisions.detail: Ratified today: D-CONF-ENTRY1 (one fn build(b: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan per package), D-CMD-OVERRIDE1 (fn test(suite: TestSuite), fn bench(suite: BenchSuite)), D-ENTRY-VALUE1 (fn run() -> App; fn dev() replaces the dev default). This ballot only renames the parameter types and gives dev and run a context.

options.name: Named after the command

options.name: Keep current names

decisions.title: May a function borrow a #Persist binding for writing?
decisions.situation: A #Persist binding keeps game or app state across a hot reload, and functions may already write to it with total += 1. Passing it to a helper with bump(&total) is rejected today, and the two compilers even give different wrong errors. The vote decides whether a write borrow of a pinned binding is allowed. We recommend allowing it, because it is the same write the function could already do directly.
decisions.gist: Can `bump(&total)` write to a `#Persist` module binding through a write parameter?
decisions.lesson: A `#Persist` module binding keeps its value when `jet dev` reloads changed code, and a function may write to it directly. A write parameter (`value: &Int`) lets a function change the caller's variable. The question is whether the two combine.
decisions.story: Mia is building a game with jet dev. Her score is `#Persist score := 0`. She moves the scoring code into a helper `add_points(points: &Int, n: Int)` and calls `add_points(&score, 10)`. Today that fails to compile, although `score += 10` in the same place works.
decisions.detail: Fixture tests/ui/static_mutable_borrow.jet. Today the Rust oracle reports E0355 (a policy at a prohibited scope) and the Jet compiler reports E0145 (#Persist on a binding that is not module-level). Both are wrong for this program: the binding is module-level, and D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A makes a #Persist binding writable from a function. No decision says whether a write borrow counts as such a write. Edge cases: a hot reload happens between calls, never while a borrow is live; a borrow of an ordinary module binding stays E0111.

options.name: Allow the write borrow
options.detail: A #Persist binding may be passed to a write parameter. The program prints 1. Ordinary module bindings stay read-only from functions (E0111).
options.technical: Sema treats &persist_binding as a write place like a direct assignment; the borrow ends at the call. The fixture becomes a run example with golden output 1.

options.name: Direct writes only
options.detail: Passing a #Persist binding to a write parameter is rejected with a dedicated error that teaches a direct write or returning the new value.
options.technical: Sema reports one registered diagnostic at the &total argument; the fixture snapshot records it.

comparisons.note: Swift lets a global variable be passed to an inout parameter with &. See https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/functions/#In-Out-Parameters

recommendation.why: D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 already makes a pinned binding writable from a function; a write parameter is the same write, done by a helper.
gains: Helpers work on pinned state with no special rule.

losses.loss: Module state can change inside a helper call.
losses.mitigation: The & at the call site shows the write, and only #Persist bindings allow it.

whyNot.reason: It adds a second rule for the same write and forces game code to be restructured.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more reach for pinned state, marked by & at every call.

decisions.title: How diagnostics name Core library types
decisions.situation: When an error mentions a Core library type, Jet prints an internal path such as module:14:source-root:0 followed by the name. Nobody can read that, and it differs between the two compilers. The vote picks one readable naming rule for every message. We recommend the plain name, with the module path added only when two different types in one message share that name.
decisions.gist: When an error message mentions a Core type such as `Secret`, how should it be named?
decisions.lesson: Error messages name the types involved. User types already print as their plain name. Core library types currently leak an internal path such as `module:14:source-root:0::…::Secret` or `<corelib>/core.crypto::Secret`.
decisions.story: Leo reads the raw bytes of a `crypto.Secret` by mistake. The error says the problem is with `module:14:source-root:0::core::crypto::Secret`. He wanted to see `Secret`.
decisions.inWild: expected `HashMap<String, u32>`, found `Vec<u8>`
decisions.detail: Fixtures: tests/ui/crypto_secret_bytes_exposure.jet (E0510), tests/ui/path_builtin_not_core_record.jet (E0112/E0108), tests/ui/ui_facade_single_uinode_identity.jet. The registry templates print `{Type}`, and user types print their leaf name. No decision fixes Core type naming. Edge case: a user type named like a Core type in the same message.

options.name: Plain name, path on a clash
options.detail: Core types print as their plain name. When two different types in one message share that name, each prints as module path plus name, as the user would write it (crypto.Secret).
options.technical: One shared type-display function strips internal module identities and qualifies only names that collide within the message; every diagnostic uses it.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `Secret` needs #Unsafe

options.name: Always the plain name
options.detail: Every type prints as its plain name, with no qualification.
options.technical: The shared type-display function keeps the last path segment.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `Secret` needs #Unsafe

options.name: Always the module path
options.detail: Core types always print with their full dotted module path.
options.technical: The shared type-display function prints the dotted Core module path.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `core.crypto.Secret` needs #Unsafe

comparisons.note: rustc prints the shortest name that is unique in the crate graph ("trimmed paths"), and the full path only when names clash. See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/73996

recommendation.why: Messages stay as short as user-type messages, and the rare clash still reads unambiguously.
gains: Readable messages with no internal paths, and no ambiguity.

losses.loss: The same type can print two ways in different messages.
losses.mitigation: The longer form appears only when the short one would be ambiguous.

whyNot.reason: It prints two different types the same way when names clash.
It makes every Core message longer for a clash that rarely happens.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare longer names, in exchange for short messages everywhere else.

decisions.title: A prep value inside a function
decisions.situation: A prep block computes a value while the program is built. A test expects such a block inside a function to be refused with an error saying it is not supported yet, while D-PREP-SURFACE2 says prepared values use ordinary names. Neither compiler gives that error today. The vote decides whether a local prep value is part of the language; we recommend yes, built once and baked in.
decisions.gist: Does `lanes :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }` inside a function compute its value at build time?
decisions.lesson: A `prep { … }` block runs while the program is built, and its last expression is its value. At module level `NAME :: prep { value }` is ratified. A fixture expects a local `lanes :: prep { … }` inside a function to be rejected with E0391, which says the form is not supported yet.
decisions.story: Kai's renderer needs the number of lanes. He writes `lanes :: prep { calculate_lanes() }` inside `run` so the work happens once at build time instead of every run.
decisions.detail: Fixture tests/ui/prep_block_value_unsupported.jet; its comment cites D-PREP-SURFACE2=A and expects E0391. D-PREP-SURFACE2=A: prep is always an expression whose final expression is its value, and prepared values use ordinary names. A 'not supported yet' diagnostic conflicts with the greenfield rule of one canonical current form. Edge cases: the prep body may not read run-time locals; it runs once per build, not per call.

options.name: Supported
options.detail: A local prep binding is computed at build time. The fixture becomes a run example with golden output 8, and E0391 is removed.
options.technical: Comptime evaluates the block once per build; codegen emits the constant. The prep body may not reference run-time locals (existing prep rules).

options.name: Module level only
options.detail: A prep value inside a function is rejected with a permanent error that teaches moving it to a module-level `NAME :: prep { … }`.
options.technical: E0391 is reworded as a permanent rule with a fix; the fixture keeps its snapshot.
options.code:
LANES :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }
fn run() { print(LANES) }

comparisons.note: Zig evaluates a comptime expression inside a function and bakes the value in. See https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime

recommendation.why: D-PREP-SURFACE2 already says prepared values use ordinary names, and a local value keeps build-time work next to the code that needs it.
gains: One rule for prep values everywhere, with no 'not yet' error.

losses.loss: The compiler must fold local prep values.
losses.mitigation: The same evaluator already folds module-level prep values.

whyNot.reason: It splits one feature by location and turns a 'not yet' into a permanent restriction.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more compiler work for a uniform rule.

decisions.title: Do method calls into Core count toward the rights a program needs?
decisions.situation: Before a program runs, Jet works out which rights it needs (reading the environment, reading files and so on) and stops with E1803 when the application has not decided them. The self-hosted compiler follows method calls such as `Path.home()` into Core and finds the Env and FS.Read rights they use. The Rust compiler only follows plain function calls, so it never sees those rights. Eleven run goldens (io/path, io/args_spec, dyn/bytes_datetime, io/system_projection and others) expect the program to run with no grants, which matches the Rust result. The vote decides which result is the rule.
decisions.gist: Does `Path.home()` in a program make it need the Env right before it runs?
decisions.lesson: A program's rights are the effects it can reach. Rust's check skips method calls, so a program that reads the home directory through `Path.home()` is treated as needing only IO.
decisions.story: Mia writes a small tool that prints her home directory with `Path.home()`. Under one rule it runs straight away; under the other Jet first asks her to grant Env, because that is what the tool reads.
decisions.inWild: deno run --allow-env main.ts   # Deno asks for the env right whenever Deno.env is reached, however it is called
decisions.detail: Jet: Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Authority.jet:153 walks call edges, method calls included. Rust: crates/jet-pkg-model/src/EffectBudget.rs:638 entry_effects over an effect call graph that records only bare-name calls (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/OSTarget.rs:503-506). Edge cases: trait method calls through a box, closures passed to Core, generic Core functions. Under A the eleven goldens gain the grant they need in their package.jet (authority.holds) and keep their output.

options.name: Every call counts
options.detail: Method calls into Core count like plain calls. The eleven goldens declare the rights they really use and keep their output.
options.technical: Keep the Jet walk; add authority.holds rows to the eleven golden packages; Rust stays the old route and is not changed.

options.name: Match the Rust compiler
options.detail: Only plain function calls count. The goldens run unchanged with no grants.
options.technical: The Jet walk skips method-call edges into Core, as Rust does.
options.code: fn main() { print(Path.home()) }   // runs with no grant

comparisons.note: Deno checks the env right at the point of use, however the code reaches it. See https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

recommendation.why: A right that a method call reaches without being counted is a hole in the check. Any program could read files or the environment through a method.
gains: The rights check sees everything the program can do.

losses.loss: Eleven goldens need a one-line grant in their package.
losses.mitigation: Their printed output does not change.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a known gap in a safety check to match an old compiler's omission.

recommendation.tradeoff: A grant line in a few examples for a rights check with no gap.

decisions.title: Rewriting another package's code needs one line naming that package
decisions.gist: Should a build need one line naming a dependency before compile-time code may rewrite that dependency's functions?
decisions.lesson: A rewrite replaces the body of a function that is already written. An application's build may let a library rewrite the application's own code. A rewrite could also reach into a dependency, such as a database library: code you did not write and may never have read. The lock file already pins each dependency's exact contents, so a permission can name a package without copying hashes.
decisions.story: Ines hands her compiler value to a tracing library so it can wrap her route functions. The library also wants to wrap every query function inside her database package. Under option A the build stops with an error that names the database package and prints the one line to add. She reads it, decides she wants traced queries, and adds the line. Her teammate sees that line in review.
decisions.inWild:
Jai: any metaprogram may modify any procedure it sees, including ones from imported modules; there is no per-module consent. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai

Rust: a crate can refuse a power at its root with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and the refusal is visible in source. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes
decisions.detail:
Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md). The owner named A, an explicit `meta.allow_rewrite(package:)` call in the application's build, and B, allowed by default as in Jai. C is today's ratified rule, included as the honest third option.

Depends on D-META-COMPILER1. This ballot applies only if that ballot ratifies the `Compiler` value. If it does not, this ballot is moot. Until this ballot rules, D-META-COMPILER1 limits rewrites to the application's own package, and D-META-OPTIN2's target records stand.

Amends D-META-OPTIN2=A. Under A, its `metaprogramming_targets` records (package identity, source digest, exact declarations list) are removed. The per-package call replaces them, and the lock file supplies the digest. OPTIN2's rule that a rewrite never changes the dependency's cached source stays. D-META-RECONCILE1=A quoted the same records as the dependency-target rule; that reference now points here.

Keeps D-JAI-EXPERT1=A: `Meta.Code.Rewrite` stays an effect leaf that must be held, and a deny from a team or organization file still wins over this call. Default holding is D-META-HOLD1.

Why per package and not per function: rewrites usually follow markers across a package, and a per-function list goes stale on every update. The `meta` lens shows the exact functions changed, so review keeps per-function detail without a hand-kept list.

Profile: short. One mechanism, three options, no new syntax; `allow_rewrite` is an ordinary method on the Core `Compiler` type.

options.name: Name the package in the build
options.detail:
The application's build may rewrite its own code once it has a compiler value. To rewrite another package's functions, the same build must first call `meta.allow_rewrite(package: "orm")`. Without that line, the rewrite stops with an error naming the package and the line to add.

The rewrite applies only to this build's copy of the locked version. The dependency's cached source never changes, and other projects using the same package are not affected.
options.technical:
`Compiler.allow_rewrite(package: String)` records consent for one package, by its locked identity. The lock already pins the package contents, so the consent covers exactly the locked version; an update shows as a lock change in review. A rewrite of a declaration from a package with no consent fails with a registered error at the `rewrite_body` call, naming the package, the function and the fix line.

A consented rewrite follows the same checks as any rewrite. Its effect facts are inferred again, and every affected caller, in the dependency's copy or in the application, is checked again at the end of the round.

Adding new declarations is not a rewrite and needs no consent. Core and the standard library are packages like any other under this rule. The `meta` lens of `jet inspect expand` groups every rewrite by target package. Effect rules still apply: `Meta.Code.Rewrite` must be held, and an organization or team deny still wins.

options.name: Allowed by default
options.detail: Once the application passes its compiler value to a library, that library may rewrite functions in any package the build uses, as in Jai. Nothing in the source names the packages it touches.
options.technical: No consent record exists. The `meta` lens still lists rewrites after the fact, and a team can deny `Meta.Code.Rewrite` entirely.

options.name: Keep exact records
options.detail: Keep today's written rule. The application's package file lists each dependency it may rewrite, with that package's source hash and the exact functions allowed.
options.technical: The ratified records name package identity, source digest and an exact declarations list. No globs and no transitive grants. An update changes the digest and invalidates the record.

comparisons.note: A metaprogram that intercepts the workspace sees every procedure, from any module, and may modify it. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
A crate root can forbid a power, and the line is visible in source and review. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes

recommendation.why: A keeps full rewrite power but makes changing someone else's code a choice you can see. One line per package is cheap, and the lock already pins what it covers.
gains: No silent changes to code you did not write.

losses.loss: A dependency update can change what a rewrite touches.
losses.mitigation: The lock change shows in review, and the meta lens lists every rewritten function by package.

whyNot.reason: B lets any library you hand the value to change any dependency, with no line saying so.
C makes you copy hashes and function lists by hand, and every update breaks them.

recommendation.tradeoff: One line per rewritten package, in exchange for no silent changes to other people's code.

surface.gist: Should a build need one line naming a dependency before tools may rewrite that dependency's functions?
surface.lesson: A rewrite replaces the body of a written function. Your build may let a library rewrite your own code. A rewrite could also reach a dependency, such as a database library, whose code you never read. The lock file already pins each dependency's exact contents.

current.note: Nothing can rewrite yet. The written rule, not yet built, lists each target with a hash and function names.

wild.note: Jai lets any metaprogram modify any procedure, from any module. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30.

decisions.title: The power to create a Compiler value is named once in the package file
decisions.gist: Must a project name compiler control in its package file before its build can create a Compiler value, or is it on by default?
decisions.lesson: Every package file has one `authority` block that lists the powers the package holds, such as network access. Ordinary powers are on unless denied. Expert powers are off until the project names them, and the trust prompt shows that change when you open a cloned project. The question is which kind the power to control the compiler should be.
decisions.story: Theo clones a game project and opens it. Its build creates a compiler value and rewrites hundreds of functions. Under option A, the clone's package file names that power, so the trust prompt shows it before anything runs, and CI fails with the exact line if it is missing. Under option B, nothing outside the build file says so, and Theo learns about it only if he reads that file.
decisions.inWild:
Rust: a crate can refuse a power at its root with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, one visible line. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes

Deno: programs get no file, network or subprocess access unless a flag or config names it. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

Jai: every metaprogram may drive the compiler, with no grant at all. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
decisions.detail:
Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md) and asked the author to pick the default from Jet's goals: beginner safety, auditability and pragmatism. The proposal leaned toward on-for-the-application. This ballot recommends the opposite, for the reasons below.

Spelling: the proposal wrote a TOML-style `[meta]` table with `compiler = "none" | "root" | "any"`. Jet's package file is Jet record syntax, and D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A puts every power in one `authority` block. So option A is the proposal's `none` and option B is its `root`. The proposal's `any` is not offered: D-META-COMPILER1 lets only the application's build create the value.

Why A. Beginner safety: a beginner never sees compiler control unless a tutorial asks for it, and then the error prints the one line. Auditability: the trust prompt, CI and an organization file all read the package file, not build code. Pragmatism: the cost is one line, once per project, which the error prints and `jet fix` can add.

Why not double gating: `b.compiler(app)` is the use, not a second gate. The package line is the only permission. That matches D-META-OPTIN2=A, where the owner chose a package-level opt-in over a package-plus-every-run opt-in.

Under A no ruling is replaced: it confirms D-JAI-EXPERT1=A for `Meta.Code` as D-META-COMPILER1 redefines it. Under B, D-JAI-EXPERT1's expert flag is removed from `Meta.Code` for the main package, and D-META-OPTIN2's rule that omission means standard mode is reversed.

Related: D-META-CROSSPKG1 decides whether rewriting a dependency needs a further line in the build. D-TRUST-LAUNCH1=A already excludes expert leaves from one-run approval, so `--trust` never turns this on.

Profile: short. One mechanism, two options, no new syntax; the `authority` block and `Meta.Code` already exist in ratified law.

options.name: Named once in the package file
options.detail:
Compiler control stays an expert power. A project turns it on with one line in its package file: `authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code] } }`. Without that line, `b.compiler(app)` stops with an error that prints the line to add.

Adding the line is a project-policy change, so the trust prompt shows it when someone opens a cloned project, and CI fails with the line instead of prompting. A beginner who never asks for compiler control never sees any of this.
options.technical:
Confirms D-JAI-EXPERT1=A for the `Meta.Code` node under D-META-COMPILER1: `$expert`, never held by default, only the main package may hold it, approved only through a project-policy edit. Holding `Meta.Code` holds its children `Rewrite`, `Raw` and `Types`; naming only `Meta.Code.Rewrite` is not enough to create the value.

`b.compiler(output)` performs `Meta.Code` and must be written in the main package's own source, so this one line governs every value. If the main package does not hold it, the call fails with a registered error whose fix is the exact `authority` line, machine-applicable through `jet fix` in an interactive edit. Organization and team files may still deny any Meta leaf, and the outermost refusal wins.

options.name: On for the application
options.detail: The application's own build may create a compiler value with no package-file line. Dependencies still never can. A team that does not want it writes `authority: { holds: { deny: [Meta.Code] } }`.
options.technical: Removes `$expert` from the `Meta.Code` node and its children for the main package only, so the main package holds them unless denied. Dependencies still cannot hold them. This amends D-JAI-EXPERT1=A for that node, and the meaning of omission in D-META-OPTIN2=A.

comparisons.note: One line at the crate root changes what the whole crate may do, and review sees it. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes
Powers are off until a flag or config names them, and the error names the missing permission. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
comparisons.code:
$ deno run main.ts
error: Uncaught (in promise) NotCapable: Requires net access to "example.com:443", run again with the --allow-net flag
$ deno run --allow-net=example.com main.ts

comparisons.note: Any metaprogram may drive the compiler; there is no grant to write or review. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
comparisons.code: #run build();   // build() may intercept and modify the whole program

recommendation.why: Rewriting a whole program is the strongest power Jet offers. One package-file line makes it visible to the trust prompt, CI and reviewers, and costs an expert one line, printed by the error.
gains: A cloned project cannot rewrite code without the trust prompt showing it.
One rule for every expert power.

losses.loss: An expert writes one more line before the first use.
losses.mitigation: The error prints the exact line, and `jet fix` can add it.

whyNot.reason: B lets a cloned project rewrite its code with nothing outside the build file saying so.

recommendation.tradeoff: One line per project, in exchange for compiler control that is always visible and approved.

The same rule as every other expert power.
