decisions.title: Byte streams gain read_into, which appends what arrives to a caller-owned buffer, so a steady read loop allocates nothing
decisions.situation:
Every read from a network connection hands back a fresh piece of memory holding the bytes. The runtime fills its own reusable block, then copies the bytes into a new list for the caller. The web server and the encrypted-connection reader then append that list to a buffer they already own.

So each read asks for memory and copies twice. The recommendation is A: a read form that appends straight into a buffer the caller owns, so a steady read loop stops asking for memory.
decisions.gist: Should byte streams gain read_into, which appends what arrives to a buffer the caller owns, so steady reads allocate nothing?
decisions.lesson: Reading from a network connection today hands back a fresh piece of memory each time. Busy servers read thousands of times a second. This vote decides whether Jet adds a way to read into memory the program already holds.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A buffer is a byte list a program keeps and reuses. A short read returns fewer bytes than the limit. Allocation is asking for new memory.
decisions.story: Ana's proxy forwards traffic in a loop. Under A, she keeps one buffer, clears it after each forward, and the loop asks for no new memory once it has warmed up.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: Read fills a slice the caller owns.
n, err := conn.Read(buf)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether byte streams get a read form that writes into a caller's buffer, and its shape. read(limit) stays.

Today, with the a0.0.43 compiler (dev c460ba91e5). Probe r02 reads a local TCP pair in a loop of server.read(4096) and prints read 4. Probe r03 calls server.read_into(buffer, 4096) and gets E0102, TCPStream has no method read_into.

Where the cost is. net_tcp_read_result in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/NetHandleRoutes.jet:67-118 now reuses a per-stream read block (net_read_buffer_take, :175). It still allocates a 48-byte scratch per call (:78). net_read_publish_bytes (:208-211) allocates an exact-size list and copies the bytes into it.

The hot callers on dev. Core/Http/Server.jet:1217 and 1226, Core/Http/Client.jet:735 and 746, Core/Net/Tls.jet:1104 and Core/Net/Net.jet:287. Tls.jet:1106 extends its own rx buffer with each result, the exact append A performs in place.

The per-stream block reuse that an earlier draft called pending has landed on dev. It removed the limit-sized allocation, but the exact-size list and its copy remain, so D's internal-reuse path is already spent.

Measured on a0.0.43, built programs, five runs each. 100,000 rounds of a 4,096-byte write and read on a local TCP pair take 1.09 s median (m1), about 11 µs a round. Appending each chunk to a held buffer, as TLS does, measures the same within noise (m2, 0.98 s).

Copying a 4,096-byte list 100,000 times takes 0.026 s median (m3), about 0.26 µs. So the list and copy A removes are about 2% of a local read round. Peak memory stayed near 14.5 MB in every run.

The case for A is therefore a loop that asks for no memory, which D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A asks of Core and which devices need. It is not raw speed.

The paired cell. A arrives with a two-program cell in the canonical performance manifest, as AGENTS.md requires of a surface added for performance. One program loops on read(4096); its twin does the same work with read_into into one held buffer.

The pair records wall time, allocations per read and peak memory. Ratification waits until read_into strictly beats read on it; any loss stays on a card.

What A does. n: stream.read_into(buffer, limit) appends at most limit bytes to the end of buffer and returns the count, 0 at end of stream. A limit below 1 is an invalid-input error, so 0 always means end of stream. A deadline form, read_into(buffer, limit, deadline:), matches read's.

It takes buffer by & as the parameter declares, so the call passes plain buffer. Bytes go straight from the socket into buffer's spare room, and the read's scratch lives with the stream. The list grows only when that room is short. TCP, Unix and TLS streams and file readers get the same method.

Clear already keeps a byte list's room when the list is not shared (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:3093-3117). So a loop that clears buffer after use stops allocating after the first reads. If the loop hands the bytes somewhere that keeps them, clear gives buffer fresh room; the kept bytes need their own memory anyway.

Precedent. Core's encoders already read this way through a private core.encoding.__read_into, used by Csv.jet, Stream.jet and Xml.jet. A makes the same move public, without that helper's empty-list rule.

Ratified decisions. A fits D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A, which prefers caller-owned buffers in Core. It keeps D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B: the Reader trait keeps exactly read, and read_into is an inherent method.

Beginner path. Keep writing chunk: stream.read(4096); nothing changes. Expert path. Hold one buffer and call read_into in the loop; the HTTP server and TLS reader switch the same way.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Generic Reader code cannot call read_into. The four hot stream types cover the measured callers, and a trait default can follow later without breaking them.

What remains. A buffer that is never cleared keeps growing. That is the caller's list, visible in their code, and the limit caps each read.

Other options. B fills from index 0 up to the buffer's length, as TlsLead first drafted and as Go does. C adds read_into to the Reader trait for every Core byte source. D adds nothing and relies on internal reuse.

Their best cases. B matches Go and Rust slices. C makes middleware generic. D adds no surface. Their costs: B needs a zero-filled buffer, which Core can only build by pushing bytes, and appenders still copy. C amends D-NETIO-CONTRACT2's trait law. D keeps one allocation and copy per read.

options.technical: Inherent method on TCPStream, UnixStream, TLSStream and file readers, with a deadline form. Reads into spare capacity with the stream's own scratch, grows only when short; 0 at end of stream; limit below 1 is invalid input. Reader trait unchanged. HTTP server, client and TLS record reader switch to it. Arrives with a paired two-program cell (read against read_into); ratification waits until it strictly wins.

decisions.title: No warnings: jet fmt rewrites style, tidy errors never stop jet run or jet dev, and jet check and jet build list them and fail
decisions.situation:
The owner agreed that Jet should have no warnings: a finding is an error or nothing. The owner added a builder-friendly rule. Tidiness never stops jet run or jet dev, while jet check and jet build list everything and fail, so the list is a to-do list.

The ratified rule says warnings and lints never fail a build by default. This ballot reverses it and changes how four ratified checks report their findings, without changing what they find. Keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: Should Jet drop warnings, so jet fmt fixes style and jet check fails on untidy code that jet run still runs?
decisions.lesson: A warning is a message that says something may be wrong but lets the program build anyway. People learn to ignore them, and real problems hide among them. This vote decides whether Jet keeps warnings, or makes each finding a style fix, a listed error, or nothing.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A lint is a check for code that works but is probably not what was meant, such as an import nothing uses. Style is how code is laid out and spelled when the meaning is the same.

A tidy error is a new kind of finding under A. It never stops jet run, jet dev or jet test, and it makes jet check and jet build fail.
decisions.story: Ada's game runs, and jet check prints four warnings and says ok. She ships it. Months later the warnings number two hundred, and the one that mattered, a never-read result, is lost among them.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How findings that are not plain errors reach the user, and which commands fail on them. It does not change what any check finds. Real errors, where a program has no single meaning, stop every command as today.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe n01 has an unused import, an unused local, a final return, a positional Bool argument and an unused private function. jet run prints TOTAL 6 and exits 0. jet check prints four warnings, now shown by name: PositionalBoolParameter, RedundantFinalReturn, UnusedLocalBinding and UnusedImport. It ends ok with 4 warnings and exits 0; jet build prints none and exits 0.

No unused-function finding fires for the unused helper in a loose file. Probe n02, a := that never changes, gets no finding at all, so D-MUT-NEVER1's ratified error is still not built. Probe n03 writes loud: true at the call, and PositionalBoolParameter still fires on the declaration.

Under A, every current lint goes to exactly one of three places. First, style: a rewrite with one certain result goes to jet fmt, which applies it. Second, tidy errors: a finding that needs a person's choice is listed with its fix. Third, advice that is not about wrong code leaves the diagnostic stream and becomes a report command.

Style moves to jet fmt. Examples are a redundant final return (L0530), a redundant unit binding (L0531), compound assignment (L0503) and a positional Bool argument (L2401). For L2401, jet fmt writes the parameter's label at each call, as n03 shows by hand, and the declaration lint is deleted. Style never fails any command; jet fmt --check exists for CI.

Tidy errors keep their code, Why and Fix. Examples are unused imports, locals, parameters and private functions (L0101 to L0104), unreachable arms and code, a constant loop condition, a discarded value, a zero divisor, and floats compared with ==. D-MUT-NEVER1's never-changed :=, D-MEMBER-LIVE1's unread fields and D-IDENT-CHARS1's look-alike names become tidy errors too.

D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1's one unsuppressible warning on pub _name becomes an unsuppressible tidy error. Tidy errors are reported with error severity in the editor, and in JSON output they carry kind tidy, so a tool can tell them from real errors.

Advice becomes reports. Performance hints such as growth in a loop (L0505), hidden allocation (L0506) and whole-file reads (L2501) leave the diagnostic stream. So do complexity (L2902), undocumented public items (L2201) and doctor advice (L2101). They move under jet lint, which already takes --complexity and --a11y, and which fails only when --max is given.

Which command does what under A. jet run, jet dev and jet test never stop or print for tidy errors; jet dev's status line shows their count. jet check and jet build list every tidy error with every real error, collect-all, and exit 1 if there is any. The list is the to-do list the owner asked for.

Whose to-do list. Tidy errors are listed only for the packages being checked or built: the entry package and workspace members. A dependency's tidy errors never fail its consumer; its own jet check lists them for its author. Findings inside code made by #run, derives or templates are reported at the written template when it is in the package, and dropped otherwise.

Saying a finding is intended. #Allow(jet.Name, "reason") is a marker that exists today, with 52 uses on dev, such as #Allow(jet.RedundantFinalReturn, ...). It removes one tidy error at one site, and its reason is required. The build report lists every #Allow, so a reviewer sees each exception. Real errors and unsuppressible tidy errors ignore it.

Migration. Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet registers 69 L and W codes on dev, and DiagnosticRows.jet mirrors the same 69. Each code gets one of the three places in the cutover, by the rule above. On the seed, docs mentioned L and W codes 14,182 times, mostly in generated pages that regenerate.

Existing code that warns today will fail jet check and jet build under A. The first run lists every item, so a package sees its whole to-do list at once. jet fix applies every fix that is certain, such as deleting an unused import, and jet fmt applies style.

Beginner path. jet run always runs a program that has a meaning, however untidy. Before sharing it, jet check lists what to clean, each item with its fix, and the list ends at zero.

Expert path. CI runs jet check, jet build and jet fmt --check; all three must pass. #Allow(jet.Name, "reason") records a deliberate exception, and jet lint --complexity or --a11y with --max adds stricter reports where a team wants them.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A package that builds today with warnings fails jet build after the cutover. jet fix and jet fmt clear the certain items in one run, and jet run keeps working while the rest is cleaned.

A half-finished edit with an unused local cannot pass jet check, even when the author means to finish it later. The author either names it _name, as the fix says, or keeps running with jet run and jet dev, which never stop for it.

Other options. B keeps D-LINTPOLICY1: warnings stay, and they never fail a build. C is Go's rule: unused imports and locals are real errors in every command, jet run included, and other checks move to a separate vet command. D is Rust's rule: warnings stay by default, and a project setting or flag turns every warning into a failure for CI.

C is the strictest, and it stops a quick experiment for an unused name, which the owner's rule says tidiness must never do. D keeps warnings for people who do not turn on the setting, so the ignored-warnings problem stays for most users.

decisions.title: #Persist means only that a value survives a hot reload, and writes follow the one module-variable rule
decisions.situation:
The owner agreed that #Persist should mean only that a value survives a reload. Today the marker also makes the value writable from functions and lets it be handed to a write parameter. No other module value gets either right.

This ballot removes both write rights from the marker. Who may change a module value is then one rule for every module value. That rule is decided by the open module-variable ballot, so the two are coupled, and the cutover waits for it. Keeping today's grant is option B.
decisions.gist: Should #Persist only keep a value across a hot reload, leaving who may change it to the module-variable rule?
decisions.lesson: jet dev can swap in edited code while a game keeps running. #Persist marks a value, such as a score, that keeps its contents through that swap. Today the marker also decides who may change the value. This vote decides whether it does only the first job.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A hot reload is jet dev replacing changed code in a running program. A module variable is a name := value written outside every function.

A write parameter, written &Int, lets a function change the caller's value. A shared holder, written shared Score{…}, is a value several tasks may change safely.
decisions.story: Ada marks her score #Persist so playtests keep it through edits. She then marks an unrelated counter #Persist too, only because that is the one way a function may change it. Now the counter also survives reloads, which she never wanted.
decisions.inWild:
; Clojure: defonce survives a reload; the atom does the writes.
(defonce score (atom 0))
(swap! score inc)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only what the #Persist marker grants. It does not decide whether functions may write a plain module variable; that is the open module-variable proposal. Survival itself, its identity by module path and name, the announced restart on a layout change and D-LIVE-PERSIST1's migrations stay as ratified.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe p01 to p11 matches the seed. Probe p01 writes a plain score := 0 from a function and gets E0111, whose fix offers a shared holder, #Persist, or #Unsafe. Probe p07 shows that run itself cannot write a plain module variable either. Probe p02 marks the binding #Persist, and the same write works and prints score 1.

Probe p03 hands a #Persist binding to a function taking total: &Int, and it prints score 1; today's call site writes add_point(score) with no &. Probe p04 hands a local of run the same way, and it works. Probe p06 hands a plain module variable the same way and gets E0223, PersistentMutableBorrow. Probe p05 reads a #Persist value without writing it and prints best 10.

Probe p09 builds a module-level holder, SCORE: shared Count{value: 0}, writes SCORE.value += 1 from a function, and prints score 1. Probe p08 marks the same holder #Persist and gets E0622, ModuleGlobalNotLiteral, so D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1's persisted holder is ratified but not built. The open D-MODULE-BUILD1=A lifts E0622 for storable initializers. E0111's fix shows the holder with a lowercase name, which fails the constant casing rule.

What survival means, exactly. Under D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A, a jet dev swap already keeps every module variable's live value unless its starting value changed. #Persist adds the two cases a plain value loses. It is kept when its starting value is edited, and kept across a jet dev restart as D-DEV-STATE1=A rules, while its name and type still fit.

The rule under A. #Persist grants survival and nothing else. It grants no write access and no write parameter passing. A #Persist binding is written exactly where a plain module variable of the same kind may be written, and refused with the same error where one may not.

With today's module rule, a function cannot write a #Persist scalar. The form for changing pinned state is a holder: #Persist SCORE: shared Score{value: 0}, written SCORE.value += 1, in today's holder spelling. Probe p08 shows it is not built yet. Survival comes from the marker and safe writes come from the holder, as Clojure's defonce and atom split them.

If the open module-variable ballot passes as recommended, score := 0 becomes writable from functions on the main task, and #Persist score := 0 is writable by that same rule. A task still cannot touch it, which closes the race today's grant allows: a task can write a #Persist score while run does. No marker then changes who may write.

The coupling, engineered so no game loses pinned state. A's cutover lands in the same change as the module-variable outcome. If you accept the proposal, the write grant moves from the marker to the plain rule, and no #Persist program changes. If not, the cutover lands with D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1's persisted holder built, and jet fix rewrites each written #Persist scalar into a holder.

D-PERSIST-BORROW1's write parameter rule follows the same law. A #Persist binding may be handed to a &Int parameter exactly when a plain module variable may. Today that is E0223 for both; the module-variable outcome decides it for both at once.

Error texts. E0111's fix drops the or mark it #Persist choice from both of its copies, because the marker no longer grants writes. Its holder example is written SCORE: shared Count{value: 0}, with the constant casing; if D-SHARED-TYPE1 respells holders, the text follows it. E0223 stops naming #Persist as the exception.

Migration, a census on dev. There are 14 #Persist module bindings, all scalar; one is Examples/Tooling/DevLoop/Persist.jet and the rest are tests. #Persist appears 62 times in 32 Jet files, mostly Compiler source and fixtures, and 55 times in 18 Markdown files. On the seed, 10 of the bindings were written by a function in the same file.

Beginner path. Mark game state #Persist to keep it while editing. Change it the same way as any module value; the error that refuses a write names the holder, and later the plain variable, as the fix.

Expert path. Survival and write access are separate decisions, so a cache can be persisted read-only, and a holder can be shared between tasks without surviving reloads. Each property is visible in one place.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Until the module-variable outcome lands, a written #Persist scalar needs a holder, which is longer than score += 1. The cutover never lands before the holder or the plain rule is built, and jet fix writes the holder.

A holder for a scalar needs a one-field struct today, because probe p10 shows shared 0 refuses SCORE += 1 and printing. That scalar ergonomics question is part of the open module-state proposal, and A does not depend on its answer.

Other options. B keeps D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1: #Persist both survives reloads and grants writes. C is Elm's model: no module value survives; run keeps its state in a local, and jet dev hands run's state value to the reloaded code. D is a Smalltalk or Lisp image: every module variable survives a reload, with no marker.

C changes how every game is written, since state must flow through run and its callees. D keeps stale values the author meant to reset, such as a constant table they just edited.

decisions.title: Keep <> in every pipe step, and let E0438's fix write it into the missing first slot
decisions.situation:
A pipe step is a line starting with |>, and <> inside it stands for the value from the line above. The ratified rule says every step writes <> at least once; a step without it is an error.

The review asked whether a step without <> should pass the value as the first argument, as Elixir does. The owner kept <>, because it marks where piped data goes. A keeps the rule and makes the error's fix write <> for you; B is the review's proposal.
decisions.gist: Should a pipe step keep writing <>, or should a call step without <> take the value as its first argument?
decisions.lesson: A pipe passes a value down a chain of steps. Jet marks where the value lands with <>, as in |> add(<>, 10). Some languages drop the mark and put the value first. This vote decides whether Jet's steps keep the mark.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A pipe step is a line starting with |>. <> stands for the value from the step above. E0438 is the error for a step that never uses <>. A fix is the rewrite an error offers to apply for you.
decisions.story: Ivo writes |> double() and |> add(10) out of Elixir habit and gets E0438 twice. Under A, jet fix turns the first into double(<>). For add, both slots take an Int, so his editor offers add(<>, 10) first, and a later reader sees exactly where the value went.
decisions.inWild:
# Elixir: the value is the first argument of each call step.
3
|> double()
|> add(10)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a pipe step may leave out <>. Pipes themselves, the <> glyph and the ?? return fallback of D-PIPE1=A are unchanged.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), as on the seed. Probe p02 writes 3 |> double(<>) |> add(<>, 10) and prints 16, and 3 |> add(10, <>) prints 13. Probe p01 writes |> double, |> double() and |> add(10), and each is E0438, PipeStepWithoutValue. Its fix today is general: write <> where the value goes, or end the pipe before this step.

Probe p03 writes |> print("done") in the middle of a pipe. That is also E0438, and here the error is doing its job: the step ignored the value, which is almost always a mistake.

The rule under A. Every step writes <>, as ratified, and E0438's fix gets exact. A bare function name of one parameter becomes name(<>). A call exactly one argument short becomes a call with <> in the one slot whose parameter accepts the value's type. A name that is only a method of the value's type becomes <>.name(…).

No silent wrong placement. jet fix applies the fix only when exactly one placement fits. When several slots accept the type, as in add(10) with two Int parameters, the error lists each placement. The editor offers each, first slot first, and jet fix leaves the site for a person. Otherwise the fix stays the general one.

So the typing cost of the mark becomes one jet fix, and the reader still sees where the value lands in every step.

Census on dev, unchanged from the seed. Pipes are rare. 13 lines in 4 Jet files start with a step. Outside the compiler's message strings, 18 steps sit in 7 files. 5 pass <> as the whole first argument and 5 call a method on it there, as Int.parse(<>.trim()). 4 put it in a condition, a lambda or a comparison, and 4 are error tests with no <>.

So 9 of the 14 working steps would need <> even under a first-argument rule, and those steps would mix two styles.

Beginner path. Write <> where the value goes; if you forget, jet fix writes it. Expert path. The same rule everywhere: a step is any expression, and <> may appear more than once or deep inside.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A step written the Elixir way fails once. The improved fix rewrites it exactly, so the cost is one command, not a lookup.

What remains. The common first-argument step carries two characters, <> and a comma, that Elixir leaves out. That is the price of the mark you chose to keep.

Other options. B is the review's proposal, guarded: a call one argument short takes the value first, so a complete call like print("done") still fails. C is Elixir's rule unguarded. D is F#'s bare function name. E fills the last argument, as OCaml and F# do.

Their best cases. B shortens 5 steps with no silent change to a complete call. C is the shortest. D reads cleanly for one-argument functions. E suits curried libraries.

Their costs. B leaves no mark, so a reader must know the callee's arity to see where the value goes. C turns a forgotten value into a silent wrong call. D adds a second step form. E puts the value where Jet's argument order rarely expects it.

options.name: Keep <>; a better fix
options.detail: Every step writes <>, as ratified. E0438's fix writes <> into the one slot that fits, and offers each slot when several do.
options.technical: D-PIPE1=A unchanged. E0438 fix: a bare one-parameter name gets (<>); a call with exactly one required argument missing gets <> in the one slot that accepts the piped type; a method-only name gets <>.name(…). jet fix applies it only when one placement fits; with several, the editor offers each and jet fix leaves the site.

options.name: Bare function name
options.detail: A step that is only a function name calls it with the value; other steps write <>.
options.technical: F#'s point-free step. A second step form beside expressions with <>.

options.detail: A call step without <> takes the value as its last argument.
options.technical: OCaml and F# application order. Most Jet functions take their subject first.

First argument, with _ for a named slot.

recommendation.why: A keeps the mark you chose: every step shows where the value lands. The better fix removes the typing cost, and half of real steps need <> elsewhere anyway.
gains: Every step shows where the value goes.
A forgotten value is still caught.
The Elixir habit costs one jet fix.

losses.mitigation: jet fix inserts it; it is the mark you chose to keep.

whyNot.reason: B hides where the value goes behind the callee's arity.
C turns a forgotten value into a silent wrong call.
D adds a second step form.
E fights Jet's subject-first argument order.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two characters per step, for a visible value everywhere.

decisions.title: Types as values and type switches, amending the ratified TypeKey
decisions.situation:
A ratified rule gives a running program an opaque key object that carries a type's exact identity; it is not built yet. The owner later asked why types as values would be a downside, since they allow switches on types. This ballot offers that: a type's own name becomes a value of type Type where a Type is expected.

Option A amends the ratified key and two reflection rules: that types stay types, and that one reflect call handles every value. Options B and F keep the ratified key. The owner's question is not itself a ratification.
decisions.gist: Should a type name be usable as a value of type Type, so programs can key maps and switch on types?
decisions.lesson: A running program sometimes needs to treat a type as data: count game components by type, or pick a handler for each kind of message. Today Jet has an approved but unbuilt key object for that. This vote decides whether the type's own name can be that value instead, with a switch on it.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A type's identity is what makes two types the same or different; Box<Int> and Box<String> differ, and two names for one type agree. A type switch picks an arm by a type's identity. It does not convert a value.

A descriptor is the small record a running program keeps for one type's identity. Type info, under D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1, is the larger record of fields and methods kept for reflection.
decisions.story: Rui writes a game whose systems count components by type and describe each kind. Today the display path of a value's type is his only key, and probe k07 shows Box<Int> and Box<String> print the same path. He wants to write counts[Position] and a switch on the type.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a running program names a type with a Type value whose source spelling is the type's own name, and switches on it. It amends D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A, which chose an opaque reflect.TypeKey. It also amends two rules of D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1: types stay types, and one reflect call handles every value. Options B and F keep the key as ratified.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), as on the seed. Generic type switches work: k01's if T == { } prints a different line for each component type, and k02 and k03 fail with E0003 without else. k07 shows reflect.of(x).path() is the same for Box<Int> and Box<String>. t: Rock is E0636, TypeAsValue (p09), and type_of is E0102 (k08, p08).

More facts on t6c. The ratified TypeKey is not built: dev has no TypeKey or reflect.key in any Jet file. A user type named Type is legal (k05), and a local declaration can shadow a Prelude name such as Dyn (k04). p05 shows a closed enum switch with no else. None of these probes runs A, B's key or E.

The rule under A. Type is a Prelude type whose values are type identities. A bare type name is a Type value only where a Type is expected. Those places are a parameter, field or result of type Type, a [Type: V] map key and a [Type] list element. They also include the other side of == with a Type, and a switch pattern on a Type.

Anywhere else a bare type name stays a type, so t: Rock is still E0636. Its fix offers Rock{…} for a value, or Type{Rock} for a Type value, the same typed-literal form as U8{1}. So a missing constructor brace can never bind a Type by accident, but a Type-accepting call still accepts any type identity, whether intended or not.

Identity. Two Type values are equal when they name the same type, as D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1 already requires. Aliases agree. Nominal types differ even with equal fields. Generic instances differ by their arguments. A function type's identity is its full signature, as D-META-REFLECT2's CallableSignature records it: parameter types and passing modes, result, error contract, effect row, calling convention and generic bindings.

Callable identity reuses canonical sema equality, including labels, zones, access modes, view provenance and identity-bearing policies. Defaults remain facts, not evaluated identity inputs. A Type value grants no authority: it cannot construct, cast, call, or reach private members. It is a plain value that compares, hashes, prints and can be sent between tasks.

type_of. type_of(x) gives the static type of x, worked out while compiling. Its argument must be a name or a field path such as p or p.pos. A call or other expression is an error whose fix is to bind the value first. So type_of reads no value, borrows nothing, runs nothing and has no effects.

Erased values. For a value whose static type is an erased carrier, such as Dyn, a trait value or the Any of D-PRIM-ANY1, type_of gives the carrier's type, never the payload's. The payload's identity comes from the carrier itself, as box.type under D-PRIM-ANY1. So one name never means two different things.

Type switches. if t == { Position -> … else -> … } on a Type value compares identity at run time, arm by arm. Type is an open set, so else is required, as for generic switches today. A duplicate arm is an error. The switch binds no payload; taking a payload out of an erased value is the Any ballot's job. if T == { } on a generic parameter stays a compile-time choice.

Printing and names. print(t) shows the type's full package path, such as game.Position or game.Box<Int>. When two linked packages share a path, such as two versions of one package, the display adds the version. Equality never compares display text, so a display collision cannot make two types equal. Version alone may not distinguish separately loaded packages with equal name and version; display also needs a package-identity qualifier then.

Reflection, an explicit amendment. D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 lets one reflect call handle every value. A amends that for one written type: reflect(t), where t is written with static type Type, is a compile error. The error says t names a type, and offers t.info() for the type it names, or reflect(Type) for the info of Type itself.

Inside generic code, reflect(x) on a parameter of type T keeps its value meaning even when T is Type. It then gives the info of Type itself, an opaque Prelude type with no public fields. So a generic helper never reads a Type value as if it were the type it names.

The schema. t.info() returns the same reflection value that reflect(T) returns for the type t names, or an InfoError. InfoError has two cases, each naming the type and its package. NotKept means the image that declares the type kept no info for it. Unloaded means that package's code has been released. The Type value itself is inspected with print(t), ==, hashing, and reflect(Type).

The strongest same-call alternative makes reflect(t) reflect the type t names, with no second operation. It is shorter. But then either reflect's meaning depends on whether the call sits in generic code, or a generic helper reads a Type value as a Position. A refuses only the written case that would mislead. E shares A's rule; B and F leave reflect unchanged.

A Type value is one word. It is the same 56-bit key of canonical identity that dev's trait values already carry in their first word (JetIR BuildTraits.jet), and the key D-PRIM-ANY1's box checks. Equality is one compare, and hashing reads the word. Two identities sharing a key stop the build, and keys of separately built packages are compared at load.

What the program keeps, by setting. Each type that becomes a Type value keeps a descriptor holding its key and display path, under every setting including none. Fields and methods are not in it. Under none, t.info() is a registered compile error naming the type_info setting.

Under requested, the default, reflect calls keep what D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 says. A program that calls t.info() also keeps the type info of every type that becomes a Type value somewhere in it. The build report lists those types and their sizes, so the cost is visible. reachable and full keep their ratified retention rules.

Descriptors across packages. Each type identity has one descriptor per process. The linker merges descriptors by identity: canonical package identity including checked content, module path, declaration revision, then generic type and value arguments, recursively. A package loaded while running adds its descriptors to the process table and reuses any that already exist.

Packages loaded while running. Each image, the program or a loaded package, keeps type info by its own build's rules. A package built for loading keeps info for every type it exports or makes into a Type value, since its loader may call t.info(). Its build report lists that cost. Kept info includes the field type graph, transitively, as D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1's type graphs do.

Privacy. t.info() shows the members visible to the calling code: public members always, and package-private ones only when the caller is in the type's own package. The check compares package identities at run time, so a Type value from a loaded package grants no new access.

Code lifetime. A type info value holds method, default and body references into its package's code, and so does a function value. The loader counts these references for each loaded package. Unloading retires a package at once for new lookups, but its code and info stay resident until that count reaches zero. Type values hold only descriptors, so they never keep code alive.

After release, t.info() on that package's types returns Unloaded, and no stale method reference can run. Descriptors are never freed, so unloading cannot leave a Type value pointing at nothing. Identity is session-local, as D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1 says: it is not a format to store or send between processes.

Hot reload. A type's identity includes its declaration revision and the identities of its field types, recursively; mutually recursive types are hashed as one group. When Position's shape changes, every type that holds a Position, such as Box<Position>, gets a new identity too. A type whose transitive field types are unchanged keeps its identity.

The real cost of never freeing descriptors, and its bound. Only hot reload grows the table: a reload that changes no type's shape adds nothing, and a release program never reloads. As an unmeasured estimate, 1,000 reloads that each change 50 types keep 50,000 descriptors of a key and a path, a few megabytes.

A jet dev restart frees them, and D-DEV-STATE1=A keeps every #Persist value across that restart. A loaded package adds its descriptors once per distinct identity, so loading the same package again adds none.

The name Type. A user declaration named Type shadows the Prelude Type in its own module, as k04 shows for Dyn; core.Type stays reachable. The census finds one user declaration named Type, in Compiler. jet fix offers a rename, by declaration identity.

Migration from the ratified key. reflect.TypeKey becomes Type, reflect.key<T>() becomes T in a Type context or Type{T}, and reflect.of(x).key() becomes type_of(x). The old names are removed in the same change, with no aliases. The census finds no use of TypeKey or reflect.key in code, because the key is not built, so the code migration is empty.

Other counts, by git grep -c on dev. There are 59 calls to reflect.of in 29 files, which keep working, and 6 mentions of type_of in 3 files. The seed's census found 12 generic type switches, which keep working. These are regex counts.

Beginner path. Write counts[Position] = 2 and if t == { Position -> … }. If you write t: Rock by mistake, the error offers Rock{…} or Type{Rock}.

Expert path. Function types, generic instances and types from loaded packages all have exact identity. The build report lists what t.info() keeps, and type_info none forbids it. t.info() returns NotKept or Unloaded instead of guessing, and an unloaded package's code stays resident while any info or function value still refers to it.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A program that calls t.info() keeps type info for every type it makes into a Type value. The build report names that cost, and generic reflect(T) avoids it. Descriptors are never freed, so repeated hot reloads grow memory without bound until the dev process restarts.

Type joins the Prelude, so a user type named Type now shadows it; that affects one declaration in the tree. A bare type name is a value in some places and a type in others. Those places are exactly where a Type is expected, and every other place reports E0636 with both fixes. reflect(t) on a written Type is refused, so reflection gains a second operation, t.info().

Option B in full. Keep D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A: reflect.TypeKey, reflect.key<T>() and reflect.of(x).key(), with the same exact identity, session-local meaning and descriptor lifetime. Branching uses chains of if key == comparisons; there is no type switch on a key. Nothing is migrated, and type names never appear in value position.

Option C repeals D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1. Maps are keyed by display paths from reflect.of(x).path(), derived rather than typed by hand. Two types with the same path collide, as k07 shows for generic instances. D also repeals the runtime key and keeps only generic switches on type parameters, so a runtime registry falls back to paths.

Option E. Runtime Type handles and type switches through a library constructor: reflect.type<T>() makes a reflect.Type, and type_of(x) returns one. Type names stay types except in switch patterns. It shares A's identity, retention and descriptor rules, and replaces TypeKey rather than living beside it.

Alternative F separates two choices that A bundles: exact-key switching and bare type names as values. Its only new surface is a checked comparison table on TypeKey. Its descriptors and lifetime are the ratified key mechanism, not another type representation.

decisions.title: Should an unresolved scratch-memory escape be refused rather than silently copied?
decisions.situation: Should an unresolved scratch-memory escape be refused rather than silently copied? Scratch memory holds temporary work that is cleared together. Noor joins two temporary names into text that must survive. Building that text in its final storage can avoid a copy, but uncertain destinations need a stated rule. We recommend final placement first and an explicit repair when a no-copy escape cannot be proved.
decisions.gist: Should an unresolved scratch-memory escape be refused rather than silently copied?
decisions.lesson: Build the finished result where it will live. Moving ownership is not necessarily copying bytes. A surviving reference into cleared scratch is invalid under either option.
decisions.explainer: An escape is a surviving dependency on arena storage, not every value created during a block. Scalars, old values and stable resource handles can leave when their owned graph contains no arena dependency. Copying bytes cannot duplicate a resource's identity or finishing duty.
decisions.story: Noor joins ada and lin, closes the arena and prints ada;lin. Both choices produce the same text; only their fallback for uncertain lifetimes differs.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative Standard ML join; MLKit infers storage from lifetimes, with no Jet performance claim.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTransact.jet:253-260 evaluates context guards and releases non-deadline guards. Both options extend this existing Context allocation route, not an extra `_in` API family.

D-CONTEXT1=A already requires safe scratch rewind and relocation of survivors. Final-destination construction is a valid optimization under that contract, not a new allocation selector. The remaining owner gate is whether automatic relocation remains a permitted fallback. F amends that fallback; E keeps it. Neither option requires an avoidable copy merely to cross a brace.

F propagates destination and retention facts through ordinary checked calls and interfaces. Known temporary allocations use the selected arena. A surviving owned graph is built directly in its destination or transfers compatible storage. A true conflict is refused; move creation outside scratch or explicitly copy a copyable graph into proved final storage. E uses the same placement analysis but may relocate when needed. E can therefore accept some programs F refuses; that is a real ergonomic advantage, not a slower implementation by definition.

Beginners use the default allocator. Experts install the existing arena context, inspect placement and choose explicit repairs for uncertain lifetimes. Follow the entire reachable graph, including captures, interior aliases, shared cells, retaining stores and task handoffs. A stable resource identity cannot be copied or relocated as bytes. Older containers keep their allocator. Partial construction, errors and cancellation settle owned values exactly once before rewind. No implicit arena-lifetime extension is allowed.

The printed join only tests the computation. The inspected guard lowering is not actual allocator routing. Before any no-copy or speed claim, measure allocations, copy counts and peak storage on both a returned text and a retaining-container workload. No performance superiority is asserted here.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Made the actual amendment explicit and gave the ratified policy the same placement optimization; removed mandatory-copy and duplicate allocator-API alternatives.

decisions.title: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head?
decisions.situation: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head? A lookup may return a value, no match or an error. Kai needs three different answers without repeating the lookup. Both choices make that same pattern table fit on one line and retire the result-only short form. We recommend adding compact layout to the existing table, without another expression head.
decisions.gist: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head?
decisions.lesson: Missing data is different from a failed lookup. List each outcome when they need different answers. Compact and expanded tables must use the same patterns, ownership checks and control-flow rules.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A result is a value or an error. An arm table is if subject == { … } with one arm per case. A single-arm if tests one case, as in if r == .Ok(n) -> …. The ?? fallback gives a value when the result is an error.
decisions.story: Kai calls lookup for -1, 0 and 7. Every choice prints -1, 0 and 7 after exactly one lookup per input.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative comma-separated general match for the same three outcomes.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/ExpressionForms/ResultHandlers.jet:1-3 and :99-105 already lower the short handler to ordinary pattern branches. Both options extend that canonical pattern route; neither adds a second result evaluator.

C adds comma separators and optional trailing commas to ordinary pattern tables. F additionally permits `subject ? { arms }` as a general short head. Both retire the result-only `? name -> ... ! name -> ...` spelling in a coordinated cutover, explicitly amending D-RESULT-DECON2=B. The compact feature is general to enums, not only error carriers. Ordinary automatic propagation and ?? remain unchanged.

The shared program uses the ratified flat Int? Problem! cases: .Val, .None and .Err. There is no nested .Ok(.Val(...)) carrier. Evaluate the subject once, run only the selected arm and retain branch-local bindings. Return, break and next retain their enclosing targets; no callback is inserted. Ordinary move/borrow, cleanup, finishing duties and secrecy tags apply.

Beginners use propagation or ?? for simple fallbacks. Experts expand the same table for multi-step arms. Closed sets list every case explicitly; an else arm cannot hide a newly added closed case. Open sets keep the existing else requirement. Missing and duplicate arms use the same checker. Format by width and comments; do not maintain separate compact and expanded AST meanings.

The strongest smaller change was already option C. The prior recommendation preferred a new head mainly because it was shorter, without evidence that the existing head imposed meaningful friction. C supplies the compact three-outcome expression without that extra spelling. F remains a genuine organization alternative under I8, not a second runtime mechanism. The migration must preserve subject evaluation, control targets, binding hygiene and drop timing.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Changed the recommendation to the strongest smaller extension and removed the false second-runtime-mechanism framing.

decisions.title: Let safe tree-building helpers work without letting shared objects keep each other alive forever
decisions.situation: Shared objects stay alive while another owner points to them. A loop of owning links can therefore keep unused objects alive forever. The compiler refuses a simple tree built through a helper in the probe, even though building the child directly works. This affects reusable code as well as memory safety. Choose how much the compiler should prove before accepting a write. We recommend better write checks, with collection still an explicit choice for real loops.
decisions.gist: Should safe tree-building helpers work without enabling hidden collection?
decisions.lesson: Think of owning links as people holding each other's tickets: a circle never gives its tickets back. A weak link is an address, not another ticket. A tree needs no circle of owners. The question is how to distinguish that tree from a real circle.
decisions.explainer: Reachability includes owned containers, erased payloads and callback captures, not only visible Shared fields. A collector also needs exact external-root accounting and safe cleanup. A graph sketch alone proves neither.
decisions.story: Ada wants a root with one child. Today putting child creation in make_child makes the tested program fail. She should not have to give up reusable helpers to get a safe tree.
decisions.inWild: Rust documents strong Rc loops as possible leaks and offers Weak links. That is useful explicit control, but safe Jet promises leak freedom too. Source comparison, not a Rust execution claim.
decisions.detail:
Same job in every option: create a root, create a child through a helper, attach it, and print 1. Every code pane is proposed canonical Jet. Shared{value} is the owner's ratified construction spelling; the available compiler still requires the old keyword for this probe. Beginners keep ordinary owned values; shared ownership is needed only when several owners need the same object. Experts use weak back-links or the existing explicit collection policy for real loops.

Observed on the t17a a0.0.43 compiler with jet run -: the helper program, written with the compiler's shared keyword, fails E0221 at root.kids.push(kid.copy()). Replacing that argument with a freshly constructed child prints 1, exit 0. This checks a false refusal, not a collector or a memory-leak measurement. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/SharedCycles.jet:151-159 accepts some fresh expressions, including lambdas; that shortcut is not evidence that captured ownership is harmless. No old retained-feed claim is carried forward without a new run.

A checks writes, not recursive type declarations. Track the owned graph through aliases, containers, captures, erased payloads and reachable calls. Publish checked summaries with ordinary interfaces. Unknown reach means not proved, not a fabricated exact loop. A store is accepted only if it cannot create an uncollected owning loop. Later mutation must preserve that proof. This is greater acceptance where proved, not a promise to decide every possible program.

A, B and C retain D-GC-OPTIN1=A: opted types may participate in collection; unopted cycles remain forbidden. Every participant in a collected owning loop must meet that policy. Collection must eventually reclaim unreachable loops, account for external roots, and honor the existing consuming cleanup and task rules. No resurrection hook or second cleanup protocol is introduced. Cyclic resources that need to call dying neighbors must be settled before collection.

B explicitly reverses #6281's companion memory card c2 requirement that refusal occur at writes, not declarations. C preserves write-site checking but leaves the helper refusal. D explicitly replaces collection opt-in; it is not already authorized. Allowing safe-code leaks was removed as a misleading normal alternative: it violates I1 unless the owner separately changes that invariant.

Adversarial verdict: A holds only within stated proof limits. Two attempts remove conservative refusals: propagate helper summaries and track aliases after calls. Neither makes arbitrary mutable graphs decidable. When proof is missing, name the uncertain link and offer weak links, IDs or explicit collection rather than unsafe acceptance. B and C are genuinely simpler; D is genuinely more convenient for arbitrary loops but adds collection where the owner currently forbids it. No speed or zero-pause claim is made.

decisions.title: The shared keyword is retired, and Shared{value} builds a shared cell
decisions.situation:
The owner's language review ruled that the shared keyword goes and that Shared{value} is the spelling. Today counter: shared Counter{hits: 0} builds a lock-guarded cell of type Shared<Counter>. That spelling was ratified, with the rule that shared expr constructs the cell.

A amends only that construction form. Plain field access, one atomic step per statement, #Transact, the Shared<T> type and the sharing menu stay, respelled. Keeping the keyword is option B.
decisions.gist: Should a shared cell be built as Shared{Counter{hits: 0}}, retiring the shared keyword and the Shared.new leftover?
decisions.lesson: A shared cell lets several tasks read and change one value safely, one statement at a time. Today a keyword builds it, while its type is written Shared<Counter>. This vote decides whether the type's own name builds it, the way other Jet values are built.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside other work. A shared cell is a value that several tasks may use at once; a lock inside it lets one statement in at a time.

Shared<Counter> is the type of a shared cell that holds a Counter. A keyword is a word the language reserves for its own grammar.
decisions.story: Ada sees Shared<Counter> in a parameter and writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} to make one. The compiler says it needs Shared but got Counter. The working spelling is the lowercase word shared, which she would not have guessed from the type.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how a shared cell is written when it is built. What a shared cell does, how its fields are read and written, how several steps commit under #Transact, and how lock order is checked do not change.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe h01 builds counter: shared Counter{hits: 0}, passes it to two tasks, and prints 1, 2 and hits 2. Probe h02 writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} and probe h03 writes Shared<Counter>{Counter{hits: 0}}; both are E0108, This needs Shared, but the value is Counter.

Probe h04 uses shared as a local name, and it works and prints shared 3, so the word is already contextual. Probe h05 writes Shared.new(Counter{hits: 0}) and it works and prints hits 1. E1115 RetiredSharedNew is registered for that form, with status Retired, so it never fires.

The rule under A. Shared{value} builds a cell that holds exactly one value, and its element type is inferred from that value. Shared<Counter>{value} names the element type, for when the value alone does not settle it. The value moves into the cell, and cloning the cell clones its handle, as today.

Why braces. In Jet a type name followed by braces builds a value of that type: Counter{hits: 0} builds a struct, and [Int]{1, 2} builds a list from its elements. Shared{value} is the list form with one element. The project's rule says a construct is a word, a marker or a library name. A shared cell is a runtime value with a type, so its library name builds it.

What is refused, each with a fix. Shared{} and a cell with two values say a cell holds one value. A field list such as Shared{hits: 0} says to build the value first, and its fix writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} when the expected type names Counter. E0108 for a Counter where a Shared<Counter> is needed gains the fix: wrap it as Shared{value}.

Retiring the old spellings. shared expr becomes one registered retirement error whose fix rewrites it to Shared{expr} by parse node. shared becomes an ordinary name everywhere; it leaves the reserved list, and the KW_SHARED spelling and its four references are deleted. Shared.new(value) gets E1115 back with an active status and the same fix.

Fix texts that spell the keyword are updated. E0111's fix today shows score: shared Count{value: 0}, which itself fails, because a module constant needs an ALL_CAPS name (probe p09). Under A it shows SCORE: Shared{Count{value: 0}}. E1101's menu becomes: give it (^), freeze it (freeze), or share it (Shared{value}).

D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A writes a module-level shared holder with the keyword; under A the same holder is written #Persist STORE: Shared{Storage{...}}. Probe p09 shows today's module-level holder works: SCORE: shared Count{value: 0} is written by a function and prints score 1.

Scalars are unchanged by this ballot. Probe p10 shows shared 0 builds a Shared<Int>, but SCORE += 1 and printing it are refused today. Under A, Shared{0} builds the same Shared<Int> with the same rules, so wrapping a scalar in a struct stays the working form.

Migration. The seed's census script counted 402 constructions: tests 149, Compiler 134, Core 59, Jetpack 26, Examples 16, Tools 7 and Docs code blocks 11, plus 23 prose mentions. On dev, git grep -cE for shared followed by a capital, digit, bracket or paren finds 413 in Jet files, comments included. Shared.new( appears 9 times. jet fix rewrites every construction in one run.

Beginner path. The type a parameter asks for, Shared<Counter>, is also how to build one: Shared{Counter{hits: 0}}. There is one spelling to learn, and the old one prints the new one in its fix.

Expert path. Shared<Counter>{make_counter()} pins the element type when a generic value would infer something else. Expert guards, Condition, #Transact and freeze are unchanged, and a cell inside a struct field or a list is built the same way.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} has one more pair of braces than shared Counter{hits: 0}. The braces show where the held value starts and ends, which the keyword left to the reader's sense of precedence.

402 constructions and the docs that teach the keyword must change. jet fix rewrites them by parse node, and the retirement error teaches the new form to anyone who types the old one.

Other options. B keeps the keyword as D-CONC-SHARE1 ratified. C is Rust's style, Shared.new(value), which works today through h05's leftover path. D is a marker on the binding, #Shared counter: Counter{hits: 0}, at its best case: no new construction syntax, and the binding reads as a Counter that tasks may share.

D hides a change of type behind a marker: the binding's type is Shared<Counter>, yet it is written as a Counter. Under the project's rule, markers carry compile-time properties of a declaration, not the type of a runtime value. C adds a second way to build values next to the brace form every other type uses.

One construction form across open ballots. Jet's conversions and typed literals already use braces: Int{b.len}, U8{1}, and Type{Rock} in the open type-value ballot. The open Any ballot spells its box Any(value). If both pass, the box follows this ballot's form, Any{value} and Any.Owes{value}, so every wrapper is built the same way; its type patterns keep parentheses.

comparisons.note: Library constructors, often two of them, build a shared lock-guarded value.
The Synchronization library's Mutex type builds the guarded value.
A library class wraps a value for atomic access; no keyword exists.

recommendation.why: A builds a cell with the type's own name, the way every other Jet value is built. It frees the shared word and closes the Shared.new leftover.
gains: The type a parameter asks for is also how to build one.
One spelling: the keyword and Shared.new both teach Shared{value}.
shared becomes an ordinary name, and a fix text that failed is corrected.

C adds a constructor function beside the brace form that every other Jet type uses.
D hides a change of type behind a marker and cannot build a cell inside an expression.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two extra braces per cell, in return for building it with the name of its type.

decisions.title: The arrow always comes first after the parameters, and the error-first unit order is retired
decisions.situation:
The owner's language review agreed that the arrow should always come before the result, and that the error-first order should be invalid. Today a function that returns a value writes its arrow first. A unit function that can fail writes its error first, or has no arrow at all.

A later ruling already writes a failing unit function as -> ! SaveError, which assumes the arrow-first order. A reverses the ratified error-first order and keeps one arrow and the fused effect arrow. Keeping the error-first order is option B.
decisions.gist: Should every signature put its arrow before the result and the error, so a failing unit function writes -> ! IOError?
decisions.lesson: After a function's inputs come up to three things: what it may touch, what it returns, and how it can fail. Today their order depends on whether the function returns a value. This vote decides whether one order holds for every function.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The effect arrow, such as -[FS.Write]>, lists what a function may touch; -> is the arrow with no effects listed. The result is the type a function returns on success.

The error contract, such as ! IOError, names how the function can fail, and ! Never says it cannot. A unit function returns no value.
decisions.story: Ada writes load with the arrow first and copies its shape for save, which returns nothing. The compiler refuses the arrow before a unit contract and tells her to write the error first. She now keeps two orders in her head for one idea.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only the order of the parts that follow a function's parameters. Which effects, results and errors a function has, and how they are checked, do not change. Lambdas keep D-LAMBDA-IFACE2's rule: they write no result or error type, and their arrow starts the body.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), probes are written in today's built spelling, String IOError!, and match the seed. Probe s01 writes load arrow first, save error first and check_name with no arrow; it runs and prints hello. Probe s02 writes save as -[FS.Write]> IOError! and check_name as -> IOError!.

Both lines of s02 are E0003: a unit-fallible error contract comes before the effect arrow, and a unit-fallible signature has no ->. Probe s03 tries the Swift order for a value and gets E0080, because a type may follow the arrow only where the result goes. Probe s04 shows -> Never! refused like s02. Probe s05 shows the same rule inside a function type.

The rule under A. After the parameters, a signature has either nothing or exactly one arrow, -> or -[Effects]>. After the arrow come the optional result type and then the optional error contract, in that order. A unit function that can fail writes the arrow and then the contract alone.

Every form under A. With nothing to say, fn(x) { } has no arrow. Pure forms: fn(x) -> Int, fn(x) -> Int ! ParseError, fn(x) -> ! IOError and fn(x) -> ! Never. With effects the arrow is -[FS]> in the same position: -[FS]> { }, -[FS]> String ! IOError and -[FS]> ! IOError. The empty row -[]> works the same way.

Function types read the same way, so fn(String) -[FS.Write]> ! IOError is a parameter type. Trait methods and extern declarations follow the same order. The entry point keeps its default: run: fn() { } is fallible with Err, and an expert pins it as run: fn() -> ! Err.

Reading a contract. After the arrow, a spaced ! starts the error contract; a type before it is the result. So -> ! IOError is a unit function that can fail, -> String ! IOError returns a String or fails, and -> String cannot fail. A lone type with no ! is the result.

Spelling. D-ERR-CONTRACT1=A, ratified, writes the error contract as String ! ParseError, and its own unit example is save: fn(n: Int) -> ! ParseError. So that ruling already assumes this order, and its retirement of String ParseError! lands with this ballot's cut. One jet fix run applies both.

That spelling is not built yet. On t6c, probe s09 writes -> String ! SaveError and gets E0003 at the result, so every probe here uses today's String IOError! spelling. The programs in this ballot show the ratified spelling.

What becomes an error. Today's error-first order fn(x) IOError! -[FS]> and the arrowless contract fn(x) IOError! both become one registered retirement error. Its fix moves the contract after an arrow and respells it: -> ! IOError or -[FS]> ! IOError. A bare -> with nothing after it, and -> Unit, stay illegal, as D-SIG-AFTER1 says.

The four E0003 texts that teach the old order are deleted with their fixes; the census finds exactly four, in Compiler, tests and Docs. The retirement fix works on parsed nodes, keeps comments and source locations, and moves only the contract and arrow tokens. It rewrites function types inside parameters, fields and aliases too.

Migration, from the census script re-run on dev. Error first with an effect row: 1,606 signatures (Core 605, Jetpack 698, Compiler 114, Tools 123, tests 45, Examples 9, Docs 12). Arrowless unit-fallible, not Never: 1,807. Arrowless Never!: 3,859. So A changes about 7,272 signatures.

Value signatures with effects, a result and an error already use A's order: 2,250 of them, and they change only in D-ERR-CONTRACT1's respelling. The counts come from regular expressions over source text, so they are estimates; the fix works on the parse tree and reports each edit. The owner's review figures for Core came from a different count.

Beginner path. One sentence covers every function: after the inputs, write an arrow, then what it returns, then how it fails. A function with nothing to say after its inputs has no arrow. The retirement error prints the rewritten line beside the old one.

Expert path. Function types, trait methods, extern declarations and generic signatures share the one order, so a signature copied into a type annotation needs no edit. Effect rows, error unions such as ! DbError | TimeoutError, and ! Never all sit where they sit for a value function.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. About 5,700 unit functions that can fail gain an arrow, 3,859 of them Never functions. jet fix writes the arrow in one run, and the formatter never removes it. A failing unit function is three characters longer, the arrow and its space; that is the price of one order.

Readers and tools that learned the old order meet the retirement error. It is registered, so jet fix applies it across a package in one run, and the error names the new order on the exact line.

Other options. B keeps the error-first order: unit signatures that can fail put the error first or have no arrow, and value signatures put the arrow first. Under the ratified spelling that reads fn(p) ! IOError -[FS.Write]>, and B would also amend D-ERR-CONTRACT1's unit example, -> ! SaveError.

C is Swift's order for every function: the error contract before the arrow, then the result, as in fn(p) ! IOError -[FS.Read]> String. D moves only the effect form, so -[FS]> ! IOError is required and a pure fn(x) ! IOError keeps no arrow.

C moves the 2,250 value signatures with effects and errors, and every pure value signature with an error. It reverses D-SIG-AFTER1's rule that the result follows the one arrow. decisions.title: Teach three ways to hold changing state: a plain value, Shared across tasks, and a Pool with IDs for graphs
decisions.situation:
Jet has seven ways to hold a value that changes: a plain value, Shared, Pool with ID, Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak, beside #Persist and module state. The docs and examples show them as peers, so a beginner must choose among seven.

The owner's language review proposed teaching three, with the rest kept for experts. This is a teaching rule, not a language change, and it extends the ratified short-path rule for examples.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's beginner path teach three ways to hold changing state, with Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak kept for experts?
decisions.lesson: A program's values change as it runs: a score goes up, tasks count hits, a tree grows. Jet has seven tools for holding such values. Most programs need only three. This vote decides which tools a beginner is taught first.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A holder is how a value that changes is kept. Shared lets tasks change one value safely. A Pool stores many values and hands out IDs, so a tree can point both ways. Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak are finer tools.
decisions.story: Sam counts hits from two tasks. Coming from Java, he reaches for Atomic, and Jet answers E1102: Atomic can't cross into a task. Under A the first page on changing state shows him Shared, which works.
decisions.inWild:
// Go's advice: share memory by communicating.
results := make(chan int)
go func() { results <- work() }()
total += <-results
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which holders the beginner path teaches, and in what order. No holder is added or removed; experts keep every one.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe s01 uses the three proposed holders: a plain score, a shared hit count changed by two tasks, and a Pool tree with a parent ID. It prints score 10, tasks 2, hits 2, leaf leaf.

Probe s02 writes the same program with Cell and Atomic, as a reader from Java or Rust would. Cell works. Atomic<Int> passed to a task is E1102, and its Why says the compiler has no registered ownership facts for Atomic.

So that refusal is a missing registration, not a rule, and this ballot does not lean on it. Probe s03 writes Go's way: tasks return values, and it prints score 10, hits 2.

Census on dev, Jet files in Examples, comment lines skipped, by git grep. shared or Shared is on 43 lines, Pool< or ID< on 10, guard_edit, guard_read, guard_write and guard.value on 12. Cell is on 4, Weak or downgrade on 4, #Persist on 1 and Atomic on 0. So the examples already lean toward the three.

What A changes. The guide's chapter on changing state teaches three holders, in order. First a plain value, the default. Then Shared, for one value changed by several tasks. Then a Pool with IDs, for graphs and trees.

Cell, Atomic, guards, Weak, #Persist and module-state rules move to an expert chapter, each with the problem it solves. Examples/Memory keeps the three at its top level and moves the rest under an Expert folder.

A registry check makes it stick. When a beginner holder solves the problem, an error's first fix names it. An expert holder may come first only when none of the three solves it, and then the fix links its chapter.

The check lists today's rows to reword. E0111 suggests the shared keyword with a lowercase module name, which itself fails; under A it shows the ALL_CAPS module holder, a Shared. E1102 suggests rebuilding an owned copy, and under A it names Shared first.

What stays. Every holder keeps its API: D-SHARED-API1, D-POOLID-API1 and D-SHAREDGUARD1 are unchanged. Expert pages link from each error that needs them.

Beginner path. Change a plain value; share it across tasks with Shared; build a graph with a Pool. Expert path. Cell for change behind a read-only view, Atomic for lock-free counters, guards for holding a lock, Weak for back links, #Persist for state across reloads.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A reader from Rust or Java looks for Atomic first. Every error that mentions Atomic links the expert chapter, and E1102 names Shared as the fix for a value several tasks change.

What remains. Shared costs a lock where Atomic would not. For a beginner's counter that cost is small, and the expert chapter shows when Atomic is worth it, once its ownership facts are registered.

Other options. B keeps today's peers. C teaches two, a plain value and Shared, and builds graphs from shared nodes with Weak back links. D teaches one, a plain value, and has tasks return results, as Go and Erlang advise; Shared and Pool become expert.

Their best cases. B hides nothing. C is one holder fewer. D is the smallest first step. Their costs: B leaves the beginner to pick among seven. C teaches Weak, the hardest part, to beginners. D leaves no beginner answer for a value several tasks must change.

options.technical: Go's and Erlang's message-passing advice, on Jet task results.

comparisons.note: Share memory by communicating.
Many holders, taught as peers.
Values first; classes and weak for graphs.
Entities and IDs for game graphs.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one answer per need: a value, a value tasks share, and a graph. Experts keep every tool, one link away.
gains: One beginner answer per need.
Errors stop suggesting expert tools first.
No API changes.

losses.loss: Readers from Rust or Java look for Atomic first.
losses.mitigation: Errors that mention it link the expert chapter; E1102 names Shared first.

D has no beginner answer for shared change.

recommendation.tradeoff: A lock where Atomic would do, for three clear answers.

decisions.title: One strictness field in package.jet names four levels, script, app, library and hardened, each a fixed bundle of today's policy keys
decisions.situation:
Jet already has many separate rigor settings: 20 scoped policy keys, 10 package policy fields, the authority block and named test profiles. A team that wants a careful package must know which ones to turn on.

A probe package that turns on harden, sentries, a lint and an authority list runs. A package that writes one strictness level is refused as an unknown field.
decisions.gist: Should package.jet get one strictness field whose four levels turn on fixed bundles of today's policy keys?
decisions.lesson: Jet can check a program more or less strictly, but each check is its own setting. This vote decides whether one word in package.jet picks a level. Each level turns on a fixed set of the existing checks.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A policy key is one package.jet setting, such as harden: true. The authority block lists the powers a package may use. A sentry is a runtime check kept in the built program.
decisions.story: Ben's team ships a parser that other teams depend on. Under A he writes strictness: .Library, and jet check refuses any change to a public function's effects or errors that would break those teams.
decisions.inWild:
// TypeScript: one switch turns on a family of checks.
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true } }
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether one field names a level, and what each level turns on. Every level is built from checks that exist today.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Policy.jet lists 20 scoped policy keys, such as unsafe, check_removal, sentries and lint_allow. package.jet's policy block also takes contain, harden, unsafe, expert, deps, claims, licenses, sources, exceptions and lints. The authority block holds allow, deny and grants.

Probe today sets policy to harden, sentries .On and a lint deny, plus an authority allow list, and prints 42. Probe dial writes strictness: .Library and gets E1215: strictness is not part of the Package vocabulary.

What A does. package.jet gets one field, strictness, with four values. A missing field keeps today's behavior exactly, so no existing program changes.

jet new writes no level, so a first program meets no new check. The cli and web templates, which ship programs to other people, write strictness: .App with their allow list already filled in.

.Script is today's default: effects are inferred and summarized, and no manifest is needed. .App adds the authority requirement. The package must have an authority allow list, which turns on D-EFFBUDGET1=D's opt-in enforcement. The error offers the inferred list as its fix.

.Library adds a stable public surface. A change to a public function's types, effects or errors that would break callers is refused until the author accepts it. The inferred signature is what is checked, so nothing new is written in source, as D-HONEST-SIG1=A says.

Where that surface lives. If the open API ballot passes, it is package.api, and .Library turns on its --locked check in every jet check. If it fails, .Library requires written effects and errors on public items instead, with the inferred text as the fix.

.Hardened adds the safety keys. It sets harden: true from D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, sentries .On and unsafe .Obligations from D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1=A. It also makes jet test run D-HARDENED1=A's hardened profile.

Levels only tighten. A package may add any key on top of its level. To loosen a key the level sets, the package picks a lower level and adds the keys it wants. This keeps D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A's rule that policy only tightens.

jet explain strictness lists each level's keys, and jet inspect guarantees prints the level a package chose. The levels are fixed lists in one Jet table, so a new key joins a level by one row.

Ratified decisions. A uses D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A, D-EFFBUDGET1=D, D-EFFECTS-BLOCK1=B, D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1=A and D-HARDENED1=A unchanged. D-MATURITY1=B's #Hardened marker is a doc label on an item; the .Hardened level is a package setting.

Census on dev, by git ls-files and git grep. The repository holds 2,490 package.jet files, 2,173 of them in tests. 207 write an allow list, and 51 write a policy block. None of them changes under A, because a missing field keeps today's behavior.

Beginner path. A first program never sees the field, since jet new writes none. Expert path. One word picks a level, and extra keys tighten further; jet explain strictness lists what each level turns on.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A team that wants .Hardened minus one key must drop a level and add keys back. jet explain strictness prints the exact key list to copy.

What remains. The levels are a fixed judgment about which checks belong together. A team with a different judgment writes the keys one by one, as it does today.

Other options. B keeps separate keys. C is one strict: true switch, as TypeScript has. D puts the level on the build profile, so one package builds at different levels.

Their best cases. B adds nothing to learn. C is the simplest name. D lets a nightly build run harder checks than a daily one. Their costs: B leaves the team to find the keys. C has only two levels. D lets a published package's level differ by build.
