decisions.title: How a build names a field's type when it declares a struct with meta.add_struct
decisions.situation: A build can declare a new struct while it runs, by calling meta.add_struct with a list of fields. Each field record has a name and a type. Today the type is text, such as "I64", which the build host turns into source for the new struct. That text check only blocks a few characters, so the type "I64, extra: String" quietly adds a second field. The ratified rule also passes a reflected field's type, which reflection gives as a TypeId, not text, so the rule contradicts itself. This vote decides what a field's type is: a TypeId, text, or either. We recommend a TypeId, written in the build file when it can see the type, and looked up by text when it can't.
decisions.gist: When a build declares a struct with meta.add_struct, is each field's type a TypeId, a text spelling, or either?
decisions.lesson: A type passed as a value keeps its identity and is checked where it is written. A type passed as text is checked only when the build runs, and it is read again in the new struct's module, where its name can mean a different type.
decisions.explainer:
A TypeId is the compiler's name for one checked type. Reflection gives one for every field, as field.type. Programs cannot make a TypeId from text; under A they can only ask the compiler for one it already issued.

A text spelling is a String such as "I64" or "[Point]". The build host pastes it into source for the new struct when the build runs.

The build function and the app can live in separate files. A build file sees only the types it declares or imports. A type only the app declares is invisible to it, unless both files import the module that declares it.

A type written as a value means a type name where a value is expected, such as String in CompilerField{name: "label", type: String}. Any other spelling goes in braces, as in TypeId{[String]}. D-PRIM-TYPEKEY2 A ratifies both spellings for a Type value, Rock and Type{Box<Int>}. Neither is built yet.

A lookup by text, meta.find_type("Point"), asks the compiler for the TypeId of one type the app declares. It returns that identity or None, and the text itself never becomes source.
decisions.story: A build reads the fields of a struct called Source, drops one, and renames another. It adds two hand-written fields, label of type String and tags of type [String]. It also adds a field at of type Point, which only the app declares, so the build file can't name it. It then declares a new struct, Shape, from that list with meta.add_struct. Every option builds the same Shape; they differ in how the hand-written, app-only and reflected types are written.
decisions.inWild: Zig builds a struct type at compile time with @Type, and each field's type is a type value, never a string. That works inside one compilation. Across the build-to-app split, Zig's build.zig passes values to the app by generating Zig source text (std.Build.Step.Options), so Zig also falls back to text there. C++26 reflection (P2996) declares a struct with define_aggregate, and each member's type is a reflection value such as ^^int. Rust procedural macros emit types as token streams, which the compiler checks only after expansion, like a text spelling. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
The ratified row reads: meta.add_struct(name, fields, scope: module) declares the struct name of fields, a list of CompilerField{name:, type:} records. Their names and types may be computed, as in a reflected field's f.type. The build host refuses a type that is not one type's spelling.

D-META-REFLECT2 A (2026-09-21) says FieldInfo's type is a TypeId, an opaque compiler-issued identity that user code cannot make from casts or strings. D-REFLECT-FIELDTYPE1 A named that field type. So the row's own example passes a TypeId into a String slot, which the checker refuses (E0108).

On dev today the two CompilerField rows disagree. The core.compiler index field row says TypeId (commit G6Decl-72), the literal row says String, and a build that writes a literal crashed the IR. The staged fix G6Meta-addstruct1 makes both rows String. It fills the index with the printed type name and has reflected sites write field.type.name. Every other type in that index stays a TypeId.

The host's check is a block-list of characters (jet_driver_meta_type_text_plain in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/BuildAdapter.jet), not a type parser. Probe inject: the type "I64, extra: String" passed it. The generated struct got a second field, extra, and the app printed a value stored there. So the row's promise that the host refuses non-type text fails today.

A TypeId's name is the type as its declaring module wrote it (type_name in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Types/Types.jet). The checker resolves such a name relative to the module that reads it. The new struct lives in a different module, which reads the name again in its own scope. A printed name can then fail to resolve there, or name a different type with the same short name.

Some printed forms are display-only and do not parse at all, such as a quantity's Quantity<dimension, base; identity>. Probe roundtrip: "Point", "Int?", "[String:Int]" and "fn(Int) -> Int" worked as text. The spellings "geo.Point" and "[geo.Point]" for a dependency's type crashed the compiler.

Text can name types a build file cannot see. Probe split: a separate build.jet named the app-only type "Point" and the app printed 9. In that build file, the bare name Point is E0107. Probe forward: a second add_struct named the struct an earlier call made, "Inner", and also "[Inner]" and "Inner?"; the app printed 7.

Type written as a value is not built for any type. Probe typevalue: Type itself is E0119, and Point passed as an argument is E0636. [Point] parses as a list literal, and Int? parses as Int followed by the ? operator. Type arguments, as in name_of<[Point]>(), accept every spelling today.

Migration under A is mechanical. jet fix writes a String literal as a bare name or a braced spelling when the text, read from the build file, names the same type the host finds in the app. Every other literal, and every computed text, becomes meta.find_type(text) with a failure for None.

In this repository the edit is small. Four test files write literal types, all I64 or I32, and jet fix rewrites them. The bad_type case computes its text and moves to find_type, which returns None for it. The typed and raw_denied cases already pass field.type. No example or Core file builds a CompilerField.

REVISION AFTER THE OWNER'S QUESTION (2026-11-12)

The owner called the TypeId direction solid and asked for its downsides to be designed away. The earlier A carried five costs. Four are gone, and one remains with a mitigation.

Computed type text, a type only the app declares, and a list of a struct made earlier in the build all failed under the earlier A. They now go through one lookup, meta.find_type(text). It returns a TypeId the compiler issued, or None. The text never reaches the new struct's source; only the identity it found does.

Function types needed a one-line alias, and compound spellings relied on name lookup to tell a type from a list literal. Braces remove both. TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int} and TypeId{[String]} reuse the ratified Type{Box<Int>} form. A type inside braces parses like a type argument, and probe typepos shows type arguments accept every spelling today. In a bare value position, [Point] reads as a list and Int? as the ? operator (probe typevalue).

The checker work for bare names and braces was listed as a loss. It is shared build work, and difficulty never ranks an option. The split between Type and TypeId predates this ballot. Both values now take the same two spellings, and the expected type picks one, so nothing new is learned.

ATTACKING THE LOOKUP

Forging. D-META-REFLECT2 A says user code can't make a TypeId from casts or strings, so that no program forges an identity. find_type returns only the identity of a type the compiler already declared, or None, so it forges nothing. A amends that sentence to allow this one lookup.

Injection. find_type reads exactly one type spelling. The text "I64, extra: String", which adds a field today (probe inject), returns None.

Scope. Names resolve as the app's root module sees them, plus every struct this build has already made, so "[Inner]" works after Inner is made. A short name that two modules declare finds nothing, and the build writes the module path, as in shapes.Point. The host still refuses, when the build runs, a type the new struct's module is not allowed to see.

Timing. The build already reads the app's declared types through b.program.packages() (spec.md, fn build), so a lookup needs nothing the build lacks. find_type, the braced form and add_struct's returned TypeId are proposed and UNCHECKED.

WHAT REMAINS

A type named by text is checked only when the build runs. That cost can't be removed, because the text exists only then, as with a config file. It is minimized: find_type returns None, so the build must handle a miss, and written and reflected types never take this path.

options.name: A TypeId, written in the build file or looked up by text
options.gist: CompilerField.type is a TypeId. Reflected types pass as is, written types are checked where written, and other types are looked up by text.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type becomes a TypeId. A reflected field's type passes as is. So does a field list from the core.compiler index, whose types are already TypeIds on dev.

A type the build file can see is written there, and checked there. A plain name such as String or geo.Point is written bare where a TypeId is expected. Any other spelling uses braces: TypeId{[String]}, TypeId{Int?} or TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int}. These are the two spellings D-PRIM-TYPEKEY2 A already ratified for a Type value.

A type the build file can't name is looked up by text. meta.find_type("Point") returns the TypeId of that one type, or None. It reads exactly one type spelling and resolves names as the app's root module sees them, plus every struct this build already made. So it covers a type only the app declares, "[Inner]" after an earlier add_struct, and type names read from a config file.

The text is never pasted into source. meta.add_struct returns the new struct's TypeId, so a later call can use it directly. The host writes each field from its TypeId. It still refuses, when the build runs, a type the new struct's module is not allowed to see. A misspelled written type is a check error at the call, and a String where a TypeId is expected is E0108.

options.name: A text spelling, as today
options.gist: CompilerField.type stays a String the build host reads. Reflected sites write field.type.name.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type stays a String. A hand-written type is its spelling in quotes, and a reflected field passes field.type.name. Any type the app can see can be named, including a type only the app declares and a struct an earlier call made. A reaches the same types through its lookup, but keeps the identity it finds.

B must replace the host's block-list with a parser that accepts exactly one type, to close the hole probe inject found. That repair is part of this option. Errors still come only when the build runs.

A reflected type loses its identity on the way. Its printed name is read again in the new module, where it can fail to resolve or name a different type. The index's CompilerField.type is then the only String type in an index of TypeIds.

options.name: Either a TypeId or a text spelling
options.gist: CompilerField.type accepts a TypeId or a String. Reflected sites pass field.type; hand-written types stay quoted.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type accepts either, so the field needs a union type, TypeId | String. A reflected field passes field.type, a TypeId. A hand-written type is a quoted spelling, which the host reads when the build runs.

Two ways to name the same type stay in one field, against I8. The text path keeps every cost of B, including the parser repair.

recommendation.why: A keeps every type's identity from reflection to the new struct, and checks a written type where it is written. Text is only ever looked up, never pasted into source, so the hole that added a field cannot occur. Every type in the core.compiler index stays a TypeId.
gains: Reflected and index field lists pass through unchanged
A misspelled written type is a check error at the call, in the editor too
Config text, app-only types and structs made earlier still work, by lookup
No text a build supplies is pasted into source

losses.loss: A type named by text, from a config file or known only to the app, is checked only when the build runs.
losses.mitigation: find_type returns None for a miss, so the build must handle it, and its text can never add a field. Written and reflected types never take this path.

whyNot.reason: B pastes text that is read again in another module, where a reflected type's name can mean a different type. Every mistake shows up only when the build runs.
C keeps two ways to name one type in one field, against I8, and its text path keeps every cost of B.

recommendation.tradeoff: One cost remains. A type named by text is checked when the build runs, and the build must handle a miss. Every other type keeps its identity and is checked where it is written.

decisions.title: Whether a C callback can ever read the task context
decisions.situation: The ratified context rule says a C callback receives no context, and that reading context there is an error until the callback installs one. The adversarial review found that the second half cannot happen. The callback rule only admits a small foreign-thread-safe subset, and that subset refuses every #Context block. A foreign thread also has no context record to install into. So the clause names a form nobody can write. This vote picks one rule. Either the clause is dropped and a callback never reads context, or the callback rule gains a form that attaches a context for a callback. We recommend dropping it.
decisions.gist: Should a C callback never read context, or gain a form that installs one first?
decisions.lesson: A C callback runs on whatever thread the C library chooses. Jet code there has no task, so it has no task context to read. Giving it one means building a context record on a thread Jet does not own.
decisions.story: A program hands a comparison function to a C sort routine. The comparison runs on the C library's thread. A helper it might call reads context.deadline to decide how long to wait. Option A refuses that read when the program is checked. Option B lets the callback open a #Context block, which builds a fresh root context for the call, so the read sees no deadline.
decisions.inWild: Jai marks a C-callable procedure #c_call. It receives no context, and it must push one with push_context before it calls code that needs it. Go's cgo callbacks run Go code on a thread Go attaches on entry, and a callback gets no request context unless it is passed explicitly. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
D-CONTEXT-EFFECT1=F says: a C callback, like Jai's #c_call, receives no context; reading context there is a registered error until the callback installs one. D-CABI-CALLBACK1=A admits a callback only from a checked foreign-thread-safe subset. Sema checks that subset in Calls/Checking.jet, and it refuses #Context blocks. On a foreign thread the runtime has no control block, so there is no current context record.

Today a context read in a callback is refused through the generic subset error, E3203. F asks for a registered error that names the context read.

options.name: A callback never reads context
options.detail: Drop "until the callback installs one". A C callback reads no context, directly or through anything it calls. Sema refuses a read with a registered error that names the context field and the callback. The subset stays as D-CABI-CALLBACK1 ratified it. If the subset later admits calls, the same reach fact that keys #Memo also refuses a callee that reaches a read.

options.name: A callback may install a context first
options.detail: Amend D-CABI-CALLBACK1: a callback may open a #Context block as its outermost statement. Entering it attaches a fresh root context record to the foreign thread for the call, and leaving it detaches the record. Reads inside see that record: thread from the attach, deadline None unless the block sets one. Reads outside it are refused with the same registered error as A.

recommendation.why: A states the rule the code already enforces, with a clearer error. B needs a context record on a thread Jet does not own, and a block form the callback subset refuses for good reasons.
recommendation.tradeoff: A callback cannot reuse code that reads context. It must take what it needs as arguments.
gains: One rule with no new form.
The error names the context read.

losses.loss: Callback code cannot call helpers that read context.
losses.mitigation: Pass the value in an argument, or read it before handing the callback over.

whyNot.reason: It adds a runtime attach path for one rare need and widens the callback subset.

surface.gist: Should a C callback never read context, or gain a form that installs one first?
surface.lesson: A C callback runs on a thread the C library picks. Jet has no task there, so there is no context to read. Giving it one means building a context on a thread Jet does not own.

current.note: The rule says reads are refused until the callback installs a context, but no install form exists.

wild.note: A #c_call procedure has no context and must push one before calling code that needs it.

options.name: A callback never reads context
options.gist: Drop the install clause. Any read in a callback is a named error.
gains: Matches what the code already enforces.
losses: Callbacks cannot call helpers that read context.

options.name: A callback may install a context first
options.gist: An outer #Context block attaches a fresh context for the call.
gains: Callbacks can reuse code that reads context.
losses: Adds a runtime attach path on foreign threads.

recommendation.why: A callback runs on a foreign thread that has no context record. The callback subset already refuses #Context blocks, so A only states that rule.
gains: One rule and no new form.

losses.loss: Callback code cannot read context through helpers.
losses.mitigation: Pass the needed value in as an argument.

whyNot.reason: A runtime attach path for a rare need.

recommendation.tradeoff: A helper shared with callback code must take its settings as arguments.

decisions.title: Which public Core API the web battery calls once the web app layer leaves Core
decisions.situation: Card #6445 moves the web app layer out of Core into the first-party web battery (D-WEB-HOME1=A). Core gets no private powers, so the battery may call only public Core API. Today that layer reaches the runtime through names only Core may use. They are the live-query store and its WebSocket publish, the process-wide shared cell, the startup environment, a coded runtime stop and private HTTP fields. Eleven compiler rules also key on the core.web module name. This vote decides which public Core API replaces those private calls. We recommend A: host powers stay in Core modules that own them, and the battery becomes plain Jet.
decisions.gist: When the web app layer leaves Core, which public Core API should the web battery call for the powers it uses privately today?
decisions.lesson: A library outside the standard library can only use what the standard library makes public. Moving code out forces a choice: publish general tools anyone may use, publish narrow ones that keep each power in its owner, or let first-party packages keep private access.
decisions.explainer:
Core is Jet's standard library, compiled with the toolchain. Names that start with two underscores are Core-private. A package that uses one fails to compile with E0067.

The web app layer is Core/Web: pages, forms, router, store, tables, live queries and browser storage, about 7,100 lines. It also holds core.web.browser, the browser automation library. The battery is Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/web, a package that ships with Jet; `jet add web` adds it.

The beginner path is the same in every option. A program writes `use web`, calls web.app(), adds routes and serves. Only the battery's own source and the compiler rules behind it change. The expert path is someone writing their own battery that needs the same powers. Option C gives them the most, A gives them what Core modules already own, and B gives them nothing new.
decisions.inWild: Next.js and Remix are npm packages, not part of Node; they use only public Node APIs plus their own compiler plugins. Phoenix LiveView is a Hex package on top of Phoenix.PubSub, a public publish-subscribe library. Bun exposes server.publish(topic, data) as public API for WebSocket topics. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
The private calls in Core/Web today, by count. core.mem.__process_shared (8, browser storage). core.sys.__startup_env (3) and __env_value (1, browser automation). core.net.ws.__connect (2) and core.web.browser.__ws_set_timeout (2, browser automation). core.web.__live_load, __live_replace and __live_publish (1 each, the live store). core.web.__contract_stop (1, OpenAPI). Private core.http fields: __router_mux, mux.__route, server.__state and app.__state.

The live store is shared. Core's app module (Core/App/App.jet) uses core.web for live bindings and sync sessions. So app cannot stay in Core while the store leaves.

The runtime bindings behind the live store are jet.runtime.web live_load, live_replace and live_publish. They are priv, and Guest.jet sema_guest_runtime_binding admits only the generated Core interface and the runtime package.

The compiler rules keyed on core.web, each to become a marker or trait. One: web.form lowering, Calls/Http.jet:590-716. Two: App route checks, Calls/Methods.jet:1304, 1315 and 1345. Three: the table.column schema check E2475, Calls/Core.jet:1549 and Direct.jet:1926. Four: web.openapi(mux), Calls/Http.jet:789-803.

Five: live, subscribe, push, invalidate and sync, Calls/Live.jet:61 and Http.jet:807. Six: the CLI web graph matching web.app, store, form and query.live by name, WebGraph.jet:512-1002 and Entry.jet:911. Seven: runtime handle rows for core.web types, RuntimeHandles.jet:225-273. Eight: effect rows, CoreDeclarations/Calls.jet:444, 493 and 549, and Taint.jet:319 and 342.

Nine: thread-confined browser types, Ownership/Crossings.jet:144. Ten: fixed signature rows, CorePlatformSignatures.jet:308-312 and 635-658, and all of WebCoreSignatures.jet. Eleven: ring rows, Rings/RingLayer.jet:17 and 100-111.

Rule four goes away with #6055 c2, which removes server.mux(). Under every option except D, rules one, two, three and six become markers the battery declares. Under A and C, rules seven, eight and ten shrink to the rows of the Core modules that stay.

Migration. The card's owner order applies: `use core.web` becomes an ordinary unknown module, with no teaching error or fix. About 470 files mention core.web today, 230 of them conformance cases.

options.name: Host powers stay in the Core modules that own them; the battery is plain Jet
options.gist: Browser automation and the browser host calls move to core.browser, the live store moves to app, and the battery calls only their public API.
options.detail:
Three moves inside Core, and no new general primitive.

One. core.web.browser becomes core.browser with its members unchanged. It keeps its private calls (startup environment, WebSocket connect and timeout), because it stays in Core.

Two. The browser host calls move beside it. core.web.on(path: String, title: String, handler: fn(WebEvent)) -[Browser]> and core.web.value(key: String) -[Browser]> String become core.browser.host.on and core.browser.host.value. core.web.storage.local and .session become core.browser.storage.local and .session, with get(key: String) -> String?, set(key: String, value: String), remove(key: String) and clear(). Storage keeps core.mem.__process_shared, because it stays in Core.

Three. The live store moves into Core's app module, which already presents it. Live<T, E>, app.live, app.subscribe, app.push, app.invalidate, app.state(binding: Live<T, E>) -> Loadable<T, E> and app.live_stats() -> String keep their signatures. The jet.runtime.web bindings stay priv and move under app. The battery calls app.invalidate and never sees the cell.

OpenAPI no longer stops the program. web.openapi(site: App) returns String OpenAPIError!, an ordinary typed error, instead of the E2805 stop. The battery's App owns its route table under D-ROUTE-ONE1=A, so it needs none of core.http's private fields.

Compiler rules become four markers the battery declares: #Form on a model struct, #RouteTable on App, #ColumnOf on table.column's name parameter, and #WebApp on web.app(). The checks behind them stay compiler code, keyed on the marker instead of the module name.

options.name: First-party batteries may declare runtime bindings
options.gist: The battery declares its own jet.runtime bindings, as Core does today, and keeps its private calls under its own names.
options.detail:
sema_guest_runtime_binding also admits packages under Jetpack/Provider/Batteries. The battery declares #Import(c) priv live_load: fn() -> [U8] = "jet_web_live_store_load", and likewise live_replace and live_publish, and calls them directly.

The other private Core calls get battery copies in the same way: the process-wide cell, the startup environment and the WebSocket connect. Browser automation and browser storage move into the battery with the rest of core.web.

The live store is shared with Core's app module, which cannot depend on a package. So the live store and app's live and sync functions move into the battery too, and app keeps only auth.

Compiler rules become the same four markers as A.

The cost is a second trust tier. First-party batteries can do what no other package can, so a third-party battery can never match the web battery. The runtime's binding rules, which today cover only Core, now cover Jetpack.

options.name: Core publishes general primitives; the battery builds the rest
options.gist: Core makes the process-wide cell, WebSocket topic publish and startup environment public; the battery rebuilds the live store and storage on them.
options.detail:
Three new public Core functions. core.mem.process_shared<T>(init: fn() -> T) -> Shared<T> returns one value per process, made on first use. core.http.server.publish(topic: String, event: String) -[Net]> sends an event to every WebSocket joined to a topic, as Bun's server.publish does. core.sys.startup_env() -> [String: String] is the environment as the process started.

The battery then holds everything core.web holds today: browser automation, browser storage and the live store. Core's app module cannot use a package, so its live and sync functions move into the battery, and app keeps only auth. The live store uses process_shared for its cell instead of the runtime's compare-and-replace cell. That is a lock instead of a lock-free retry, [INFERENCE] slower under contention and not measured.

OpenAPI returns a typed error, as in A. Compiler rules become the same four markers as A.

Any program may now hold hidden process-wide state with process_shared, which Core keeps private today. publish reaches every connection on a topic from anywhere in the program.

options.name: Defer: core.web stays in Core until v1 release preparation
options.gist: No new API. #6445 waits, and the web app layer keeps its private access.
options.detail:
core.web stays where it is. The battery keeps calling `use core_web: core.web` as it does today. Card #6445 stays open until v1 release preparation (#6068). Work that the card names as sequenced after it, the image pipeline of #4695, continues on core.web and moves with it later.

Nothing breaks and nothing is built now. The cost is that Core keeps a 7,100-line app framework with eleven compiler rules keyed on its name, against the ratified D-WEB-HOME1=A.

recommendation.why: A moves the layer out without giving any package a private power and without publishing a general hidden-state tool. Each private call stays in the one Core module that owns its concept, and the battery uses that module's public face.
gains: The battery compiles as an ordinary package; a third-party battery could do the same
No new general primitive: process-wide state and runtime bindings stay inside Core
Core's app module keeps live queries and sync, so app programs do not change

losses.loss: Core gains core.browser, core.browser.host and core.browser.storage, and keeps about 2,400 lines of browser code.
losses.mitigation: Browser automation is a test tool used outside web apps, and the host calls are Core's browser boundary. Neither belongs to the app framework the card moves.

losses.loss: web.openapi now returns a typed error, a signature change for its callers.
losses.mitigation: Registered routes already reject a bad contract at compile time, so callers handle an error that only hand-built contracts can raise.

losses.loss: Four new markers, each with compiler checks behind it.
losses.mitigation: Each replaces a check that exists today keyed on the module name, so no new check is added.

losses.loss: Programs that wrote web.live must write app.live.
losses.mitigation: The owner order for #6445 moves every in-repo caller in the same change, with no teaching error.

losses.loss: A frees the battery from private HTTP fields only once App owns its route table, which #6055 c2 has not built yet.
losses.mitigation: #6055 c2 lands first, on core.web where it lives today, and #6445 moves the finished table.

whyNot.reason: B makes first-party batteries a privileged tier that no other package can match, and moves app's live and sync out of Core.
C makes hidden process-wide state and program-wide publish public for every program, and moves app's live and sync out of Core.
D leaves a 7,100-line framework in Core against the ratified D-WEB-HOME1=A and keeps #6445 open.

recommendation.tradeoff: The battery gets no special access, but Core keeps the browser module and the live store under its own names.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Checked against Core/App/App.jet, which already forwards state and live_stats to core.web, and Core/Web (6,974 lines); the claims hold. One gap: A needs the App route table of #6055 c2 first, now a stated loss.

decisions.title: Core's file readers and writers for JSON, CBOR, CSV and XML: take the Prelude's byte-stream traits, reorder the layers into six groups, or move to new paths
decisions.situation: D-CORE-LAYERS1=A puts Core in four checked layers, where a lower layer may not use a higher one. It also promises that no import or API changes. Readers that turn a file into JSON or CBOR events sit low, but take a file, and files sit higher. The owner asked why byte traits would not be a good idea. They are the best design, with two costs named below. Jet's Prelude already declares Reader and Writer traits for byte streams, though user code cannot name them as a bound yet. If the codecs take those traits instead of a file, nothing low names files, and no public path changes. We recommend A.
decisions.gist: Should Core's codecs take the Prelude's byte-stream traits, should Core reorder its layers, or should the file readers move to new paths?
decisions.lesson: Jet's core library is sorted into layers, where lower parts may not use higher ones. Readers that turn a file into JSON or CBOR events sit in a low layer but use files, which sit higher. This vote picks a fix: let the readers take any byte stream, reorder the layers, or move the readers to new names.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Core is Jet's built-in library. A layer is a group of Core modules that may use only its own or lower groups. An adapter is a function that connects a format, like JSON, to a file. A path is the import name, like core.encoding.json.

A trait is a set of methods a type promises to have. A byte-stream trait says only: you can read bytes from me, or write bytes to me. A file, the terminal and a network stream can all promise that.
decisions.story: Ana streams a large catalog.json with json.reader over an open file. Under A her program is unchanged, and the same json.reader also reads from stdin or her own type. Under B her program is unchanged, but every JSON program loads the files code. Under C she imports core.files.json instead.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How the Core layer check of D-CORE-LAYERS1=A turns on without breaking its promise of no import or API change.

The owner's question (q0mbsiry). The owner asked why byte traits would not be a good idea. The posted ballot charged them three costs: two new public traits, 75 compiler lines to reroute, and 7 names that still move. On a closer look none of the three holds.

The traits exist but are not open yet. Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:228 declares Reader with read(limit) -> [U8], and :233 declares Writer with write and write_all. Nothing implements them, and seed b14 refuses a user bound on them (probe r1: E0301, Reader is not a trait). A opens both as ordinary bounds; the same shape with a local trait already runs (probe r3). A adds read_into to Reader, as TLS streams already spell it, so a codec can read without a new list per chunk.

FileReader fits with a thin impl. Its read and read_into are compiler routes today, not Jet methods (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/StreamHandles.jet:163, documented at Core/Files/Files.jet:329). So impl FileReader.Reader is two one-line methods that call them.

One name is shared. core.term already has a public Reader: the binary cursor behind Reader.over(bytes) and read_u8 (Core/Term/Term.jet:24). D-NETIO-CONTRACT1 names it the byte-stream type; A amends that, so the trait is the contract and the cursor one type that implements it. The two stay apart by path, as Go's io.Reader and bufio.Reader do.

The 75 compiler lines are private routes. Today the compiler knows the codecs' FileReader handles by name. Pillar 5 of the philosophy says Core uses no private compiler hook a user library could not. A generic codec is ordinary Jet, so those routes are deleted, not rewritten.

The 7 names need no move. The posted C moved them because the ratified table put crypto, data, csv and WebSocket below what they use. A places those four modules one layer higher instead. Crypto joins files, and data, encoding.csv and net.ws join services. Their paths stay.

The census, on dev 0f41dd417c. The ratified table gives 67 upward lines in 20 module pairs. A's table gives 31 lines in 11 pairs, none new. 25 are codecs naming files, which the traits remove: cbor 20, of which 19 are test fixtures, Core.encoding's Stream and CborStream parts 2, and json, jsonl and xml 1 each. Hex and ETF naming archive are a private move in every option. Meta, rt, sync and TLS are cleared by staged moves.

Cost at run time. A generic function is built once for each type a call reaches (spec.md, Generics), so json.reader over a FileReader is built for FileReader alone. [INFERENCE] Each chunk then costs one direct call, as today; the Core speed gate checks it. A call through a type parameter charges its effects to the caller (spec.md 2725), so json.reader(file) still needs FS.Read and json.reader(stdin) needs IO.

Load cost. Measured with seed b13 on a17e4f4491, a json.parse program loads 29 Core units and 1.95 MB of Core source. 5 units and 0.29 MB of that are the files chain: files, its path kernel, sys, process and term. Under A and C json.parse loads none of them; under B it always does.

Sources. Go encoding/json: pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#NewDecoder. Rust serde_json: docs.rs/serde_json/latest/serde_json/fn.from_reader.html. Python json.load: docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.load. Java Reader and InputStream: docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/io/InputStream.html.

options.name: Codecs take the Prelude's Reader and Writer traits; four modules change layer
options.detail:
json.reader, jsonl, cbor, csv and xml readers and writers take any type that implements the Prelude's Reader or Writer. FileReader and FileWriter implement them, so every call written today still works. Crypto moves up beside files, and data, encoding.csv and net.ws move up to services. No public path changes.

Beginner path: pass an open file, as today. Expert path: pass term.stdin(), or write impl MySource.Reader for a socket, a decompressor or a test buffer.
options.technical:
Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet: Reader gains read_into: fn(&self, &buffer: [U8], limit: Int) -> Int IOError!, with read kept. OwnedTraitRows.jet opens Reader and Writer as bounds user code can name. FileReader, FileWriter, core.term's Reader cursor and its StdinHandle, Stdout and Stderr implement the traits; FileReader's methods call its routed read and read_into. The 11 codec constructors and the 10 reader and writer types become generic: fn<R: Reader>(input: &&R, ...). Core.encoding's Stream and CborStream parts take the trait.

The compiler's private FileReader and FileWriter codec routes are deleted, about 75 lines in 20 files. Cbor's 19 file test fixtures read a small test-local Reader. Core/package.jet moves crypto to the files layer, and data, encoding.csv and net.ws to services. Hex and ETF's kernels move privately, as in every option.

options.name: Six groups; adapters stay
options.detail: This was the posted A. Amend the ratified table to six groups. Files and the system basics sit below the codecs, crypto and archive; data and CSV join services. No public path changes. Every codec still names files, so any JSON or CBOR program loads the files chain.
options.technical: Core/package.jet lists six groups: Prelude; Data; OS (sys, files, process, tasks, term); Formats (the codecs, crypto, compute, archive); System; Services, with data, csv and net.ws. Three private moves remain: sys owns the hostname read, cbor owns CborStream, and json owns the JSON file engines.

options.name: Adapters move to new paths
options.detail: This was the posted B. Keep the ratified four layers. The file adapters move under core.files, and the other upward public names move beside what they use. Thirty public names change path, such as core.encoding.json.reader to core.files.json.reader.
options.technical: Public moves: the json, jsonl, cbor, csv and xml readers and writers go to core.files.<codec>. crypto's file_seal, file_open and FileCryptoError go to core.files.crypto, and data's csv_reader and json_reader to core.files.data. data.status and require_bridge go to core.process, csv.query to core.db and ws.upgrade to core.http.

comparisons.note: Codecs take io.Reader; os.File, net.Conn and bytes.Buffer implement it. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#NewDecoder
serde_json reads any io::Read, including std::fs::File and TcpStream, built once per type. Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/latest/serde_json/fn.from_reader.html
json.load takes any object with a read method. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.load

recommendation.why: A is the design Go, Rust and Python ship, and Jet already has its traits. It keeps every public path, so the no-API-change promise holds. It lets codecs read any byte stream and deletes private compiler routes, and a JSON program no longer loads the files code.
gains: No public path or call changes.
Codecs read files, stdin and any user type that implements Reader.
json.parse no longer loads 5 Core units and 0.29 MB of files code.
About 75 private compiler routing lines are deleted.

losses.loss: The codec signatures become generic: fn<R: Reader>(input: &&R).
losses.mitigation: Callers write the same call. Each use is built for its own type, so a FileReader read stays one direct call per chunk [INFERENCE]; the speed gate checks it.

losses.loss: Four modules change layer: crypto, data, encoding.csv and net.ws.
losses.mitigation: Each is one row in Core/package.jet, and none changes its path.

losses.loss: A network stream reads with a deadline, which Reader has no place for.
losses.mitigation: A one-line impl fixes the deadline per stream; the deadline stays explicit.

losses.loss: The trait Reader and core.term's binary cursor Reader share one name.
losses.mitigation: They differ by path: the cursor is always written term.Reader and implements the trait, as Go's bufio.Reader implements io.Reader. Renaming the trait ByteReader is the fallback if the owner prefers distinct names.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the codecs tied to files, so every JSON program loads the files code, and the codecs read nothing else. A gets the same path stability without that cost.
C moves 30 public names to new paths and still ties each codec to files.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generic codec signatures and four layer rows, for codecs that read any byte stream and no public path change.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: BallotReview-3. The review probed whether user code can bound on the Prelude Reader; it cannot yet. It added the shared term.Reader name and FileReader's routed methods, and softened the machine-code claim.

decisions.title: Rounding: every rounding keeps the number's own type and Int{} is the one conversion, every rounding returns a Float, or some roundings return an Int
decisions.situation: Rounding turns a number with a fraction into a whole number. Jet has five roundings: trunc, floor, ceil, round and round_even. Today four of them take a Float and return a whole Float, but math.round returns an Int. None of them accepts a Decimal, a Fraction or an Int, so math.round(7 / 2) does not build, because 7 / 2 is the exact Fraction 7/2. The owner asked what the best behavior would be, and suggested that each rounding keep the type it is given. This vote decides what type each rounding returns. We recommend A, the owner's design: an Int stays an Int, a Float stays a Float, and Int{...} is the one way to get an Int.
decisions.gist: Should every rounding return the same type it was given, with Int{} as the one way to get an Int?
decisions.lesson: Rounding 2.5 to a whole number has two common rules. Ties away from zero gives 3, and ties to even gives 2. Rounding a Float gives a whole Float such as 3.0, which is not yet an Int. This vote picks what type each rounding returns and how a program gets an Int.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A tie is a value exactly halfway between two whole numbers, such as 2.5. Ties to even picks the even neighbor, so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. A Float is a fast binary number with a fraction. A Decimal is an exact base-ten number, and a bare 2.5 in Jet code is a Decimal. A Fraction is an exact ratio; dividing two Ints gives one.

Int{x} converts x to an Int when x is whole, and stops the program otherwise. A trait is a set of methods a type promises to have; generic code accepts any type that has them.
decisions.story: Bo keeps prices as Floats and rounds halves to even, as banks do. Under A, math.round_even(price * 100.0) gives 12.0, and Int{...} around it gives the Int 12. His report averages Int counts: math.round(total / days) works under A because total / days is an exact Fraction, and Int{} around it gives the Int. Under B, C, D and E that line does not build until he writes Float{total} / Float{days}, which is no longer exact.
decisions.inWild:
# Julia: round keeps the argument's type; round(Int, x) converts.
round(2.5)        # 2.0, a Float64
round(7 // 2)     # 4//1, a Rational stays a Rational
round(Int, 2.5)   # 2, the program asked for an Int
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The type each core.math rounding returns, for every number type Jet has, and the one way to turn a rounded value into an Int.

The owner's question (q0tnkm9j). The owner asked for the best intended behavior, and proposed that an Int stays an Int, a Float stays a Float, and Int{} converts. Option A is that design, worked out for every number type. Options B to E are the posted options, renamed: B was A, C was B, D was C and E was D.

Today on dev 0f41dd417c. Core/Math/Math.jet declares trunc, floor, ceil and round_even as fn(n: Float) -> Float, and round as fn(n: Float) -> Int, ties away from zero. Decimal has its own round, floor and ceil methods, ties away (Math.jet:15507). Fraction has none. math.Rounding (Math.jet:14307) already names the five rules: TowardNegative, TowardPositive, TowardZero, TiesToAway and TiesToEven.

A correction to the posted ballot. It said the exact Int{f} conversion is built. It is not on dev: seed b14 refuses Int{<Float>} with E0112 (Constructors.jet:2272). The work is a submission waiting in the inbox (G3Core2-float-int-exact-r2). That submission makes Int{f} convert a whole, finite, in-range Float and stop otherwise with E3010, and makes checked(Int{f}) give None and saturating(Int{f}) clamp. Every option here assumes it lands.

A third gap. Under A, Int{} must also convert a whole Decimal and a whole Fraction. Seed b14 refuses both with E0108 (probe r6_int_from_exact.jet), and no submission covers them yet. A needs that work before Int{math.round(total / days)} builds.

A second correction. The posted program wrote dollars: 0.125. A bare 0.125 is a Decimal, and seed b14 refuses math.round_even of a Decimal with E0112 (probe r4_posted_program.jet). Under A that line works.

What A builds. A Core trait Roundable with one method, rounded(mode: Rounding) -> Self. math.trunc, floor, ceil, round and round_even become fn<T: Roundable>(n: T) -> T, each passing its own fixed mode. Float, F32, Decimal and Fraction implement it. Int and every sized integer implement it by returning the value unchanged.

A user number type joins by writing one impl. Generic functions are built once per type a call reaches (spec.md: a generic function is built only for the instances a call reaches), so no run-time type test remains.

What earlier decisions A amends. Card #6313 c5 says math.round_even(f) -> Int and that round and round_even stop on NaN; under A the stop lives only in Int{}. Today math.round does not stop: it returns 0 for NaN and clamps infinities and huge values to the 64-bit ends (probe r7, Math.jet:13900). The inbox submission makes it stop. D-CONVERT-TRAIT1=A's sample line Int.from(reading, rounding: .NearestEven) becomes Int{math.round_even(reading)}, so one spelling remains. D-FLOAT-INT1=A's roundings keep their names and rules.

Sources. Julia: docs.julialang.org/en/v1/base/math/#Base.round-Tuple{Type,%20Any}. Swift: developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/floatingpoint/rounded(_:). Python: docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#round and the __round__, __floor__, __ceil__ and __trunc__ hooks. Rust: doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html#method.round_ties_even. C23: roundeven.

options.name: Every rounding keeps the number's type; Int{} is the one conversion
options.detail:
math.trunc, floor, ceil, round and round_even each take any number and return the same type. A Float gives a whole Float, an F32 a whole F32, a Decimal a whole Decimal and a Fraction a whole Fraction. An Int, or any sized integer such as U8, comes back unchanged. round ties away from zero and round_even ties to even, as today.

To get an Int, wrap the result: Int{math.round(x)}. Int{} converts a whole value exactly and stops on NaN, an infinity or a value out of range; checked(Int{...}) gives None instead of stopping.

Beginner path: math.round(x) just works on whatever number x is, and printing shows the type (3.0 for a Float). Expert path: x.rounded(mode) when the rule is a value chosen at run time, and impl MyFixed.Roundable to make a user number type round like the built-in ones.
options.technical:
Core/Math/Math.jet: add Roundable: trait { rounded: fn(self, mode: Rounding) -> Self }. Float and F32 implement it with the IEEE operations: NaN and infinities come back unchanged, and -0.5 rounds to -1.0 or -0.0. Decimal implements it with exact digit rounding, adding ties-to-even and trunc beside today's round, floor and ceil. Fraction uses exact integer arithmetic, and Int and every sized integer return the value unchanged.

The five functions become fn<T: Roundable>(n: T) -> T Never!, each passing a constant mode. The build's performance gate must show the same machine code as today's direct Float calls. Decimal's separate round, floor and ceil methods go, since Roundable covers them.

Rewrite the 63 call lines that want an Int as Int{math.round(x)}. Update E0112's fix text, which now suggests math.round(value) to get an Int, the core-library.md rows, LibcCensus.jet and card #6313 c5.

options.name: Every rounding returns a whole Float; convert with Int{}
options.detail: This was the posted A. math.round becomes Float to Float, ties away from zero, like C's round and Rust's f64::round. All five roundings take a Float and return a whole Float, and Int{math.X(f)} is the one Int path. A Decimal, a Fraction or an Int must be turned into a Float first.
options.technical: Core/Math/Math.jet: round becomes fn(n: Float) -> Float Never!, ties away, returning NaN and infinities unchanged. Rewrite the 63 call lines that want an Int to Int{math.round(x)}. Update the core-library.md row, the LibcCensus note for lround and llround, and card #6313 c5.

options.name: Only round_even stays a Float; round keeps returning an Int
options.detail: This was the posted B. round_even stays the C23 roundeven, Float to Float, and Int{math.round_even(f)} gives the Int. math.round keeps returning an Int. Today it returns 0 for NaN and clamps an infinity; with the inbox submission it stops by itself on those and on values out of range. Card #6313 c5's text is corrected to that spelling.
options.technical: No change to Core/Math/Math.jet, Core.rows, the musl case or LibcCensus. Card #6313 c5: replace New math.round_even(f) -> Int with Int{math.round_even(f)}.

options.technical: Core/Math/Math.jet: rename round_even to round_ties_even (35 lines there) and add round_even: fn(n: Float) -> Int Never! returning Int{round_ties_even(n)}. Move the other 7 call lines, both core.math rows in Core.rows, the core-library.md row and LibcCensus.jet.

options.name: Both, under two names: add round_even_int
options.detail: This was the posted D. math.round_even stays Float to Float, and a new math.round_even_int(f) returns an Int and stops on NaN, an infinity or a value out of range. core.math gains one public function.

comparisons.note: round, floor, ceil and trunc return the argument's own type, for floats, rationals and integers. round(Int, x) converts. Source: docs.julialang.org/en/v1/base/math/#Base.round-Tuple{Type,%20Any}

x.rounded(rule) returns Self for every floating-point type, with a rule enum like Jet's Rounding. Int(exactly:) converts and fails on a fraction. Source: developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/floatingpoint/rounded(_:)
comparisons.code:
let r = (2.5).rounded(.toNearestOrEven)  // 2.0
let n = Int(exactly: r)                   // Optional(2)

comparisons.note: round(), math.floor and math.ceil accept int, float, Fraction and Decimal through the __round__, __floor__ and __ceil__ hooks, but return an int, and round ties to even. Source: docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#round

f64::round and f64::round_ties_even return f64; integers have no rounding, and the program converts with as, which saturates silently. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html#method.round_ties_even

recommendation.why: A is the owner's design and the best one. A rounding never changes what kind of number you have, and Int{} is the one place a type changes or a program can stop. It is the only option where rounding an exact Decimal or Fraction stays exact, and where generic code can round any number. Julia ships the same design.
gains: One rule for all five roundings: the result has the argument's type.
Exact numbers stay exact: math.round(7 / 2) is the exact 4, with no trip through a Float.
Generic code can round any number: fn<T: Roundable> works for Float, Decimal, Fraction, Int and user types.
Converting to an Int is always written Int{...}, so a reader sees every place a value can stop the program.

losses.loss: Code that wants an Int writes Int{math.round(x)}: a wrapper around each rounding.
losses.mitigation: A typed binding is already written px: Int{...}, so the wrapper is the type itself. Passing a rounded Float where an Int is wanted is E0112, whose fix inserts Int{...}.

losses.loss: A beginner may expect math.round(2.7) to print 3 and sees 3.0 for a Float.
losses.mitigation: The .0 shows the type, and math.round(2.7) on the bare literal 2.7, a Decimal, prints 3. Float rounding prints a whole Float in Julia, C and Rust too.

losses.loss: Each wrapper passes its rule as a value, so a slow build must not branch on it at run time.
losses.mitigation: The rule is a constant in each wrapper, which the optimizer folds. The build's performance gate must show today's machine code for Float.

losses.loss: Int{} over a whole Decimal or Fraction is not built on any branch, and A depends on it.
losses.mitigation: It is the same exact conversion the inbox submission adds for Float, over exact types, so a whole value converts with no rounding at all.

whyNot.reason: B makes every rounding a Float, so a Decimal, Fraction or Int must be turned into a Float first. That throws away exactness exactly where the program chose an exact type.
C keeps two shapes: round returns an Int and stops by itself, while the other four return a Float. A reader must remember which is which.
D moves the mismatch instead of removing it: round and round_even return an Int, the other three a Float, and the C23 function gets a second name.
E adds a sixth function that does what Int{math.round_even(x)} already does, so there are two ways to write one thing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Programs that want an Int write Int{...} around the rounding, for one rule that holds for every number type, exact or not.

decisions.title: Memory a program still holds and keeps growing: count it as the program's data listed by jet audit retention, make it carry a visible mark, or forbid it
decisions.situation: Safe Jet promises that a program does not leak memory. A leak here means memory nothing can reach any more but that is still taken. Jet frees such memory by rule. A program can still keep data it can reach and let it grow without end, such as a cache told to keep every answer or a global list it appends to forever. The owner said this should be allowed, as the posted A proposed, but shown to the user with an inspect command. We recommend A with that report: jet audit retention lists every place in a program that can keep growing, and nothing else changes.
decisions.gist: Should growing data a program still reaches count as its own data, listed by jet audit retention, or need a mark, or be forbidden?
decisions.lesson: A leak is memory a program lost track of but never gave back. Retention is memory the program still holds on purpose, such as a cache or a log. Jet already frees lost memory by rule. This vote decides whether retention that grows without end is allowed, and how a programmer finds it.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Reachable means some live name, global, task or cache can still get to the memory. A bound is a cap on how many entries a store keeps. #Memo marks a function whose answers are kept and reused. Shared{...} is a value many places can read and change.

An audit command reads a program without running or changing it and prints a list. jet audit copies already lists hidden copies this way, and jet inspect audit copies is the same command.
decisions.story:
Ana writes a log service. It keeps every line in a global list so a status page can show them all. After a week the process uses 2 GB. Under A the program builds as written. Ana runs jet audit retention, and its first row names LOG at main.jet:2 as a store that can grow without a bound, so she caps it.

Under B the global needs a #Grows mark before it builds. Under C the global list does not build at all, and the log must live inside run.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether data a program can still reach, but lets grow without a bound, breaks safe Jet's no-leak promise, and how a programmer sees where it can happen.

The owner's answer (q1ma08a2). The owner said growth should be allowed, as the posted A says, and communicated to the user with an inspect. A now includes that report. Options B and C are unchanged.

The three constructs. #Memo(bound: none), a module Shared{...} global whose type holds a growable collection, and a collection a never-ending task keeps appending to. Each can grow while still reachable, so no freeing rule applies. The audit document the posted ballot cited, Docs/audits/2026-11-12-safe-jet-memory-retention.md, is not in the repository on any branch. Card #6567 c4 still owes that audit, and this ballot states the list itself.

Today. spec.md: a #Memo function keeps 128 results by default, and #Memo(bound: none) makes it unbounded. A seed run of the program below prints kept 100000 lines and exits 0. jet audit copies --json on it returns an empty audit.copies report, and jet audit retention does not exist yet.

The neighbor command. jet audit memory already exists (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/AuditMemory.jet). It reads a bounded ledger of what earlier runs held. Retention is its static partner: the places that can grow, listed before the program runs.

What the report lists, and how exactly. The first two kinds are exact, read from types and marks. A #Memo with bound: none is listed, and one with the default or a number is not. A module Shared global is listed when its type contains a list, map, set or String at any depth. A global of fixed-size data is not.

The third kind is a syntactic check. It lists a push or insert into a collection declared outside a loop, when that loop walks no range or finite collection and has no break or return. A bare loop, a loop on a condition and a loop over a channel qualify; loop i in 0..<100000 does not. A queue that also pops is listed though it stays small, so the row says may grow. Growth reached only through another module's function is not traced.

Why no warning. D-NO-WARNINGS1=A ratified that Jet has errors and no warnings, so the report is a list the programmer asks for. The existing #Policy(copies: .Explicit) pairs with jet audit copies; retention needs no policy, since every listed store is legal.

The leak witness. #6567 c7 adds a runtime check that counts live allocations at exit on O0, O1 and O2. Under every option it drops globals, memo stores and task results first, then counts.

options.name: Reachable data is the program's own, and jet audit retention lists where it can grow
options.detail:
The no-leak promise covers memory nothing can reach. Data a live global, cache or task still reaches is the program's own, as in Rust, Go and Swift. jet audit retention lists every store in the program that can grow without a bound, with its place, kind, name and type.

Beginner path: write the program as today; run jet audit retention when memory grows, and the first rows name the stores to cap. Expert path: jet audit retention --json in CI, failing the build when the stores array is not empty.
options.technical:
spec.md memory safety gains one sentence. The no-leak guarantee covers unreachable allocations; reachable retention, including #Memo(bound: none) and module Shared globals, is program data.

cli.md gains jet audit retention [--json] [<entry.jet>], also jet inspect audit retention, choosing and checking the entry as jet audit copies does. The text form is unbounded stores: N, then one row per store, sorted by path and offset: <path>:<line>:<col>  kind=<memo|global|loop>  name=<name>  type=<type>.

--json emits the audit.retention status envelope with a stores array of {path, line, column, kind, name, type, exact}. A source that does not check reports its diagnostics with exit 1. #6567 c7's witness frees globals, memo stores and task results before it counts.

options.name: Unbounded growth needs a visible mark
options.detail: A module global whose Shared value holds a list, map or set must carry a new #Grows mark. #Memo(bound: none) is already such a mark and stays. Without #Grows the global is a compile error that names the mark. A reviewer can search for #Grows and bound: none.
options.technical: New marker #Grows on module globals. A new registered diagnostic, with a ui snapshot, rejects an unmarked module Shared global that holds a collection. spec.md and syntax-decisions.md gain rows. The witness behaves as in A.

options.name: No unbounded store in safe code
options.detail: #Memo(bound: none) is removed; a cache gives a number. A module Shared{...} global may hold only fixed-size data, so a list that keeps growing must live inside run or a task. Every store that can grow is then owned by a function and freed when it returns.
options.technical: Remove bound: none from #Memo (spec.md, syntax-decisions.md, Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet, sema FunctionHeaders.jet). A new registered diagnostic rejects a module Shared global whose type holds a list, map, set or String, with a ui snapshot.

comparisons.note: A static collection may grow without end; Rust's safety promise is about freed and dangling memory, not growth. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/fn.forget.html (leaking is safe).
A package-level slice grows freely; the garbage collector frees only what nothing reaches. pprof's heap profile shows where held memory was allocated, at run time. Source: pkg.go.dev/runtime/pprof.
ARC frees unreachable objects; a global array that keeps growing is the program's data. Xcode's memory graph shows what holds it, at run time.

recommendation.why: A keeps the promise exact: Jet frees by rule every byte the program can no longer reach. The new report shows every store that can grow without a bound before the program ever runs, which Rust, Go and Swift do not offer.
gains: The promise has one exact meaning: nothing unreachable stays allocated.
jet audit retention lists every unbounded store before the program runs.
No new mark or error; the report follows jet audit copies and sits beside jet audit memory.
CI can fail on any listed store with the --json form.

losses.loss: A program can still grow a global list until the system runs out of memory.
losses.mitigation: No language can stop growth of data the program still reads. The report names the place, so the fix is one line.

losses.loss: The loop rows are a syntactic check: a queue that also pops is listed, and growth through another module is missed.
losses.mitigation: Memo and global rows are exact, and loop rows say may grow. The exit witness still catches real leaks.

losses.loss: Nobody sees the list unless they run the command.
losses.mitigation: Jet has no warnings by decision. The --json form lets a project fail CI on any listed store.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second mark beside bound: none for the same meaning, and a global still grows once marked. The report shows the same places without a new rule.
C removes bound: none, which programs use for exact caches, and forces shared logs and tables into run, where they grow just the same.

recommendation.tradeoff: Growth of held data stays the program's choice, and one command shows every place it can happen.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: BallotReview-3. The review traced the jet audit dispatch and narrowed the loop rule, which would have listed the sample's range loop. It added jet audit memory and card #6567 c4.

decisions.title: Background tasks still alive when run returns: cancel them with a short grace, keep today's rule, forbid them, or end the process at once
decisions.situation: A background task is work a program starts with detach() and does not wait for. When run returns, such a task can still be alive. Today a waiting task, such as a ticker that sleeps between ticks, stops the program with error E3013 and exit status 70. A task stuck in a loop that never waits keeps the process alive forever. Past 4,096 tasks, waiting ones are not even cleaned up. This matters for servers, tickers and anyone who wants a clean, prompt exit. You are asked what happens to background tasks when run returns. We recommend cancelling every one, giving them one second to clean up, and then exiting with run's own status.
decisions.gist: When run returns, what should happen to background tasks: cancel with a grace, today's rule, forbid them, or exit at once?
decisions.lesson: A background task is work started with detach() that nobody waits for. When the main function run ends, some of that work may still be going. Jet must stop it cleanly, treat it as an error, forbid it, or simply end the process. This vote picks one rule.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside the rest of the program. detach() lets a task go on without anyone waiting for it. Cancel asks a task to stop, and a task notices only at its next wait, such as a sleep, a channel read or a network read. Cleanup is the code that runs as a value goes away, such as closing or flushing a file.
decisions.story: Kai starts a ticker task that wakes every second to refresh a cache, and detaches it. When run finishes, the program prints run returns. Today it then stops with E3013 and exit status 70. Under A the ticker is cancelled at its sleep, cleans up and the program exits 0 at once. Under B Kai must keep the handle, cancel it and join it. Under C, detach() is gone, so he must do the same. Under D the process ends the moment run returns, and the ticker's cleanup never runs.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What the runtime does with detached tasks that are still alive when run returns.

Today, parked tasks. After run returns, main_exit_cleanup in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet looks for tasks parked on a wait. If it finds any, it reports E3013 (Parked tasks remain at process exit). It cancels the tasks it can reach so they unwind, and the process exits 70. Tasks past the registry cap (OBSERVE_TASK_CAP, 4,096) are neither reported nor unwound. A seed run of the ticker program prints run returns, then E3013 with the ticker blocked on its sleep, and exits 70.

Today, running tasks. If no task is parked, jet_scheduler_drain_after_exit waits until no task is queued or running. A seed run of a program whose detached task runs `loop { n += 1 }` never exits; it was killed after 10 seconds.

Cancellation reaches only waits. In spec.md, cancellation is preemptive at wait points: channel send and receive, time.sleep, join, select and I/O. There is no check on loop back-edges. A seed run that cancels and then joins a task looping on `n += 1` also never returns. tasks.yield_now() is a wait point, so a loop that calls it can be cancelled.

The rest of the spec. A cancelled task unwinds and runs Drop-backed cleanup. #Shield defers cancellation until its block exits. Dropping a handle without joining or detaching is L1101, so every detach is an explicit choice.

Why it matters for memory. #6567's leak witness counts live allocations at exit. A task that is not unwound keeps its frame and captures, so the witness must either see every task unwound or leave task frames out.

options.name: Cancel every background task, wait up to one second, then exit
options.detail: When run returns, the runtime cancels every task still alive. A waiting task stops at its wait at once, runs its cleanup, closes its files and frees its memory, with no cap on how many. The exit waits until every cancelled task has unwound, or for one second, whichever comes first. A task still running after that second is in a loop that never waits. It is abandoned, the process exits, and the system takes its memory back. The exit status is run's.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet: after run returns, cancel every live task through the task registry, with no OBSERVE_TASK_CAP limit. Drain until no task is queued, ready or running, or until 1 s of monotonic time has passed, then exit. Retire E3013's exit report: its registry row, explainer page and runtime_e3013 ui snapshot, which becomes a case that exits 0. The leak witness counts after the drain and names each abandoned task instead of counting its frame. spec.md gains the rule.

options.name: Keep today's rule and close its gap
options.detail: A waiting background task still stops the program with E3013 and exit status 70, after it is cancelled and cleaned up. A task in a loop that never waits still keeps the process alive forever. The 4,096-task cap goes, so every waiting task is reported and cleaned up. A program with a ticker keeps its handle, cancels it and joins it before run returns.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet and Observe.jet: lift OBSERVE_TASK_CAP from the exit report and unwind. No other change; E3013 stays.

options.name: No task may outlive run
options.detail: detach() is removed. Every task handle is joined, so every task ends before the function that started it returns. A ticker is kept, cancelled and joined. A server that serves each connection in its own task joins those tasks through a group. A joined task in a loop that never waits still never ends.
options.technical: Remove Task.detach from Core and the sema rule that lets it discharge L1101. Retire the detach forms of E1103 and E1106, and migrate every detach() caller (Core/Http/Server.jet and others) to task groups. spec.md D-DETACH1 is superseded.

options.name: End the process the moment run returns
options.detail: This is the model of Go and of Rust's standard threads. When run returns, the process exits at once with run's status. Background tasks stop where they are, without cancelling and without cleanup, and the system takes their memory back. Nothing can hang the exit, and nothing waits.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet: after run returns and the main task's own cleanup, flush stdout and exit without draining the scheduler. Retire E3013's exit report and the exit unwind. The leak witness leaves every live task's frame and captures out of its count. spec.md gains the rule.

comparisons.note: When main returns, the process ends; goroutines stop at once and their deferred calls do not run.
When main returns, the process exits; spawned threads stop without running their destructors.
Runtime shutdown drops spawned tasks at their await points and runs their destructors; a task that never awaits blocks a blocking shutdown, so shutdown_timeout bounds it.
asyncio.run cancels the tasks still pending when main returns and waits for them to unwind.

recommendation.why: A gives every program a clean exit with run's status. Every task that waits, which is almost every background task, cleans up and frees its memory at once. A loop that never waits can delay the exit by at most one second, so nothing hangs. It is Tokio's shutdown_timeout as the default.
gains: A ticker or server task no longer turns a normal exit into status 70.
Every waiting task's cleanup runs at exit, with no 4,096 cap.
No exit hangs: a loop that never waits costs at most one second.
No new syntax; detach() keeps its meaning of not waiting.

losses.loss: Background work still in progress at exit is cut short.
losses.mitigation: Join the task when its work must finish, or put that work in #Shield, which finishes before the cancel lands.

losses.loss: A loop that never waits is abandoned after one second without its cleanup.
losses.mitigation: Its memory goes back to the system and the leak witness names the task. Calling tasks.yield_now() in the loop makes it cancellable.

losses.loss: E3013 no longer reports a background task stuck on a wait at exit.
losses.mitigation: A task whose end matters is joined, and L1101 already forces that choice.

whyNot.reason: B keeps stopping normal programs with ticker or server tasks with status 70, and a loop that never waits still hangs the exit.
C removes detach(), which servers and tickers use, and a joined loop that never waits still hangs.
D is fastest, but it skips every background task's cleanup, so files go unflushed and connections unclosed, and the leak witness cannot see task memory.

recommendation.tradeoff: Up to one second of exit for a loop that never waits, in exchange for cleanup in every task that waits.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. The first draft hid that a task looping without a wait never reaches a cancel point, and it omitted the Go and Rust std exit. The revision checks that hang on the seed, adds a 1 s grace to A, and adds D.

surface.gist: When run returns, should background tasks be cancelled with a grace, stop the program, be forbidden, or just die?
surface.lesson: A background task is work started with detach() that nobody waits for. When run ends, some may still be going. Today a waiting one stops the program with status 70, and a loop that never waits hangs it. This vote picks the rule.

current.note: Today a sleeping detached ticker stops the program with E3013, status 70.

options.name: Today's rule, no cap

gains: Every waiting task is reported.
losses: Tickers and servers exit 70.

options.name: No detach
options.gist: Every task is joined before its starter returns.
gains: No task outlives run.
losses: detach() and its callers migrate.

options.name: Exit at once
options.gist: The process ends when run returns; tasks just die.
gains: Fastest exit.

recommendation.why: Every waiting task cleans up at once. A loop that never waits costs at most one second, so the exit is clean and never hangs.
gains: No status 70 from tickers.
No exit hangs.
