losses.mitigation: Join it, or wrap it in #Shield so it finishes first.

whyNot.reason: Normal programs keep exiting 70.
Removes detach(); loops still hang.
Skips all task cleanup.

recommendation.tradeoff: At most one second of exit, for cleanup in every waiting task.

decisions.title: Sending on a closed channel: return a SendError that hands the value back and passes up like any failure, return the Closed error, stop the program, or keep dropping it
decisions.situation: A channel carries values from a sender to a receiver. Today sender.send(v) returns nothing. When the receiver has closed or gone away, Jet throws v away and carries on, so the program never learns the value was lost. Card #3239 c61 says a send on a closed channel must be an error. The owner asked for the best design with no regard for existing code. This vote decides what a send on a closed channel does. We recommend A: send fails with a SendError that hands the value back, and a send nobody handles passes the failure up like any other.
decisions.gist: When the receiver is gone, should send fail and hand the unsent value back, fail without it, stop the program, or drop it?
decisions.lesson: A channel has two ends. The sender puts values in and the receiver takes them out. If the receiver leaves first, the sender has nowhere to put the value. Today Jet throws the value away and says nothing. This vote picks what happens instead.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A closed channel is one whose receiver called close() or was dropped. A failure passes up when a function stops and hands its error to its caller. In Jet a call that can fail passes its failure up by itself, with no extra mark. A function that names no error type still fails with the general error Err, so run and task blocks can pass failures up.

A conversion, written impl X -> Err, tells Jet how to turn error X into Err when it passes up. Without one, a call that can fail is refused (E2402) until the caller handles it with ??.
decisions.story: Ana runs a worker task that sends results to a logger task. The logger stops early. Today every result vanishes. Under A her worker's bare send line fails, the worker ends, and its join reports why. Where she cares, she writes ?? and gets the unsent result back in err.value. Under B she gets the failure but not the result. Under C the whole program stops. Under D nothing changes.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What Sender.send returns, what it does when the channel's receiver is closed or dropped, and what a send that nobody handles does.

The owner's question (q4k1qwo1). The owner asked for the best theoretical greenfield design. Option A is that answer. It is the posted B, with the cost the posted ballot charged it removed: a bare send now passes its failure up instead of being refused. Options B, C and D are the posted A, C and D.

Today's send. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Concurrency.jet types sender.send(v) as Unit. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Channel.jet jet_rt_native_sender_send leaves its loop when the channel is closed or has no receiver, then drops the value with coll_slot_drop. receive() -> T !Closed reports the other direction.

Why the posted ballot charged A and B 282 edited lines. A bare call that can fail, inside a function whose error type can't take that failure, is refused with E2402. Compiler/Prelude/Errors.jet declares impl X -> Err for Core errors such as IOError, but none for Closed. So a bare send in run or a task block was refused.

How A removes that cost. Core declares impl SendError -> Err and impl Closed -> Err beside the other Core errors. Probe s4_declared_conversion.jet shows the effect with a stand-in error: a bare failing call is accepted in a plain function, in a task block and in run. The failure passes up, join reports it, and run ends with a located message.

What remains. A send inside a function that promises Never!, or names another error type with no conversion, still needs ?? or a conversion. Each such line is listed by E2402 with a fix. Seed b14 does not yet apply a conversion declared on a generic error to its instances in run (probe s1); the build must, since SendError<T> is generic.

What is never silent under A. A value the channel accepted stays receivable after the receiver closes: probe s3 prints got 1 and got 2 after close. A value the channel refuses comes back in err.value. Only values still queued when the last receiver is dropped are freed with it, as in Rust, Go and Kotlin. Freeing runs each value's drop, so what a value holds is released.

Try_send. D-CONC-BACKGROUND1=A (card #3239 c38) ratified an ownership-returning Sender.try_send. Under A both sending calls hand the value back, so the two agree.

Sources. Rust std::sync::mpsc::SendError: doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/mpsc/struct.SendError.html. tokio: docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/mpsc/error/struct.SendError.html. crossbeam: docs.rs/crossbeam-channel/latest/crossbeam_channel/struct.SendError.html. Go: go.dev/ref/spec#Send_statements. Kotlin: kotlinlang.org/api/kotlinx.coroutines/kotlinx-coroutines-core/kotlinx.coroutines.channels/-channel/ (Undelivered elements). Trio: trio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference-core.html#trio.BrokenResourceError.

options.name: send fails with SendError<T>, which hands the value back and passes up like any failure
options.detail:
sender.send(v) returns nothing on success and fails with SendError<T> when no receiver remains. err.value is the value that was not sent, moved back to the caller.

Beginner path: write sender.send(v) bare. In run, a task block or any function that names no error type, a failed send passes up like any other failure, with a message naming the send. Nothing is lost silently.

Expert path: write sender.send(v) ?? handler to keep err.value, retry on another channel, or reply to whoever asked. Inside a function that fails with Closed, a bare send passes up as Closed.
options.technical:
Core declares #Error SendError: struct<T> { value: T }, impl SendError -> Err, impl SendError -> Closed and impl Closed -> Err. Concurrency.jet types send as Unit !SendError<T>. Channel.jet's send returns the slot to the caller instead of calling coll_slot_drop, as the ratified try_send must.

Error conversion lookup must apply impl SendError -> Err to every SendError<T>; seed b14 refuses that in run (probe s1). Lines inside Never! functions, or functions with another named error, gain ?? or a conversion, each listed by E2402 with a fix. spec.md Channels states the closed-send rule, and card #3239 c61 names SendError<T>.

options.name: send fails with Closed, the error receive uses
options.detail: This was the posted A. sender.send(v) fails with Closed when no receiver remains, and the value is dropped. The same impl Closed -> Err as in A lets a bare send pass up. A program that needs the value must keep its own copy before sending.
options.technical: Concurrency.jet types send as Unit !Closed. Channel.jet returns the Closed failure after coll_slot_drop. Core declares impl Closed -> Err. try_send, ratified to hand its value back, then disagrees with send.

options.name: send stops the program
options.detail: This was the posted C. send returns nothing. A send on a closed channel stops the whole program with a located message, as Go panics. No caller can recover, so a server whose one logger task ended stops entirely.
options.technical: Channel.jet raises a registered stop where it now drops the value. Concurrency.jet keeps Unit. spec.md Channels states the stop.

options.name: Keep dropping, and write it down
options.detail: This was the posted D. send keeps returning nothing and a send on a closed channel drops the value. The spec states it. Card #3239 c61, which forbids a silent rail, is rewritten.
options.technical: No code change. spec.md Channels documents the drop; card #3239 c61 is amended.

comparisons.note: std::sync::mpsc, crossbeam-channel, tokio and flume all return Err(SendError(value)) once the receiver is gone, handing the value back. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/mpsc/struct.SendError.html
Sending on a closed channel panics, and a receiver that just stops reading makes the sender block forever. Source: go.dev/ref/spec#Send_statements
comparisons.code: ch <- 7 // panics if ch is closed

comparisons.note: send throws ClosedSendChannelException and the element is lost; an onUndeliveredElement callback was added so programs can release resources an undelivered element holds. Source: kotlinlang.org/api/kotlinx.coroutines/kotlinx-coroutines-core/kotlinx.coroutines.channels/-channel/
send on a memory channel whose receivers are closed raises BrokenResourceError; the value is not returned. Source: trio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference-core.html#trio.BrokenResourceError

recommendation.why: A is the only option where a send can neither lose a value silently nor take the value away from a caller who wants it. With Core's conversions, the common bare send costs nothing to write: it passes up like any failure. Rust's four main channel libraries chose the same hand-back, and Kotlin added a callback because losing the value hurt.
gains: No value is ever dropped without a failure the program can see.
The unsent value comes back, so a program can retry, reroute or reply.
A bare send still works in run, task blocks and plain functions: the failure passes up.
send and the ratified try_send agree: both hand the value back.

losses.loss: A send inside a function that promises Never!, or names another error with no conversion, needs ?? or a conversion.
losses.mitigation: E2402 lists each line with its fix. That is the rule for every call that can fail, so nothing new is learned.

losses.loss: Values still queued when the last receiver is dropped are freed with it.
losses.mitigation: Freeing runs each value's drop, so a file or reply it holds is closed, not leaked; Kotlin needed onUndeliveredElement because its values have no drop. A receiver that must account for every value drains with loop v in receiver after close, which probe s3 shows still yields queued values.

losses.loss: The error type carries the value type, SendError<Int>, so a function naming it writes the type.
losses.mitigation: Most code never names it: a bare send converts to Err or Closed, and ?? handlers read err.value without naming the type.

whyNot.reason: B reports the failure but destroys the value, so a program that must reroute or release it has to copy every value before sending. It also disagrees with the ratified try_send.
C stops the whole program when one receiver ends, and gives a caller no way to recover.
D keeps the silent loss that card #3239 c61 exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Sends inside Never! functions write ?? or a conversion, for sends that never lose a value silently and always give it back on request.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: BallotReview-3. The review reran the probes and checked card #3239 c61 and c38 and the spec's conversion rules. It added that freed queued values run their drop.

decisions.title: Branching on an enum: single tests stay free; else over several cases is an error with an instant fix
decisions.situation: An enum is a type with a fixed list of cases, such as a shape that is a circle, a square, a line or a dot. Code that tests a few cases and ends in else quietly takes any case added later, and the program gives a wrong answer with no error. A package must also be able to add a case without breaking its users. This vote picks how Jet catches later cases while keeping the most common code free. We recommend an error with an instant fix, and #Open for package enums that grow.
decisions.gist: When code tests one enum value against several cases, how do we catch a case added later, with the least writing?
decisions.lesson: An enum has a fixed list of cases. The bug to prevent: code that tests a few cases and ends in else quietly takes any case added later. One test of one case stays free. The options differ in how much the writer must type to keep later cases from slipping into else.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here, shown on the one program this ballot uses throughout.

```jet
Shape: enum {                  // an enum: a type with a fixed list of cases
    Circle(radius: Int)        // a case that carries a value, its radius
    Square(side: Int)          // a case that carries its side length
    Line                       // a case that carries nothing
    Dot
}
```

A case test asks whether a value is one case. shape == .Circle(r) is true for a circle, and r is then its radius.

A chain is if ... else if ... else, with one case test per branch. Its final else takes every case not tested above, including cases added later.

A table names the value once and gives one arm per case, as in if shape == { .Circle(r) -> 3 * r * r ... }. The arrow -> gives the arm's result, and | joins cases in one arm. A table over an enum must name every case, so an else arm there is refused.

The rest means the cases that code does not handle one by one, such as Line and Dot in area.
decisions.story: Ana writes area(shape) as a table: a circle, a square, then else for the rest. The editor marks the else and offers the fix, and one keystroke turns it into .Line | .Dot. Months later Ben adds Triangle, and the build stops at Ana's code until he decides what a triangle's area is. A key handler that should treat every other key, now or later, the same writes .. and is never stopped.
decisions.inWild:
OCaml: warning 4, off by default, flags a fragile match, one whose wildcard would silently take constructors added later. A polymorphic variant type can be named, type flat = [ `Line | `Dot ], and the pattern #flat matches any of its members.

Swift: a switch over an enum must be exhaustive. For an enum that may grow, @unknown default runs for unknown cases, and the compiler warns when a known case is not named.

Rust: a match must be exhaustive, and the wildcard _ takes the rest silently. The opt-in Clippy lint wildcard_enum_match_arm flags that wildcard.

Kotlin and Java: a when or switch over an enum or sealed type must be exhaustive, and else or default may take the rest.

These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
What Jet does today. Every example here ran with the gate-p66 jet on dev 03d5f7b309. The v4 probes hold the exact programs this ballot shows, with their outputs.

The table form of area checks clean and runs (t1). Add Triangle to Shape, and it stops with E0307: This `if` doesn't cover every case — missing: Triangle. The fix line says: Add an arm for: Triangle (t2).

The chain form of area, ending in else, gets two warnings, L0302 and L0507, and runs (t3). With Triangle added, it still runs and returns 0 for a triangle (t4).

Area can also be written as separate ifs, one after another, that each return:

```jet
area: fn(shape: Shape) -> Int {
    if shape == .Circle(r) -> return 3 * r * r   // one test; return leaves area
    if shape == .Square(s) -> return s * s
    0                                            // the rest: every other case gives 0
}
```

That form gets no finding at all. With Triangle added, it checks clean and returns 0 for a triangle (t5, and v3 probe r1). The same holds when the ifs assign to a result instead of returning (v3 probe r4).

Two more escapes. A second test hidden in an else block, else { if shape == .Square(s) ... }, gets no L0302. A table with a plain true-or-false arm, such as verbose == true, may keep an else over an enum, and that else takes Dot silently. A guarded arm, .Circle(r) && r > 10, does not count as covering Circle, and that part is already right: E0307 names Circle.

The rule every option shares. It applies when code tests one value, a name or a field path, against two or more cases. The tests may sit in one chain, one table, or separate ifs in a row in one block. Those ifs have nothing between them and no body that changes the value. Such code must name every case, and else cannot stand for the rest.

An else whose whole body is another if on the same value counts as part of the chain. When separate ifs each leave (return, next, break or panic), the rest is the code after them. When they fall through, the rest is doing nothing. Either way, a case added later stops the build. A true-or-false arm may sit among the tests, but it covers no case.

What stays free. One test is free whatever its pattern, with or without an else, so if shape == .Line | .Dot { … } else { … } is free. So are tests with other code between them, and ifs whose body changes the value (a state machine stepping state). So is a test through a helper such as shape.is_round(). The rule covers every closed set: an enum, an optional, a result and a union.

L0302 retires under every option, since Jet has no warnings.

How big the change is. A rough scan of dev finds 35 chains with two or more tests of one value. A rerun on 03d5f7b309 finds 11 of them ending in else, where the first count said 13. It also finds 5 if { } tables that test one value twice or more, all ending in else, so 16 sites have an else to replace.

Separate ifs are the commonest form. Scans of one-line ifs alone find 130 groups whose bodies leave and 33 that fall through, over two or more cases. The scans are v3/exitscan.awk and v3/sepscan.awk. They skip block bodies, so these counts are lower bounds. The scans read text, not types, so the chain and table counts are upper bounds.

Some rests are long under every option. Two chains ending in else test the compiler's Type, which has 24 cases, so each else stands for 22. Expr has 51 cases. And ir_builtin in BuildRoutes.jet tests 13 of TBuiltinOp's 214 cases before handing the rest to ir_builtin_on.

Which syntax is new. Options B and C add no syntax: every line of their programs runs today (t1, t6 and t7). They add only the new error E0644. Option A adds the case set line, Flat: .Line | .Dot, and the pattern .Flat. Today that line is a parse error (t8).

Why A's case set is written with dots. Name: .A | .B reuses the colon that declares a name and the dotted or-pattern a table arm already writes. So | keeps its meaning, one case or another.

The undotted Name: A | B already means a union type wherever a Name: line sits today. In a struct body it is a field of type Line | Dot, and at file scope it is a union alias (v3 probes r2 and r2a). No option adds a glyph, and the range .. and the spread ... are not used.

options.name: An error with an instant fix
options.detail:
Most common first. One test of one case stays free: if order == .Paid { … }. A table naming every case stays free. Two or more tests ending in else over one of your own enums is an error, and one quick fix replaces the else with the cases it stands for. A rest meant to take every other case, now or later, is written .., as .Case{field, ..} already means every other field.

Packages can add cases. An enum a package marks #Open may gain cases in a minor version; users' tables over it need a .. arm, and single tests stay free. When an update adds a case, jet update lists every .. arm that now takes it, so nothing changes silently. An unmarked package enum is closed: adding a case is a major version, and jet publish says so.

Evidence: Docs/Research/2026-11-16-enum-branching-in-real-code.md. In Rust, 20% of public enums opt into non_exhaustive, and 80% stay closed.
options.technical:
E0641 already refuses else over an enum in a table. A extends it to a chain of ifs over one value. Sema recognises that chain by the same subject test it uses for tables (I8).

.. is a table arm for every remaining case, including later ones, as in .Case{field, ..}; _ keeps its one meaning, ignore a slot. #Open is a Core marker declared like any other (#6849). A table over another package's #Open enum without .. is an error whose fix adds the arm. Non-enum subjects keep else.

options.name: A tidy error before build
options.detail:
One test of one case stays free. Two or more tests of one enum value may be a chain of ifs or a table, as today. Their rest may be typed as else. jet run, jet dev and jet test accept it, so trying code costs nothing.

jet check and jet build report such an else as a tidy error (D-NO-WARNINGS1), naming the cases it stands for. jet fix replaces it with them, such as .Line | .Dot. From then on a case added to the enum stops the build at every place that does not name it. A rest meant to take every other case, now or later, is written .. and is never stopped; a key handler is the usual example.
options.technical:
Today E0641 already refuses an else over an enum in a table, everywhere, and its fix writes the cases. A moves E0641 to the tidy tier, so run, dev and test accept the else, and applies it to a chain of ifs over one value too. Sema recognises the chain by the same subject test it uses for tables, so both forms get one rule (I8).

.. is a new table arm meaning every remaining case, including later ones, as .Case{field, ..} means every other field; no Jet code uses .. as an arm today. Non-enum subjects (Int, String) keep else unchanged, since their cases cannot be listed.

decisions.title: Mapped files: keep borrowed bytes stable by cloning the file, else holding it, else copying it; copy always; copy on every read; or let the bytes change
decisions.situation: A mapped file is a file the program reads as if it were already in memory. files.map(path) gives Jet code a borrowed view of the bytes with no copy. Today another program can change those bytes while the view is borrowed, and a probe saw a borrowed byte change from 3 to 9. If the other program shrinks the file, the next read kills the process with SIGBUS. Safe Jet promises a borrowed value does not change under you. The owner asked whether A's downsides can be engineered away. Most can: A now asks the file system for a free private clone of the file first, and only holds or copies the file where no clone is possible. We recommend A.
decisions.gist: When another program writes a file Jet has mapped, should borrowed bytes stay put through a clone, hold or copy, be copied first, be copied per read, or change?
decisions.lesson: Mapping a file lets a program read a huge file without loading it first: the operating system brings in each page when the program touches it. The bytes still belong to the file, so another program can change them while Jet is reading. Jet's rule is that a borrowed view never changes under you. This vote picks how mapped files keep that rule.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A view is a borrowed window into bytes someone else owns; it is not a copy. A clone, or reflink, is a new file that shares the original's disk blocks. It costs no time and no space until one side writes; the writer then gets fresh blocks and the clone keeps the old ones.

A lease is a Linux promise to the program that holds it: before another process may write or shrink the file, the kernel tells the holder and makes the writer wait. Copying means reading the bytes into new storage, which costs time and space equal to the file's size.
decisions.story:
Mia's log tool maps a 2 GiB log and scans it for errors. One night a rotation script truncates the log mid-scan. Today her tool dies with SIGBUS. Under A, on her btrfs laptop or her Mac, Jet mapped a clone, so the script never waits and the scan finishes. On an ext4 server the script waits about 0.7 s while Jet copies the 2 GiB.

Under B every map first copies 2 GiB. Under C each read copies and two reads can disagree. Under D her scan sees whatever the file says at each moment.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What a safe borrowed view from files.map sees when another process writes or truncates the file, and where zero-copy mapping lives.

The owner's question (q3huikf3). The posted A held the file with a lease and copied where it could not. Its five costs were real: writers stalled, a 45 s deadline could stop the program, many hosts copied, a signal was reserved, and Windows refused writers. This version removes most of them by trying a clone first. The costs that remain are named in the recommendation with their price and their best mitigation.

Today's map. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/CompilerMapped.jet jet_std_files_map opens the file read-only, takes a shared flock (advisory, so non-Jet writers ignore it), and calls mmap with PROT_READ and MAP_PRIVATE. A private mapping is not a snapshot on Linux: pages not yet copied show the file's current bytes.

What the card says. #6706 c1: a safe borrowed view must not observe a byte change made by another process after the borrow, or the safe API no longer hands out such a view. c2: a truncation during safe access gives a typed error or a registered fault, never a raw SIGBUS.

The clone probe. clone_probe.py clones a file into an unnamed temp file on the same file system, maps the clone, then overwrites and truncates the original. On btrfs, a 64 MiB clone took 0.06 ms and a 1 GiB clone 0.10 ms. The mapping still read the old byte at the old length. On ext4 and tmpfs the clone call failed with ENOTSUP, which is the signal to fall back.

Where a clone works. Linux btrfs, xfs (reflink is the default since xfsprogs 5.1), bcachefs, and OpenZFS 2.2 with block cloning on. macOS APFS through fclonefileat. Windows ReFS, including Dev Drive, through FSCTL_DUPLICATE_EXTENTS_TO_FILE. FreeBSD ZFS through copy_file_range. NFS 4.2 and SMB servers that support a server-side clone. Ext4, tmpfs, f2fs and NTFS cannot clone. [INFERENCE] Clone time grows with the number of extents, so a heavily fragmented file clones slower than the probe's fresh file.

Disk space. A clone shares blocks only until the original changes. If another program rewrites or truncates the file while it is mapped, the clone keeps the old blocks, so the space is not freed until the map is dropped. A fallback copy needs free space equal to the file. When the temp file cannot be written, files.map fails with its IOError, as it does today when the file cannot be opened.

The other probes. lease_probe.py shows the lease path: a writer waited 18-32 ms while a 64 MiB map was copied, and lease_probe.py stall shows the kernel's 45.2 s deadline. copy_cost.py shows a 1 GiB map opens in 0.05 ms at 32 MiB RSS, while a copy took 0.36 s and 1056 MiB RSS.

Sources. Linux ioctl_ficlone(2): man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/ioctl_ficlone.2.html. fcntl(2) Leases: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fcntl.2.html. macOS clonefile(2). Windows: learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/winioctl/ni-winioctl-fsctl_duplicate_extents_to_file. memmap2: docs.rs/memmap2/latest/memmap2/struct.Mmap.html. Java MappedByteBuffer and Go syscall.Mmap, as in the comparisons.

options.name: Stable map: map a clone where the file system can, hold the file where it can't, copy as the last resort
options.detail:
files.map keeps zero-copy views and makes them stable. First Jet asks the file system for a private clone and maps that, so another program's writes never reach the view and never wait. Where no clone is possible, Jet holds the file with a lease on Linux or deny-write sharing on Windows, and copies only when a writer arrives. Otherwise it copies into an unnamed temp file, so even files larger than memory map.

Beginner path: write files.map(path); nothing else changes. Expert path: mapped.kind() reports Clone, Held or Copy, and an #Unsafe raw map remains for shared live bytes.
options.technical:
Map time, in order. A file system that cannot be written at all, such as squashfs or erofs, maps the file directly. A read-only mount alone does not count, since a bind mount or a network server can still write the file. Next, clone into an O_TMPFILE in the file's own directory or another writable directory on the same mount. Linux uses FICLONE, macOS fclonefileat with an unlink, Windows ReFS FSCTL_DUPLICATE_EXTENTS_TO_FILE and FreeBSD copy_file_range. Any refusal falls through.

On local Linux ext4, tmpfs and f2fs, take the posted lease: F_SETSIG SIGRTMAX, F_SETLEASE F_RDLCK. At a break, copy into an unnamed temp file on the same mount and map it over the same address with MAP_FIXED. NTFS opens without FILE_SHARE_WRITE.

A lease is taken only for a file that copies well inside lease-break-time, about 4 GiB at 100 MB/s and the 45 s default. Larger files, refused leases and other hosts copy at map time into an unnamed temp file. Truncation can no longer fault a safe view, which meets c2.

options.name: The safe map is a copy; zero-copy mapping moves behind #Unsafe
options.detail: files.map(path) reads the whole file into the program's memory, as files.read_bytes does, and keeps the MappedFile API (window, lines, len). Views are stable because they borrow the copy. Zero-copy mapping becomes an expert call inside #Unsafe that hands out raw reads, never a safe view.
options.technical: jet_std_files_map reads the file into an owned buffer instead of calling mmap; the drop frees the buffer. Add an #Unsafe raw map in core.files whose reads go through checked raw access and whose truncation fault is c2's registered stop. Web gets the same copy.

options.name: VolatileBytes: no borrowed views; every read copies
options.detail: files.map returns a map that never lends a view. mapped.read(start, count) copies the bytes it asks for at that moment, and lines() yields copied lines. Searching and counting run inside the runtime over the live pages. Two reads can disagree if another program wrote in between. A read past a shrunk end stops with a registered message.
options.technical: MappedFile loses window, window_len and the View<U8> lines iterator; it gains read(start, count) -> [U8] !IOError, a copying lines() and runtime scan kernels (find, count, checksum). c2's registered SIGBUS stop is required.

options.name: Keep views and let them change: a mapped view is shared with other programs
options.detail: files.map keeps today's zero-copy views. The spec states that another program may change a mapped file's bytes at any time, so a mapped view can read different values at different moments. The compiler never assumes a mapped byte stays the same between reads. A read after a shrink stops with a registered message.
options.technical: No API change. Sema marks map views as externally mutable, so no optimization reuses a loaded mapped byte. c2's registered SIGBUS stop is required. Card #6706 c1 is rewritten to accept change.

comparisons.note: memmap2 marks every file-backed map constructor unsafe, because the map is undefined behavior if the file is modified in or out of process; the caller must prevent that.
comparisons.code: let map = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? }; // UB if the file changes

comparisons.note: syscall.Mmap returns a plain byte slice that shows other processes' writes. A read after truncation crashes the program unless debug.SetPanicOnFault turns the fault into a panic.
comparisons.code:
m, _ := syscall.Mmap(fd, 0, size, syscall.PROT_READ, syscall.MAP_SHARED)
first := m[0] // may change later

comparisons.note: MappedByteBuffer documents that its content can change at any time when the file changes, and that touching a truncated region throws an unspecified exception, possibly later.
comparisons.code:
MappedByteBuffer buf = ch.map(MapMode.READ_ONLY, 0, ch.size());
byte first = buf.get(0); // may change

comparisons.note: cp --reflink=auto clones where the file system can and copies otherwise. A uses the same clone-else-copy rule, at map time. Source: www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/cp-invocation.html
comparisons.code: cp --reflink=auto big.log snapshot.log   # instant on btrfs, xfs

recommendation.why: A keeps both the promise and the speed. On file systems that clone, the map is zero copy, never makes a writer wait and has no deadline or reserved signal. Elsewhere it holds the file or copies with the same meaning. The remaining costs apply only on file systems that cannot clone.
gains: A borrowed mapped byte never changes, on every host.
On btrfs, xfs, APFS and ReFS, a 1 GiB map is a 0.10 ms clone and no writer ever waits.
A shrink by another program can no longer fault a safe view.
Copies go to an unnamed temp file, so files larger than memory still map.

losses.loss: On ext4, tmpfs and f2fs, the first writer waits while Jet copies: 18-32 ms for 64 MiB, and non-blocking opens fail once.
losses.mitigation: It happens once per map. A program that must never stall a writer reads with files.read_bytes.

losses.loss: On those file systems the runtime reserves signal 64, and storage slower than 100 MB/s can still miss the 45 s deadline.
losses.mitigation: Big files copy at map time instead; a miss is a located stop while the writer still waits.

losses.loss: Hosts without clone or hold copy at map time, and NTFS refuses other programs' writes while the map lives.
losses.mitigation: The meaning is the same everywhere. A file already open for writing on NTFS is copied instead.

losses.loss: A clone or copy holds disk space: a rewritten or truncated original frees nothing until the map is dropped, and a copy needs space equal to the file.
losses.mitigation: Space returns when the map is dropped. A map that cannot get its copy fails with IOError, and files.read_at reads a part without either.

whyNot.reason: B copies every map on every host, even where a free clone gives the same stability with no copy.
C removes borrowed views from maps, so every line a program keeps is a copy, and two reads can disagree.
D gives up Jet's promise that a borrowed value doesn't change under you.

recommendation.tradeoff: On file systems that cannot clone, a short writer wait or a map-time copy, for stable zero-copy views everywhere a clone exists.

decisions.title: Reads of another process's /proc entry: the child read joins Exec and a kernel lock replaces the lock read, both reads join their operation, declare FS.Read, or remove both
decisions.situation: D-HOST-NONCE1 said some small host reads belong to the operation that makes them. Two reads found since then look at a different process. When Jet starts a program with a memory or open-file limit, it reads that child's /proc entry to tell which limit stopped it. When a secrets-vault write finds an old lock, it reads the /proc entry of the program that left it. The owner asked for the best greenfield design, and said old code is never a reason to pick a worse one. We recommend A, which was the posted D. The child read is part of Exec, and the vault uses a lock the kernel drops when its holder exits, so it reads no /proc entry.
decisions.gist: Should the child read count as part of Exec, and should the vault switch to a lock the kernel releases, so it reads no other process?
decisions.lesson: Some operations look at the host to do their job. A process start with a memory limit watches the child it started. A vault write that finds an old lock checks whether the program that left it still runs. This vote decides whether those looks are part of the operation, need a permission, or should go away.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. /proc is a folder Linux fills with live facts about each running program, one entry per process id (pid). An effect is a permission that a function's row names, such as Exec to start programs, Secret to use the secrets vault, or FS.Read to read files. A denial such as --deny=FS.Read refuses every call whose row needs that effect.

A kernel lock, such as flock, is a lock on an open file that the operating system releases by itself when the program holding it exits or crashes. Docs/spec/reference/host-reads.md lists each read the runtime makes under another effect, and whether a denial covers it.
decisions.story:
Ravi's grading helper starts each student's program with a 32 MiB memory limit. His package allows Exec and IO, and he runs it with FS.Read denied. He wants an over-limit program to report ResourceLimit(.Memory). He also stores an API key in the vault, and last week his laptop died during a vault write.

Under A and B the memory error keeps working. Under A his next vault write proceeds at once, because the kernel dropped the dead writer's lock. Under B he waits ten minutes. Under C every process start needs FS.Read. Under D the memory error is gone.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether two runtime reads of another process's /proc entry belong to the effect of the operation that makes them, or are replaced or removed.

The owner's question (q2i7dehp). The owner asked for the best greenfield design, and noted the posted ballot passed over D only because older toolchains would need updating. That is not a valid reason, so the recommendation moves to D, now listed first as A. The other options are renamed: B was A, C was B, and D was C.

The first read, H22. HostSpawn sets the kernel limits RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_NOFILE in the child before it runs. While a limited child runs, Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ProcessExecutionLimits.jet reads /proc/<child>/status (VmSize) and lists /proc/<child>/fd. When VmSize comes within 1 MiB of memory_limit, or the descriptors reach open_file_limit, Jet stops the child. The run then fails with IOError.ResourceLimit(.Memory) or ResourceLimit(.OpenFiles).

The kernel reports neither limit by a signal, so without this read Jet cannot tell these failures apart from any other. No other interface gives a per-process open-file count. That is why every option except D keeps the read.

The second read, H23. The vault lock is .jet/.secrets.age.lock, created with O_EXCL. A writer records its pid and its start time, read from its own /proc/<pid>/stat (VaultLinux.jet:768). A later writer that finds the file waits until it is ten minutes old (VaultLinux.jet:853). Only then does it read the recorded owner's /proc entry and decide whether the owner is gone.

Why a kernel lock is better, not just cheaper to rule. Under A the writer opens the lock file and takes flock, through HostFileLock.jet, the leaf core.files locks already use. The kernel releases it the moment the holder exits, so there is no stale state, no ten-minute wait and no pid. The pid check is also wrong when the vault sits on a shared network folder, where a pid names a process on another machine. The revision and hash checks that choose the current or backup store stay.

Older Jet builds. A Jet from before the change takes no flock and expects a pid= line. A new Jet that finds an old-format file treats it as held by an older Jet. It refuses with a message naming the file, and never steals it.

The reverse is stricter. The new file is never removed, so once a new Jet has written a vault, an older Jet refuses every write to it. The older Jet reports the vault locked until someone deletes .jet/.secrets.age.lock.

Jet is greenfield and owes its older builds no compatibility, so A accepts this, and a release note names the file. If mixed builds ever must share a vault, the writer can unlink the file on release and recheck the file's identity after locking. That costs one stat per write and removes the file between writes.

The rule A adds. spec.md Effects extends the D-HOST-NONCE1=A sentence with one case. Reading the state of a child process the operation started, its /proc entry or a control group (cgroup) the operation created for it, belongs to the operation's effect. host-reads.md H22 moves to ruled and H23 to fixed.

Relation to other ballots. D-HOST-NONCE1=A is the rule this one extends. D-NET-HOSTREADS1=A covers TLS reads and is unaffected.

options.name: Count the child read as part of Exec, and replace the stale-lock read with a kernel lock
options.detail:
This was the posted D. Reading the /proc entry of a child the operation started belongs to Exec, so the typed memory and open-file errors stay. The vault lock becomes a flock the kernel drops when its holder exits, so no vault call reads another process's entry, and a crashed writer's lock is free at once.

Beginner path: nothing to learn. Limits report which one stopped the child, and a crash never blocks the vault. Expert path: host-reads.md lists the one remaining read, and --deny=FS.Read says exactly what it does not cover.
options.technical:
spec.md Effects extends the D-HOST-NONCE1 sentence with the started-child case, naming its /proc entry and any cgroup the operation creates for it. host-reads.md H22 moves to ruled.

VaultLinux.jet opens .jet/.secrets.age.lock with O_CREAT and takes flock through HostFileLock.jet, waiting under the call's deadline. The file is never unlinked, which avoids the unlink race of lock files. It drops vault_process_start, the pid and start-time fields, the pidfd check and the ten-minute age check. A file holding the old pid= format is refused as held by an older Jet, with a message naming the file. host-reads.md H23 becomes fixed. No Core row changes.

options.name: Count both reads as part of their operation
options.detail: This was the posted A. The rule gains two named cases: the child the operation started, under Exec, and the owner recorded in a lock file the vault's own protocol wrote, under Secret. Nothing changes for programs, including the ten-minute wait after a crashed writer.
options.technical: spec.md Effects extends the D-HOST-NONCE1 sentence with both cases. host-reads.md H22 and H23 move to ruled. No runtime change.

options.name: Declare FS.Read on the operations that make them
options.detail: This was the posted B. Rows are fixed in the source, so every process start and run that can carry a limit names FS.Read, and so does every vault write. A package that allows Exec but not FS.Read can no longer start a program, even one with no limit.
options.technical: core.process start and run entry points, the pipeline runners and core.crypto.vault prepare and commit add FS.Read to their rows. The compiler's call effect rows and IR route effects follow.

options.name: Remove both reads
options.detail: This was the posted C. The child read goes: the kernel still enforces the limits, but a child that hits one ends however its own code handles the failed allocation or open. The run no longer says which limit stopped it. The vault lock becomes the same kernel lock as in A.
options.technical: Delete ProcessExecutionLimits.jet's polling and the parent-side stop, and the ResourceLimit(.Memory) and ResourceLimit(.OpenFiles) results with their cases. The vault change is A's.

comparisons.note: File locks such as fs2's lock_exclusive and std's File::lock use flock, which the kernel releases when the holder exits; no pid file is involved. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.lock
comparisons.code:
let file = File::create(".secrets.age.lock")?;
file.lock()?;   // released by the kernel if this process dies

comparisons.note: A unit's MemoryMax is enforced by a cgroup, and systemd reads that cgroup's memory.events to report that the limit stopped the unit. It reads the state of the child it started to report the cause, as A rules. Source: www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html
comparisons.code:
systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=32M ./student
# result: oom-kill, read from the cgroup's memory.events

comparisons.note: --allow-run grants starting programs, and Deno gives no limits of its own. Reading a child's /proc entry needs --allow-read like any file. Source: docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security
comparisons.code:
const child = new Deno.Command("./student").spawn();
await Deno.readTextFile(`/proc/${child.pid}/status`); // needs --allow-read

recommendation.why: A keeps the typed limit errors that only the child read can give, and rules that read under the narrowest case: the child the operation itself started. It removes the other read entirely and fixes two vault weaknesses. A crashed writer no longer blocks it for ten minutes, and a pid on another machine can no longer fool it.
gains: Programs keep ResourceLimit(.Memory) and ResourceLimit(.OpenFiles).
No vault call reads another process's /proc entry; a crashed writer's lock is free at once.
The rule grows by one narrow case, and host-reads.md has no open rows.
Exec and Secret grants keep working with FS.Read denied.

losses.loss: A denial of FS.Read does not stop the parent reading its own child's /proc entry.
losses.mitigation: The read returns only which limit stopped the child, never file contents, and host-reads.md names it.

losses.loss: Once a new Jet has written a vault, an older Jet build refuses every write to it until .jet/.secrets.age.lock is deleted.
losses.mitigation: Jet owes older builds no compatibility, and a release note names the file. Unlinking on release, with an identity recheck after locking, removes the file between writes if mixed builds must share.

losses.loss: The child read is a 1 ms sample, so a child that jumps past the limit between samples meets the kernel limit with no typed error.
losses.mitigation: This is today's behavior under every option but D. A cgroup the operation creates gives exact memory reports and falls under the same rule.

whyNot.reason: B keeps three flaws a kernel lock removes. It reads another program's /proc entry, waits ten minutes after a crash, and trusts a pid that is wrong on a shared network folder.
Rows are static, so C charges FS.Read to every process start and vault write, even with no limit or old lock, which breaks the common Exec-only grant.
D drops the typed memory and open-file errors, and nothing else can give them.

recommendation.tradeoff: One named read of the operation's own child stays under Exec, for typed limit errors and a vault that reads no other process.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: BallotReview-3. The review checked the /proc reads and the vault lock code. A never-unlinked lock file locks older Jet builds out for good; that cost is now named with its mitigation.

decisions.checkInstructions:
In the Jet repository, read Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ProcessExecutionLimits.jet. process_execution_memory_used reads /proc/<pid>/status for VmSize, and process_execution_files_used lists /proc/<pid>/fd. The 1 MiB memory threshold is at line 97.

Read Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/VaultLinux.jet. Line 768 reads the writer's own pid and line 769 its start time from /proc. Line 853 is the ten-minute age check, and lines 857-862 read the recorded owner's fields, its /proc entry and a pidfd.

Read Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/HostFileLock.jet: jet_fs_lock_try_raw and jet_fs_lock_wait_raw call flock (syscall 73) with LOCK_EX, and the final drop closes without unlinking. That is the leaf A's vault lock uses. host-reads.md rows H22 and H23 are open on dev. VaultLinux.jet lines 857-862 also show what an older Jet does with a file it cannot parse: it reports the vault locked and never steals it. Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.

decisions.title: F32 remainders: give rem_quo, remainder and fmod an F32 result under their own names, add _f32 names, or keep the Float results only
decisions.situation: rem_quo divides one number by another and returns two parts: what is left over, and the whole number of times it went in. For 6.5 and 2.0 that is 0.5 left over and 3. Today the left-over part is always a Float, a 64-bit number, even when both inputs are F32, a 32-bit number. math.remainder and math.fmod also answer a Float for two F32s. Floor, hypot, frexp, modf and most other math functions answer in the argument's width. The math card asks for C's float forms remquof, remainderf and fmodf. This vote decides how a program gets them. We recommend A: these three follow the width rule too.
decisions.gist: Should math.rem_quo, remainder and fmod give an F32 remainder for F32 inputs, as most math functions do?
decisions.lesson: A Float is a 64-bit floating-point number and an F32 is a 32-bit one. Most math functions answer in the width you give them: math.floor of an F32 is an F32. The three remainder functions, rem_quo, remainder and fmod, answer with a Float today. This vote picks how an F32 program gets an F32 remainder.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. rem_quo divides a by b and rounds the quotient to the nearest integer, ties to even. It returns what is left over plus that integer's low 31 bits and sign, as musl's C does. remainder returns the left-over part alone. fmod cuts the quotient toward zero. Widening an F32 to a Float is always exact. F32{x} narrows a Float back. It stops the program when x is a NaN or an infinity, which are values outside every number range.
decisions.story: Mia reduces an F32 angle into one turn and needs to know which quarter it fell in. Under A she writes math.rem_quo(angle, quarter) and gets an F32 remainder, as math.floor(angle) gives an F32. Under B she must know to write math.rem_quo_f32(angle, quarter). Under C she widens both inputs and narrows the remainder with F32{}. Her program then stops on the first angle that is a NaN, where C's remquof hands the NaN back.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a program gets C's remquof, remainderf and fmodf, which card #6700 c5 requires as the float forms of every C23 math.h function. frexpf and modff are not on this ballot. Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreSignatures.jet already gives frexp and modf generic rows over the argument's float type (lines 369-379).

Today, run on the seed compiler. With two F32 arguments, math.rem_quo, math.remainder and math.fmod each answer a Float (probe f2). CoreSignatures.jet line 405 types remainder and fmod as Float only, and rem_quo is a Float source function. Passing the result where an F32 is wanted is E0112. Most other functions keep the width: math.floor of an F32 is an F32 (probe f1).

How the other functions keep the width. sema_call_try_core_math_f32 in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Core.jet widens two F32s, calls the Float source and rounds the result once to F32. That rounding never stops: a NaN stays a NaN.

Why that round trip is exact here. The remainder of two binary32 values is itself a binary32 value, and widening is exact. So computing in Float and rounding once gives exactly remquof's remainder, and the quotient is the same integer. A zero divisor or an infinite dividend gives a NaN, as C specifies. No new F32 source is needed.

Narrowing in a program. F32{x} stops with E3010 on a NaN or an infinity (probe f3), and F32.from_float returns an Err for them. Jet has no public narrowing that passes them through.

Why no new record type. The result is an anonymous named tuple, (rem: Float, quo: Int), not a record. A tuple with an F32 field needs no new type declaration.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner under A writes math.rem_quo(a, b) and gets a remainder in their width, with no conversion to learn. An expert who wants a Float remainder widens first, the same under every option. An expert porting C maps remquof, remainderf and fmodf to their Jet names under A, and to three _f32 names under B. Under C each becomes two widens, the call and a guarded narrow.

options.name: Same names, F32 remainder
options.detail: math.rem_quo, math.remainder and math.fmod follow the rule most core.math functions follow: two F32 arguments give an F32 result. rem_quo's quotient stays an Int. Float arguments keep today's Float results. No new public name.
options.technical:
Signatures for two F32s: rem_quo -> (rem: F32, quo: Int), remainder -> F32 and fmod -> F32.

CoreSignatures.jet: line 405's Float-only row for fmod and remainder becomes generic over the float type, and rem_quo gains a generic tuple row like frexp's. Calls/Core.jet: sema_call_try_core_math_f32 adds remainder and fmod to its member list, and rounds only the rem field of rem_quo. The round trip is exact, so no F32 source port is needed.

docs/core-library.md and Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet name the F32 forms. Proof: the F32 exact corpus case gains rows for all three against musl 1.2.5's remquof, remainderf and fmodf on O0, O1, O2 and web.

options.name: Separate _f32 names
options.detail: Three new public functions, math.rem_quo_f32, math.remainder_f32 and math.fmod_f32, return F32 results. The plain names keep returning a Float for two F32s. A program picks the width by the name, as C picks remquo or remquof.
options.technical: Signatures: rem_quo_f32: fn(a: F32, b: F32) -> (rem: F32, quo: Int), and remainder_f32 and fmod_f32: fn(a: F32, b: F32) -> F32. Each uses A's exact round trip. Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows exports them in both core.math rows, and docs/core-library.md gains three rows. New public Core API: three names.

options.name: No F32 form; widen and narrow
options.detail: Nothing new. A program widens both F32s to Float, calls the Float function and narrows the remainder with F32{}. The narrowing is exact for every finite remainder, but F32{} stops the program on a NaN, so a program that may see one checks math.is_nan first. The card's c5 text is amended to say the three remainder functions have a Float form only.
options.technical: No Core or compiler feature. Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet notes that remquof, remainderf and fmodf are the Float calls on widened arguments. Card #6700 c5 text: these are not separate forms. This program runs today on the seed compiler (probe f1).

comparisons.note: One function per width; the quotient comes back through a pointer.
comparisons.code:
int quo;
float rem = remquof(a, b, &quo);

comparisons.note: No remquo in std; the libm crate has one function per width.
One float width; math.remainder gives no quotient.

recommendation.why: A gives the three remainder functions the rule most core.math functions already have, frexp and modf included: F32 in gives F32 out under the same name. The result is exact, no public name is added, and a NaN passes through as in C.
gains: One rule: the remainder has the argument's width, as floor, hypot and frexp do.
No new public names; remquof, remainderf and fmodf map to the names a program already uses.
The F32 result is exact and a NaN passes through, with no guard to write.
No new F32 source: the exact round trip reuses the Float functions.

losses.loss: The result's width comes from the arguments, so a reader must know their types to know the remainder's.
losses.mitigation: Most core.math functions already work this way; the editor's hover shows the type, and widening first asks for a Float.

whyNot.reason: B adds three public names for a choice most core.math functions make by the argument's type, so F32 code has two styles.
C makes F32 programs write three conversions per call, and F32{} stops on a NaN where remquof returns it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The remainder's width follows the arguments, as for most math functions, for one rule and no new names.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: BallotReview-3. The fresh review probed the seed and found remainder and fmod also answer a Float for F32s, so A now covers all three. It showed the Float round trip is exact, removing the port cost.

decisions.title: How the web package puts its app on a network port: one serve call in core.http, a public route table, the app kept in Core, or HTTP in the package
decisions.situation: The web toolkit, the code behind web.app(), is moving out of Jet's built-in library into an installable package called web. A package may use only the public parts of the built-in library. Today the app builds its route table and starts its server through 15 hidden calls in the HTTP module. The build of an earlier vote, one route table on web.app(), also removes every public way to start a server. So once the move lands, the web package has no public way to listen on a port. You are asked which small public door the HTTP module keeps. We recommend A: one call that serves one handler, a ready handler for a folder of files, and a route pattern whose match alone tags a request with its route.
decisions.gist: Once web.app() moves into the web package, what is the best public door for that package to start a server?
decisions.lesson: A web app needs two things: a route table that picks the code for each address, and a server that listens on a port. The route table is moving into the web package. The server stays in Jet's built-in HTTP module. This vote picks the public calls that join them.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Core is Jet's built-in library. A package, or battery, is an installable library outside Core; the web package is one. A public call is one any program may use. A private name starts with two underscores, and only Core itself may use it.

A route table maps an address, like GET /hello/:name, to the code that answers it. A handler answers one request with one response; Core's handler type is HTTPHandler, and a function written where an HTTPHandler is expected becomes one. Listening means opening a network port and waiting for requests.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small app: web.app(), one app.get route, then app.bind and serve. Under A, B and D her program is the same. Under A the web package serves her table through one Core call, server.listen. Ana can also serve a folder with no package at all: server.listen with server.static_dir("public"). Under B the package wraps a public Core route table, server.mux(). Under C her pages move to a second value. Under D the package parses HTTP itself.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The public Core calls the web package uses to serve its route table once core.web leaves Core.

The gap. Card #6445 moves core.web, router included, into the web package under D-WEB-HOME1=A; core.http and core.net stay in Core. D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A says that package uses public Core calls only, with no new general primitive, and that its compiler rules become markers it declares. A double-underscore name is refused outside Core with E0067.

D-ROUTE-ONE1=A makes web.app() own the one route table and removes server.mux(). Its build, the #6055 c2 submission, also removes server.serve, server.bind, serve_once, serve_once_listener, static_files, cors, request_id and http.serve. On dev today, core.http.server already has no mux, bind or serve, and HTTPServer keeps local_addr, serve, wait and shutdown(grace:).

What the app uses today. Core/Web/Web.jet calls 15 private core.http.server names, 36 times. Building the table uses __mux_new, __route_add, __route_add_dynamic, __route_add_custom, __handler and __layer_add. Its options use __static_files, __cors_handler and __request_id_handler. OpenAPI uses __mux_routes, __route_parse and __route_openapi_path. Serving uses __bind, __serve_once and __server_on. __server_on is how app.serve tells a busy port from other failures before it tries the next port.

The routing code also writes two private request fields, the path values and the matched route, which request.param and server.access_log read. Route registration stops with E2804, E2805 and E2808 through core.rt.__coded_stop, which is private too.

What stays public under every option. The helpers response, response_body, json, static_file, static_file_range, tls, sse, cors_policy and the access log helpers. HTTPServer with its methods. HTTPHandler with handle; a function written where one is expected becomes one, and the compiler checks its captures as handler captures. The #Server.Get route markers.

How A removes the earlier downsides. serve_once is a method on the server listen returns, as Python's handle_request is. static_dir returns a handler, as Go's FileServer and Deno's serveDir do, so a folder needs no package. Only Core's RoutePattern.match tags a request with its route, so no code can forge one. Literal routes keep E2804 at check time; only a computed pattern meets the run-time stop.

Is A's server.listen a general primitive? No. D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A turned down process-wide shared state, a publish reachable from anywhere and the startup environment. Its rule is that a host power stays in the Core module that owns it. Listening on a port is core.http.server's own job. listen holds no route table, so it is not the second builder D-ROUTE-ONE1=A removed.

Sources. Deno.serve and serveDir: docs.deno.com/api/deno/~/Deno.serve, jsr.io/@std/http/doc/file-server. Go ListenAndServe, FileServer, StripPrefix and Request.SetPathValue: pkg.go.dev/net/http. Python socketserver handle_request: docs.python.org/3/library/socketserver.html. Node http.createServer: nodejs.org/api/http.html. Bun.serve: bun.sh/docs/api/http.

options.name: core.http.server serves one handler and answers a folder; routing, CORS and request ids move into the web package
options.detail:
Core keeps a server that answers every request with one HTTPHandler. The web package owns everything about routes: the table, matching, the 404, 405 and OPTIONS answers, middleware, CORS and request ids. web.app() hands its table to Core as one handler. Core keeps what belongs to one request and its connection: framing and limits, TLS, WebSocket upgrade, the status for a handler error, and the safe answer for files under a folder.

Beginner path: web.app(), app.get, then app.bind or app.serve(), unchanged. A folder of files needs no package: server.listen("127.0.0.1:8080", server.static_dir("public")). Expert path: server.listen with any handler, for a health probe or a proxy, with TLS and graceful shutdown the same way.
options.technical:
core.http.server gains two functions, one HTTPServer method and one small type, RoutePattern. Each replaces a private call.

listen: fn(on: String | TCPListener, handler: HTTPHandler, *, tls: HTTPServerTLS?{None}, deadline: Duration?{None}) -[Net]> HTTPServer HTTPError!
It replaces __bind on an address and __server_on on a bound listener. So app.serve still sees a busy port from core.net.tcp_listen and tries the next one. A failed bind or a bad TLS identity is HTTPError, as app.bind reports today.

HTTPServer.serve_once: fn(self) HTTPError! -[Net, FS.Read, Time]>
It answers the next connection, for tests, replacing __serve_once. It sits beside serve, wait and shutdown on the server listen returns.

static_dir: fn(root: String, *, prefix: String{""}, index: Bool{true}, dotfiles: Bool{false}, follow_links: Bool{false}) -> HTTPHandler Never!
Its handler is today's static mount answer: the dot-dot, dotfile and symlink checks, index.html, content type, ETag, 304 and byte ranges. It drops prefix from the path first. The web package's app.static_files routes {prefix}/* to it, so the folder escape checks keep one home.

RoutePattern is an opaque type with three operations.
route_pattern: fn(text: String) -> RoutePattern HTTPError!
match: fn(self, request: HTTPRequest) -> HTTPRequest?
overlaps: fn(self, other: RoutePattern) -> Bool.
 A pattern that does not parse is an Err worded as E2805. match returns the request tagged with the path values and the template only when the path really matches. So request.param and server.access_log work on routed requests, and no code can set a tag that did not match. overlaps is the clash test.

HTTPHandler stays in core.http.server. The package wraps its table in a function written where an HTTPHandler is expected, so the compiler's handler capture check still applies. A probe stores route functions in a list and wraps them this way. A handler's Err becomes a status in Core, as today: BodyTooLarge 413, InvalidFraming 400, UnsupportedEncoding 415, anything else 500.

Into the web package go HTTPMux, the table and its order, the 404, 405 with Allow, OPTIONS * and HEAD answers, middleware layers, CORS, request ids, route input decoding and OpenAPI. The one-pattern parser and matcher stay in Core behind RoutePattern, a narrow amendment to D-WEB-HOME1=A, which moves the router. The custom method check uses the public http.valid_method and http.method_parse.

Which clashes are found when. A route whose pattern is a literal or a constant gets E2804, E2805 and E2808 at check time, keyed on the #RouteTable marker the package declares. A probe shows two literal app.get rows refused with E2804. A pattern computed while the program runs is not seen by the check; the same probe with a computed pattern passes it.

That computed route is checked when it is added: overlaps finds the clash, and route_pattern's Err finds a bad pattern. The package words each through its own Diagnostic type, so the stop text carries the code, what, why and fix. The stop itself is a panic, E3001, because the coded stop is private to Core.

options.name: server.mux() and its HTTPMux route table become public again; the web package wraps it
options.detail:
Core keeps the route table type, HTTPMux, public with its get, post, mount, middleware, static_files, cors, request_id, bind and serve_once methods. web.app() builds one and adds pages on top.

Beginner path: web.app(), unchanged. Expert path: server.mux() builds a route table with no web package. That is the second builder D-ROUTE-ONE1=A removed, so two tables can again hold routes for one address.
options.technical:
core.http.server exports mux: fn() -> HTTPMux Never! again. HTTPMux's methods become public: the verbs get, post, put, delete, patch, head, options and custom, plus mount and middleware. static_files(prefix, root), cors(policy) and request_id() are public too. HTTPMux also lists its rows publicly, because web.openapi reads them.

Serving is mux.bind(address, tls:, deadline:) -[Net]> HTTPServer HTTPError! and mux.serve_once(listener) HTTPError! -[Net, FS.Read, Time]>. The web package's App holds an HTTPMux and forwards to it. Route stops stay coded, because the table stays in Core.

A route a program puts on its own mux is not in the app's table. So E2804 cannot see a clash between the two tables, and jet explain --routes lists only the app's rows. The compiler lowers route rows twice: once on HTTPMux in Core and once on #RouteTable in the package. This reverses part of D-ROUTE-ONE1=A.

options.name: The app type and its route table stay in Core under core.http.server; pages, forms and their markers move to the web package
options.detail:
The App type, with routes, binding and serving, stays in Core with its private calls. The web package keeps pages, forms, islands and the build steps. A package can add methods only to its own types, so pages cannot be App methods: they go on a second value, web.Site, that adds rows to the App.

Beginner path: a program with routes only is unchanged; a program with pages writes site: web.site(app) and site.page(...), two values for one app. Expert path: core.http.server.app() works with no web package.
options.technical:
App moves from Core/Web/Web.jet into Core/Http as core.http.server.App. It keeps its route table and its bind, serve, serve_once, static_files, cors, request_id and middleware methods, and its private calls stay private because it is in Core.

An external inherent method must be in the module of its type (spec, methods), so page, layout, loader, action, the render modes and assets move to web.Site. web.Site adds GET and POST rows to its App through App's public methods, so one table still holds every row.

#RouteTable is declared by Core, not by the battery, so the battery declares three of D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A's four markers; the rule stays keyed on a marker. C amends D-WEB-HOME1=A, whose card #6445 moves the router out of Core.

options.name: No serve call in Core for the package: the web package reads and writes HTTP itself over core.net
options.detail:
Core keeps its HTTP client and helpers but no server entry the package uses. The web package accepts TCP connections from core.net.tcp_listen, reads HTTP/1.1 requests, applies limits, runs TLS and writes responses.

Beginner path: web.app(), unchanged. Expert path: a program with no package has no server; it uses the web package or writes HTTP over core.net itself.
options.technical:
The package needs new public Core calls for what is private today. The server side of TLS is core.net.tls.__server and __server_context. A WebSocket upgrade uses the socket number and an upgrade cell: core.net.__tcp_fd, http.__upgrade_cell and http.__upgraded. Requests and responses are built by http.__server_request and http.__response.

A public socket number lets any code act on a connection the server owns. That is a general primitive of the kind D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A turned down. HTTP/1.1 framing then has two homes: core.http's client in Core and the server in the package. HTTPServer and its shutdown report leave Core.

comparisons.note: ListenAndServe takes one Handler. FileServer is a Handler for a folder. Request.SetPathValue (Go 1.22) lets any code tag a request; A lets only a real match do it. Its ServeMux panics on a clashing pattern at registration. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http
Deno.serve takes one handler; routers such as Hono are libraries above it. The std serveDir answers a folder for a request. Source: https://docs.deno.com/api/deno/~/Deno.serve
http.server serves one handler class; socketserver's handle_request answers one request on a bound server, the shape of serve_once. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/socketserver.html
http.createServer takes one request listener; Express builds its router on top and adds no request id by default. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html

recommendation.why: A gives the web package one public door, the shape Go, Deno, Node and Python ship. Each part stays with its owner: connections, TLS and file safety in Core, routes in the package. One table holds every route, as D-ROUTE-ONE1=A asks. The package needs no private Core call, and a folder of files needs no package at all.
gains: The web package serves through public Core calls only.
Route matching has one home, so E2804 sees every clash.
A program with no package serves one handler or a folder, with TLS and graceful shutdown.
Middleware keeps Core's HTTPHandler and the compiler's handler capture check.
The folder escape checks keep one home in Core.
Literal routes keep E2804 at check time; a computed route's clash still prints E2804 with its why and fix lines.
Only a real match tags a request with its route, so no code can forge path values.

losses.loss: Core gains four public items: server.listen, server.static_dir, HTTPServer.serve_once and the RoutePattern type.
losses.mitigation: Each replaces a private call that does the same job, and none holds a route table.

losses.loss: A route whose pattern is computed while the program runs and clashes stops as a panic, E3001, with E2804's text inside.
losses.mitigation: Literal and constant routes, the common case, are refused at check time with the full E2804 report.

whyNot.reason: B brings back server.mux(), a second route builder, so a clash across two tables escapes E2804 and jet explain --routes, and the compiler lowers route rows in two places.
C keeps the router in Core against D-WEB-HOME1=A, and splits one app into two values, because a package cannot add page methods to Core's App.
D makes a socket number public for WebSocket upgrades, a general primitive D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A turned down, and gives HTTP/1.1 framing two homes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four small public items in Core, for a web package with no private Core call, one route table and a file server without a package.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. The reader asked that the forgeable route tag and the run-time clash be engineered away. v3 r2 mints the tag only by a real match and keeps literal clashes at check time.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Read Core/Web/Web.jet on dev for the 36 calls to 15 private core.http.server names. Among them are __handler, __route_add, __layer_add, __static_files, __mux_routes, __bind, __serve_once and __server_on. rt.__coded_stop raises the route stops.

Read Core/Http/Server.jet. HTTPHandler is at line 154, HTTPServer at 278 with local_addr, serve, wait and shutdown(grace:). __serve_once is at 568, __static_files at 607 and __static_serve at 1832.

Read Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Lambdas.jet:1474, where a function becomes an HTTPHandler, and Calls/Http.jet:400-423 for the handler capture check.

Probes on the batch-8 compiler. b6445/wrap: a list of stored route functions, wrapped in a function where an HTTPHandler is expected, answers a parsed request. b6445/diag: a package-declared Diagnostic type prints E2804 with What, Why and Fix in a run-time stop.

b6445/clash: two literal app.get("/a/:id") rows are E2804 at check time. b6445/clash_computed: the same clash with one pattern built at run time passes the check. Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.
