decisions.title: Amending D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A: on every Core stream the plain name takes text and the _bytes name takes bytes, and Writer is write_bytes plus flush
decisions.situation: You ratified D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A: the JSON, CBOR, CSV and XML writers write through the Prelude's Writer trait, and the screen's Stdout and Stderr are Writers too. Two facts block that as written. Writer's write takes bytes, but Stdout's write takes text, and one type cannot have two methods named write. And Writer has no flush, so a log watched with tail -f shows nothing until the program ends. We recommend A. Every Core stream follows the rule core.files already uses: the plain name takes text and the _bytes name takes bytes. Writer becomes write_bytes, which writes every byte or fails, plus flush.
decisions.gist: Which names do Core's streams and the Writer trait use, so the screen, files, sockets and codecs fit one rule?
decisions.lesson: A codec turns values into JSON, CSV, CBOR or XML bytes, and under the ratified plan it writes through a Writer. Core names its write methods two ways today. Files and the screen say write for text and write_bytes for bytes. A child's stdin, a TCP socket and the Writer trait say write for bytes, write_all for every byte, and write_text for text. Writer also has no flush.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Bytes are a list of U8 values, written [U8]; text is a String. A trait is a named set of methods; a type that has them implements the trait, and generic code can accept any such type. The Prelude is the part of Core every program sees without a use line. A default body is a method body the trait itself supplies, which a type may replace.

A buffered writer collects bytes in memory and hands them to the operating system in large pieces. Flush means: hand over whatever is collected now. tail -f is a Unix command that prints the lines a file gains while another program writes it.

A partial write takes some of the bytes, maybe not all, and returns how many it took. The caller must loop until every byte is taken.
decisions.story:
Ana's service logs events to a JSONL file, prints a summary on the screen, and sends frames to a peer over TCP. Her teammate watches the log with tail -f.

Under A her screen line stays out.write("summary"). She calls log.flush() after each event, and tail -f shows each event as a whole line. Her socket code says conn.write_bytes(frame), which sends every byte or fails. She can point a JSONL writer at term.stdout() or at the socket.

Under B a codec cannot write to the screen. Under C she writes out.write_text for the summary, and conn.write(frame) may send part of the frame. Under D her teammate sees records only in bursts. Under E her own writer type needs two impl blocks.

Under F she hands term.stdout().binary() to a codec. Under G a buffering writer she forgets to give flush still compiles, and the log stalls. Under H conn.write(frame) still means a partial byte write while out.write means text.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The write and read method names on Core's streams: Stdout, Stderr, FileWriter, FileReader, a child process's pipes, TCPStream and UnixStream. It also decides the methods of the Prelude's Writer and Reader traits. It amends D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A and changes nothing else that vote decided.

Core's first naming rule. core.files says read(path) and write(path, text) for text, and read_bytes(path) and write_bytes(path, bytes) for bytes (Core/Files/Files.jet:954-992). Stdout and Stderr say write(text), write_line(text), write_bytes(bytes) and flush (Core/Term/Term.jet:113-152).

Core's second naming rule. A child's stdin says write(bytes), which takes what the pipe accepts and returns the count, then write_all(bytes) and write_text(text). The sources are ProcessHandles.jet:516-545 and core-library.md:2988-2989. TCPStream has the same three, and its read(n) gives bytes while read_text(n) gives text (NetworkHandles.jet:102-114). The Writer trait has write(bytes) returning a count, and write_all (Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:249-253).

The trait's partial write is used by no one generically. FileWriter implements Writer.write by writing every byte and returning the length (Files.jet:430-436), so its write is never partial. The codecs only ever write whole buffers and flush.

Partial writes are a known trap. Rust's write may take part of a buffer, and Clippy denies ignoring its count as a correctness lint, unused_io_amount. Jet's own code falls in it: Doctor.jet:116 and Repl.jet:620 call child.stdin.write(bytes) and drop the result. A body larger than the pipe takes would be cut short with no error.

Go removed the trap at the contract. io.Writer's Write must return an error if it writes fewer bytes than given (src/io/io.go), so generic code never loops. A gives write_bytes that same contract.

Default bodies work. Probe r3 runs on the seed-b17 compiler. A user trait declares write_bytes and flush, with default bodies for write(text) and write_line(text). Counter implements only the two required methods. Screen replaces write with its own. A generic function calls all four through the bound and prints counter bytes 11 flushes 1, then screen texts 1 bytes 7. The Prelude's trait rows carry no default bodies today (OwnedTraitRows.jet:45-48), so A adds that.

Flush today. Each codec writer's flush calls the file's flush directly, at CborStream.jet:694, Csv.jet:729, Stream.jet:1525 and :2001 and Xml.jet:304. Under D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A a codec holds a generic W, so it can call only the trait's methods. FileWriter buffers its writes (Files.jet:400-401). Without a trait flush, nothing reaches the file until the buffer fills or the program ends.

The held-back line end. The JSONL and CSV writers hold back each record's line end until the next write or finish (Stream.jet:1955-2013, Csv.jet:660-671). Probe p4 shows that after each flush the file holds one whole line fewer than the records written. Every option with a codec flush, all but D, has the codec's flush write the pending line end first. A finished file's bytes stay the same as today.

The missing last line end was never a mark. JSON Lines calls a final line terminator strongly recommended but not required (jsonlines.org). RFC 4180 section 2 says the last CSV record may or may not have an ending line break. So no reader can take a missing last line end to mean an unfinished file.

The beginner path. The core.term reference teaches out.write("done") (core-library.md:2260). It keeps working under A, B, F and H, and is E0112 under C. Today's E0112 fix line for bytes passed to a text write says to use interpolation (probe p3), which is the wrong advice.

One write for both kinds cannot work. A method whose parameter is String | [U8] does not satisfy a trait method taking [U8]: review probe r1 gets E0907. Review probe r2 shows an impl may add -[IO]> to a trait method that declares no effect, so Stdout's IO methods can implement Writer.

Size of the change, which weighs for no option. census-v3.mjs over the 20,620 .jet files at dev 8e1c67443b counts 195 write_all calls, 53 write_text and 80 read_text. It lists 137 lines for a hand read of byte reads and partial writes. Under A, Stdout's and Stderr's call sites do not change.

options.name: One rule on every Core stream: the plain name takes text, the _bytes name takes bytes; Writer is write_bytes, which writes every byte or fails, plus a required flush
options.detail:
Every Core stream says write(text), write_line(text) and write_bytes(bytes), as core.files and the screen do today. On the read side, read gives text and read_bytes(limit) gives up to limit bytes. Stdout and Stderr keep every name they have and implement Writer.

The trait. Writer requires write_bytes(bytes), which writes every byte or returns an error, and flush. It supplies write(text) and write_line(text) as default bodies over write_bytes, so a user writer writes two methods. Reader's read(limit) becomes read_bytes(limit); read_into is unchanged.

A partial write is no longer in the trait. A child's stdin, TCPStream and UnixStream keep it as write_some(bytes), which returns the count taken, for code that must stop at a deadline. The name says it may stop early.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") is unchanged, and so is the reference example. A file writer and a socket now take text the same way. Expert path: generic code over W: Writer writes text or bytes, and flush pushes a codec's records to the file.

Edge cases. Code written with Rust or Go habits, conn.write(frame) with bytes, is E0112, and the fix line names write_bytes. A codec's flush writes the record's pending line end first, then flushes its writer. A cut log ends on a whole line, which JSON Lines and CSV already treat as a complete file.
options.technical:
Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet and OwnedTraitRows.jet:45-48: Writer becomes { write_bytes: fn(&self, bytes: [U8]) IOError!; flush: fn(&self) IOError!; write: fn(&self, text: String) IOError! { self.write_bytes(text.bytes()) }; write_line: fn(&self, text: String) IOError! { self.write_bytes("{text}\n".bytes()) } }. The Prelude's trait rows gain default bodies, using the rule user traits already follow (Examples/Modules/Library.jet:10-17; probe r3). Reader becomes { read_bytes(limit); read_into(buffer, limit) }.

Core/Term/Term.jet: Stdout and Stderr keep write, write_line, write_bytes, flush and is_tty, and wrap write_bytes and flush in impl Writer { }. Their own write and write_line replace the defaults with stdio_write. StdinHandle and the cursor reader rename read to read_bytes.

Core/Files/Files.jet: FileWriter's write_all becomes write_bytes, and its fake partial write at :433-436 is deleted. It gains write(text) from the default, and keeps write_line, flush and fsync. FileReader's read(max) becomes read_bytes(max).

The handle rows follow. In ProcessHandles.jet:516-545 a child's stdin write becomes write_some, write_all becomes write_bytes, and write_text becomes write. The child's stdout and stderr read becomes read_bytes. NetworkHandles.jet:102-133 does the same for TCPStream and UnixStream, and read_text(n) becomes read(n). In StreamHandles.jet:160-171, FileWriter's write_all row becomes write_bytes and FileReader's read row becomes read_bytes.

E0112 gains a fix line for a [U8] argument passed to a text write that names write_bytes. Each codec's flush writes its pending line end, then calls the trait's flush. The renames run as one cutover with every call site, sized by census-v3.mjs.

options.name: Names stay as they are; Stdout and Stderr do not implement Writer; Writer gains flush
options.detail:
Every stream keeps today's names. Stdout and Stderr keep write(text) and write_bytes(bytes) and are not Writers, so no codec can write to the screen. Writer keeps write(bytes) returning a count and write_all, and gains flush. The codec flush behaves as in A.

Beginner path: unchanged. Expert path: to stream records to the screen, encode a batch to text with jsonl.to_string and write it. That builds the whole batch in memory, outside the codec's size limits. A Linux or macOS program can open /dev/stdout as a file; Windows has no file path for a redirected stdout.

Edge cases: the two naming rules stay, so write means text on the screen and on files but bytes on a socket. The partial write stays in the trait.
options.technical: Core/Term/Term.jet is unchanged. D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A's list of Writer types drops Stdout and Stderr. Traits.jet's Writer gains a required flush, and the codec flush changes are A's. No call site changes.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write("logging to events.jsonl\n")
log := jsonl.writer(files.append("events.jsonl"))
log.write(record)
log.flush()
// jsonl.writer(term.stdout()) is refused: Stdout is not a Writer.
out.write(jsonl.to_string(records))
conn.write_all(frame)

options.name: Byte-first names, as Rust: write and write_all take bytes and write_text takes text on every stream, Stdout included; Writer gains a required flush
options.detail:
Stdout and Stderr read like a child's stdin and a TCPStream: write(bytes) returns the count taken, write_all(bytes) writes every byte, and write_text(text) writes text. write_bytes goes away. FileWriter gains write_text. Writer gains flush.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") is E0112, and the reference example moves to out.write_text("hi"). Expert path: as in A, with write, write_all and flush in a user writer.

Edge cases: the plain name write takes part of the bytes, so code that forgets the count can lose bytes silently, as Doctor.jet:116 does today. core.files keeps write(path, text) for text, so files and streams still use two rules.
options.technical: Traits.jet: Writer { write: fn(&self, bytes: [U8]) -> Int IOError!; write_all; flush }. Term.jet: Stdout and Stderr gain write(bytes) and write_all, rename write(text) to write_text, and delete write_bytes. FileWriter gains write_text. The codec flush changes are A's. About 60 text writes and 18 write_bytes calls on the screen change.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write_text("logging to events.jsonl\n")
log := jsonl.writer(files.append("events.jsonl"))
log.write(record)
log.flush()
conn.write_all(frame)
files.write("notes.txt", "text")   // the file function still takes text

options.name: Names as in A, but flush stays on the concrete writers only; codec writers lose flush, and finish hands the writer back
options.detail:
The names follow A. Writer requires only write_bytes. Codec writers lose their flush method, since a generic codec cannot reach its writer's flush. finish ends the line, writes the closing bytes and hands the writer back, so the program can flush and close it.

Beginner path: write records, then file := log.finish() and file.flush(). Expert path: as in A without flush.

Edge cases: nothing a codec writes is certain to reach the file before finish. A long-running log fills FileWriter's buffer before any bytes appear, so tail -f sees records in bursts. A crash loses the last buffer.
options.technical: Traits.jet: Writer { write_bytes; write and write_line by default }. Every codec writer's flush (Cbor.jet:23, Json.jet:252, Jsonl.jet:33, and the four push types) is deleted. Each finish returns W instead of nothing. The renames are A's.
options.code:
log := jsonl.writer(files.append("events.jsonl"))
log.write(record)
// no flush: tail -f sees records only as the file buffer fills
file := log.finish()
file.flush()

options.name: Names as in A, with flush in a separate Prelude trait, Flush, and codec writers ask for both
options.detail:
The names follow A. A second Prelude trait, Flush, holds flush. Each codec writer takes W: [Writer, Flush], so its flush works as in A.

Beginner path: identical to A. Expert path: a user writer implements two traits to reach a codec; one with only Writer is refused at the constructor.

Edge cases: as in A. Jet has no where clause, so a codec cannot offer flush only to writers that have it. Every writer passed to a codec needs Flush, so the two traits always appear together.
options.technical: Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet gains Flush: trait { flush: fn(&self) IOError! }. FileWriter, Stdout, Stderr, TCPStream and a child's stdin implement both. The codec constructors and types take <W: [Writer, Flush]>. OwnedTraitRows.jet opens Flush as a bound user code can name. Every other change is A's.
options.code:
writer: fn<W: [Writer, Flush]>(output: &&W) -> JSONLWriter<W> EncodingError!
// A user writer: impl Writer { write_bytes } and impl Flush { flush }.

options.name: Stdout and Stderr keep text names only; out.binary() returns a byte Writer over the same buffer, as Python's sys.stdout.buffer
options.detail:
Stdout and Stderr keep write(text), write_line(text), flush and is_tty. Bytes move to a view: out.binary() returns StdoutBytes, a Writer over the same stdout buffer. Writer gains flush, and the codec flush works as in A. Other streams keep today's names.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") unchanged. Expert path: jsonl.writer(term.stdout().binary()) streams records to the screen.

Edge cases: text and bytes share one buffer, so they keep call order. The name write means text on Stdout but bytes on its own binary view, a child's stdin and TCPStream. Each screen stream needs a second type.
options.technical: Core/Term/Term.jet gains StdoutBytes and StderrBytes, each holding the fd, with write, write_all and flush routed to stdio_bytes and stdio_flush, and impl Writer. Stdout.binary() and Stderr.binary() return them. write_bytes is deleted; its callers write out.binary().write_all(bytes). The codec flush changes are A's.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write("logging to events.jsonl\n")
screen := jsonl.writer(term.stdout().binary())
screen.write(record)
screen.finish()
conn.write(frame)   // bytes, and may send part of them

options.name: As A, but Writer's flush has a default body that does nothing, as Java's OutputStream
options.detail:
As A, except Writer declares flush: fn(&self) IOError! { Ok() } as a default body. FileWriter, Stdout and Stderr write their own flush; a user writer may leave it out.

Beginner path: as in A. Expert path: a user writer implements write_bytes alone, and adds flush only if it buffers.

Edge cases: a buffering user writer that forgets flush compiles. Its codec's flush then returns Ok without pushing bytes, so a tailed log stalls with no error.
options.technical: Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet: Writer as in A, with flush: fn(&self) IOError! { Ok() }. Every other change is A's.

options.name: The trait renames its partial write to write_some, Stdout keeps write for text, and a child's stdin and TCPStream keep write for bytes
options.detail:
Writer becomes write_some(bytes) returning the count, write_all(bytes) and flush. Stdout and Stderr keep write(text) and write_line(text), rename write_bytes to write_all, and gain write_some. FileWriter gains write_some. A child's stdin and TCPStream keep write, write_all and write_text.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") unchanged. Expert path: a user writer implements three methods, one of them a partial write.

Edge cases: the name write means text on Stdout and Stderr but bytes on a child's stdin and a TCPStream. Moving code from one to the other gives a type error, not wrong output. The partial conn.write trap stays.
options.technical: Traits.jet: Writer { write_some: fn(&self, bytes: [U8]) -> Int IOError!; write_all; flush }. Term.jet: write_bytes renamed write_all; write_some added; write(text) kept. FileWriter gains write_some. The codec flush changes are A's. A child's stdin and TCPStream need write_some as a second name for their write before they can implement Writer.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write("logging to events.jsonl\n")
out.write_all(bytes)
child.stdin.write(bytes)   // bytes, and may send part of them
conn.write_text("hello\n")

comparisons.note: io.Writer has one method, and its contract forbids a silent short write: Write must return an error if it writes fewer bytes than given. Generic callers never loop. A's write_bytes takes this contract. Flushing lives on bufio.Writer and the optional http.Flusher. Source: https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/io/io.go
comparisons.code: n, err := w.Write(frame) // n < len(frame) implies err != nil

comparisons.note: Write::write may take part of a buffer, and write_all takes all of it; flush is required. Clippy denies an ignored write count as a correctness lint, unused_io_amount, because the short write is a common bug. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#unused_io_amount
A text stream's write takes text, and sys.stdout.buffer is the byte stream beneath it, sharing its order; the shape of F. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout

Writer takes text and OutputStream takes bytes, two type families; OutputStream's flush has a body that does nothing, the shape of G. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/io/OutputStream.html#flush()

recommendation.why: A extends the rule files and the screen already use to every Core stream: write takes text and write_bytes takes bytes. So out.write("hi") keeps working and one name never means two kinds. Writer's write_bytes writes every byte or fails, as Go's io.Writer does, so the short-write trap Rust lints against is gone. A required flush with a line-ending codec flush lets a tailed log show each record.
gains: write, write_line and write_bytes mean the same on files, the screen, pipes and sockets.
The beginner's out.write("hi") and the reference example are unchanged.
No generic write can silently send part of a buffer.
A user writer joins every codec with two methods.
Codecs stream straight to the screen with their limits, and a tailed log shows each flushed record.

losses.loss: Pipes, sockets, FileWriter and Reader rename their byte methods, so Rust or Go habits like conn.write(frame) with bytes are E0112.
losses.mitigation: It fails at compile time, never at run time, and the fix line names write_bytes. The renames land in one cutover with every call site.

losses.loss: Every Writer must write flush, even one with no buffer.
losses.mitigation: It is one line, flush: fn(&self) IOError! { Ok() }. A default body, option G, would let a buffering writer forget it and pass silently.

losses.loss: Generic code over a Writer cannot write part of a buffer and stop at a deadline.
losses.mitigation: Pipes and sockets keep write_some for that, on the concrete type. No codec needs it, and Go's io.Writer makes the same choice.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two naming rules and leaves the codecs unable to write to the screen except through a whole batch in memory.
C breaks the beginner's out.write("hi"), keeps a plain write that may send part of the bytes, and still disagrees with core.files.
D cannot show a record before the file buffer fills, so a tailed log stalls and a crash loses the last buffer.
E puts flush in a trait that every codec, Core's only generic writer user, asks for anyway, so a user writer needs two impl blocks.
F needs a second type per screen stream, and write still means text on the screen but bytes on pipes and sockets.
G lets a buffering writer that forgets flush compile, and its codec's flush then pushes nothing, with no error.
H keeps write meaning text on the screen but bytes on pipes and sockets, and keeps a partial write in the trait.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pipes, sockets and FileWriter rename their byte methods once, and every writer writes flush, for one naming rule across Core, no silent short writes, and logs that show each flushed record.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main, which did not write this rework. The pass attacked A on unbounded text reads, short writes at a deadline, a required flush on unbuffered writers, and text names on sockets. Each holds: read_bytes(limit), write_some, a one-line flush, and E0112 with a fix line naming write_bytes.

decisions.title: Should Jet try a fully data-parallel compiler design?
decisions.situation: Most compilers handle code one piece at a time: look at this node, then its children. A data-parallel compiler instead runs each pass as operations over whole tables at once, like a spreadsheet formula applied to a whole column. That can use wide vector hardware, and graphics cards, which normal compilers cannot. It has been shown for small languages, not yet for a language as rich as Jet. Jet's speed plan reaches its 30-million-lines-per-second goal on ordinary processor cores, so this is about going past the goal or rescuing a step that falls short. You are asked whether, and when, to explore it. We recommend A: one bounded prototype of one pass, started once the plan meets its goal or a step stalls, with a bar it must clear.
decisions.gist: Should Jet fund one bounded prototype of a compiler pass written as whole-array operations, and when?
decisions.lesson: A new shape of algorithm can use hardware the usual one cannot, but it must beat the usual one on every core.
decisions.explainer: A pass is one step of the compiler, such as name resolution. A column is a flat list of values, one per node. SIMD means one instruction working on many values at once. A GPU is a graphics card used for general computing. Wall time is the time on the clock from start to finish.
decisions.story: Even with 32 threads, a one-node-at-a-time compiler hits a ceiling. Vector instructions handle many values per step, and a graphics card has thousands of small cores, but both help only if the work is written as whole-column operations.
decisions.inWild: Co-dfns and Pareas are research compilers. No production compiler for a large language works this way.
decisions.detail:
Prior art: Co-dfns, Aaron Hsu's APL compiler (thesis, 2019), runs its passes as array operations on a GPU. Pareas (Voetter and others, 2022) lexes, parses and generates code on a GPU.

The plan's exit (#5479 c3, 30M lines/s) is budgeted inside 32 CPU threads: step 6 (#5479 c9) allows at most 1 µs of CPU per line. Jet has no general GPU compute path today; `GPU` is an effect root for graphics and game operations. The plan's steps 0 to 5 are staffed by one agent.

Under A, the prototype starts once #5479 c3 lands, or earlier if a plan step stalls below its gate. One pass is rewritten as array operations over #6793's flat columns: name resolution, or type propagation for a subset. It runs on CPU vector instructions, and on a GPU only if Jet has a GPU compute path by then. The bar to continue: at least 4x less wall time than the scalar pass running on all 32 threads, on the c1 corpus, with identical results and diagnostics.

Below the bar, the prototype is recorded as evidence and stopped. Under D, the same prototype starts as soon as #6793 lands.

decisions.title: Should 'checking time grows in step with the code' be a language rule?
decisions.situation: Some language rules can make the compiler's work grow much faster than the code: doubling a file can quadruple, or worse, the time to check it. Swift's slow type inference on long arithmetic and Rust's trait solver on deep generic code are known examples. Jet already has a scaling test that fails when a compiler step grows too fast on its sample programs. But no language rule says every rule must keep pace, so a rule that no sample exercises can still blow up on someone's code. You are asked whether 'checking keeps pace with the code' becomes a language rule. We recommend A: adopt the rule, audit today's rules once, add a scaling sample per rule, and ballot only real language changes.
decisions.gist: Should every language rule check in time that grows in step with the code, with one audit of today's rules?
decisions.lesson: Compile speed is partly a language-design property: a rule that can blow up will eventually blow up on someone's code.
decisions.explainer: 'Proportional' (linear) means twice the code takes about twice the time. The rule allows a little more, N log N, the cost of sorting a list, which is what Jet's scaling test already accepts. 'Super-linear' means much more, such as four times. Type inference is the compiler working out types you did not write. A trait solver finds which implementation of an interface a call uses.
decisions.story: A generated file has a 20,000-arm choice. If the checker's work grows with the square of the arms, the file takes minutes and gigabytes to check, and nothing warned anyone in advance.
decisions.inWild: Go was designed for fast compiles, with simple inference and no overloading. Swift's expression type checker is known for 'expression too complex' errors. Rust's trait solver can be slow on deep generics. Zig and Jai keep inference local.
decisions.detail:
Today: Tools/perf/scaling (Tower #4319, #4601) compiles generated program shapes at growing sizes. It fails when a compiler phase or work counter grows faster than k * N log N, but it covers only the shapes it generates. #5910 c61 (open) adds one shape: a 20,000-branch chain must check with peak memory growing at most linearly from 1,000 to 20,000 branches.

One audit candidate is visible in code. The ownership last-use query reads the rest of a body's statements at a use (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/LastUse.jet). That may be quadratic in a long body with many moves; it is not measured.

Under A, the rule is written in Docs/spec: checking takes at most N log N time and memory in the program's size. Compile-time code a user writes is excluded, because it is the user's own program.

One audit in Docs/audits lists every rule whose cost can grow faster: inference, overload and trait resolution, exhaustiveness, flow typing, ownership, generic instantiation depth and compile-time evaluation. Each finding gets a shape in Tools/perf/scaling. A finding that is only slow checking code is fixed under a card like any bug. A finding that needs the language to change gets its own ballot.

options.gist: Checking keeps pace with the code (at most N log N). One audit lists today's exceptions; slow code is fixed as a bug, and only language changes get ballots.

decisions.title: Should the compiler keep a syntax tree, and in what form?
decisions.situation: A syntax tree is the compiler's in-memory outline of a program, one entry for each piece of code, built while reading the text. Jet builds it from many small boxes; in one measured run, copying and freeing such boxes, with similar compile-time values, took a fifth of the busy time. The tree is not where the finished program gets faster: every optimization runs later, on a lower form of the code. We recommend A: keep one compact outline per file, a flat list that the checker, formatter and editor all share.
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep one compact syntax list per file, drop the syntax tree, or keep today's tree of small boxes?
decisions.lesson: Keep the outline, but make it a flat list: the cost was the boxes, not the outline.
decisions.explainer:
A syntax tree, also called an AST, is the outline the parser builds from source text. The checker reads it to find errors. It then writes a checked body for each function. The lowering step turns the checked body into IR, a simple instruction list. The optimizer and the machine-code generator work only on IR.

A flat list stores the outline as a few plain arrays: kind, position and size per entry, children before their parent. It needs no boxes and no pointers, so it is cheap to build, copy and free.
decisions.story: Priya's team has 200,000 lines of Jet. Every `jet build` and every editor keystroke reads all of it into small boxes, copies some of them, and frees them. A compact list per file removes that waste without taking anything away from the formatter, the editor or the optimizer.
decisions.inWild: Zig parses each file into one flat node list (std.zig.Ast: tokens, nodes and extra_data arrays). zig fmt, the compiler and the language server read that list. Carbon's toolchain stores its parse tree as one flat array in postorder (toolchain/docs/parse.md). Rust checks ownership on MIR with liveness, not on syntax (RFC 2094). Tiny C emits code while parsing, with no tree, but has no generics, ownership or formatter to serve.
decisions.detail:
Where optimization happens. All 17 optimizer passes run on IR (Compiler/JetIR/Source/Opt.jet:97, IR_OPT_PASS_NAMES). JetIR, JetBackend and JetEval never name the parser's types: their `.Expr` matches are variants of the checked body (BodyLambdaBody.Expr). So the outline's form cannot change the finished program. Rust (MIR), Go (SSA), Swift (SIL) and Zig (AIR) also optimize on a lower form, never on the syntax tree.

What it costs today. The parser builds boxed payload enums (Expr 51 variants, Stmt 35, Item 24, Pattern) in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST. Clones and drops of these trees and comptime values were 20.5% of busy samples on the measured slice and 7.8% on `check main.jet` (Docs/research/fast-compiler-architecture-2026-09-30.md, line 83). The ownership last-use query walks the remaining statements' trees by name for each question (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/LastUse.jet). The driver's route and plugin scans walk the trees too (Loader.jet, PluginFacts.jet).

Under A, the parser writes one flat postorder record per file into the file's arena. It holds the lexer's token columns plus node columns: kind tag, span, subtree size, first token and payload. This is #6793 S4. The Expr, Stmt, Pattern and Item enums and the Func struct are deleted, and every reader uses accessors. The checker, formatter, language server, semantic index and driver scans read the same record.

Generic and compile-time bodies keep their node ranges for later use. The rest of a file's record is freed once its bodies are checked (#6793 S7). The ownership last-use rule moves to one backward liveness pass over the checked body, so the checker no longer walks syntax ahead. The proof is #6793's: the self-host fixed point, byte-identical ui snapshots and cases, and the c1 throughput cell (#5479 c1).

options.name: One flat syntax list per file, shared by every tool
options.gist: The parser writes a compact list per file. The checker, formatter and editor read it, and ownership moves to the checked body.
options.detail: No boxes, no clones, one parser. Generic and compile-time bodies keep their slice of the list. The rest is freed after checking. The optimizer is unchanged, because it already runs on IR. The list keeps every token with its byte span, comments and blank lines included, so jet fmt stays lossless. Code a compile-time splice generates is written as rows of its own generated file. An editor change re-reads only the edited file.

options.name: Keep today's tree of small boxes
options.gist: Every piece of code stays its own box, copied and freed as today.
options.detail: No change to the parser or its readers. The per-function pipeline (#5479 c8) still fuses later steps.

options.name: No stored syntax for ordinary code
options.gist: The parser feeds the checker directly. Generic bodies are re-read from text, and the tools get their own parser.
options.detail: Ordinary bodies go straight from parser notes to the checked body. Generic and compile-time bodies are re-parsed for each use. The formatter and editor keep a separate tree-building parser.

recommendation.why: A removes the measured cost, the boxes and their copies, and keeps everything the outline is for. The finished program is unchanged, because optimization runs on IR.
gains: No per-entry boxes or copies, part of a measured fifth of busy time
One parser and one list for the checker, formatter and editor
Optimization of the finished program is unchanged

losses.loss: Generic and compile-time bodies keep their part of the list after checking.
losses.mitigation: Only those bodies' slices stay. They are flat arrays with no boxes, and every other entry is freed once its file is checked.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the boxes and copies that, with compile-time values, took a fifth of busy time in one run, for no gain.
C needs a second parser for the tools, re-parses generic bodies for every use, and saves little over a flat list.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generic bodies keep a small flat slice after checking, in exchange for no boxes, one parser and an unchanged optimizer.

decisions.title: How far should the compiler go in tuning operating-system costs?
decisions.situation: When a compiler handles a gigabyte of code per second, small operating-system costs add up. Examples are each new page of memory the system hands out, each separate file read, and each step of writing the output. These are fixed costs every compile pays. Linux offers ways to pay them in bulk; other systems offer different ones. Fast paths can also backfire: Jet's memory allocator turns large pages off today, because on a busy machine they can stall every thread. You are asked how far Jet's compiler should go. We recommend A: per-system fast paths inside the shared runtime, each kept only where a measurement shows a gain, with identical output everywhere.
decisions.gist: Should the compiler use operating-system fast paths such as large memory pages and batched file reads, and where?
decisions.lesson: At high speed fixed costs dominate, so pay them in bulk, but only where a busy machine measures a real win.
decisions.explainer: A memory page is the unit the system hands out, usually 4 KB. A large page is 2 MB, so far fewer hand-outs are needed, but each is slower to set up. Pre-faulting means asking for the pages up front. io_uring is a Linux way to submit many file reads at once. An arena is a block of memory a compiler step fills and then frees all at once. The program image is the runnable machine code the compiler produces.
decisions.story: `jet run hello.jet` compiles a tiny program, yet it still pays these fixed costs: memory handed out a page at a time, and each file read on its own. With bulk paths those costs shrink for every compile, large or small.
decisions.inWild: The mold linker pre-sizes its output file and spreads its work over every core. Zig's compiler once never freed memory until exit and dropped that policy as compile-time work grew. Most compilers use the general allocator and plain reads.
decisions.detail:
Today: `jet run` and `jet dev` link the program image and run it from memory (jet_cli_launch in Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet). They write a file under `.jet/build` only when the system refuses executable memory.

The runtime allocator deliberately keeps 4 KiB pages: alloc_region_map in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet sets MADV_NOHUGEPAGE. Its reason: a first touch of a huge page zeroes 2 MiB, and an advised huge region compacts memory on fault. That stalls every allocating thread on a loaded host. The runtime has no io_uring or other batched read path.

Under A, the compiler's phase arenas (#6793 S7) may use large pages and be pre-faulted in one call. That holds only where the size is known up front and the c1 throughput cell (#5479 c1) shows a gain on both an idle and a loaded host. The general allocator keeps its 4 KiB pages. Source files are read in one batch: io_uring on Linux, plain reads elsewhere. The runtime and precompiled Core (#6328 c22) sit at fixed places in the image, so each compile only patches its own code.

All of it lives in the shared runtime (I9) and changes timing only, never output. Each fast path has the plain path as its tested fallback. Arenas are freed in bulk at phase end, so nothing is left for process exit to clean up (I1).

options.gist: Large-page arenas, batched reads and a pre-laid-out image wherever the system offers them and a measurement shows a gain; identical output everywhere.
options.detail: Fast paths live only in the shared runtime; a system without one uses the plain path. Each is kept only where the c1 cell shows a gain on an idle and a loaded host. Proof: identical goldens on every system, timings reported per system.

hello

options.gist: No system-specific fast paths.
options.detail: One plain path on every system.

options.name: Linux fast paths only
options.gist: Tune Linux and leave other systems on the plain path.
options.detail: Fast paths on Linux only.

options.name: Never free compiler memory; let exit release it
options.gist: Skip freeing during a compile and let the system reclaim everything when the compiler exits.
options.detail: The compiler's own memory is never returned while it runs. Each compile saves the cost of freeing, but peak memory grows with everything the compile ever held. It needs an exception to I1, which says safe Jet cannot leak.
options.code:
$ jet run hello.jet
hello
# nothing freed until the compiler exits

recommendation.why: A cuts fixed per-compile cost wherever a system allows it, keeps only measured wins, and never changes output.
gains: Lower fixed cost for every compile
No output differences
No regression on loaded machines

losses.loss: More runtime code for each system's fast path.
losses.mitigation: Fast paths sit behind one runtime interface, the plain path is the tested fallback, and a path that measures no faster is dropped.

whyNot.reason: B leaves fixed costs that dominate small compiles.
C leaves other systems slower for no design reason.
D trades unbounded memory growth for a small saving that arenas freed in bulk already give.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some per-system runtime code in exchange for lower fixed cost everywhere.

decisions.title: May a fast vector scan skip clean code before the compiler's checks?
decisions.situation: Before Jet builds a program, it checks the code for mistakes, one small piece at a time. Processors have vector instructions that look at 16 to 64 pieces in one step, which could speed up the common case of code with no mistakes. The risk is two versions of a check that disagree, or error messages that change. We recommend A: a fast vector scan only marks stretches that might hold a mistake, and today's precise check alone writes every message and answer.
decisions.gist: Should a fast vector scan mark which stretches of code need checking, while today's checks still write every message?
decisions.lesson: Use the fast path only to decide where to look; let one precise path decide what to say.
decisions.explainer: A vector instruction, also called SIMD, does the same small test on 16 to 64 values at once. A diagnostic is an error or warning message with its place in the source. A filter is a quick test that answers either 'certainly fine' or 'maybe not'. A 'maybe' only sends that stretch to the precise check, so a cautious filter costs a little time and never changes a message.
decisions.story: Sam saves a 5,000-line file and the editor rechecks it. Almost every line is fine. A vector scan clears most of the file in a few steps, and the precise check looks only at the stretch around Sam's typo. Sam sees the same message, in the same place, as before.
decisions.inWild: simdutf's validate_utf8_with_errors checks text 64 bytes at a time with vector instructions. When a block fails, it rewinds and runs its scalar validator from there to report the exact error position (src/generic/utf8_validation/utf8_validator.h). simdjson finds structure with vectors and parses values with scalar code. Most compilers check node by node with no vector filter.
decisions.detail:
Today every check after lexing is scalar: it looks at one token or node at a time. The optimizer already turns a plain counting loop over bytes into SSE2 vector code (JetIR OptReduce.jet:190 calls Compiler/JetBackend/Source/X64/Count.jet). Jet's lane types, such as U8x16 and U8x32, define each operation as the scalar operation applied lane by lane. So the same source runs on every machine (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md, SIMD lanes; D-SIMD3=B).

Under A, the scalar check stays the only code that writes diagnostics or computes results, such as which declaration a name means. A vector filter runs first over blocks of 64 tokens or nodes. It answers 'certainly clean' or 'maybe' per block. Each 'maybe' block, with its neighbors at the edges, goes to the scalar check. A filter tests a simpler, wider condition than its check, for example 'any token of these kinds'.

Filters are written in plain Jet with lane types or loops the optimizer turns into vector code, never with unsafe processor intrinsics. A machine without vector units runs the same code lane by lane. A differential test runs every check over all test corpora and generated inputs twice, with filters on and with filters off. Diagnostics must be byte-identical and results equal. A filter lands only where the throughput cell (#5479 c1) shows a gain. It depends on #6793's flat columns (S4); the lexer's own vector classifier is #5910 c6.

options.name: Vector scan marks the spots; today's check writes every message
options.gist: A portable vector filter clears clean blocks. The existing precise check runs on the rest and alone writes messages and answers.
options.detail: One implementation of each rule. The filter only chooses where the check looks. A test with filters on and off must give byte-identical messages and equal results. A filter may clear a block only by a rule that is conservative by construction: every byte in it belongs to a class the precise check accepts without context. Generated inputs and fuzzing run the on/off differential.

options.name: Scalar checks only
options.gist: Every check keeps looking at one piece at a time.
options.detail: No change. Checks of clean code cost the same as today.
options.code:
// A misspelled name; every token is checked one at a time.
show: fn(name: String) { print("hello {nmae}") }

options.name: Full vector checks that write their own messages
options.gist: Each chosen check is rewritten in vector form, which reports errors itself, with a coarser place or order.
options.detail: A second implementation of each rule. Messages may point at a block instead of the exact token, or come in a different order.

recommendation.why: A speeds up checking of clean code, which is almost all code, while one precise implementation still writes every message and answer.
gains: Clean code is cleared many pieces per step
Messages and answers come from one implementation
Same code on every machine, no unsafe intrinsics

losses.loss: A filter bug could call a block clean and hide a mistake.
losses.mitigation: Filters test a wider, simpler condition than the check. The on-and-off test over every corpus and generated input fails on any difference.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the speed-up for clean code unused, with no gain in correctness over A.
C keeps two versions of each rule that can drift, and makes messages less exact.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small filter beside each chosen check, guarded by an on-and-off test, in exchange for faster checking with unchanged messages.

decisions.title: Programs for machines without an operating system: how the compiler checks the Core code they call
decisions.situation: Some programs run on a bare chip with no operating system and often no memory heap, the pool that growing lists draw from. The compiler refuses a list the program builds itself there, but it skips Core, the standard library, by name. So a program that calls a Core function which grows a list passes the check and then fails on the chip. Jet already has a check that proves a function never uses the heap, and it already looks inside Core. You are asked how code the program does not write is checked for such a chip. We recommend running that one existing proof from the program's start, for Core and every package alike, and showing each problem on the program's own line.
decisions.gist: On a chip with no heap, how should the compiler check the Core and package code a program calls?
decisions.lesson: A heap is the memory pool a program borrows from when a list grows. A chip with no heap is like a kitchen with no fridge: a recipe that needs one cannot work. Jet can already prove that a function never touches the heap. Today that proof is only used when a programmer asks for it. This vote decides who gets checked on a chip without a heap, and where the warning appears.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A heap is the memory a program asks for while it runs, for example when a list grows. A no-OS machine is a chip with no operating system, such as a microcontroller board; it may have no heap unless the program brings one. Core is Jet's standard library; it ships with the compiler. A package is any other library a program uses. A function is reached when the program's run function can call it, directly or through other functions.

The heap proof is the check behind -[!Mem.Alloc]>, a mark a programmer can put on a function today to promise it never uses the heap. The compiler then follows every call from that function, into Core and packages too, and refuses the first one that allocates.
decisions.story: Mia writes firmware for a sensor board with no heap. Her total function calls combo.count_from(0, 2, n), which grows a list. Today the check passes, and the board has nothing to grow the list into. Under A the check stops on her count_from call. The note shows the path total, then count_from, and the line inside count_from that grows the list. Under B the error appears inside Core's own file, which she cannot edit. Under C nothing is reported, as today.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a no-OS machine's missing heap and missing OS services apply to code the program does not write: Core, and other packages. The card's criterion is that Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Scopes.jet no longer tests for Core.

What changed since the first version. The first A added a second, new walk that summed up what each function needs. Probing showed Jet already has that walk: the heap proof behind -[!Mem.Alloc]> (Effects/Checks.jet:3984, sema_effect_memory_search). It already enters Core bodies. So the new A adds no walk. It runs the existing proof from the program's start, closes two gaps in that proof, and fixes where its message points.

Today, as the code reads at a03eea6ac0. sema_scope_environment_no_os (Scopes.jet:561) returns false for every Core module (module_is_core, line 562). E3303 refuses each list and map literal written in a non-Core body (Expressions/Literals.jet:485 and :607). E3301 refuses an OS-only Core module call (Calls/Core.jet:675) and #Live (Statements.jet:10239). TargetDenials.jet skips Core functions at line 74 and reports a Core callee's denied effect at the caller at line 91 (E1123).

Probe results on the batch 3b compiler (2d2afdbb12 plus 8ed9de963c), target board.sensor_v1. Probe user_list: a list the program writes is E3303 at main.jet:2. Probe core_call: total calling combo.count_from prints ok, though count_from grows a list (Core/Math/Combinatorics.jet).

The heap proof today. Probe deny_alloc_core marks a function -[!Mem.Alloc]> and calls core.compute.profile_f32_strict, whose text template allocates. The check refuses it with E0921 and the path main.label -> core.compute.profile_f32_strict, so the proof enters Core. Its caret lands on main.jet:10:1, past the end of the 9-line file, because the Core file's position is shown in the program's file. Probe deny_alloc_user finds a list built in a helper, with the path main.total -> main.helper.

Two gaps in the proof. First, its events are list and map literals with items, text templates, arena and Shared construction (Checks.jet:3370-3418). An empty list that then grows by push is not an event, so probe deny_alloc_direct (out := [Int]{}, out.push(n)) passes -[!Mem.Alloc]>. That is the count_from shape. The proof also skips nothing by name, so no Core test is needed there.

The second gap refuses too much. A generic call whose type argument is known still counts its bound method as open dispatch. Probe deny_alloc_round marks total -[!Mem.Alloc]> and calls math.round(x) on a Float: E0921, though Float's rounding never allocates. A trait-value call is refused the same way, even when its only implementation is heap-free (probe deny_alloc_trait_free). A function passed as a value is followed (probe deny_alloc_value).

A, in full. A no-OS machine whose profile has no allocator puts an implied heap denial on the program's roots: run and each function an Output links, the roots TargetDenials uses. The heap proof runs once from each root. The per-literal E3303 check in Literals.jet is deleted, so only reached code is judged. Growth operations become heap events: list push, insert and append, map insertion, and text building.

A also seals dispatch, as the stack proof already does in a program build: a trait-value call may run any implementation the program holds, so the proof walks each one. Probe stack_trait_seal shows that seal naming the one implementation. A generic call on a known type walks just that type's method. Only a library checked alone stays open, and it gets no implied denial.

Placement under A. A finding inside the program's own package is shown at its own line, as today. A finding inside Core or another package is shown at the program's call where the path leaves the program's package. The note lists the path and the file and line that allocate. The same rule replaces both module_is_core tests in TargetDenials.jet (lines 74 and 91), so E1123 and E3301 place the same way. E3311 (capability rows) is outside this decision.

Cost. The proof is a breadth-first search that visits each reached function once (Checks.jet:3984-4011). Probe cost: a run that calls five core.math functions, checked six times with and without -[!Mem.Alloc]> on run and score. Both took about 240 ms each time (236 to 325 ms with the mark, 237 to 404 ms without), so no difference shows above noise.

B checks Core in place. The Core test is deleted. Core bodies the compile checks get E3303 and E3301 in Core's own files. Bodies checked up front (trait impls, close methods) are judged whether reached or not. Bodies taken from the stored Core record were checked without a machine, so B also needs that record split per machine.

C keeps the skip and publishes it. The Core test becomes a package-level field any package may set, for example target_neutral: true in package.jet, and Core sets it. Such packages are never checked against the selected machine.

Scale. Core has 205 panic lines whose message is a text template, out of 1272 panic lines; none are in Core/Math. Under A, a reached template allocates, so a heapless program that reaches one is refused at its own call. That is the truthful answer: on the chip the message could not be built.

options.name: One heap proof for every package, shown on the program's own line
options.detail:
A chip with no heap means the program promises not to use the heap, the same promise -[!Mem.Alloc]> makes. The compiler runs that existing proof from the program's start. It follows calls into Core and packages alike, with no exception by name.

A problem in the program's own code shows on its line, as today. A problem inside Core or a package shows on the program's call that leads there. The note shows each step of the path and the exact line that uses the heap.

Beginner path: nothing to write; the error names the call to change. Expert path: the same mark, -[!Mem.Alloc]>, proves any one function heap-free on any machine.
options.technical:
Delete the module_is_core test from sema_scope_environment_no_os and the per-literal E3303 checks in Literals.jet. When the selected machine is no-OS with no allocator fact, add an implied Mem.Alloc denial to each root (entry run and Output-linked functions) and run sema_effect_memory_project from it.

Report E3303 for that implied denial, and E0921 for a written one. Add heap events for growth: list push, insert and append, map insertion, and text building. In a program build, let sema_effect_memory_search take the targets sema_effect_stack_seal computes, and follow a node's instance_reaches, so no dispatch with known targets counts as open. The note names the implementation that uses the heap.

Place a finding whose owner is outside the entry package at the entry package's last call on the path, with a note naming the path and the event's file and line. Replace module_is_core at TargetDenials.jet:74 and :91 with the same entry-package test. UI snapshots: freestanding_core_reach_e3303 and memory_denial_core_path_e0921.

options.name: Check Core in place, like another package today
options.detail: The Core skip is deleted. Each Core body the compile checks gets the same per-line errors a package body gets, shown inside Core's source.
options.technical: Delete the module_is_core test from sema_scope_environment_no_os. Core bodies checked for the program's machine report E3303 and E3301 in Core files. Bypass the stored Core record on no-OS builds, or keep one record per machine, so stored bodies are checked too. TargetDenials and the heap proof are unchanged.

options.name: Keep the skip and let any package claim it
options.detail: Core keeps its skip, now as a package setting any package may claim. Packages that claim it are never checked against the selected machine.
options.technical: Replace module_is_core in sema_scope_environment_no_os with a package flag read from package.jet (target_neutral: true). Core's package row sets it. Document the field in the package manifest reference.

comparisons.note: An API marked @available for newer systems is refused at the caller's line, not inside the library. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/attributes/#available
comparisons.code: render()  // error: 'render()' is only available in macOS 13 or newer

comparisons.note: A no_std crate cannot name std; a dependency that uses std fails while that dependency compiles, inside its own source. Source: https://docs.rust-embedded.org/book/intro/no-std.html
comparisons.code:
#![no_std]
extern crate alloc; // only with a #[global_allocator]

comparisons.note: Functions that allocate take an Allocator argument, so the caller sees the need at its call. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Memory
A freestanding build has no malloc; a call to it fails only at link time, with no source line. Source: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/C-Dialect-Options.html

recommendation.why: A uses the heap proof Jet already has, for Core and packages alike, so no code is exempt by name and nothing new is walked. Each error lands where the programmer can act, with the full path.
gains: No exception for Core: Core is checked by the same proof as every package.
No new walk: the existing heap proof runs once per root, with no measurable cost (about 240 ms with or without it).
Errors land on the programmer's own line, and the note keeps the exact line that uses the heap.
Only reached code is judged, so an unused Core function never fails a build.
The written -[!Mem.Alloc]> mark gets the same fixes: growing lists count, generic and trait-value calls with heap-free targets pass, and its message points at a real line.

losses.loss: A package's heap or OS error is shown at the calling program's line instead of inside the package.
losses.mitigation: The note lists the path and the package's own line, and checking the package itself shows the error in place.

losses.loss: Counting list growth can refuse an existing -[!Mem.Alloc]> function that grows a list.
losses.mitigation: Each one breaks a promise it already made; the cutover fixes every such function in the repository.

whyNot.reason: B shows errors inside Core files the programmer cannot edit, judges Core code the program never reaches, and needs a stored Core copy per machine.
C keeps the hole: a heapless program can call code that needs a heap and hear nothing until it fails on the chip.

recommendation.tradeoff: A package's error moves to the caller's line with the full path, and broken heap promises now fail, in exchange for one proof that checks every package the same way.

In the Jet repository at a03eea6ac0, read Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Scopes.jet:561-562, Expressions/Literals.jet:485 and :607, and TargetDenials.jet:26-110 (Core tests at lines 74 and 91). Read the heap proof in Effects/Checks.jet: events at 3370-3418, sema_effect_memory_search at 3984-4011 and E0921 at 4924-4939.

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G3Core2/probe/b6144/. They are user_list, core_call, cost and eight heap probes: deny_alloc_core, _user, _direct, _value, _generic, _round, _trait_free, and stack_trait_seal. Run each with jet check main.jet. Add --target=board.sensor_v1 for user_list and core_call. The last five heap probes ran on the batch 8 compiler (a03eea6ac0). Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet --update.

surface.lesson: A heap is the memory a list grows into. Some chips have none. Jet refuses the program's own lists there but skips Core by name. Jet already has a proof that a function never uses the heap, and it already looks inside Core. Whichever option wins, Core functions that grow lists stay unusable on such chips.

wild.note: A missing platform API is refused on the caller's line. Source: Swift book, @available.

recommendation.why: One existing proof checks Core and packages alike, costs nothing measurable, and puts each error on the programmer's own line with the full path.
gains: No exception for Core.
No new walk.

losses.loss: Package errors move to the caller's line.
losses.mitigation: The note keeps the package's line; checking the package itself shows it in place.
