decisions.title: How code takes one type back out of a list of mixed values
decisions.situation: Some lists must hold values of different types chosen by other code. Log fields are the common case: log.info("saved", 14, "notes.txt", 120ms) carries an Int, a text and a Duration. Jet keeps such values in a list of a trait the types opt into, and printing each one works today. But the log writer wants one type back, to print a Duration as milliseconds, and Jet has no way to ask a trait value for its type. The vote decides how that question is written. We recommend a type arm: if field == .Duration(d) means "if this field is a Duration, call it d".
decisions.gist: A list holds values of different types. How does code ask "is this a Duration?" and get it back?
decisions.lesson: A Jet list holds one type. To mix types, the types opt into a shared trait, such as Field below. Printing each value already works. What Jet cannot do today is ask one item "are you a Duration?" and use it as a Duration. The options differ in how that question is written and when a wrong question is caught.
decisions.explainer: A Jet list holds one element type, so to mix 14, "hi" and a Point that type must fit all three. It can be a fixed set of types, a trait each stored type opts into, or Any under option E. A value held as a trait is a trait value. Under E or C, the type arm .Point(p) runs only for a stored Point and binds it as p; else takes the rest. Under option B a trait method returns the Point.
decisions.story: Lin writes the log writer for her team's service. Each log line carries extra fields: a user ID, a file name, how long the save took. She wants every field printed as is, except a Duration, which should print as milliseconds. Today she cannot take the Duration back out of the field list.
decisions.detail:
This ballot challenges a frozen wall: "no top type" stands among the walls in Docs/audits/whole-language-frame.md:32. Docs/audits/whole-language-audit-prompt.md:17 says such a challenge must carry worked code, the measured cost of the wall today, and a named amendment. The worked code is each option's program. Option E adds Any and needs the amendments below. Options B and C keep the wall.

D-ANY-JAI1 (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:751-754, card #169) has three parts. Heterogeneous varargs are trait-bounded, parts: ...Renderable. There is no top type, so general Any is rejected. Its ratified story, an inspector panel for game entities, is served by reflect.of, the read-only floor in Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:2550-2593. D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 (Tower card c3gdynamic, ratified 2026-06-30) also chose "No general Any", and rejected an Any gated to boundaries with an explicit downcast.

reflect.of needs no opt-in. Probe x10 keeps reflect.of of 14, "hi", a Point and 69.420 in one list. It prints each type name and value on O0, O1 and O2. Over a trait value it reports the internal key, module:14:…::Shown, not the stored type (n09, n13, #6845 c16). It cannot give a value back: the floor has no runtime type registry, and get, copy and equal stay declined (core-library.md:2589-2593).

E would supersede D-ANY-JAI1's no-top-type part and keep its varargs part and reflect.of. Ten more places would change. D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1's "No general Any" is superseded on Tower. D-UNIONTYPE1's sentence "Does not reopen D-ANY-JAI1" (line 765) is struck. D-TYPESWITCH1's "no Any type (D-ANY-JAI1 stands)" (lines 796-797) becomes "unions, or Any for an open set". The Dyn note's "(D-ANY-JAI1 stands)" (line 5355) is dropped; Dyn still holds data only.

Docs/spec/spec.md:7235-7236 leaves "Deliberately absent", and Any gets a spec section. Typed selection (syntax-decisions.md:1166-1169) says a checked downcast of a foreign value is not Jet syntax; it gains an exception for the checked case over an Any. The frozen wall loses "no top type". Card #744 c10, "D-ANY-JAI1 remains intact", is recorded as superseded. Docs/proposals/reflection-2026-11-04.md:66 points to D-PRIM-ANY1. Examples/Types/NoAnyAlternatives.jet is rewritten to say when Any beats an enum, a generic, ?T or Dyn.

An earlier draft offered A: the same Any, entered only through a written box, Any{value}. Its merit, from Docs/research/2026-11-09-any-type.md:253-256, is that an argument not written Any{...} is refused at compile time. The review rules allow three options, so A is kept as a variant of E in its design-away record. A keeps E's law cost, makes Any the only trait whose conversion is written, against S48, and Any{...} still accepts every value.

Option C keeps D-ANY-JAI1, D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1, reflect.of and the frozen wall, and amends two ratified sentences. D-TYPESWITCH1's "Run-time dispatch over mixed values uses unions" (line 796) becomes "uses unions, or type arms over a trait value". Typed selection's last clause (line 1169) gains "or held as a trait value and selected with a type arm". Its foreign-value clause is unchanged, since a trait value is a Jet value. Its loan rules (lines 1163-1166) apply to a type arm's binding as written.

C also extends D-UNIONTYPE1's member arm, .Point(p) (lines 760-762), to a trait subject, and "Does not reopen D-ANY-JAI1" stays true. spec.md:945-948 on trait values gains the type arm. E0305's sema texts change (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Patterns.jet:294, :338). So does its Prelude entry (Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:4702-4716): its safety reason, "would read the value's bytes as that type", and its expert path, "none", gain the checked arm.

C also amends spec.md:641-646, landed with dev a1c3325a65. Its first sentence keeps two same-named types as two members, each value keeping the member it was built as; C keeps it, and the leaf rule below relies on it. Its second sentence makes a bare .Point arm name neither member (E0305) and lets a table keep its else without E0641; its third offers named cases. C replaces both with the next paragraph's text, so one rule names a type over a union and a trait value (Patterns.jet:152-169).

"A bare .Point arm names the member Point names in type position there; a package's own Point is .Point(p) beside geo.Point. If Point names no type there, it names the one member whose leaf is Point. A generic's one instance takes its generic's name and leaf; two instances spell their arguments, .Box<Int>(b), as do generic arms over a trait value. Any other bare arm is E0305, offering .geo.Point(p). So every member has an arm; an else in a table is E0641."

So spec.md:903-905's rule, an else over a union is E0641, holds with no exemption. Coverage.jet:988-991 exempts two module members of one leaf today, but not two instances of one generic (f01b); C removes it. E0307's fix at Coverage.jet:521-523 names the arm each missing member takes, in place of "no arm can name" (a04, a04b, a09, f05, f06). E0641's fix offers each member's arm, never the internal tags .M_Box_Int_ it offers today (f01c, f01d, m33, #6839 c55).

Two agent notes are corrected. Docs/audits/2026-10-07-owner-notes-digest.md:113 says a trait value has no downcast. Docs/research/evidence-2026-09-29/3389-typed-selection.md:100-101 says a foreign downcast helper needs its own ballot; C is not foreign, and this ballot records it anyway.

C is not D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1's rejected option C. That option was a boxed Any that any value could become, with an explicit downcast at interop edges. Under option C no type exists that every value fits. A value enters a trait value only if its type opted into that trait, and an arm may name only such a type.

The wall's measured cost, counting each program's body: E's is five lines. B's open-set form is eleven (review probe x7): a three-line trait, three impl lines, one carrying a one-line override, and the five-line loop. C's is nine: a one-line empty trait, three empty impl lines and E's five lines (c1). B's named-enum form adds a five-line enum, writes .Num(14) for 14, and reads with an eight-line table (r8).

Jobs and today's answers on p210, the same on O0, O1 and O2. A type the caller picks uses D-TYPESWITCH1's generic type table: g1 prints 15 and hi, and a bare 2.5 takes the Decimal arm (x4). A known set uses a named enum: r8 prints the four lines, and f1 adds 2.5 as a Float payload. A single union value runs (b3, f2), but not as a generic function's parameter (a07c, #6839 c49); a union list is an internal compiler error (#6839 c26, r6).

An open set uses a user trait: x7 and b13 print every item and take the Point back. That holds for local and inline-module types (v01e). A file-module type in the user's trait passes checking, then stops ir.build with an internal compiler error, and a direct call is E0102 (v01, v01b, v01c). So B's and C's open set across files needs #6839 c39.

A call with mixed arguments, such as print or format (comment #111), uses D-ANY-JAI1's trait-bounded variadic with no box: x5 prints 14, Float{69.420}, hi and the Point. reflect.of inspects a concrete value (x10), and Dyn holds loose data (d1). Typed lookup by a type parameter, the clip's get_ini_field($T), is Dyn's decode<T> or Core/Encoding/Ini.jet:125-140's typed getters under every option.

D-LITCARRIER1=D (syntax-decisions.md:2107-2113) makes a bare 2.5 a Decimal and Float{2.5} a Float. A type table sends a bare 2.5 to its Decimal arm (x4). The ratified suffix 2.5f is not built; it gives E0134 (x2, #4730 c6). Float{69.420} enters a trait list and prints 69.42 (x6), and enters ...Printable varargs (x5). So the clip's 69.420, read as Jet reads it, is a Decimal.

A Decimal cannot enter a trait value today. With no impl, a bare 2.5 entering a trait list stops the compiler (x3), where a Bool gets E0112 (x12); #6727 c9 asks for E0112. impl Decimal.Shown {} is E0301 although spec.md:927-929 allows it (x1, #6839 c30). impl math.Decimal.Shown {} passes checking and crashes ir.build on "unlowered … type math.Decimal" (x1c, #6727 c9). A Decimal at a ...Printable bound gets a wrong E0904 (x5b, x5c, #6839 c30).

These defects fall on B and C, whose programs box a Decimal into a user trait; Float{69.420} works for them today (x6). Under E an Any holding 69.420 holds a Decimal, so .Decimal(d) matches it and .Float(f) does not. Whether boxing a Decimal into Any would share x1c's crash cannot be probed, since Any does not exist.

Under E, recovery is D-UNIONTYPE1's member test, .Point(p), extended to an open set. A table over an Any needs else, because types are an open set, as D-TYPESWITCH1 already requires for type tables. An Any holding a Dyn matches .Int(n) as the type Int, never as Dyn's Int case. A generic instance such as .Pair<Int, String>(p) does not parse today (E0003, g6). A list, an optional or a function value has no arm spelling, so it reaches else; Go's type switch names those types.

Option C lets a type arm test a trait value. In if item == .Point(p), item is a Shown value; the arm runs only when the stored type is Point, and binds it as p. The arm must name a type that implements Shown, and any other type is a compile error, as Go requires of its type switch cases. A table needs else, because another module may add an implementer; D-TYPESWITCH1's open-set rule already says so.

Over a trait value or a union, C's arm names a type as type position names it at that spot. A local type, or one imported with use geo.[Point] after use geo, is .Point(p). A type from another module is .geo.Point(p): the path after the dot, as the impl head impl Local.types.Named writes one (spec.md:3619-3622, D-IMPLDOT1). An arm through an alias names its target, as D-TYPESWITCH1 says of type tables.

Over a trait value the name resolves by scope, so a new module never changes an arm. Over a union, a name that type position does not know falls back to the one member with that leaf, as o7's arm does. A package's own Point is .Point(p) beside geo.Point; today only an else reaches it, binding nothing (a04b, f05). A name for a non-member type, or a leaf two members share with neither in scope, is E0305, naming both and .geo.Point(p) (v03, a09).

So where Point names a type, .Point(p) names it throughout the file, over a union or a trait value. Where it names none, each union's arm names that union's own Point member, as .Red names each enum's own case. Over Int | geo.Point and Int | geo2.Point, the same text binds geo.Point and geo2.Point (k01). Today E0305 offers named cases and spells a local member filestem.Point, which fails (a04c, #6839 c52). Mine(Point) | Theirs(geo2.Point) runs (f04), but changes the type and every construction site.

A named case is never ambiguous: its name is the union's own, as an enum case's is. A type of its name in scope leaves its arm alone, today and under C (z02), an imported one too (a06). So does a case carrying the same-named struct, Point(Point) | Int (a05). No member may share a named case's name (E0363).

This keeps today's bare arms that work, such as o7's .Point(p) over Int | geo.Point. Letting type position alone decide over a union would refuse that arm, since only geo is in scope; hence the leaf fallback. Three kinds of program change, all at compile time with a fix. The bare arms of v03 and m31b bind today; under C both are E0305. A union whose named case shares a member's leaf (y09d) becomes E0363. No working arm changes meaning: a04 and f03 are E0305 today.

Edge cases follow. A member imported with use geo.[Point], or an alias naming it, is the same type, so it is not ambiguous. An alias named Point for another type is E0305, as v03's local Point is. A qualified arm, .geo.Point(p) or .outer.inner.Point(p), is never ambiguous; today both fail (n03b, v11, #6839 c35). A generic member such as .Box(b) needs #6833 c3, which names that spelling over an Any, a union and a trait value (v05, k04).

Two instances of one generic, Box<Int> | Box<String>, share the leaf Box. Over Int | Box<Int> the bare .Box(b) names Box<Int>; today it is E0305 "doesn't belong", local or imported (v05, k04). Over boxes.Box<Int> | kit.Box with no Box in scope, two members have the leaf Box, so the bare .Box(b) is E0305 naming both. Today it binds kit.Box, and boxes.Box<Int> takes only the internal tag .M_Box_Int_ (m31, m31b, #6833 c5).

With two instances, each arm is .Box<Int>(b), and the bare .Box(b) is E0305 naming both. Today that arm also says "doesn't belong", and E0641's fix offers the internal tags .M_Box_Int_ | .M_Box_String_, which bind (f01-f01d). C refuses them with E0305, as it refuses the identity tag (a08, #6839 c55).

A named case whose name is a member type's leaf, as in Point(Int) | geo.Point, is refused with E0363, as D-ALT-CASES1 refuses Point(Int) | Point (y09b). A qualified member's name is its last segment, so this is D-ALT-CASES1 as written. Today that union is accepted and the bare .Point(n) binds the case (y09d, #6839 c43). spec.md:641-643 already calls geo.Point and map.Point two types named Point. y09b's E0363 is followed by an E0305 whose fix does not parse (z07, #6839 c47).

None of this spelling works everywhere today. With file modules, .Point(p) over Int | geo.Point runs, and an alias arm works in a type table (o7, o8i). With inline modules the bare arm is E0305 (n03a, n04), and use geo.[Point] is E0611 (n14, #4723 c12). The dotted arm .geo.Point(p) is E0107 with an empty name (n03b, o8a, #6839 c35). An alias in a union arm is E0305 (o1, o8e, #6839 c38). These are C's build criteria.

A worse defect sat under the spelling rule. On p207, with file modules, geo2.Point | map2.Point was accepted as one member, and a map2.Point{name: "harbor"} printed as Point { x: 35184415600640, y: 2 } (o8f, o8b). Dev a1c3325a65 fixed it: on p209 the union keeps two members, and the bare .Point(p) is E0305 naming both, with a named-case fix. spec.md:641-646 now says such an arm names neither member and a table keeps its else without E0641. #6839 c36 is met.

Inline modules have more naming gaps. A type-table arm cannot name geo.Point (E0608, o5b). An alias of an inline-module struct is not its target: a call says "wants geo.Point, but this is geo.Point" (o5c), and a type-table arm through it takes else (o5). The same alias works with a file module (o7, o8i). These are #6839 c37.

A stored enum whose case shares a type's name does not change the arm. Over a Shown value, .Point(p) names the type Point; a stored Item.Point(…) is an Item and takes an .Item(i) arm or else. A union behaves so today: over Item | Point, Item.Point(…) takes .Item (o6). No lint warns, since implementers change with the build and such a warning would come and go. Union clashes stay E0363, because a union is closed.

A union value passed as a trait value boxes the member it holds, with that member's own key, so .Int(n) matches a boxed Int. Every member must implement the trait; otherwise the call gets E0905. Boxing the union's own identity was rejected, since every member arm would then miss. Today the call is an internal compiler error (n01, #6839 c34).

An arm may not name a trait; that is E0305, with a fix pointing to the trait's methods. Testing for a second trait needs trait-to-trait conversion, an internal compiler error today (#6727 c7). Type tables refuse a trait arm too (n11, E0119), so both forms keep one rule. Go, Swift, Java, C# and Kotlin allow such a test; C can add it later as an arm, by its own decision, since #6727 c7 refuses that conversion under B and C.

A union may not hold a trait member: Shown | Int is refused at the type with E0363. E0363 already says an anonymous union holds concrete closed types, not trait objects (Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:5866-5880). A trait written by its name slips past that check today (v04, #6839 c40). The fix is a named enum, or a Shown value with Int implementing Shown.

E0363's check looks inside member types, including lists, maps, optionals, results, tuples, named cases and generic arguments (FailureLaw.jet:1540-1561). So c40's fix refuses [Shown] | Int and S(Shown) | Int too, as it already refuses a trait object or a function type there. [fn(Int) -> Int] | Int is E0363 today, then a cascade E0641 (z03, #6839 c48); [Shown] | Int is accepted (y10). The fix is a named struct holding the list, a closed member.

Accepting .Shown(s) as a member arm instead would put an open set inside a closed union. Then .Point(p) over Shown | Int would have two meanings, a member or a reach into the box; today it is E0305 (w06). So an arm naming a trait has no union exception.

D-TYPESWITCH1's identity rules apply to type arms. An alias is its target; a distinct type, F32 or Int? is not Int, so a stored UserID takes else (o5). The bare arm .Point -> runs the same test as .Point(_), as over a union today (o3). A Shown? subject takes no type arm, as (Int | Point)? takes none today (o4, E0305); unwrap it with Val(item) first (o4b).

Only named types implement traits (impl [Int].Shown is E0003, b6), so under C no unnameable value is ever stored; a list rides in a one-field struct (b7). A generic implementer such as Pair<Int, String> needs #6727 c6 to be stored and #6833 c3's arm spelling to be named. #6833 c3 names that spelling over an Any, a union and a trait value. Under E, #6727 c7 converts a trait value to Any keeping its inner key; under B and C it refuses the conversion (m43, m46).

An expert writes one generic function for a library: recover: fn<T: Shown>(item: Shown) -> T? from item, whose body is if item == .T(p) -> return Val(p), then None. The arm .T(p) names the type parameter, so each instance compares against its own type's key. The name take is reserved (E0003, n07b); recover is an ordinary name (o2). Today a type parameter in a type-table arm is E0119 (x8), and a trait method cannot take its own type parameter (x9).

recover returns a read view. The checker tracks it only while a plain local holds it: moving or changing the owner then is E0212 (w01b, w02b, y11, h01, h03, m01-m03). A value-producing if or table loses it, even with the call in a branch (h06, h08-h10). So does a lambda, struct, tuple, map, enum payload, list, defer, method value or Shared cell holding it, or a Shared owner (a01, a03b, e01-e09, h02, h05). A plain arm binding escapes too (e10, h11): the hole is the loan checker's, not C's.

A case payload already leaves this way through -> Point? from item: from an enum (w01), a union (w02) or a list (v07, v07b, v07c). The loan survives generic instantiation (y04, y05), and the view cannot be written (y11b).

What runs is not yet a pointer. At O0, a function under from item and the same function without it emit identical IR (y12). Each allocates a new 24-byte T? cell, copies the payload's bytes and retains its shared heap block; jet audit counts only the form without from as a copy. Rust's downcast_ref also returns a borrow, &T, but as a pointer with no allocation, and needs a 'static type.

So the copy is gone from direct use, not from the machine. Its address differs from the payload's on O0, O1 and O2: mem.address_of needs no audit gate (spec.md:3164-3166; z01, z01b). Through an escape its value differs too: with the owner rewritten, the held view still reads 41 (e11, h12, a03b). The ranking rests on b8, not on this: B's program copies too (b13), and a library trait's user cannot add B's method (b8, m41-m46).

A checked loan needs a lowering change and a complete loan checker. The lowering makes a T? from result a pointer into the owner's payload. A value converted at the call, or read through a Shared handle, lives in a cell released right after it (z04 IR; a03b IR op 70). That cell must outlive the result, or the call is E2305, as for a temporary. A path returning a value no owner holds (z05) keeps its own cell and a caller's drop, or is refused.

The checker must keep the owner borrowed through every holder: a lambda, local, stored or returned (#6839 c50), a Shared read (c51) and every carrier (c54). So must branch joins (c56; spec.md:1963-1965, 2057-2059, 2066-2069). Moving or rewriting the owner while a holder lives is E0212. No task receives the view, also inside a Shared cell (E1102: a02; e09 passes today). Every from result and arm binding needs this: #6839 c46, after c50, c51, c54 and c56 (y12, z01b, z04, z05, a01, a03b, e01-e11, h02, h05, h06-h12).

Other subjects follow the enum rules. A temporary subject's view cannot leave its statement (E2305: y06b, y06c). A && subject moves the payload out with no from (y07); a from clause naming a && parameter is accepted, then its call gets a misleading E0209 (y07b, #6839 c45). An arm over a & subject binds read-only, as an enum's does (y08, E0205 blaming item: #6839 c44). So C has no downcast_mut analogue.

A copy is written, Val(p.copy()), with no from clause, and the caller owns it (w04). Today an unmarked Val(p) of a read value with no from clause also copies (n15b, v08); a bare return is E0120 and a take E0201 (v08, v08b). #6839 c41 refuses that hidden copy, since Jet never hides a clone (spec.md:1892-1895). A Val(p) under a from clause naming its owner stays a view; c41 spares it.

B's trait method can lend the same way, point: fn(self) -> Point? from self (w03). On p209 the loan was not tracked through dispatch: the list moved or changed while the result lived (w03b, w03c), and the result was a copy (y01). Dev c1fca7426c, in batch p210, tracks it: w03b, w03c and y01 are E0212 on O0, O1 and O2 (#6839 c42; the copy remains c46's). B's shared program copies with self.copy() (b13). C needs no c42: a trait value's loan without dispatch is tracked (y03, y05).

Today C's program fails at the arm with E0305 on O0, O1 and O2 (c1, and c3 for a table), plus a cascade E0107 on the arm's binding (#6839 c53). Its other lines compile, but a value of a trait with no methods prints as an empty line (c2, c2b, #6845 c15). The box already stores its type key at offset 0 and the payload at offset 8 (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTraits.jet:332-354, :457).

The arm adds no storage and no allocation. An arm loads the 8-byte key, compares it with a constant and views the payload behind it; q1's 32-byte struct sits at offset 8 of its 40-byte box (q1 IR). The key is the first 56 bits of a SHA-256 of the type's identity, plus one (BuildTraits.jet:9-28). The key depends on that identity alone. recover's T? result allocates its own cell today, as the copy form's does (y12 IR, O0).

Today a key collision panics (BuildTraits.jet:21-24). #6845 c18 makes it a registered diagnostic naming both types, as the collect-all rule requires. C needs c18, since the key is what an arm tests.

A table of N type arms costs up to N compares, where a union's tag can switch. C's compiler work is the pattern checker, the IR compare, the arm spelling for qualified, imported and alias names, union-to-trait boxing, the spec and an example. It also changes E0305's texts and Prelude entry and E0307's and E0641's fixes, and removes the E0641 exemption (Coverage.jet:521-523, :988-991). A beginner writes the .Point(p) they already use for unions; an expert writes one recover<T> for a library.

Declarations are public by default, and priv is the only hiding form (spec.md:3509-3512, 3568-3569). So under C a caller can arm any public type a library stores behind its trait values. The library then cannot change that type without breaking those arms. Go's errors blog names the cost: "wrapping an error makes that error part of your API" (go.dev/blog/go1.13-errors). Its errors.As still "behaves like a type assertion", C's mechanism.

Two remedies were weighed. A signed marker, #!Debug (spec.md:953-954), opts a type out of a derivable trait. Using one to seal type arms would add a second hiding form beside priv, against spec.md:3568. Rust 1.86 asks the trait's author to opt in with an Any supertrait; that would bring back B's loss for every library trait whose author did not opt in. C keeps priv as the one hiding form.

A priv type cannot be named outside its package, or outside its module when declared inside one (S18, syntax-decisions.md:2531-2538). So a type arm cannot reach it, and it takes else. From a file module a priv struct is refused today, though with E0119 where E0605 belongs (o8d, #4723 c13). Inside an inline module it leaks with no diagnostic (n12, n12b, #4723 c11). print and reflect.of already show a library's concrete type and name (n05), so C adds recovery, not disclosure.

B checks at compile time that a type opted in: a String with no impl is E0905 (b9e). Taking a type back needs a trait method per type, as point() does in x7. That bites only for values a library hands over already boxed as its own trait: the user cannot add a method there, and .Point(p) is E0305 (b8). For the user's own trait, a method gives back any type (b13). B's matching gain is control: a library decides which types callers take back.

The library trait's user has no other route. A free type table sees only the trait, so a library Point takes else (m41). Adding a method to the library trait from outside is E0003, and a second impl of it is E0902 (m42, m45). A trait of the user's, implemented for the library's Point, would reach it only through a conversion that keeps the key. That conversion is an internal compiler error today (m43, m46), and #6727 c7 refuses it under B and C.

One constraint holds for every option and is stated once. A stored type the reader did not plan for reaches else under E and C, and has no method under B. Probe r7 stores a Point3 and prints found a Point: false on O0-O2. Full compile-time checking of recovery comes only from a closed set: a table over the named enum that forgets .At is E0307 (b12).

What Any would gain is real. Under E no stored type needs an impl line, so the clip's Table(string, Any) works with no declarations. A list, an optional or a closure goes in without a wrapper struct, though taking one back needs an arm spelling (#6833 c3). Comment #4 calls this the case where sum types are clumsy. B and C pay one impl line per stored type.

Prerequisites differ by option. Trait-value printing, #6845 c13, is met (x7, r9), so print(item) works for every option. Every trait value carries a key, so every option needs #6845 c18. E needs generic trait values (#6727 c6) and trait-to-trait conversion (#6727 c7). B's and C's open set across files needs #6839 c39, and c6 only if a generic type opts in. A bare Decimal needs #6727 c9 and #6839 c30 under B and C.

C also needs the type arm and its spelling rules (#6833 c3 and c5, #6839 c35, c37, c38, c43, c47, c52 and c55, #4723 c12-c13). It needs union-to-trait boxing (#6839 c34), a trait member refused in a union with one report (#6839 c40, c48) and no hidden copy in Val (#6839 c41). Its view must keep its loan through every holder (#6839 c50, c51, c54, c56). It needs private types enforced (#4723 c11) and empty-trait printing (#6845 c15).

Today every option allocates per stored value. A conversion to a trait value allocates a heap box and copies the payload, read arguments included: a 32-byte struct allocates 40 bytes and copies 32 (q1). A union argument allocates 24 bytes (b3 IR), and a named-enum list allocates per element (b4 IR). A union or enum has a known size and can be stored inline, while a trait value or an Any needs a box or a bounded inline buffer.

Odin's any is a data pointer and a type ID, and a literal passed to it lives in the caller's stack frame. A written box, A's variant, would show the allocation that E hides. Inline storage for small values is G11 work for every trait value, proved by a paired cell. O1 and O2 IR could not be read, because jet emit refuses both with E2102.

Closed-world dispatch is today's implementation, not law: BuildTraits.jet stops on an unknown key at jet_rt_unreachable. D-LIB-DYNTRUST1=A ratifies loadable .jetlib libraries, pinned to one compiler identity, with a checked export table (Docs/spec/reference/library-reuse-and-linking.md:116-139). An Any from a loaded library (E) and a type arm on a loaded trait value (C) need type identity shared across libraries. A trait value (B) needs the same dispatch. This is #3102 c17.

Defects found on the way are filed apart from this ballot. Trait-to-trait conversion and a closure in a trait list are internal compiler errors (#6727 c7, c8). The Decimal defects are #6727 c9 and #6839 c30, and 2.5f is #4730 c6. Reviews 4-11 filed #4723 c11-c13, #6839 c34-c58, #6845 c16-c18 and #3102 c17. The empty-trait print is #6845 c15, [Printable]{14} is #6839 c32, and x9 is #6839 c31.

If E wins, #6833 c3 carries three build duties: generic arguments in member arms, unnameable types reaching else, and the provenance diagnostic for a view of a local escaping through Any. If C wins, it carries the first and third for trait values and unions, and #6833 c5 carries the arm spelling rules above. Today a read trait value returned as-is is E0120 (l1). #6833 c4 holds E's diagnostic snapshot for the extended member test. C's refusals are snapshotted under #6839 c35, c38 and c40.

If B or C wins, E0119 on the name Any should point to an enum, a trait or reflect.of. Today fn(value: Any) says only "There's no type called Any" (x11, #6839 c33). E0350, which once named D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1, is retired (Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:5563). The adversarial review is Docs/audits/any-type-info-pointer-2026-11-15.md, from mining run any-NXt-20261115. Recall audits 1 and 2 failed and the run was re-mined after each; audits 3-11 passed, audit 11 (seed 14666) matching 125 concepts with no miss.

options.name: Any with implicit conversion
options.detail: Any is a Core trait every type implements, so a value converts to it implicitly, as to every trait. print shows the concrete value, and the type arm .Point(p) tests the stored type and binds it. The intended output is 14, hi, Point { x: 1, y: 2 } and 1. Today this stops at the first item with E0112, because no type is called Any (probe e1). It also needs #6727 c6 and c7.
options.technical: Sema adds the Core trait and records each type the program converts to Any. The dispatch switch must cover those types, every implementer of a trait value converted to Any, and every generic instance converted inside generic code. Converting a trait value keeps its inner key; ir_trait_box already returns a trait value unchanged. The pattern checker extends D-UNIONTYPE1's member test to an Any subject and requires else. Build duties sit on #6833 c3.

options.name: No Any: fixed lists, and trait methods to take a type back
options.detail: No Any; D-ANY-JAI1 stands. A known set uses a named enum, the documenting form D-UNIONTYPE1 keeps, and a table that forgets a case is E0307 (probe b12). An open set uses a user trait: print(item) shows each value, and a default point() returns None except in Point's impl. The program prints the four lines twice on O0, O1 and O2 on p210 (probe b13). A union list, the other known-set form, is an internal compiler error today (#6839 c26).
options.technical: No compiler change. The trait value boxes as spec.md:945-946 says. A type with no impl is refused where it enters: a String gets E0905 (probe b9e). Taking a type back needs a trait method per type. For the user's own trait that works (b13); a library trait's user cannot add one, and .Point(p) over it is E0305 (b8, m41-m46). A library decides which types callers take back. A Decimal entering the trait needs #6727 c9 and #6839 c30; Float{69.420} works (x6).

options.name: No Any: type arms over a trait value
options.detail: No Any; D-ANY-JAI1 and D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 stand. Each stored type opts into a trait with one empty line, and print(item) shows each value. The type arm .Point(p) tests the trait value's stored type and binds it, with else required in a table. Each arm must name a type that implements the trait; a type from another module is .geo.Point(p). The intended output is E's. Today the arm is E0305 (probe c1), and an empty trait's value prints as an empty line (c2, #6845 c15).
options.technical: The pattern checker accepts a type arm over a trait value when the named type implements the trait, resolving the name as type position does, and requires else in a table. IR loads the box's type key at offset 0, compares it with the arm type's key, and binds a read view, which recover<T> returns under from item. The arm adds no storage or allocation. A union passed as a trait value boxes its member (#6839 c34). An arm naming a bounded type parameter compares against each instance's key.

recommendation.why: C asks the question in one checked arm, for any trait, without adding a type every value fits.
gains: The same arm form as enums: .Duration(d).
Arms are checked when compiling.

losses.loss: Needs compiler work first.
losses.mitigation: B's form runs today and stays valid.

losses.loss: A caller can depend on which types a library stores.
losses.mitigation: A table needs else, and a private type cannot be named in an arm.

whyNot.reason: With Any, a wrong question is found only when the program runs.
B needs a method per type, and a library's users cannot add one.

recommendation.tradeoff: Compiler work buys checked type questions without Any.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: AnyReview11. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation on p210: every route from a user to a library trait's type stayed closed, and every move of a view's owner was refused. It repaired the generic arm rule for boxes.Box<Int> | kit.Box and tied B's loss to #6727 c7.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Probes ran on the p210 batch compiler (dev 7f902dd915) at $JET_STATE_ROOT/lander3-tmp/gate-p210/tree/Compiler/JetCli/.jet/build/jet. Its identity is jet@a0.0.45#8e7e97c2b52745d37c75a7c6a78688ef33bc908c74df3d3499e197dea8dea508, in the IDENTITY file beside the binary. Set JET_COMPILER_IDENTITY to it and unset JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT. The tiers are flags: -O0, -O1 and jet build -O2; --optimize=basic does not exist (E2102). Every file line number cited (spec.md, core-library.md, BuildTraits.jet and the rest) is at dev 7f902dd915; Tower criteria are quoted as they stood on 2026-11-16.

Every probe this ballot cites, the eleven reviews' probes included, is in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/AnyBallot/probes. Run ./run.sh NAME.jet there. It writes NAME.p210.out (jet run -O0), NAME.p210.O1.out (jet run -O1) and NAME.p210.O2.out (jet build -O2, then the binary), each ending in its exit code. MODE=emit FLAGS=--ir writes O0 IR as NAME.p210.ir.out. All three tiers matched for every probe.

Every probe also matched its p209 output (NAME.p209.out, dev a1c3325a65), except five. w03b, w03c, y01 and y02 are E0212 on p210, which carries #6839 c42's check (dev c1fca7426c); y01's IR is p209's. n05's reflect.of now names the private type Secret, not M3LibSecret. On p209 and p210, o8b, o8f and vf f are E0305 (c36, met); their p207 outputs record the old defect. y09b's E0363 now has a cascade E0305 (#6839 c47).

File-module probes are named by folder: ./run.sh o7_file_module/main.jet, o8_file_modules/NAME.jet, vf/NAME.jet or fm/NAME.jet. Their outputs sit beside the others, as o7_file_module, o8X_file_NAME, vf_NAME and fm_NAME.

Re-run b13 for B; c1, c2, c2b and c3 for C; e1 for E. For C's arm spelling re-run n03a, n03b, n04, n14, o1, o7, o8a, o8b, o8e, o8f, o8h, o8i, v03, v11 and w07. For privacy re-run n05, n12b and o8d. Re-run r7 and b12 for the shared fall-through and the closed set, x10 and n09 for reflect.of, and x3, x4, x6, x1, x1c and x5b for Decimal. If an option wins, re-run its program with the built feature on every tier.

Unprobed edges: a comptime value as an Any, a move-only resource in an Any or a trait value, a key collision (source reading only, #6845 c18), and executing the web build. Also unprobed: O1 and O2 IR (jet emit refuses both, E2102), and key stability across builds that add a module. z06 lends a Close enum payload under from; it closes once.

surface.gist: A list holds values of different types. How does code ask "is this a Duration?" and get it back?
surface.lesson: A Jet list holds one type. To mix types, the types opt into a shared trait, such as Field below. Printing each value already works. What Jet cannot do today is ask one item "are you a Duration?" and use it as a Duration. The options differ in how that question is written and when a wrong question is caught.

options.gist: Every value fits in Any with no opt-in, and a type arm takes it back.
gains: No opt-in lines.

options.gist: The trait gets one method per type code wants back.

options.gist: The arm .Duration(d) asks a trait value for its type and binds it.

decisions.title: C library features Jet leaves out on purpose: floating-point flags, thread attributes, signal masks and message queues
decisions.situation: The C standard library is the toolbox every C program on Linux uses. Jet is replacing it with its own Core library, and a census lists each C function and the Jet call that does its job. Thirteen groups still have no Jet counterpart, because C threads, signals and arithmetic work differently from Jet's. For example, C sets a hidden overflow flag after a multiplication, while Jet shows the overflow in the result itself. Someone porting a C program meets these gaps first. You are asked whether Jet should copy these thirteen groups or say plainly that Jet does not need them, naming the Jet way for each. We recommend naming the Jet way and not copying them.
decisions.gist: Should Jet copy thirteen C library groups that clash with how Jet works, or say they are not needed and point to the Jet way?
decisions.lesson: A new kitchen does not need a part for every gadget of the old one. If the new oven has a built-in timer, the old clip-on timer is not missing. Jet does many C jobs in another place: an overflow shows in the value itself, and a task is stopped by cancelling it. This vote decides whether those old parts are copied anyway.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. libc is the C standard library. A census is a list of every libc function and its Jet counterpart. A task is Jet's unit of concurrent work, like a C thread. A signal is a message the operating system sends to a process, such as Ctrl-C. A mask blocks some signals for a while. A floating-point flag is a hidden note C keeps when arithmetic overflows or loses precision.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a C tool that checks an overflow flag after a long calculation, and that stops a worker thread with pthread_kill. Under A the census row for fetestexcept says to check the result with math.is_inf or math.is_finite. The row for pthread_kill says to call cancel on the task. Ravi writes those two lines. Under B Ravi finds core.sys.fenv and a per-task kill call, which only some machines support, and the rest of Jet never sets or reads them.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The owner's 2026-11-08 rule (Q18) is parity coverage: each libc gap is either filled with idiomatic Jet, or carries an owner ruling that Jet does not need it. Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet lists 277 families; 33 are GAP. This ballot covers the thirteen whose C shape clashes with a Jet rule. The other GAP families are being filled: complex and Bessel functions, run-once, task-local storage, semaphores, read-write locks, descriptor duplication, terminals, sockets, shared memory, fences and pthread_atfork.

The thirteen families follow, each with the Jet way its row would name.

1. fenv.h exception flags (feclearexcept and six more). There are no sticky flags: the result carries the fact (math.is_inf, math.is_nan, math.is_finite), and checked integer arithmetic stops on overflow.

2. fenv.h rounding and environment (fegetround, fesetround and eight more). Jet fixes round-to-nearest-even; directed rounding is math.floor, math.ceil, math.trunc and Decimal's rounding modes.

3. pthread_attr_*. A task takes no attributes; stack and placement belong to the runtime.

4. pthread_getschedparam, pthread_setschedparam and pthread_setschedprio. There is no per-task priority; the scheduler is fair.

5. pthread_mutexattr_*, the prioceiling calls and pthread_mutex_consistent. Jet has one lock kind (tasks.lock), with no robust, priority-ceiling or process-shared locks.

6. pthread_condattr_*. Deadlines use the monotonic clock, and conditions are not shared between processes.

7. pthread_spin_*. Use tasks.lock; whether to spin is the runtime's choice.

8. pthread_kill. A task handle's cancel() stops one task.

9. sigprocmask and the sigset family (sigaddset through sigaltstack). Signals arrive as values through process.signals, so nothing needs blocking.

10. posix_spawnattr_getsigmask and setsigmask. These follow item 9.

11. mqueue.h. Use channels inside a process, and pipes or sockets between processes.

12. fmtmsg. Use core.log.

13. gethostid. core.sys.hostname and core.sys.uname name the machine; libc's 32-bit host id is neither stable nor unique.

pthread_atfork is not in this ballot, because core.sys.fork exists.

Under A each row becomes coverage NotNeeded, with a note citing the owner ruling on #6696 and naming the Jet way. LibcCensus.jet already checks that a NotNeeded note cites the ruling.

options.name: Say not needed, and name the Jet way
options.detail: The thirteen groups stay out of Jet. Each census row says not needed and names the Jet call that does the job.
options.technical: In Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet, set coverage .NotNeeded on the thirteen GAP rows (fenv x2, pthread_attr, schedparam, mutexattr, condattr, spin, pthread_kill, sigset, spawnattr sigmask, mqueue, fmtmsg, gethostid). Each note cites 'owner ruling on #6696' and names the Jet API. No Core change.

options.name: Copy them into Core
options.detail: Core gets a floating-point flag module, thread attribute records, signal masks and message queues, with the C names translated.
options.technical: Add core.sys.fenv (test, clear, raise, round mode), task attribute records, a per-task signal call, sigset values with process masks, and POSIX message queues as runtime rows on Linux. Every engine must save and restore the floating-point state around task switches, and the web engine has none of them.

comparisons.note: std has no fenv, no signal masks and no thread priorities; the libc crate exposes raw calls.
No floating-point flags, goroutines take no attributes, and os/signal delivers signals on a channel.

recommendation.why: Each of these jobs already has one Jet way, and copying the C shape would add a second mechanism that most engines cannot honour.
gains: One mechanism per job: overflow in the value, cancel for tasks, signals as values.
Every census row still names where the job is done.

losses.loss: A C program ported line by line has no same-named call for these thirteen groups.
losses.mitigation: The census row for each C name prints the Jet call to use, so the porter finds it from the C name.

whyNot.reason: B adds hidden global state and second mechanisms, Linux-only rows the web engine cannot support, and task-switch costs for every program.

recommendation.tradeoff: No same-named C calls for thirteen groups, in exchange for one Jet way per job on every engine.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Use the Jet repository at 81b426cf46. Run JET=<jet> jet Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet from the root and read its Gaps by area section. The thirteen families are the GAP rows at LibcCensus.jet lines 120, 121, 257, 281, 284, 296, 297, 301, 304, 306, 334, 359 and 376.

Check that Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows exports core.math is_inf, core.tasks lock, core.process signals, core.log, and core.sys hostname, uname and fork. A task handle's cancel() is used at tests/run/Concurrency/StopBoundaries.jet:82. Option A's program prints overflowed. Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.

surface.lesson: C keeps hidden flags, thread settings and signal masks. Jet does those jobs elsewhere: an overflow shows in the value, and a task is stopped by cancelling it.

current.note: Today the census lists these groups as gaps with no answer.

wild.note: Go has no float flags and delivers signals on a channel.

options.name: Name the Jet way
options.gist: Each group is marked not needed, with the Jet call to use.
gains: One way per job.

losses: No same-named C calls.

proposed.code:
if math.is_inf(big) -> print("overflowed")

options.name: Copy them
options.gist: Core gains flag, attribute, mask and queue calls.
gains: C code ports name for name.
losses: Hidden global state.
Linux-only calls.

recommendation.why: Each job already has one Jet way, and the copies would be second mechanisms most engines cannot honour.
gains: One way per job.
The census still names each answer.

losses.loss: No same-named C calls for these groups.
losses.mitigation: Each census row names the Jet call.

whyNot.reason: Hidden state, second mechanisms and Linux-only calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: No C names for thirteen groups, for one Jet way everywhere.

decisions.title: Whether a distinct type codes as its base without a marker
decisions.situation: A distinct type such as TaskID: distinct String is its own type over a base, String here. Today it has a wire form only if it carries #CodableAsBase, the marker D-CAPBUNDLE1 gave it in 2026-07. A #Codable struct with an unmarked TaskID field fails jet check with E2411 on that field. Its fix line says to add #[Codable] to TaskID, which is accepted but still fails. The ratified web app shape (D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1 A) writes model.jet with unmarked TaskID and ProjectID fields inside #Codable records, and card #6819 c1 asks for that to work. This vote decides how a distinct type gets its base's wire form. Under A it does by default, the way a qualifying plain struct already gets a codec (D-AUTODERIVE1 E). Under B it keeps needing the marker. Under C it forwards every trait its base derives, printing and ordering included. We recommend A.
decisions.gist: Does a distinct type such as TaskID: distinct String get its base type's wire form by default, or only with #CodableAsBase?
decisions.lesson: A default that a plain struct already follows should also cover a distinct type over a codable base. Otherwise typed IDs, the common case on the wire, need a marker that adds no meaning.
decisions.explainer:
A distinct type is a new type with the same values as its base. TaskID: distinct String holds text, but a TaskID cannot be passed where a ProjectID is wanted.

A wire form, or codec, is how a value becomes JSON and back. #Codable asks for both directions; #Encode and #Decode ask for one.

Since D-AUTODERIVE1 E, a plain struct or enum whose fields all have a wire form gets one without a marker. #!Codable opts a type out, and the auto_derive lint can deny the default in a package.

#CodableAsBase is the marker that gives a distinct type its base's wire form today: a TaskID is written as the String it holds.
decisions.story: The web app model from the ratified shape: two distinct ID types and a #Codable Task that holds them, sent to and from the browser as JSON. The same file is written under each option.
decisions.inWild: Rust's serde needs #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] on each newtype. serde_json then writes a newtype struct such as struct TaskId(String) as its inner value. #[serde(transparent)] matters mainly for other formats and for wrappers with named fields. Kotlin's kotlinx.serialization needs @Serializable on a value class, which then encodes as its one property. Go encodes a defined type such as type TaskID string as its underlying type with no annotation. Swift's Codable needs a conformance on each wrapper type. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
Today, on dev 26afb1a0e6 with the gate-p62 jet, a #Codable struct with an unmarked distinct Int or distinct String field is E2411 twice on the field. One error is for serializing and one for decoding. With #CodableAsBase on the distinct type, json.to_string and json.decode<Task> round-trip {"id":7,"name":"a"}.

With #Codable on the distinct type instead, jet check accepts the marker and still gives E2411 on the field. The parser keeps only bundle markers on a distinct type (parser_distinct_marker_derives in JetParser Declarations/Types.jet). It drops an auto-derive marker silently, so the fix line's advice does not work. A staged fix (GoalsB-1-e2411-distinct-fix) makes that fix line name #CodableAsBase for now.

A hand-written codec on an unmarked distinct type already works. With impl TaskID.Encode and impl TaskID.Decode written by hand, a #Codable record prints {"id":"0193a5e0"}. Decoding "t1" is refused with [at `id`: not a UUIDv7: t1]. A range-bounded distinct Int(1..10) marked #CodableAsBase refuses 11 as a field error, not a panic.

Spec: spec.md says a distinct type forwards only the traits it names (D-CAPBUNDLE1), and syntax-decisions.md says #CodableAsBase exposes base coding. Equality already comes with every distinct type whose base has it. The web app shape proposal (A.6 finding 1, TR4) records that the checked crewboard files had to drop #Codable from Logic, because no distinct ID derives a codec.

Edge cases are written under each option.

options.name: A distinct type codes as its base by default
options.gist: A distinct type whose base has a wire form gets the base's wire form with no marker. #!Codable opts out; #CodableAsBase retires.
options.detail:
A distinct type follows D-AUTODERIVE1 E for coding. When its base has a wire form, the distinct type has the same one, written as the base value. It needs no marker as a field, a list element or a top-level value (json.to_string(id)).

The default holds for an imported distinct type too. A #Codable record in the UI package that holds logic.ProjectID codes it with no marker, so the cross-package codec facts include distinct types. #!Codable on the distinct type opts it out. A package that denies auto_derive must mark it #Codable, which on a distinct type now means base coding.

Printing, ordering and Debug keep D-CAPBUNDLE1: a distinct type forwards them only when it names them (#Printable, #Comparable), as the ratified model.jet does. Only the wire form gets the default, because an ID needs it to cross a boundary. Printing and ordering change what a program shows and allows; option C defaults them too.

A hand-written codec wins over the default, the same rule as for structs (SerdeItems.jet: an unmarked hand codec stays the only one). An ID type that must refuse some base values writes impl TaskID.Decode with its own check. It needs no marker or opt-out. This is how #3709 c23 is met: an ID decoder accepts only UUIDv7 text, so "t1" in a crafted request is refused with 422.

Nested: Inner: distinct Int and Outer: distinct Inner both code as an Int. A base with no wire form (a #!Codable struct, a function) gives none. A #Codable record holding it is E2411 at the field, and the fix line names the base.

Decode errors are the base's errors at the same path: "id": "x" for a distinct Int is the Int decode error at $.id. A range-bounded distinct such as distinct Int(1..10) decodes through its checked conversion, so 11 is a decode error at the field, not a panic.

E2411 changes with the rule. Its Why line no longer says that only types that opt in have a wire form, which is already untrue for structs since D-AUTODERIVE1 E. It names the type in the path that has none instead. Its union-member fix text stops naming #CodableAsBase.

#CodableAsBase becomes redundant and retires in one cutover. After it, the marker is the plain E0927 (jet.UnknownAppliedRule: "#CodableAsBase isn't a known applied rule"). That is the generic error for any marker the registry does not hold, with no teaching text (D-LANG-MIGRATE1). The rewrite registered in jet fix deletes the marker and is the migration route. The Core and repository sweep comes first, per the tightened-rule rule.

The cutover changes 33 tracked files on dev 26afb1a0e6. Compiler has 14: JetCli SyntaxDictionaryData, JetDriver CoreReach, and JetFoundation PreludeMarkers, DiagnosticRows (the E2411 union fix text), OwnedTraitRows, OwnedTraits and its test. The rest of Compiler is JetSema Derives, Items, SerdeItems and DistinctForwardSourceFixtures, and Prelude Markers, Traits and Diagnostics.

Outside Compiler: Examples/Types (2), tests (9: 4 cases rows, 3 ui files, 1 fuzz file) and Docs/spec (2). Then the generated Docs/site E2411 page, Tools/editors (4 grammars) and one Tools/agent-eval facts file. The other 10 files that name it are dated audits and the Tower store, which stay as history.

options.name: Keep the marker: #CodableAsBase on each distinct type
options.gist: A distinct type codes as its base only with #CodableAsBase, as today. The card and the proposal's model.jet add the marker to each ID type.
options.detail:
D-CAPBUNDLE1 stays as ratified: a distinct type forwards only the traits it names. Every ID type that crosses the wire carries #CodableAsBase. #6819 c1 is amended to say so, and the web app shape's model.jet adds the marker to TaskID and ProjectID.

A hand-written impl TaskID.Encode or impl TaskID.Decode wins and needs no marker, as today. So an ID type that must refuse "t1" (#3709 c23) writes its own decoder under B too.

The E2411 fix line names #CodableAsBase for a distinct type (the staged fix). Its Why line says a distinct type has a wire form only with that marker or a hand codec. That replaces the stale "only types that opt in have a wire form". #Codable written on a distinct type becomes an error that names #CodableAsBase, so the marker that looks right but does nothing stops being accepted.

Nested: Outer: distinct Inner needs its own #CodableAsBase, and Inner must have a wire form. A base with no wire form is E0905 at the marker, naming the trait and the base. Decode errors are the base's errors at the same path, and a range-bounded distinct decodes through its checked conversion, as under A.

options.name: A distinct type forwards every trait its base derives
options.gist: A distinct type gets its base's Printable, Debug, Comparable, Encode and Decode by default; #!Trait opts one out. #CodableAsBase retires, and #Printable and #Comparable on a distinct type become redundant.
options.detail:
A distinct type follows D-AUTODERIVE1 E for every auto-derivable trait. Printable, Debug, Comparable, Encode and Decode come from the base when the base has them, as Equatable already does today. #!Printable, #!Comparable or #!Codable on the distinct type opts one out. A package that denies auto_derive names the traits it wants.

#Numeric stays a marker: operators are what a distinct type exists to withhold, and structs do not derive them either. A hand-written implementation wins, as under A, so a validating ID decoder is impl TaskID.Decode (#3709 c23). The default reaches imported distinct types as under A. Decode errors, nesting and range-bounded bases behave as under A.

C supersedes more of D-CAPBUNDLE1 than A. #CodableAsBase retires with the same plain E0927, the same jet fix route and the same 33-file cutover. #Printable and #Comparable on a distinct type become redundant too. The jet fix rewrite deletes them, which adds every file that writes them on a distinct type to the sweep, the ratified model.jet included.

Edge cases: every ID prints and sorts by its base value with no marker. That suits logs and stable listings. But a sort or a < over IDs then compiles where the author meant no order. A distinct type over a sensitive String prints it unless it opts out with #!Printable.

recommendation.why: Typed IDs on the wire are the common case in every app the web shape describes, and a struct of codable fields already codes with no marker. A makes a distinct type follow the same codec default, so the ratified model.jet checks as written and a typed ID never needs a marker to cross the wire. Printing and ordering stay opt-in, because they change what a program shows and allows.
gains: The ratified model.jet checks as written, with no codec marker on its ID types
The codec follows the struct default (D-AUTODERIVE1 E); Printable and Comparable forwarding stay per D-CAPBUNDLE1
A marker retires instead of a new one being taught

losses.loss: A distinct type made to keep a value apart, such as a token over String, now has a wire form unless its author opts out.
losses.mitigation: #!Codable opts it out, and the auto_derive lint can deny the default per package. The ratified model keeps secrets as #Secret String, not as distinct types (proposal line 574: webhook_secret: #Secret String?). A #Secret field is refused on the wire today: a #Codable struct with a #Secret String field is E2411 on that field (probed with the gate-p62 jet).

losses.loss: It amends ratified D-CAPBUNDLE1, which said a distinct type forwards only the traits it names.
losses.mitigation: Only coding changes; ordering, printing and arithmetic still need their markers, so the forwarding rule stays for every trait that changes behaviour.

losses.loss: It costs a compiler change and a sweep. The codec check, the derived codec for a distinct type in its own and importing packages, and the E2411 text change. jet fix removes #CodableAsBase from 33 tracked files.
losses.mitigation: The derived codec already exists for #CodableAsBase (SerdeItems.jet sema_serde_items_distinct_codec); A makes it the default and deletes the marker path. The source sweep is one jet fix run; the Compiler rows are listed under A.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a marker on every ID type that only says the type may be written as its base. A plain struct never needs one, yet the ratified model.jet and every app built from it would carry it.

C also makes every ID print and order by its base with no marker. A wire form is what an ID needs to cross a boundary. Printing and ordering change what a program shows and allows, so a sort over IDs or a printed sensitive value would compile unasked. The ratified model.jet already writes #Printable on its IDs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Typed IDs code with no marker, at the cost of amending D-CAPBUNDLE1 for coding and asking authors of value-hiding distinct types to opt out.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: GoalsA-1. The non-author review (ballots/D-CODABLE-DISTINCT1.review.md) found G1-G7, and GoalsB-2 applied every one. GoalsA-1's confirmation of the fixes is pending.

decisions.title: How a method is passed where a function value goes
decisions.situation:
Today crew.tell with no parentheses is E0302: Crew has no field tell. A callback that calls a method is written as a closure, fn(id) { crew.tell(id) }. Its parameter type comes from the function type the callback's parameter expects. Card #6824 asks for a shorter way to pass a method.

The owner ruled that v1's options (A plain read binds, B closure only, C Crew.tell, D crew.tell(..)) are not good enough. This v2 starts from three facts. Jet already lets the expected type decide what a short form means: D-SUBJECT-CALL1 makes .label() mean fn(c) { c.label() }, but only where a one-parameter function is expected. Every short mark is taken: <> is the pipe-step value, .. is the inclusive range and ... the spread, and crew.tell() reads as a call with no arguments. A free function is already a value anywhere: f: greet holds greet.

Under A, crew.tell is the method with crew bound only where a function type is expected, and stays an error everywhere else. Under B the closure stays the only form, with a fix that writes it. Under C, Crew.tell names the method with the receiver as its first parameter. Under D, fn crew.tell marks the bound value with the existing fn keyword. We recommend A.
decisions.gist: Where a function type is expected, should crew.tell, read without parentheses, pass the method with crew bound, while every other read without parentheses stays an error that suggests the call?
decisions.lesson: A method passes as a callback with no closure exactly where the reader already sees that a function is expected, the rule .label() already follows. So a forgotten call can never turn into a value.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here, shown on the one program this ballot uses throughout. Every line runs today (v4 probe u1).

```jet
Crew: struct {
    name: String                                  // a field: data each crew holds
    tell: fn(self, id: Int) -> String { "{self.name} hears about task {id}" }
    label: fn(self) -> String { self.name }       // a method with no other parameter
}
```

A method is a function declared in a type, such as tell. Its self parameter is the value it is called on, the receiver. A call writes parentheses: crew.tell(1).

```jet
each: fn(ids: [Int], notify: fn(Int) -> String) {   // notify has a function type
    loop id in ids -> print(notify(id))
}
```

A function value is a function passed or stored without being called, such as each's notify. Its type, fn(Int) -> String, is a function type.

```jet
each([1, 2], fn(id) { crew.tell(id) })   // prints Ada hears about task 1, then 2
```

A closure is a function value written in place, here fn(id) { crew.tell(id) }. It captures names such as crew from where it is written.

The expected type is the type a place requires. Here notify requires fn(Int) -> String, so the closure's id needs no written type. A call argument, a struct field, a typed list element and a declared return type all have one.

```jet
crews.map(.label())   // subject shorthand: means fn(c) { c.label() }
```

Subject shorthand is allowed only where a one-parameter function is expected (D-SUBJECT-CALL1).

A bound method value is a function value made from a method and one receiver, such as crew.tell under A. Calling it calls the method on that receiver.

A method takes self to read its receiver, &self to change it, or &&self to consume it. Fields and methods have separate namespaces (D-MEMBER-NAMESPACE1 A): a read without parentheses names the field, a call names the method.
decisions.story:
A crew passes its tell method to each, which calls a notify callback for every task ID. The same program is written under each option.

Each option then shows two later mistakes. Someone forgets the parentheses and writes x: crew.label. Someone else adds a field tell: fn(Int) -> String to Crew, named like the method.
decisions.inWild:
C#: crew.Tell read without parentheses is a method group, C#'s name for a method not yet called. It converts to a delegate, C#'s function value, only where a delegate type is expected (ECMA-334, Method group conversions). C# 10 added a natural type, so var f = crew.Tell also works when the group has one overload (C# 10 lambda improvements proposal). Jet has no overloading (E0105), so every read names one method.

Scala 3: a method reference is eta-expanded into a function value automatically (Scala 3 reference, Automatic Eta Expansion). A method with an empty parameter list, def total(): Int, is not expanded unless a function type is expected. Scala 2 required the mark crew.tell _, which Scala 3 dropped as noise.

Kotlin: crew::tell is a bound callable reference and Crew::tell an unbound one taking the receiver first (Kotlin docs, Callable references). Since Kotlin 1.4 a reference adapts to an expected type that omits defaulted parameters.

Swift: crew.tell is a bound closure and Crew.tell the curried form, called Crew.tell(crew)(1). Swift refuses crew.bump for a mutating method of a value type: partial application of a mutating method is not allowed.

Go: t.M is a method value, evaluating t once; for a pointer-receiver method on an addressable t it binds &t, so writes reach t (Go spec, Method values). T.M is a method expression whose first parameter is the receiver (Go spec, Method expressions).

Rust: no bound method values. Crew::tell names the method as a function of the receiver. Reading crew.tell is E0615, attempted to take value of method, with the help: use parentheses to call the method. Binding is a closure, |id| crew.tell(id).

Python and JavaScript bind or lose the receiver on any read: Python's if door.is_open: is always true, and JavaScript's const f = obj.method loses this.
decisions.detail:
Today, on dev 03d5f7b309 with the gate-p66 jet. The v4 probes hold the exact program this ballot shows, with outputs in v4/results.txt. The earlier probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/GoalsB-3/bm, each with its .out.

- u1: the program runs and prints Ada, the two tell lines, then Lin and Kai.
- u2 x: crew.label and u3 each([1, 2], crew.tell) are E0302 `Crew` has no field, with the fix: check the field names. Neither suggests the call.
- u4: add a field tell: fn(Int) -> String to Crew. The closure still calls the method, but each([1, 2], crew.tell) now compiles and passes the field, with no warning.

- u5 Crew.tell is E0302 `Crew` has no static member. u6 fn crew.tell is a parse error: Expected a value, found `fn`.

- p01 each([1, 2], crew.tell) is E0302 `Crew` has no field `tell`, with the fix: check the field names. It does not suggest the call.
- p02 x: crew.total and p12 if door.is_open are E0302 at their line.
- p03 Crew.label and p14 Crew.make are E0302 `Crew` has no static member. A static method is no value today.

- p04 and p18: the closure fn(id) { crew.tell(id) } works, its parameter typed from each's notify and from map.
- p05: the subject shorthand works: crews.map(.label()), crews.map(.name) and crews.map(.tell(7)).
- p06 fn crew.tell and p09 crew.tell(..) are parse errors, so both spellings are free. p10 crew.tell(<>) outside a pipe is jet.PipeValueOutsideStep; p19 7 |> crew.tell(<>) prints Lin tells 7. p11 crew.tell() is jet.MissingArgument.

- p07: with a field step: fn(Int) -> String and a method step, each([1], box.step) passes the field.
- Examples/Basics/Functions/FunctionValueLabels.jet (f: greet) and p16: a free function is a value with no expected type. In p16, total read without a call fails only at its first use: + can't combine fn() -> Int and Int.
- p15: a function with a defaulted parameter does not pass where a shorter function type is expected.

- p20: a struct field of function type and a typed list [fn(Int) -> String]{…} take a function value. p21: a local has no written function type; (fn(Int) -> String){announce} is a parse error.
- p17: a closure calling a &self method passed down to a call writes the owner (6); stored in a struct field, its write is lost (still 6, where 11 is meant). That trap is the closure's, under every option.

A shorter closure was looked for and not found. Each short form needs a mark for the parameter: <> is the pipe value, _ is the discard, .. and ... are range and spread, and $0 or it would be a new glyph or a new reserved word. Jet's closure already takes its parameter types from the expected type, so fn(id) { crew.tell(id) } is the shortest closure without a new token.

options.name: crew.tell passes the method where a function type is expected
options.gist: Where a function type is expected, crew.tell is the method with crew bound; anywhere else a read of a method without parentheses is an error that suggests the call.
options.detail:
The rule is the one D-SUBJECT-CALL1 already uses for .label(): the expected type decides. A call argument, struct field, list element or return value whose type is a function type accepts crew.tell when tell's other parameters, result, error type and effects fit that type. The read is then the closure fn(id: Int) -> String { crew.tell(id) } with the method's own access marks.

Which places expect a function. A function type counts, and so does an optional function type (F)?, which a plain value fills under D-OPT-LIFT1. A generic parameter counts only once inference has made it a function type. The read waits for that, as a closure does today: q03's pick(announce, fn(n) { … }) and pick(fn(n) { … }, announce) both type the closure.

A union never counts, even one with a function member such as Int | fn() -> Int. There a forgotten call and the value would both fit (q01), so the read is the error that suggests the call.

Where no function type is expected, only the message changes. x: crew.total and if door.is_open stay errors at their line. The message now says total is a method and offers crew.total() as the fix, like Rust's E0615. Elsewhere a forgotten call can never become a value; where a function is expected, the method binds only if its whole type fits.

The receiver is evaluated once, at the read, as in Go, C#, Swift and Kotlin: hired("Lin").tell computes hired once and keeps the result. A name or field path is captured under the closure rules.

Field and method clash. D-MEMBER-NAMESPACE1 keeps both a field and a method of one name. Where a function type is expected and the type has both, the read is an error whatever their types. The error names both. It offers fn(n) { box.step(n) } for the method and fn(n) { box.step.call(n) } for the field.

Choosing whichever fits would let a change elsewhere swap them silently. Say the field is step: fn(String) -> String and the method is step(self, id: Int). Then each(ids, box.step) would bind the method. A library that retypes each's notify to fn(String) -> String would make the same line pass the field. So adding a field or a method can make a read an error, but never changes what it names.

p07's each([1], box.step) passes the field today and becomes that error. So A amends D-MEMBER-NAMESPACE1's sentence that a read without parentheses is the field. Where no function type is expected, that sentence stands.

Edges. A &self method binds where its closure would write the owner. Passed to a call argument, it borrows the receiver and the writes land (p17's first line). Stored, returned or put in a field over a copied receiver, it is refused with the closure-or-pass-down fix, since the write would miss.

A &self method on a temporary receiver, hired("Lin").bump, is refused as the call is (E0111, q08). Its once-evaluated receiver would be a hidden copy that keeps the writes. A &&self method is refused, since the value could run twice.

A generic method takes its type arguments from the expected function type. If they don't follow, the error asks for the closure with written types. Defaults are not filled: the expected type lists every parameter, as for a free function today (p15).

The value keeps the method's effect row and error type, and the expected type must admit them, as for a closure. A static method, Crew.make, passes the same way where a function type is expected. p14 shows that is missing today.

Beginners write each(ids, crew.tell) where an editor shows notify expects a function, and get told to add () anywhere else. Experts get the same value with no new syntax, and the closure stays for partial application and adaptation.

options.name: Closure only, with a fix that writes it
options.gist: A method read without parentheses stays an error; where a function type is expected, the error's fix writes the closure fn(id) { crew.tell(id) }.
options.detail:
Nothing changes in the language. Every callback that calls a method is a closure, typed from the expected function type (p04).

The diagnostic improves. E0302 on a method name says it is a method. Where no function type is expected it offers crew.tell(…) as the fix; where one is, it offers the closure as a structured edit that jet fix applies.

Every capture, borrow and escape rule is visible in the closure's text, including p17's lost write, which needs its own card under every option.

Beginners learn one form for every callback. Experts write nothing new and pay a closure per method callback.

options.name: Type-qualified method, Crew.tell
options.gist: Crew.tell names the method as a function whose first parameter is the receiver, fn(Crew, Int) -> String; binding one receiver stays a closure.
options.detail:
Crew.tell is Go's method expression and Rust's Crew::tell. A &self method is fn(&Crew, Int), so no write can reach a hidden copy. A static method, Crew.make, is a value the same way. The spelling is free: p03 and p14 are errors today.

Its main use, mapping or sorting over receivers, is already covered. crews.map(.label()) works today under D-SUBJECT-CALL1 (p05), so crews.map(Crew.label) would be a second spelling of it. C adds new reach only where the receiver is not the single argument, such as a two-parameter function type fn(Crew, Int) -> String.

The callback with one receiver, the case #6824 asks about, is still the closure.

Beginners keep the closure. Experts get unbound method values and static method values.

options.name: Marked reference, fn crew.tell
options.gist: fn crew.tell is the bound method value anywhere, with or without an expected type; the plain read stays an error that suggests the call.
options.detail:
The existing keyword fn marks the reference, so no glyph is added and the form reads as the function crew.tell. Today fn crew.tell is a parse error (p06), so the spelling is free. Kotlin marks the same value as crew::tell, and Jet's :: is taken.

The mark names the method even when a field shares its name, so a field can never change what it reads. It works with no expected type: notify: fn crew.tell infers fn(Int) -> String.

The value and its &self, &&self, generic, default and effect rules are A's.

The cost is a third shape for fn, after the function type fn(Int) -> String and the closure fn(id) { … }. A reader sees fn crew.tell beside fn(id) { crew.tell(id) } and has to tell them apart by the parenthesis. The form is used only for callbacks. Scala 2's similar mark, crew.tell _, was dropped in Scala 3 as noise.

Beginners learn a new form for callbacks. Experts get a value that a field can't shadow.

recommendation.why: A gives the short callback exactly where the reader sees that a function is expected, under the rule Jet already ratified for .label(). It adds no glyph or keyword shape, and every other read of a method without parentheses stays an error at its line.
gains: A method passes as a callback with no closure and no new syntax
A forgotten call is an error at its line wherever no function type is expected
A field and a method of one name never silently trade places: where a function is expected, having both is an error
One rule with D-SUBJECT-CALL1: the expected function type decides, for .label() and for crew.tell
A &self value passed down writes its owner; one stored over a copy is refused, where today's closure loses the write

losses.loss: A method read needs an expected function type, while a free function is a value anywhere (f: greet), so notify: crew.tell with no written type is an error.
losses.mitigation: The error offers the closure; a struct field or typed list gives the read its expected type (p20). The free-function read is looser today: a forgotten call to one fails only at first use (p16). A leaves it alone, and a follow-up card can ask whether free function reads should follow the same rule.

losses.loss: The bound value evaluates its receiver once, so each(ids, hired("Lin").tell) calls hired once, where the closure fn(id) { hired("Lin").tell(id) } calls it per ID.
losses.mitigation: This is Go, C#, Swift and Kotlin's rule, the one readers expect of a value. jet inspect and the hover show the bound receiver; the closure keeps the per-call form.

losses.loss: Adding a field or method that shares a name with the other turns a working method-value read into an error, even when only one of them fits.
losses.mitigation: The error names both members and writes the closure for each, so the fix is one edit. Choosing whichever fits would let a parameter retyped in another package silently swap the field for the method.

whyNot.reason: B is safe but keeps a closure that only restates the call at every method callback, though the expected type already says a function goes there and .label() already uses that fact.
C's main use is already crews.map(.label()), so it adds a second spelling for that, and it leaves the one-receiver callback, the #6824 case, as a closure.
D gives fn a third shape that differs from a closure by one parenthesis, for a form used only in callbacks; A gets the same value with no new form.

recommendation.tradeoff: Methods pass as callbacks with no closure, at the cost that a method value needs an expected function type.

hybrid.synthesis: A and C's static half do not conflict: Crew.make where a function type is expected follows the same rule, and A includes it. C's unbound instance form stays out, since subject shorthand covers its common case.

harvest.aspect: A fix that writes the closure.
