decisions.title: How a binary format feeds typed decode
decisions.situation: Typed decode turns stored data into a typed value. JSON streams straight into the value, but every other format must first build a full in-memory tree and then decode that tree. The compiler's saved Core record is the costly case: loading it builds tens of millions of tree values, so checking with the record is slower than reading Core's source again. Only Core may implement the streaming reader, because names that start with two underscores are reserved. The vote decides how a binary format gets the streaming path, and we recommend making the reader a small public Core trait.
decisions.gist: How should a program feed its own binary format into typed decode without first building a whole tree?
decisions.lesson: Typed decode turns stored data into a typed value, such as a struct. JSON text streams straight into the value. Any other format must first build a full in-memory tree, then decode that tree. Only Core may implement the streaming reader today. Whichever option wins, the compiler's saved Core record gets the streaming path.
decisions.story: Mara maintains the compiler's saved copy of the checked standard library. Loading it should beat checking the library again, but each row first becomes a large in-memory tree and then a typed value. The streaming reader that would skip the tree has a reserved name, so her package may not implement it.

options.name: Public decode source
options.detail:
Rename Core's private streaming reader trait to a public `DecodeSource` in core.encoding. Its entry becomes `encoding.decode_from<T>(source)`. The trait keeps the cursor shape the JSON reader and the tree reader already implement. Its methods are begin_object, object_members, next_key, key_is, key_text, begin_array, next_item, take_null, skip, capture and four scalar reads.

Derived types are unchanged: their generated reader takes any source. A type's own hand-written Decode impl stays over Dyn, as ratified for codecs. So this adds a format-side trait, not a second type-side surface. The compiler's record reader then implements it with no exception.

Cost: rename the trait, the entry and its lowering key. Update the two Core implementations, the generated reader's bound, the Core reference page and one test.

Edge cases: a source that miscounts members gets ordinary FieldError results, never unsafe reads. The trait has no unsafe operations. A source's `capture` must return the value at the cursor as a tree; every non-streamed type falls back to it. The name lives in core.encoding, not the root, so it collides with nothing a program does not import.

options.name: Compiler-only exception
options.detail:
Keep the trait private and add a second exception to the reserved-name rule. In a file of one of the toolchain's own packages, a reserved name Core declares is accepted in two places. Those are right after `impl` and as the head of a `.` path. Declarations, every other reserved spelling, and every file outside those packages still get E0067.

The toolchain's package census decides membership. It holds the compiler workspace's members and their in-tree path dependencies, read from the tree Core itself comes from. A user manifest cannot add to it.

Cost: the lexer rule, a parse lane in the driver and the formatter, and a UI test. That is about 530 lines, already written and checked.

Edge cases: the language server's formatting knows no toolchain lane, so it still rejects those files. Whoever points the toolchain root at a tree also supplies its Core, so the trust equals Core's. Other packages keep the tree path.

options.name: Core reads the record
options.detail:
Move the compiler's record tree format into a new core.encoding.record module. The format holds strings, shapes, a node table and typed rows. Core implements the private reader there and exposes `record.decode<T>(bytes, at)` and `record.encode(value)`.

Today no Core binary format implements the streaming reader. CBOR, Erlang term format and the rest decode through a tree, so this would be Core's first.

Cost: move about 1,400 lines of reader, plus the writer, into Core. Add a format reference and tests.

Edge cases: the layout carries compiler-only parts such as shared-node memo slots. A public format would either carry them or fork. Every record schema change becomes a Core release note. Programs gain a binary codec nobody asked for.
options.code:
use core.encoding.record

bytes: record.encode(module_row)
row: record.decode<ModuleRow>(bytes, 0) ?? return Err(err)

comparisons.note: The public Deserializer trait let bincode, rmp-serde, serde_cbor and others stream into every derived type. Its known cost is size: about thirty methods plus a visitor, which makes a new format hard to write. https://serde.rs/impl-deserializer.html
comparisons.code: impl<'de> Deserializer<'de> for &mut Reader<'de> { fn deserialize_map<V: Visitor<'de>>(self, v: V) -> Result<V::Value> { ... } }

comparisons.note: Decoder is a public protocol, so third-party formats such as MessagePack plug into every Decodable type. Its keyed and unkeyed containers are often called verbose. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/decoder
comparisons.code: struct MessagePackDecoder: Decoder { func container<Key>(keyedBy: Key.Type) throws -> KeyedDecodingContainer<Key> { ... } }

comparisons.note: Decoder and CompositeDecoder are public; CBOR, ProtoBuf and community YAML formats use them. The format API stayed marked experimental for years while its shape settled. https://kotlinlang.org/api/kotlinx.serialization/kotlinx-serialization-core/kotlinx.serialization.encoding/-decoder/
comparisons.code: class RecordDecoder : AbstractDecoder() { override fun decodeElementIndex(descriptor: SerialDescriptor): Int { ... } }

comparisons.note: Go has no format-neutral decoder interface. Each format (encoding/json, encoding/gob, msgpack libraries) repeats its own reflection walk, the failure mode a shared trait avoids.

recommendation.why: One small public trait gives every binary format the fast path, keeps the reserved-name rule whole, and matches what serde, Swift and Kotlin proved.
gains: Every format decodes without a full tree.
The reserved-name rule keeps its one exception.

losses.loss: A new public trait that Core must keep stable.
losses.mitigation: It ships with the exact methods the JSON reader already uses and tests.

whyNot.reason: It bends a ratified rule for one program and still leaves every other format slow.
Core would own a compiler-internal layout that changes with every compiler release.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core keeps one more public trait stable; the JSON reader already proves its shape.

decisions.title: Memory chokepoint: kernel files with owners and checked views; kernel files with single-use handles; a kernel of raw primitives; today's blocks plus a report; or Core only
decisions.situation: Jet code that touches raw memory opens an #Unsafe block and writes a reason. There are 1,528 such blocks, and 656 of them read, write, allocate or free memory directly. The runtime also has 248 ordinary functions that read or write at an address their caller picks, used 17,528 times with no block at the call. The owner asked that every raw memory action go through one small, heavily audited place. Probes show that moving raw operations alone changes nothing: a read after free still compiles, and a release build runs it silently. Single-use handles stopped some of these bugs. But a handle can be copied, directly or inside a struct, and the release build then reads freed memory. Jet's view checker, which already guards list and arena views, refused every read after close that the probes tried.
decisions.gist: Should raw memory live in kernel files that hand out owners and checked views, in kernel files with single-use handles, in raw primitives, in today's blocks, or only in Core?
decisions.lesson: Raw memory means reading and writing bytes at an address the program computed. If the address is wrong, or the memory was already freed, the program reads garbage or crashes, and a release build does not check. Jet makes such code open an #Unsafe block and write why it is safe. This vote decides whether those blocks may sit anywhere, or only in a few small kernel files, and what those files hand the rest of the program.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A kernel file is a file a package names as allowed to hold raw memory code. An owner is a value that holds a piece of memory and frees it when it closes. Only the kernel can make one, and Jet refuses to copy it.

A view is a window into memory that an owner hands out, like a slice of a list. Jet ties each view to its owner, so the owner cannot close, move or grow while the view is still used. A single-use handle is a value that must be spent exactly once. A release build is the fast build. It runs without the sentries that watch memory in the default and hardened builds.
decisions.story:
Ana writes a ring buffer for audio over memory she allocates herself. Today she opens #Unsafe blocks in four files. A teammate later keeps a copy of a pointer after the buffer is freed. The default build stops at the bad read, but the release build prints stale samples.

Under A, Ana puts the buffer in one kernel file. It hands out a Ring owner and views of its samples. The teammate's view, kept past the close, does not compile, and the audit report lists her one file.

Under B the Ring is a single-use handle. The teammate copies it with .copy(), and the release build still reads freed samples. Under C she calls kernel read and write functions, and the stale copy still compiles. Under D nothing changes, but the report lists all four blocks. Under E she cannot write the buffer at all unless Core ships one.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Where Jet code may perform raw memory actions, and what the rest of a program uses instead.

What the review measured. The raw primitives are already defined in three places: the core memory module, the compiler's intrinsic rows and the operating-system leaves. What is scattered is the reasoning at each use. 656 blocks address memory directly, and 248 runtime functions take an address from their caller with no block at the call. The runtime's raw code sits in 81 files of about 36,600 lines.

What probes showed. A read through a copy of a freed pointer compiles under every build, and the release build prints the stale value. Moving the read into a kernel function changes nothing, because the caller still vouches for the address. A word-sized read through a kernel function built to the same image size and ran in the same time as the direct read.

What a second, fresh review found. Single-use handles refuse forging and a plain use after release. But .copy() of a handle compiles, a struct that holds one copies freely, and a raw window handed out by one outlives it. Each case reads or frees freed memory silently in a release build. Jet's own Core memory block copies the same way.

What already works. Jet ties a view returned by an owner's method to that owner. Closing, moving or growing the owner while the view is used is a compile error, and so is returning a view of a dead owner. Owners that close themselves cannot be copied, even inside a struct, and can be lent to helpers. One escape remains: a view stored in a field of a returned record.

What it costs. With the loop in its own function, a view read runs at raw speed and a checked handle read costs 1.4 times. With the loop in the main function, the view costs 1.8 times and the handle 3.6 times. The existing raw window boxes every element, about 15 times slower.

options.name: Kernel files that hand out owners and checked views
options.detail: A package lists its kernel files in its policy. Raw memory operations anywhere else are refused, and the message names the safe type to use instead. A single-file program is its own kernel, so small scripts keep working. Kernels hand out owners: memory, regions, mappings, device registers and shared atomic words. An owner hands out views tied to itself. Beginners use lists and never see a kernel. Experts write their own kernel file, still behind #Unsafe.
options.technical:
A new policy field, memory: .Kernel([paths]), next to unsafe: .Paths. A package without it has no kernel files. A type declared in a kernel file keeps its private fields private to the kernel files, not the whole package. A kernel's public function that is not #Unsafe may not take an integer or pointer that reaches a raw address.

Owners are Close resources: copies are refused, lending is plain, and scope end closes them. Inside a kernel, mem.window(owner, pointer, count) builds a View<T> whose owner is the first argument. It replaces the copyable mem.Window<T>, which amends that row of D-RAWPTR2. Sema's existing view rules then refuse closing, moving or growing the owner while a view lives. Two gaps close first: a view inside a returned record, and the close duty of pattern bindings.

Kernel primitives are intrinsics or always inlined. The compiler's lowering rows are the kernel for generated loads, and proven accesses stay plain loads. jet audit memory lists every kernel file, raw operation, adopting or view constructor, lowering row, asm leaf and vouch block. The runtime, below Core, gets its own kernel.

options.name: Kernel files that hand out single-use handles
options.detail: The same kernel files as A, but kernels hand out single-use handles instead of owners and views. A handle carries its own bounds and is spent exactly once. Today a handle can be copied, directly or inside a struct, and a release build then reads freed memory. A handle cannot be passed to a helper function at all.
options.technical: The same policy, kernel privacy and address rule as A, with #SingleUse handles instead of owners and views. Four sema changes are needed first. Copies of single-use values must be refused, and their duty must pass through struct fields. Handles must not hand out copyable views. Lending with & must be allowed, which amends D-LIN1. A bounds-checked read costs 1.4 times with the loop in a handle method and 3.6 times with it in the main function.

options.name: A kernel of raw primitives
options.detail: Each package has one kernel of typed raw primitives: read, write, step, copy, allocate and free. Raw syntax elsewhere is refused. Callers still open an #Unsafe block around each primitive call and vouch for the address. There are no owners or handles, so the bugs the probes found still compile.
options.technical: The same policy field and report as A, without kernel privacy, owners or the address rule. Primitives are always inlined. The 42 runtime one-word wrappers become kernel primitives that callers gate, so their 17,528 calls each open a block.

options.name: Today's blocks plus a report
options.detail: #Unsafe blocks stay where they are. Jet adds the generated jet audit memory report and refuses safe functions that take a raw address. Packages may still opt in to path limits.
options.technical: The existing unsafe: .Paths policy stays opt-in. The address rule applies everywhere, so the runtime's 248 address-taking wrappers become #Unsafe functions. Their 17,528 calls open blocks or move to typed views. No new types.

options.name: Core only
options.detail: Only Core and the runtime may hold raw memory code. User code gets owners and views and nothing else, so a user allocator or driver needs Core to ship it or goes through FFI.
options.technical: Removes the user raw-pointer set the owner ratified earlier. Core's kernel and the runtime's kernel are the only kernel files; package policy cannot add one. A foreign vouch block in a user package is raw memory outside Core, so it must be banned or listed as a kernel.

comparisons.note: Unsafe code may appear in any crate. Soundness rests on module privacy, and safe code gets owners and borrowed slices that the borrow checker ties to them.
comparisons.code: let s = &v[1..];   // drop(v) won't compile while s is used

comparisons.note: Drivers may not use unsafe at all; only the core kernel and chip crates may. Privileged calls take capability objects only trusted code can make.
Span is a safe, non-escaping view of contiguous memory tied to its owner, and strict memory safety marks each unsafe use when a module opts in.
comparisons.code:
let s: Span<Int> = array.span
let x = s[i]   // checked, no copy

comparisons.note: The foreign memory API replaced raw access with MemorySegment handles that carry bounds and an arena lifetime. A closed arena turns later access into a run-time error, not a compile error.
comparisons.code:
MemorySegment seg = arena.allocate(32);
long x = seg.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 8);

comparisons.note: Raw pointers work anywhere. Allocation is explicit through an allocator argument, and safe builds keep bounds checks.
comparisons.code:
const words = try allocator.alloc(i64, 4);
defer allocator.free(words);

comparisons.note: Raw pointer code must import unsafe, which is easy to search for. Tools check the documented conversion rules at run time.
comparisons.code: p := unsafe.Pointer(&x)   // vet and checkptr check this

recommendation.why: A is the only option where every probed read after free stops compiling. It reuses the view rules Jet already enforces for lists and arenas. Its views read at raw speed in a function, and experts keep raw code in small listed files.
gains: Forged owners, reads after close, copied owners and views that outlive their owner are compile errors.
One generated report lists every kernel file, raw operation and generated load.
Word reads through a kernel cost nothing once inlined, and views read at raw speed in a function.
Experts keep raw pointers in their own kernel files.

losses.loss: There are about five audit places in this repository, plus one per package with raw code, not one.
losses.mitigation: One generated report lists them all with their sizes, and kernels stay small.

losses.loss: The runtime migration is large: raw code in 81 files and 17,528 wrapper uses.
losses.mitigation: The 42 one-word wrappers collapse mechanically into owners and views first; the rest is counted down by subsystem.

losses.loss: Release builds do not watch kernel code, so a kernel bug is silent there.
losses.mitigation: Kernel tests run under the hardened build and under fuzzing, and views shrink what the sentries must catch.

losses.loss: Views last only for their scope and stay on one task.
losses.mitigation: Owners carry long-lived memory and can be stored and lent. Shared memory uses a shared owner with checked atomic offsets, as Core's shared-word API does.

losses.loss: Two checker gaps must close before raw-backed views ship: a view in a returned record field, and the close duty of pattern bindings.
losses.mitigation: Both are criteria on this card, and the probes that show them are written.

losses.loss: mem.window gains an owner argument, which amends one row of the ratified raw-pointer decision.
losses.mitigation: The old copyable window is 15 times slower and readable after free, so nothing worth keeping is lost.

whyNot.reason: B's handles can be copied directly or inside a struct, and the release build then reads freed memory. Closing those holes rebuilds A's rules, amends the ratified single-use rule for lending, and still costs 1.4 to 3.6 times per checked read.
C moves raw reads into named functions but leaves each caller vouching for the address, so the read after free still compiles.
D shows every raw memory operation in a report but turns no memory bug into a compile error.
E takes raw pointers away from users, so allocators and drivers need Core or FFI.

recommendation.tradeoff: Several small listed kernel files, a large runtime migration and two checker fixes, for memory bugs that stop compiling and one report of every raw memory operation.

decisions.title: Keep the plain table header for comparing one value, with the hole written `<>`?
decisions.situation: A decision table is an `if` followed by a list of arms; Jet tries the arms in order and runs the first one that fits. The plain header `if light == {` compares one value with each arm. The hole header `if n % <> == 0 {` drops each arm's value into the `<>`, so the arm `15 -> "FizzBuzz"` tests `n % 15 == 0`. In September you ruled that every table needs a hole. That would change about 16,000 tables and make about 5,400 function calls in headers run again for every arm tried. You asked for the hole to be `<>`, the mark a pipe already uses for "the value goes here", so every option below spells it that way. You are asked which headers Jet keeps. We recommend keeping the plain header for comparing one value and using the `<>` hole only for tests that do more.
decisions.gist: Should a table that compares one value keep its plain header, with the `<>` hole kept for tests that do more?
decisions.lesson: A decision table is an `if` whose arms are tried in order, like a list of cases. Its header holds the test the arms share. A hole is the mark `<>` in that test, and each arm's value fills it in turn. A pipe already uses `<>` to mean "the value goes here", so one mark keeps one meaning. Whichever option wins, the rules, the formatter and the docs name one spelling for each job.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A decision table is an `if` followed by a list of arms. Each arm is a value, an arrow and what to do: `15 -> "FizzBuzz"`. Jet tries the arms from the top and runs the first one that fits.

The header is the test written after `if`, before the `{`. A plain header such as `if light == {` compares one value with each arm. A hole header holds the mark `<>`, and each arm's value fills that mark in turn: `if n % <> == 0 {` with the arm `3` tests `n % 3 == 0`.

A pipe passes a value down a chain of steps: `raw |> Int.parse(<>)`. Inside a step, `<>` is the value coming in. The `else` arm runs when no other arm fits.

A call has an effect when it does more than compute an answer: it reads input, takes a lock, changes a value or prints. Calling it twice is not the same as calling it once. A pure call only computes, so a second call gives the same answer.
decisions.story: Maya teaches Jet to new programmers with a traffic light. Her first table is `if light == { .Red -> 30  .Amber -> 5  .Green -> 0 }`. Later she shows FizzBuzz with `if n % <> == 0 { 15 -> "FizzBuzz"  3 -> "Fizz" }`. One student asks whether the light table also needs `light == <>`. Another writes `if reader.next() == <> {` and wonders why records go missing. A third ends a pipe with a FizzBuzz table and cannot tell which `<>` is the piped number. Maya wants one answer she can teach without exceptions.
decisions.detail:
What you ruled. On 2026-09-11 you chose D-IFHOLE1=A (card #3067). It says every table header holds exactly one hole and the plain header goes away in one change. It also says the header runs again for each arm tried, with no saving of the first result, even for a plain comparison. That change never ran, so the spec still teaches the plain header.

What is built today. The hole landed on 2026-11-14, spelled `_`. Jet rewrites each arm into the header, with the arm's value in the hole, and runs an ordinary list of tests. A header that is exactly `subject == _` is treated as the plain table, so it reads its subject once. That does not match your per-arm rule, so the ruling must settle it either way. Three errors, E0946, E0947 and E0948, refuse a misplaced hole or arm.

Why `<>` instead of `_`. You asked for it, and it fits. A pipe step already reads its input as `<>`, so `<>` already means "the value goes here". The `_` mark already means "ignore this" in patterns and in the catch-all arm. With `_` as the hole, one table would use it both ways, as in `if files.try_lock(path) == _ { .Val(_) -> false }`. Switching is a one-token change in the parser, plus respelling the hole's own example, spec rows and tests. A `_` written where the hole goes then gets an error whose fix writes `<>`.

The pipe rule. A pipe runs each step on the value of the line above, and the step names that value `<>`. A table inside a step could then see two meanings of `<>`. The rule in every option is the one pipes already use: inside a step, `<>` is always the step's value, even inside a lambda or a string. So a table header inside a step cannot hold a hole. A plain header there, such as `|> if <> == {`, compares the piped value and works.

What the pipe rule refuses. A table inside a step whose header needs a hole is refused with a registered error. Its fix ends the pipe one line early in a named value and starts the table with that name. The author picks the name, so `jet fix` does not apply it. A pipe written inside a hole header is fine: in `if (raw |> Int.parse(<>) ?? 0) % <> == 0 {`, the `<>` in the parentheses belongs to that pipe and the other is the hole.

How many tables would change. A scan of dev e3f8a73a8b skips comments and strings and follows headers across lines. It finds 16,351 plain-header tables in 2,724 files. By area: Compiler 6,588, Core 1,530, Examples 427, tests 2,063, Jetpack 5,135, Tools 504 and Docs 104. Markdown pages hold about 117 more. Of these tables, about 5,400 call a function in the header, and about 530 read through an index or a borrow. In Examples, 240 of 427 tables call a function in the header.

Why a call in the header matters. A header that holds a hole runs again for each arm tried. Then `if reader.next() % <> == 0 {` calls `next` once per arm, and a miss on the first arm skips a record. A test of the hand-written equivalent printed two fetches where the plain header printed one. Under your per-arm rule this holds for every table, so option B must first name about 5,400 header calls, and must do it without reordering other effects.

The effect rule. Options A, C and D keep hole headers that run per arm, so each refuses a call with an effect in one. Sema already knows each call's effects: reading input, taking a lock, printing, or changing a value through `&` or `&self`. The fix names the value first, as B does: `next: reader.next()` on the line above, then `if next % <> == 0 {`. A pure call such as `fits(<>, size)` stays, since a second run gives the same answer. D allows any call in `subject == <>`, which reads once.

When a table needs `else`. A plain table over an enum that lists every case, such as `light == {` with `.Red`, `.Amber` and `.Green`, is proven complete and needs no `else`. A hole table cannot be proven that way: Jet cannot tell that `15` and `3` cover every `n`. So a hole table that gives a value needs `else`, and today a missing one is refused. A hole table used as a statement may leave `else` out and does nothing when no arm fits.

Edge cases. A call that holds the hole, such as `if queue.try_push(<>) {`, cannot be named first, since each arm passes a different value. It gets the same error, and the fix writes the arms as plain tests: `if { queue.try_push(1) -> … }`. A call inside a lambda in the header is checked the same way. A call that only reads, such as `list.len()`, is pure and stays.

Some fixes are shown and not applied. In `total: base() + if next() % <> == 0 {`, the table does not start its statement. Moving `next()` above would run it before `base()`, so the author places it.

The same tables in each option. Take `if kind == {` in Compiler ItemHeads.jet, `if parse(...) == {` in Core Toml.jet and `if files.try_lock(path) == {` in Examples FilesRootedLifecycle.jet. A leaves all three as they are. B writes `if kind == <> {` and names `parse(...)` and `files.try_lock(path)` first, since a second `try_lock` would take the lock again. C allows either spelling of each. D writes `<>` into all three, and each still reads its subject once.

One way per meaning (I8). Jet already runs a table two ways: as a comparison against one value, or as a list of tests. A gives each way one spelling, and a `<>` in a header always means the header runs per arm. B runs every table by one per-arm rule. C gives one table two spellings with the same meaning. D keeps one shape, but its `<>` means one read in some headers and a read per arm in others.

Beginners. A learner reads `if light == {` as "compare light with each arm". Under A, the hole lesson may invite `light == <>`, which is refused with a fix that deletes `<>`. Under B and D every table looks alike, but `<>` in a plain comparison tells the reader nothing new. Under B, `if reader.next() == <> {` loses records with no warning.

Experts. Experts want one rule and no hidden repeats. A shows the read rule in the syntax and refuses a repeated effect, and B gives one rule with explicit names. C makes each review pick a spelling, and D asks readers to spot which header shapes read once.

Formatter and errors. Under A, the fix for `light == <>` deletes one token, and the parser already proves both spellings build the same table. E0948's fix must stop suggesting `subject == _`. Under B and D the formatter must learn to lay out hole tables before the change, and the change touches files in every live lane at once.

options.name: Plain header compares one value; the `<>` hole fills a shared test
options.detail:
`if subject == {` stays the one way to compare one value with each arm, and it reads the subject once. The `<>` hole is for a shared test that does more, such as `n % <> == 0` or `fits(<>, size)`. That header runs once per arm tried, so a call with an effect in it is refused, and the fix names the value first. A header that only compares with `<>` is refused, with a fix that removes the `<>`.

A hole table that gives a value needs `else`, because Jet cannot prove its arms cover every value. A plain table over an enum that lists every case needs none. In a pipe step `<>` is the piped value: a plain table works there, and a hole table names the value first. No existing table changes.
options.technical:
Amend D-IFHOLE1: drop the rule that every table holds a hole, and drop its cutover. Keep D-IF3, D-IFDIST1 and S68 for comparison headers. Respell the hole `<>`. E0437 (`<>` outside a pipe step) narrows to `<>` outside a step or a table header, E0947 retires into it, and a `_` where the hole goes gets an error whose fix writes `<>`.

The parser refuses a header whose whole test, ignoring parentheses, is `subject OP <>` or `<> OP subject`. That refusal is a registered error with a machine fix that deletes the `<>` and flips the operator when `<>` stood on the left. The queued rewrite of that header into the comparison table becomes this refusal. E0946 stays. E0948 stays, with its fix changed to `if subject == {`.

A new registered error (E0950, the next free code) refuses a call with an effect in a hole header. It reads the call's effect facts: an effect, a `&` argument or a `&self` receiver. A pure call stays. The error ships with a UI snapshot and a machine fix that binds the call to a name on the line above and reads the name in the header.

The name is the called method's name (`next`), or `value` for another call, with a number added on a clash. The fix applies only when the table starts its statement; otherwise it is shown, not applied, so no effect moves before another. A call that holds the `<>` cannot be named; its fix shows the arms as plain tests. Calls inside a lambda in the header are checked too.

A hole table that gives a value requires `else` (E0003), since its arms are tests, not cases of one type; one used as a statement may leave `else` out. A plain table keeps today's coverage rule.

Inside a pipe step `<>` is always the step's value, through lambdas and string holes, as D-PIPE1 says. A table header there that needs a hole is refused with a registered error whose fix shows the pipe split into a named value. The spec, the syntax row and Examples/Basics/DispatchHole.jet drop `shape == _` and spell the hole `<>`.

options.name: Every table holds a `<>` hole, as ratified
options.detail:
D-IFHOLE1 as ratified, with the hole spelled `<>`. Every header holds exactly one `<>`, so `if light == {` becomes `if light == <> {`. The header runs once per arm tried, even for a plain comparison. A header that calls a function gets a named value first, so the call still runs once. A table written later with a call in its header repeats the call per arm, as ratified.

A table needs `else` unless its header compares a named value with every case of an enum. In a pipe step `<>` is the piped value, so a table there names the value first. About 16,400 tables in 2,700 files change, about 5,400 with a call in the header.
options.technical:
Keep D-IFHOLE1 as written, with the hole respelled `<>`. Remove the plain-header parser path and the `it` subject name, and refuse a plain header with a registered error and a machine fix. Change the queued rewrite so a computed `subject == <>` runs per arm tried and needs a named subject to leave out `else`.

Migrate every table with a source-aware tool that names each computed subject first and moves it without reordering other effects. Inside a pipe step `<>` is the step's value, so every table there is refused with the pipe-split fix, and the migration splits such pipes too. Teach the formatter to lay out hole tables. The examples, spec and teaching pages move to the hole header.

options.name: Both headers stay
options.detail:
Keep both spellings. `if light == {` and `if light == <> {` build the same table, and both read the subject once. Both keep the plain coverage rule, so listing every case of an enum needs no `else`. The formatter keeps whichever was written. No existing table changes.

Hole headers that do more than compare work as ratified and run per arm. A call with an effect in one is refused with a fix that names the value first, as in A. Such a table needs `else` when it gives a value. Inside a pipe step `<>` is the piped value: a plain table there works, and a hole table must name the value first.
options.technical:
Keep D-IF3 and D-IFHOLE1 side by side, drop D-IFHOLE1's cutover, and respell the hole `<>`. Amend D-IFHOLE1 so a hole header whose whole test is one comparison reads its subject once, as built, with the plain table's coverage. The formatter keeps the written spelling, and the docs teach both spellings as one table.

Every other hole header runs per arm tried. The same new registered error as in A (E0950, with a UI snapshot and the same machine fix) refuses a call with an effect there. A hole table that gives a value requires `else` (E0003).

Inside a pipe step `<>` is always the step's value, as D-PIPE1 says. A plain header there compares that value. A header there that needs a hole is refused with a registered error whose fix shows the pipe split into a named value.

options.name: Every table holds a `<>` hole; a plain comparison still reads once
options.detail:
Every table header holds one `<>`, as ratified. A header whose whole test is `subject == <>` still reads its subject once, as the parser builds it today. It keeps the plain coverage rule, so listing every case of an enum needs no `else`. The change adds one token per table: `if fetch() == {` becomes `if fetch() == <> {`, with no named value and no change in behavior.

Every other hole header runs per arm. A call with an effect there is refused with a fix that names the value first, as in A. Such a table needs `else` when it gives a value. Inside a pipe step `<>` is the piped value, so no table can sit in a step, and the value is named first. The plain header is removed after about 16,400 tables change.
options.technical:
Keep D-IFHOLE1's required hole and its cutover, with the hole respelled `<>`. Amend its read rule: a header whose whole test, ignoring parentheses, is `subject OP <>` or `<> OP subject` is the comparison table over `subject`. That table reads its subject once and keeps `it`, patterns, ranges and coverage. Every other hole header runs per arm tried. There, the new registered error from A (E0950, with its UI snapshot and machine fix) refuses a call with an effect. A table there that gives a value requires `else` (E0003).

A machine fix inserts the `<>` in every table, and the parser already proves both spellings build the same table. Inside a pipe step `<>` is the step's value, so every table there is refused with the pipe-split fix, and the migration splits such pipes too. The formatter learns to lay out hole tables before the cutover.

comparisons.note: Primary reference read on 2026-11-14. A match reads its value once and lists patterns, with optional guards. A shared test such as divisibility repeats in every guard. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/match-expr.html

Primary documentation and the clojure.core source read on 2026-11-14. `condp` takes one two-input test, one value and candidate clauses, and tries the test with each candidate in order. The macro binds the value once, and plain equality uses the same form with `=`. It is the closest prior art to the hole table, and it never reads the value twice. Source: https://clojuredocs.org/clojure.core/condp

Primary documentation read on 2026-11-14. Scala writes `_` for one unnamed function input and also for the catch-all case, so one mark carries both meanings. That is the double meaning a `<>` hole avoids. Source: https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/book/fun-anonymous-functions.html

A `<>` in a header means the header runs again for each arm, so Jet refuses a call with an effect there, with a fix that names the value first. Inside a pipe, `<>` keeps its one pipe meaning.
recommendation.tradeoff: A reverses part of your 2026-09-11 choice. `light == <>` is refused with a fix, and the plain header stays. Every other hole table works as ratified, now spelled `<>`.

D keeps the required hole with a one-token change per table. But its `<>` means one read in some headers and a read per arm in others, and no table fits in a pipe step.

decisions.title: How an app declares and uses a typed database table: a table value with a key function, a marker on the row type, or SQL checked against the migrated schema
decisions.situation: A database table is a list of rows on disk that a program reads and changes. In a Jet app today, a programmer writes the SQL text for every table by hand and turns each result row into a struct with a decode call. Nothing ties a table to its row type or its key, and nothing checks the SQL against the tables. Live screens refresh a whole table after any write. This vote picks how an app names a table, its key and its row type, and how a change to the row type reaches the stored table. It also fixes the rule that each method that writes runs as one transaction. We recommend A: a typed table value made from the row type and a key function.
decisions.gist: Should an app's tables be typed values with a key function, a marker on the row type, or SQL checked against the migrated schema?
decisions.lesson: A table holds rows of one shape, and each row has a key that finds it. When the language knows the shape and the key, it can check reads and writes, keep secrets out of answers, and refresh only the screens a write touched.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A row type is the struct one row holds, such as Task. A key is the value that finds one row, such as a task's ID. A composite key is a key made of two or more fields, such as a project and an account together.

A transaction is a group of reads and writes that happens all at once or not at all. Serializable means the result is the same as if the transactions ran one after another. A row policy is a rule that decides which rows a caller may read or change.

A migration is a step that changes the stored tables when the row type changes. A full scan reads every row of a table. A read set is the list of rows a query looked at, so a later write can tell which live queries it changed.
decisions.story:
Mia builds a task board. A Task has an ID, a title, a status and a version number. A Member is found by its project and its account together.

Under A she writes one line per table: store.table("tasks", key: task_key). Her method move_task reads a task with get, checks its version and writes it back with put. Two people move the same task at once. One call wins, and the other gets Conflict, because the method is one serializable transaction.

Later she adds a due date to Task as an optional field, and jet check records the new column on its own. She renames title to name next. jet check now stops with an error naming Task.title, and its fix line is the one migration step to add.

Under B she marks the Task struct with #Table and writes the key field names in the marker. Under C she writes CREATE TABLE in a migration and every SELECT by hand, and jet check verifies each query against the migrated schema.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: how a service declares a typed table, its key and its row type, and the methods get, add, put, delete, query and search. It also fixes, for every option, the transaction rule of a method that writes.

Current code. Core/Db/Db.jet has a connection (DBConnection), a policy scope (DBScope) and an open transaction (DBTransaction). A scope runs checked SQL through query and query_one, which need DB.Read, and execute, which needs DB.Write. The SQL type checks its holes, not the tables. live binds one SELECT as a live query, refreshed when its table is written.

More current code. transaction runs SQL steps in one transaction, and migrate records SQL steps and their checksum in a ledger. db.decode turns a row and a list of column names into a struct. A row policy (RowPolicy, made by db.policy(table, expr)) accepts only true and owner == user. There is no table type. The data library's Query<T> filters, sorts, groups and collects into an ordinary list; its public Table<T> carrier was retired.

The transaction rule, the same for every option. A method of a mounted service whose effects include DB.Write runs in one serializable transaction. On SQLite that is BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so writers take turns. On a server database it is the SERIALIZABLE isolation level. A method called from another method joins the caller's transaction. A method that only reads runs on one consistent snapshot.

move_task's read, version check and write rely on this: no other writer can change the task between them. A serialization failure or a busy database retries the whole method, up to 5 attempts with a short random wait. After the last attempt the method returns DBError.Busy. A client call that ends in Busy gets 503 with Retry-After, which the client maps to app.CallError.Unreachable with a retry time.

A retried method must not repeat work outside the database. So a Net, FS.Write or Exec effect inside a method that writes is a compile error that names the call. The program queues such work with app.after_commit(fn), which runs once after the commit, or starts a job.

Out of scope: the full-text index syntax and live-query transport, which have their own cards.

options.name: A table value: db.Table<K, T>, made by store.table(name, key: fn(T) -> K)
options.gist: The row type and the key function make a typed table; queries return the data library's Query<T>.
options.detail:
A service's field is a table: tasks: db.Table<TaskID, Task>. The server opens it with store.table("tasks", key: task_key), where task_key is a function from a row to its key. A composite key is a struct key, such as MemberKey with project and account.

The key function must be pure and deterministic. It has no effects, reads only its row, and calls only functions that do the same. Each field of K is stored as a key column, and the primary key is those columns. A key function that reads a clock, a global or anything but its row is a compile error at key:, naming the read.

get(key) returns the row or None. add(row) inserts a row whose key must be new, and answers Exists or Denied. put(row) inserts or replaces. delete(key) removes a row. query() returns the data library's Query<T>, so filter, sort_by, group_by and collect mean what they mean on a list.

Filters. A filter made of field comparisons joined by && and || becomes SQL. Any other filter needs a full scan, and A makes that explicit. A filter the compiler cannot turn into SQL is a registered warning at the filter, naming the part it could not read. Writing .scan() before it says the full scan is meant and silences the warning.

Secrets and policies. The row is stored with its storage codec, which keeps #Secret fields. Answers to a client use the wire codec, which drops them. A table attaches a row policy with .guard(policy), the typed form of the ratified row-policy rule. Each query records its read set and each write its write set, so a live query refreshes only when a write touched its rows.

Schema changes. The row type is the schema, and Jet writes the steps it can prove safe. Each table's layout is kept in a schema snapshot beside the package, the way a published wire shape is pinned. jet check compares the row type and the key type with that snapshot.

A new field with a default, or an optional field, is recorded as one generated step, applied when the table opens. A removed, renamed or retyped field, or a changed key type, is a compile error naming the table, the field and the change. Its fix line is the SQL step to add, which the program lists with store.table(..., migrate: [steps]). Each step runs once and is recorded in the migrate ledger.

Edge case: renaming Task.title to name. jet check reports that tasks lost title and gained name, and suggests SQL{"ALTER TABLE tasks RENAME COLUMN title TO name"}. After the step is listed, open applies it once.

Beginner path: one line per table and plain methods. Expert path: the same store still runs checked SQL, and a scope that runs as the system can bypass a guard on purpose.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. Core/Db gains Store (db.open) and Table<K, T> with get, add, put, delete, query, search and scan. It gains Who (Account, System) and Op (Read, Insert, Update, Delete), and DBError gains Denied, Exists and Busy. Query<T> gains limit and count. T and K are #Codable; K is #Comparable. The table keeps key columns from K and one column per top-level scalar field of T for filters.

New diagnostics: an impure key function, a filter that needs a full scan (a warning), and a row type that changed without a migration step.

Proof: an example with a db.Table holding a #Secret field prints its stored and wire forms on O0, O1 and O2. A case shows a query's read set refreshing a live query after a write. A UI snapshot shows the effect error for a put without DB.Write. A case runs two concurrent move_task calls and prints one Ok and one Conflict.

options.name: A marker on the row type: #Table(name:, key:) on the struct, and db.Table<T> fields
options.gist: The row struct says which table it lives in and which fields are its key.
options.detail:
The row struct carries #Table(name: "tasks", key: [id]). A composite key lists two fields: key: [project, account]. The service field is tasks: db.Table<Task>, and store.open<Task>() binds it. get takes the key fields in order, as a tuple: self.members.get((project, account)).

The methods, the storage codec, the guard, the filter warning, the read sets and the schema changes work as in A. The key is a list of fields, so it is pure by construction. The difference is where the table is declared: on the row type, once, instead of where the table is opened.

Beginner path: one marker per row type. Expert path: as A.

Gain: the table name and key sit beside the fields they name. Loss: a row type can live in only one table, so an archive table of old tasks needs a copy of the Task struct. The key is a list of field names inside a marker, so a renamed field breaks the marker, and the key has no type of its own to pass around.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. A new #Table marker, declared by core.db, with name: String and key: a list of field names checked against the struct. db.Table<T> derives its key type as a tuple of the key fields' types. The rest is as in A.

options.name: SQL checked against the migrated schema: no table type; jet check verifies each query, like sqlx
options.gist: The program writes the migrations and every query in SQL; jet check proves each query against the schema the migrations build.
options.detail:
The service holds a database scope. A migration creates each table with SQL. jet check replays the package's migrations into a schema and checks every SQL text against it. Each table and column must exist, and the selected columns must match the struct db.decode fills. A method reads with query_one, decodes the row, and writes with execute.

Schema changes are migrations the programmer writes. A struct field with no column, or a query naming a dropped column, is a compile error at the query.

Read sets come from the parsed query: the table and the columns its WHERE clause compares. A write names its table and the key it changes, so a live query refreshes only when a write could match it.

Beginner path: learn SQL first. Expert path: full control of every statement, joins and indexes included.

Gain: what runs is exactly what is written, every query is checked, and no new table surface is taught. Loss: every table and every query is written by hand, so a get-by-key is three lines of SQL and decode. A composite key, a row policy and a #Secret column are the program's job in SQL text, and a policy stays limited to true and owner == user.
options.technical: Proposed in part. Core/Db has query, query_one, execute, migrate, decode and live today. New: a schema built from the package's migrations at check time, a check of each SQL text against it, and statement-level read sets. The transaction rule above applies. Proof: the same move_task case written in SQL, and a UI snapshot of a query naming a dropped column.

comparisons.note: A table is a value built from a name and typed columns, and queries are typed by it: the shape of A. Migrations are generated from the table values by drizzle-kit. Source: https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/sql-schema-declaration
comparisons.code: export const tasks = sqliteTable("tasks", { id: text("id").primaryKey() });

comparisons.note: One schema file is the source of the typed client and of generated migrations; a rename needs a hand-edited migration. Close to A's schema story. Source: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations
A schema macro on the row module names the table and its fields, the shape of B; migrations are written by hand. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/ecto/Ecto.Schema.html

A table! description, printed from the migrated database, types every query at compile time; migrations are SQL the programmer writes. Between A and C. Source: https://diesel.rs/guides/schema-in-depth.html
comparisons.code: table! { tasks (id) { id -> Text, title -> Text, } }

comparisons.note: Plain SQL text, checked at compile time against the migrated database or its saved description: the shape of C. Source: https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/macro.query_as.html
comparisons.code:
let task = sqlx::query_as!(Task, "SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE id = ?", id)
    .fetch_one(&pool).await?;

comparisons.note: Each mutation is one serializable transaction that the platform retries on conflict, and side effects go to scheduled functions: the transaction rule here. Source: https://docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ
comparisons.code: export const move = mutation(async (ctx, { id }) => { await ctx.db.patch(id, { status: "done" }); });

recommendation.why: A gives each table a typed key and row with one pure function, writes the schema steps it can prove safe, and reuses the data library's Query<T>. B ties a row type to one table and puts the key in field names. C checks every query, but leaves every table, key, policy and secret to hand-written SQL.
gains: A table, its key and its row type are declared once and checked at every get, put and query.
#Secret fields stay in storage and never reach a client answer.
Live screens refresh only when a write touched the rows they read.

losses.loss: New public names in core.db: Store, Table, Who, Op, and three DBError cases.
losses.mitigation: They replace hand-written CREATE TABLE, SELECT and decode code, and the query side adds no carrier: query() returns the existing Query<T>.

losses.loss: A filter the compiler cannot turn into SQL needs a full scan.
losses.mitigation: Such a filter is a registered warning naming the part it could not read, and only an explicit .scan() silences it.

losses.loss: A retried method could repeat work outside the database.
losses.mitigation: The compiler refuses Net, FS.Write and Exec effects inside a method that writes, and app.after_commit runs such work once after the commit.

losses.loss: A renamed or removed field, or a new key type, needs a migration step the programmer adds.
losses.mitigation: jet check finds the change before the app runs, and its fix line is the SQL step to add; safe additions are generated.

whyNot.reason: A row type can live in only one table, and the key is a list of field names with no type of its own.
Every query is checked, but each get-by-key is hand-written SQL and decode, and composite keys, policies and secrets stay the program's job in SQL text.

recommendation.tradeoff: A typed table costs a handful of new core.db names in exchange for checked keys, guarded secrets, generated safe migrations and precise live refresh.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Main's review found five gaps (a checked-SQL option, schema evolution, the full-scan filter, isolation and Busy, and the key function's purity), and every one is fixed in this payload.

decisions.title: Where a streamed page splits into regions: at each read's Loading branch, at an explicit deferred wrapper, or nowhere with the client finishing slow reads
decisions.situation: When a server builds a web page, some data comes back fast and some comes back slow. Today a Jet server waits for every read to finish before it sends any of the page. One slow read makes the whole page late, and the person sees a blank screen. Streaming sends the parts that are ready first, with a loading state in place of the slow parts. Each slow part then arrives on the same connection when its data is ready. This vote picks where a page splits into those parts, which we call regions, and in what order they appear. We recommend A: each read that a screen matches on is its own region, and its Loading branch is what shows until the data arrives.
decisions.gist: Should a streamed page split at each read's Loading branch, at an explicit deferred wrapper, or should the client finish slow reads itself?
decisions.lesson: A page is ready in pieces. If the server knows which piece waits on which read, it can send the ready pieces at once and fill in each slow piece the moment its data arrives.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A read is a call a screen makes for data, such as app.state(app.live(fn() { crew.board(id) })). A screen matches on its state: Loading, Failed or Loaded. The Loading branch is the code that draws the screen while the data is on its way.

The shell is the first part of the page the server sends. A region is a part of the page that the server may send later. Streaming means sending one HTTP answer in several pieces over one connection.

Layout shift is the page jumping when a late part appears with a different size. Resuming means the browser picks the page up where the server left it, without running the screen code again.
decisions.story:
Sam opens a project board. The page has a header, the board and a members panel. The board's read takes 300 ms; the header and the members panel are ready in 10 ms.

Under A the app graph says .stream(after: 50ms). At 50 ms the server sends the header, the members panel and the board's spinner, which is its Loading branch. At 300 ms it sends the board, and the spinner is replaced in place. Sam's programmer wrote no new code; the spinner was already there.

Under B the programmer also wraps the board in ui.deferred with a fallback, and an unwrapped slow read still holds up the whole page. Under C Sam sees the spinner at 50 ms too. But the browser then asks the server for the board in a second request, so the board arrives one round trip later.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: where a page streamed by .stream(after:) splits into regions, in what order they appear, and what each region carries. The graph spelling .stream(after: 50ms) is already in the web app shape.

Current code. Core/App/App.jet's state reads a live binding and returns Loadable: Idle, Loading, Failed or Loaded. On the server it runs the read at once and waits for it. App.stream is a stub in the shape proposal and is not built.

The same for every option. Without .stream the page is sent whole, after every read, as today. A page whose reads all finish before after: is sent whole too, with no swap code. A screen cached with .cache(.Public) is always sent whole, so a shared cache never keeps a page with Loading regions.

HTTP status, the same for every option. The status code and the head are fixed when the shell is sent. A 404 from a bad link comes from the route decode, which runs before the shell. A read whose Failed branch shows the graph's not-found or error view decides the status, so it holds the shell until it finishes. Any other read that fails after the shell draws its Failed branch under the 200 already sent.

Placing a late piece, for A and B. Each later piece is HTML in a template tag plus a short inline script that moves it into place. A browser with scripts off keeps the Loading branch. Requests from known search crawlers get the whole page, as Next.js does for bots.

Resume, the same for every option. Each piece carries its read's encoded result in the page's resume state. The browser never runs the read or the screen code again for that region.

Out of scope: the head and sitemap builders, install and assets, which have their own cards.

options.name: Each read is a region, and its Loading branch is the fallback
options.gist: A screen that matches on app.state is one region; no new code.
options.detail:
Each app.state read on the server starts its source on its own task. When after: passes, a read still running draws its Loading branch inside a marked region. The server then sends the shell. When the read finishes, the server draws that region's Loaded branch and sends it. A read that fails after the shell draws its Failed branch the same way.

Concurrency. A page runs at most 8 reads at once; the rest wait their turn in page order. The reads belong to the request's task group, so they stop when the browser disconnects or the request times out.

Reveal order. A region inside another region appears only after its parent. Sibling regions appear in page order: one that finishes early waits for the regions above it. Reveals are batched every 300 ms, so the page moves a few times at most, top to bottom.

Layout shift remains when a Loading branch and its Loaded branch differ in size. A Loading branch drawn at the size of its content, such as a placeholder of the board's height, avoids it.

Beginner path: add .stream(after: 50ms) to the graph; the spinners already written become the fallbacks. Expert path: a screen that must arrive whole reads its data with a plain call instead of app.state. jet inspect choices lists each region with its read.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. app.state gains a server mode that returns Loading when the stream deadline passes and records the region. The web server writes the response in chunks and bounds each page's reads at 8. The renderer marks each region's root node and orders reveals. No new public names beyond the shape's App.stream.

Proof: a case with two reads, one fast and one slow, shows the shell with the slow read's Loading branch and then its Loaded HTML. A second case shows a read that fails after the 200 status drawing its Failed branch.

options.name: An explicit wrapper: ui.deferred(fallback:, content:)
options.gist: Only code wrapped in ui.deferred streams; every other read holds up the shell.
options.detail:
A region is written by hand: ui.deferred(fallback: kit.spinner(), content: fn() { board(crew, view) }). The server sends the fallback in the shell and the content later. A read outside any ui.deferred holds up the shell until it finishes. Concurrency and placing are as in A; reveal order follows the wrappers, which can group several reads into one reveal.

Beginner path: wrap each slow part. Expert path: choose exactly which parts stream and which appear together.

Gain: a reader sees each region in the code, and grouping is explicit, as React's Suspense and SuspenseList give. Loss: two ways to say loading, the Loading branch and the fallback, and a screen needs both. A slow read that nobody wrapped makes the whole page late, which is the problem streaming is meant to fix.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. A new ui.deferred function in the ui package. The rest is as in A.

options.name: No server streaming: send the shell at the deadline, and the client finishes slow reads
options.gist: The server stops waiting at after:; the browser runs each unfinished read itself.
options.detail:
At after: the server sends the whole page with each unfinished read's Loading branch and closes the answer. The browser resumes the page, sees the unfinished reads and calls the server for each one.

Beginner path: as A. Expert path: as A.

Gain: the server sends one plain answer and needs no chunked writer. Loss: each slow region arrives one round trip later than in A. The server's work on that read is thrown away and done again. A browser with scripts off keeps the Loading branch, as in A, and crawlers get whole pages, as in A.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. app.state gains the same deadline as in A; the client runs unfinished reads through app.Remote after resume. No chunked response.

comparisons.note: Explicit Suspense boundaries mark regions, the shape of B, and SuspenseList controls reveal order. React throttles reveals to limit layout shift, and Next.js sends whole pages to bots. A borrows the ordering, throttling and bot rule but places boundaries at reads. Source: https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense

A loader returns a deferred promise and the page awaits it inside Suspense, with its own error element. Each deferred value is chosen in the loader, closer to B. Source: https://remix.run/docs/en/main/guides/streaming

An await tag streams in order with no script, or out of order with client-reorder. A only streams out of order, so A needs a script that Marko's in-order mode does not. Source: https://markojs.com/docs/await/
Suspense boundaries over resources stream out of order, and a resource read outside a boundary suspends the nearest parent. Source: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/components/suspense

assign_async loads data after the first render, and the template matches on loading, failed and ok, close to A's Loading branch. It updates over the live socket, not one streamed HTML answer. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/phoenix_live_view/Phoenix.LiveView.html#assign_async/4

recommendation.why: A streams every slow read with the Loading branches screens already have, so there is one way to say loading and no slow read can hold up the page by accident. B adds a second loading form, and C makes each slow region a round trip late.
gains: Turning streaming on is one line on the app graph; screens do not change.
Every slow read streams, so no forgotten wrapper makes the page late.
Each region resumes from its own result, with no second render in the browser.

losses.loss: A screen cannot ask for one read to hold up the shell while the rest stream.
losses.mitigation: It reads that data with a plain call instead of app.state, and jet inspect choices lists every region with its read.

losses.loss: A read that fails after the 200 status cannot change the status code.
losses.mitigation: A read whose Failed branch shows the not-found or error view holds the shell, and a 404 from a bad link comes from the route decode first.

losses.loss: Late regions can make the page jump.
losses.mitigation: Regions appear in page order, batched every 300 ms, and a Loading branch drawn at its content's size does not shift.

losses.loss: A browser with scripts off keeps the Loading branch of a late region.
losses.mitigation: Known search crawlers get the whole page, and a cached public page is always sent whole.

whyNot.reason: It needs both a fallback and a Loading branch for one wait, and a slow read nobody wrapped still makes the page late.
Each slow region costs one more round trip, and the server's work on it is done twice.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives up a per-read hold-the-shell switch and explicit grouping in exchange for streaming that needs no screen changes.

decisions.title: When shipping Core already checked would make a compile slower, which rule wins?
decisions.situation: Core is Jet's standard library: files, text, maths and more. jet already ships Core's machine code, but every compile still checks some Core function bodies from text, such as the generic ones. One rule says no compile may do that. A second rule says shipping Core precompiled must never make a compile slower or use more memory. The first try broke the second rule badly: hello took 22 seconds instead of about 1, and that design was retired. The next steps load checked bodies instead. Each load must cost under a tenth of a check, but memory and start-up can still lose. You are asked which rule wins when one step meets the first rule and breaks the second. We recommend A: speed gates every merge, small losses cannot add up across steps, and each kind of body moves only when loading it is no slower.
decisions.gist: Jet wants its standard library already checked inside jet, and no compile ever slower. When one step can't do both, which rule wins?
decisions.lesson: Two good rules can pull apart. Decide ahead of time which one gates a merge, and make the other one a measured goal rather than a silent exception.
decisions.explainer:
Checking means the compiler confirms that code is correct: names, types, effects. A checked body is a function whose checking was done when jet itself was built. Loading it means reading those saved results instead of redoing the work.

A kind of body is a group that loads the same way, such as generic functions (written once for many types) or methods of built-in types.

Peak memory is the most memory one compile uses at any moment.

The noise band is a change too small to tell from noise on a shared machine: 3% and 2 ms in time, 1 MB or 1% in memory.
decisions.story: Mia writes a six-line program that reads a file and prints it. Today jet checks 79 Core function bodies from text for it, about 74 ms of its 790 ms of CPU. If a new step loads those bodies already checked, but her compile then takes more memory or time, her compile gets slower.
decisions.inWild:
Swift ships its standard library as a binary module with inlinable bodies, and also a text interface (.swiftinterface) that a newer compiler rebuilds when the binary one can't be used.
Rust ships the standard library as rlib files: machine code plus metadata holding generic and inline bodies, which rustc decodes lazily.
Go has shipped no precompiled standard library since Go 1.20; it rebuilds it from source into a build cache.
decisions.detail:
The two rules are card #6328 criteria c22 and c37. c22 (open): Core and Prelude ship precompiled inside jet, as checked interfaces and machine code made when jet is built. `jet run` reads, scans and re-checks no Core source, and strace of hello shows no file calls on the toolchain tree. It keeps one meaning on O0, O1 and O2.

c37 (met): with precompiled Core, `jet check hello.jet` and `jet run hello.jet` take no more wall time and peak memory than with Core from sources, median of 3. It was met on 2026-11-15 by the seal stand-ins (dev c01387e368). On p143 and p144 hello tied (wall ratio 1.000), and lint, e3401, RunColdContext and Summarize got faster. Its text still names the retired record and covers only hello, so every option also rewords it.

History: the front-end Core record met part of c22 and broke c37. On gate-p62 the record jet took 22.1 to 24.4 s at 1.68 GB, against 0.76 to 1.5 s at 185 MB from sources. Its decoder cost about 10 us per row byte, and its module-sized units widened what a compile loaded. It was retired on 2026-11-14.

What ships today: Core's machine code, `jet_core.o`, built at O2 when jet is built. A call to a sealed Core function binds to it through a stand-in checked by signature only (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/CoreDemand.jet). The bodies a compile still checks from text are the kept ones. They are generic functions, function values, intrinsics, the 35 packages not built as machine code (`JET_CLI_CORE_LOWERED`), impl methods, defaults and comptime calls (note section 4).

What step B can win, measured on p155: a kept body costs 0.84 to 0.96 ms of traced CPU to check. fread.jet, six lines using core.files, keeps 79 bodies: 73.7 ms of its 790 ms user plus sys. RunColdContext keeps 591: 494.6 ms of 4,180 ms. So step B can remove about a tenth of these compiles' CPU, and less of their wall time.

Where a B step can lose: note section 3.3 fails any form whose load costs more than a tenth of the check, per body. So a step is unlikely to lose CPU on the bodies it replaces. It can lose elsewhere. A loaded body is a full owned body, so peak memory can rise. jet may grow by up to 48 MB across A and B, which costs page faults on a cold start. Setup and wider loading add fixed cost, which is where the record lost.

Never slower is defined in note section 6.2. The programs are hello, abs.jet, fread.jet, e2404, lint, e3401, RunColdContext and Summarize, under `jet check` and `jet run`. Each runs on built-in Core, with a named matching tree and with a named edited tree. The jet before and the jet after alternate over 11 warm runs, plus 5 cold runs. A program is worse when its median wall or CPU rises by more than 3% and 2 ms, or its peak memory by more than 1 MB or 1%.

Plan (Docs/proposals/2026-11-15-lazy-precompiled-core-interfaces.md): step A ships declarations, signatures, types, constants and reach. Step B ships checked bodies one kind at a time, B0 to B5 (section 4). Until the owner rules, Main's ruling on gap H16 holds: no B step that makes a 6.2 program worse merges.

Numbers so far: none for any B step. The only new ones come from the unlanded A2a patch (PrecompiledCore-4-a2a-lazy-bodies), which still parses Core text, heads first and then the kept bodies. They were measured in process, one run each, as load peak memory. A core.files, core.sys and core.process program parsed 1,376 Core bodies instead of 1,962. Its load peak fell from 103.8 to 92.6 MB. Hello's load grew 17.5 MB against 17.6 MB. No timing from that machine was valid.

Forms a kind can take are Main's choice within c22. Machine code in `jet_core.o` already serves sealed calls, and could take the lowered packages at a cost in jet's size, but not every generic instance or comptime call. The interface alone is step A; it leaves fread's 79 bodies (option C). Checked rows loaded per body are B1's form. Note section 9 rejects a mapped image of sema's tables, which hold per-process ids. This ballot decides what happens when the best form still loses.

Beginner path: Mia writes and sets nothing, and her program is the same under every option. She cannot tell which kinds load. Expert path: a Core contributor names the edited tree with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT (ruling T1). A named tree always checks Core from text, so step B never changes its speed, and the named-tree arms of 6.2 check that. The counter `core.bodies_from_text.<category>`, which step A0 adds, shows which kinds still come from text.

Edge cases. Stale artifact: the interface is part of the jet binary, written by the same check as `jet_core.o` and the seal, so nothing on disk can go stale. A Core unit whose text hash does not match its rows parses whole. Cross-tier: until B5, `jet build` at O1 and O2 checks bodies from text, so one function can be loaded under `jet run` and checked under `jet build`. The body guard and note section 8's tier proof run at every step, in every option.

Noise: the machine is shared, so a change inside the band counts as no change, and a slowdown of up to 3% or 2 ms can pass unseen in any option. A kind that stays on text keeps a text body path on built-in Core. The note does not yet say how that fits A2's proof that a compile parses 0 bytes of Core text.

Gates this ballot cannot loosen: the AGENTS.md performance gate still fails any build-time cell where Jet loses to a peer, whatever option wins. The cold compile target is 30 million lines per second. Option C leaves about a tenth of CPU in Core body checks for good, and option B lets steps drift away from that target.

options.name: Speed gates every merge; each kind of body moves only when it is no slower
options.gist: No step that slows a measured program beyond the noise band merges, and small losses cannot add up across steps. A kind of body that loads slower keeps being checked from text until a faster form exists.
options.detail:
Each B step runs note section 6.2's A/B against the jet before it. It merges only if no program is worse beyond the band, in time or peak memory. A ledger also multiplies each program's ratios over all B steps. If a product passes the band, no further kind moves until a step wins it back, so six steps cannot each spend 3%.

A kind that loses keeps checking from text, with a published row: its gap and the next form to try. c22 is claimed when every kind has moved. A kind that never wins returns to the owner with its numbers, and c22 stays open meanwhile. c37 is reworded to the 6.2 set and band.

options.name: The precompiled rule wins within a small budget
options.gist: A B step may merge even if it slows a program, up to 5% wall time and 5% peak memory.
options.detail: Each B step is timed as in A. A step whose loss is up to 5% in time or peak memory still merges, in place of A's 3% band. c37 is reworded to allow it. Best form: A's ledger caps the total at 5% per program over all of B. Without a cap, six steps could add up to 34%. c22 comes sooner only for a kind that loses by between 3% and 5%.

options.name: The speed rule wins for good; Core stays text plus an index
options.gist: Stop at step A: Core ships declarations already checked, and compiles check the bodies they use from text.
options.detail: Stop after step A. c22 is reworded: a compile may check the Core bodies it keeps from text, reading only those bodies. No B step is built. This reverses the owner's 2026-11-12 restatement that Core ships checked inside jet. Kept-body checks stay on every compile: about a tenth of CPU for fread and RunColdContext.

options.name: Nothing merges until every kind of body is faster
options.gist: Hold every B step unlanded, and land all of them at once when every program is faster.
options.detail: No B step lands on its own. Each is written and tested, and the stack waits as unlanded patches in Main's inbox, since the repository allows no extra branch. It lands in one change once the whole stack passes A's gate. Owner orders say finished work lands and is never held, so D needs an exception to them. A failure in the one large change is harder to trace to its kind.

options.name: Net never slower: all steps together must beat checking from text
options.gist: A step may be slower on its own, as long as all B steps so far, together, are no slower than checking Core from text.
options.detail:
This reads c37 as written: compare with Core from text, not with the jet of the day before. Each B step runs A's A/B, and A's ledger multiplies each program's ratios since the jet before B0. A step merges while every program's product stays within the band, even if that step alone is slower. A losing kind can then ride on the wins of the kinds before it.

No measured program ends slower than Core from text, but one can get slower than the jet of the day before. A program outside the set that uses only the losing kind can end slower than text.

recommendation.why: A keeps every measured compile within noise of the jet before it, and stops small losses adding up over all of B. It moves each kind of body as soon as loading it wins, and shows exactly what blocks c22.
gains: No measured compile gets slower than the jet before it, beyond the noise band
The ledger stops small losses adding up across steps
Each kind of body moves as soon as it wins
What blocks c22 is a published, measured list

losses.loss: c22 may close later than under B or E, or never, if some kind never loads fast enough.
losses.mitigation: Each lagging kind publishes its gap and next form (machine code, narrower rows, per-body loading), and returns to the owner with its numbers.

losses.loss: Until every kind moves, built-in Core keeps a text body path beside the loaded one.
losses.mitigation: The text path stays for named trees anyway, and the body guard compares the two paths in every build.

losses.loss: Only the 6.2 programs are gated, so another program can still get slower.
losses.mitigation: The census of note section 10 reports Core bodies by kind over every example and gauntlet program, and a program that loses joins the set.

whyNot.reason: B's 5% allowance is only 2 points looser than A's 3% band, so it buys little c22 time. It still lets compiles drift slower, against the owner's order for a measured win over no precompiled Core.
C gives up on checked bodies before any of them is measured. It reverses the owner's ruling that Core ships checked, and keeps about a tenth of CPU in Core body checks on every compile.
D holds back the kinds of bodies that already win, needs an exception to the rule that ready work lands, and makes one large change that is hard to trace.
E lets one step make a program slower than the jet of the day before, so a user who upgrades can see a regression. Programs outside the measured set lose the most.

recommendation.tradeoff: A later, possibly open c22 claim, in exchange for never shipping a measured compile slower than the jet before it.
