decisions.title: How a program makes an HTTP body: free functions in core.http, renamed Body constructors, or one name for both a constructor and a reader
decisions.situation: An HTTP body is the payload of a web request or response: some text, a form or JSON. Today a program can make one in two ways. It can call http.body_text("hi"), or it can call http.Body.text("hi"). The second form reuses the name of the method that reads a body back, body.text(limit). Jet does not let one type have two members with one name, so the compiler checks those Body calls with about 1,000 lines of special code. No library can use that code, which breaks the rule that Core is ordinary Jet. You are asked how a program should make a body. We recommend the free functions that already exist, http.body_text and its family, and removing the Body.* forms.
decisions.gist: Should HTTP bodies be made with http.body_text(...) and its family, with renamed Body.of_text(...) constructors, or should a type allow a constructor and a method with one name?
decisions.lesson: One thing should have one name. When making a value and reading it back share a name, either the language needs a special rule or the library needs special compiler help. Neither is needed if the maker has its own name.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A body is the payload of an HTTP message. A constructor is a function that makes a new value of a type. A static member is a function written inside a type and called through the type's name, such as Body.text("hi"). An instance member, or method, is called on a value, such as body.text(5), which reads the body back as text of at most 5 bytes.

A free function is one written at module level, called through the module, such as http.body_text("hi").

The compiler-side checker is code inside the compiler that knows these HTTP calls by name. Any library that wanted the same shape could not have it.
decisions.story:
Ada writes a small client. She builds a JSON body, sends it, and reads the answer as text.

Today she finds two ways in the docs: http.body_text("hi") in the core library table, and http.Body.text("hi") in the HTTP example. Both work. Later she writes her own Message type and tries the same trick, a text constructor next to a text method. Jet stops her with E0105, a duplicate definition. Core could do it only because the compiler helps Core.

Under A she sees one way: http.body_text, http.body_form and http.body_json. Her own library can use the same pattern with no special help.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: one spelling for making an HTTP body, and whether a type may have a static and an instance member with one name.

Current code, checked on dev 963b9fbd76. Core/Http/Http.jet declares Body with the reading methods bytes(self, limit), text(self, limit) and json<Target>(self, limit). It also declares the free functions body_empty, body_text and body_bytes. The spec's core library table lists those as the constructors (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md, line 1614).

The Body.* forms are not declared on Body at all. They are Body.empty(), Body.bytes(b), Body.text(t), Body.text(t, media_type), Body.form(fields), Body.multipart(fields), Body.json(value) and Body.reader(reader) with an optional length.

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Http.jet recognizes them by type and member name. It calls hidden helpers: __body_typed_text, __body_form, __body_json, __body_reader and __body_reader_sized. The same file handles Headers.new and Client.new, which have no name clash and become ordinary static members under every option.

A user type cannot copy this shape: a struct with text(words: String) and text(self) is E0105, a duplicate definition.

Callers of the Body.* forms: 8 code sites, plus 2 rows in the core library table. Seven sites are in Examples/Network/HTTP/HTTPMessageValues.jet and one in tests/ui/print_lazy_iter_view.jet. Callers of the free functions http.body_empty, body_text and body_bytes outside Core/Http: 30 sites in 8 files.

This ballot leaves out the route checks in Sema/Calls/HttpRouting.jet, which move to library markers in a separate design.

options.name: Free functions in core.http: http.body_text, http.body_form, http.body_json and the rest
options.gist: Extend the free functions that already exist and remove the Body.* forms.
options.detail:
core.http keeps body_empty, body_text and body_bytes. It adds body_typed_text(text, media_type), body_form(fields), body_multipart(fields) and body_json(value). It also adds body_reader(reader) and body_reader_sized(reader, length). Each one is an ordinary public function with its own declared signature and effects. The Body.* call forms are removed, and the compiler's HTTP body checker is deleted with them.

Beginner path: type http.body_ and the editor lists every way to make a body. The core library table already teaches this spelling.

Expert path: the same functions; a library with its own message type writes the same free-function family with no compiler help.

Cost: 8 code sites and 2 table rows change. The 30 existing free-function callers do not change.

Edge cases: a missing Body.text("hi") call gets the ordinary missing-member error, whose fix names http.body_text. Two-argument forms that differed only by count get their own names (body_typed_text, body_reader_sized), because Jet has no overloading.
options.technical:
Proposed. Core/Http/Http.jet: the hidden __body_* helpers become public body_typed_text, body_form, body_multipart, body_json<T: Encode>, body_reader and body_reader_sized with today's bodies. Headers.new becomes an ordinary static new on Headers next to headers(), and Client.new an ordinary static new on Client. Sema/Calls/Http.jet's static-constructor path is deleted.

The missing-member error E0102 gains a fix that names the free function. It applies when the type's module declares a function named for the type in lower case, an underscore and the member. Proof: the HTTP example and a ui case for the fix text.

options.name: Rename the constructors: Body.of_text, Body.of_json, Body.of_form, Body.of_reader
options.gist: Constructors stay on Body under names that differ from the reading methods.
options.detail:
Body declares static members of_empty, of_bytes, of_text, of_typed_text, of_form, of_multipart, of_json, of_reader and of_reader_sized. The compiler's checker is deleted.

Beginner path: type http.Body. and the editor lists the makers next to the readers.

Expert path: the same members.

Cost: the 8 Body.* sites and 2 table rows change. The 30 free-function callers must also move to Body.of_*, or the free functions stay as a second spelling of the same thing, which breaks the one-way rule.

Edge cases: none new; of_ is a new naming pattern that no other Core type uses today.
options.technical: Proposed. Body gains nine static members; body_empty, body_text and body_bytes are removed with their 30 callers. Sema/Calls/Http.jet's static-constructor path is deleted.

options.name: Let a type have a static and an instance member with the same name
options.gist: Body.text("hi") makes a body and body.text(5) reads one, by a new language rule.
options.detail:
A type may declare one static member and one instance member with the same name. Resolution rule: a call through the type's name, Body.text(...), picks the static member; a call on a value, body.text(...), picks the instance member. Two static or two instance members with one name stay E0105.

Edge cases. Reading Body.text without parentheses where a function is expected gives the static member, since a method is bound only on a value. A trait that declares both forms must be implemented with both. A generic call T.text(...) on a type parameter picks the static member. A name used with both forms gets a new registered error when one call could match either, such as a future form that passes the receiver explicitly.

Beginner path: today's code keeps working. Expert path: the same.

Cost: no caller changes. The free functions stay, so a body still has two spellings unless the 30 free-function sites move too.
options.technical: Proposed. Registration keeps a static slot and an instance slot per member name. Method lookup on a type name reads the static slot; on a value, the instance slot. Body declares its constructors as static members; the free functions either stay or are removed with 30 callers. Sema/Calls/Http.jet's static-constructor path is deleted. One new diagnostic code for an ambiguous call.

comparisons.note: Bodies are made with free constructors of readers, such as strings.NewReader, and passed to http.NewRequest; reading is a method on the response body, the shape of A. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#NewRequest
Body is made through From and read through methods with other names, the shape of B. Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Body.html

Static and instance members may share a base name, told apart by the receiver and argument labels, the shape of C. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/methods/
comparisons.code: struct Note { static func text(_ s: String) -> Note { ... }; func text() -> String { ... } }

recommendation.why: A keeps the spelling the spec already teaches and 30 callers already use, removes the second spelling, and needs no new language rule. B renames 38 call sites to reach one spelling, and C adds a rule for a single type.
gains: One way to make a body, the one the core library table already lists.
Only 8 code sites and 2 table rows change.
About 1,000 lines of compiler-only HTTP checking are deleted.
A user library can copy the pattern with no compiler help.

losses.loss: Typing http.Body. in the editor no longer lists the makers.
losses.mitigation: Body's doc comment names the body_ functions, and a call such as Body.text("hi") gets an error whose fix names http.body_text.

losses.loss: Forms that differed only by argument count need two names.
losses.mitigation: Each name says what it takes, body_reader and body_reader_sized, as Jet does everywhere it has no overloading.

whyNot.reason: To reach one spelling it renames all 38 sites, including the 30 that already use the spelled-out free functions, and it adds an of_ pattern no other Core type uses.
It adds a language rule and an ambiguity error for one library type, and it leaves two spellings for one body unless 30 sites move anyway.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives up listing makers under Body. in exchange for one spelling, no language change and the smallest migration.

decisions.title: How a server entry gives push notifications their provider keys: one .push(...) call with a maker per provider, one modifier per provider, or typed secret fields in the environment file
decisions.situation: A push notification reaches a phone or a browser through the company that delivers it: Apple, Google, or the browser's push service. Each of them asks the sender to prove who it is with a secret key. Jet already builds and signs every push, but no public code says where those keys come from, so an app cannot send a push today. This vote picks that code, and it matters to every app that pushes. A beginner should be able to paste it, and a deployment should keep the keys out of the source. We recommend A: one .push(...) line in the server entry, where the app names its own environment variables. It is shaped like the mail line of the ratified app shape (D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1), which is designed and not built yet.
decisions.gist: Should a server entry give push its provider keys through one .push(...) call, one modifier per provider, or typed secret fields in the environment file?
decisions.lesson: A secret such as a signing key belongs outside the code, in an environment variable the app names. The code says which variable holds which key, and the server reads them once as it starts. One place in the server entry then lists every way the app reaches people: mail and push.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A provider is the service that delivers a push: APNs for Apple systems, FCM for Android, and a browser's push service for Web Push. A credential is what proves the sender to the provider. An environment variable is a named value the host hands a program as it starts, such as SMTP_URL.

Apple's .p8 file is a signing key a developer downloads once. Google's service-account file is a JSON file with a key inside. VAPID is the key pair a Web Push sender signs with. The topic is the app's bundle ID, such as com.example.crewboard.
decisions.story:
Mia's Crewboard server sends a push when a task gets an assignee. She has Apple's key file, Google's service-account file and a fresh VAPID key.

Under A she adds one .push(...) line below .mail(...) in Web/web.jet. It names APNS_KEY, APNS_KEY_ID, FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT and VAPID_KEY. She lists the same names as secrets in env.jet. On her first deploy she forgets VAPID_KEY. The server refuses to start, naming the variable and the line, so her host's health check fails before anyone misses a push.

Under B she writes three lines, .apns(...), .fcm(...) and .web_push(...), with the same names. Mail still uses .mail(app.smtp(...)), so her entry has two shapes for one idea.

Under C she writes no push code. She declares typed push fields in env.jet, and jet dev checks the key files first. Her production host starts the program without Jetpack, so she needs a second way to hand it the same keys.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: the public code a server entry writes to give the three push providers their credentials. APNs needs a .p8 signing key, its key ID, the team ID and the topic. FCM needs a service-account JSON file. Web Push needs a VAPID private key and a contact address (the VAPID subject).

Out of scope, decided on #6800 by Main on 2026-11-16. Fixed JET_* variable names are refused. Device registration is internal: POST /__jet/push/devices and __jet_push_devices rows, through a store hook like CallOutbox. The HTTP/2 client stays inside core.http.client. A provider with no configuration is skipped and logged. Until this ballot lands, the providers build against an internal priv(package) record.

Today, at dev d6d482c5f7, Core/App/Push.jet builds each request from raw values. push_apns_token takes the team ID, the key ID and the private scalar (:243-250). push_ec_private parses a .p8 or SEC1 key (:112-124). push_fcm_token_request signs Google's assertion with the service account's RSA key (:272-285).

push_vapid_authorization signs the VAPID token with a key pair and a contact (:205-218), and push_key_pair derives the public key from the private one (:95-102). No public code reaches any of them. Core/App has no push, mail or smtp configuration at all: git grep finds none in App.jet.

The precedent is mail, still a proposal. The web entry writes .mail(app.smtp("SMTP_URL"), from: "Crewboard <crew@example.com>") (Docs/proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md:2549). Its stub is smtp: fn(url_env: String) -> Mail (:5833-5838), and 4.14 says app.mail sends through the transport the entry names (:3578-3580).

Rules every option shares. The app chooses every variable name. The server reads each one once as it starts, through core.sys.getenv (Core/Sys/Sys.jet:2104), and keeps the value as a #Secret String. Jetpack's dotenv secrets list keeps those values out of plans, logs and images (Docs/spec/reference/jetpack-epoch5.md:493-496). If an allow list is given, each secret must be on it (Jetpack/EnvModel/Source/Environment/FactReaders.jet:399-405).

A named variable that is unset or empty refuses the start before the port opens. The error names the variable, the argument and the source line. A key that does not parse refuses the start the same way, with Push.jet's own reason, such as "the key is not on P-256". A variable may hold the key file itself or its base64 on one line, so a multi-line .p8 or JSON file fits any host.

Edge cases. Apple's sandbox and production hosts are chosen per device: registration records which one the app build uses, and one .p8 key serves both. The FCM project ID comes from the service-account file's project_id field. A device whose provider is not configured is skipped and logged. The browser gets the VAPID public key from the server, so the app never writes it twice.

More edge cases. A new VAPID key breaks old browser subscriptions, so the client compares keys as it starts and subscribes again. A push service that answers 404 or 410 drops that subscription. Rotating any key means changing the variable and restarting. APNs and FCM tokens live an hour at most (Push.jet:246, :280), so nothing could switch faster anyway.

Tests need no variables: app.test_host sends to local fake providers with keys it makes, as #6800 c1's proof does. Proof rows are proposed in each option's technical text.

options.name: One .push(...) call with a maker per provider: .push(apns: app.apns(...), fcm: app.fcm(...), web: app.web_push(...))
options.gist: The server entry names the push transport the way it names the mail transport, and each maker names its own environment variables.
options.detail:
The entry gains one builder, .push, with three optional named arguments. app.apns, app.fcm and app.web_push make the three provider values, as app.smtp makes the mail one. An argument ending in _env names an environment variable, the convention of smtp's url_env in the ratified app shape. Every other argument is a plain value that is safe in git: the team ID, the topic and the contact.

Beginner path: paste the .push line, put the three files' contents in .env, and list the names as secrets in env.jet. Leave out a provider the app does not use. A missing variable stops the start with its name and line.

Expert path: choose names per deployment, keep values in the host's secret store, and rotate a key with a rolling restart. A push is a job, and a stopping server leaves its unfinished jobs for the next one (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:5680-5686).

A second .push(...) on one app refuses the start, naming both lines.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. core.app gains App.push: fn(self, apns: APNs?{None}, fcm: FCM?{None}, web: WebPush?{None}) -> App. It gains apns: fn(key_env: String, key_id_env: String, team: String, topic: String) -> APNs.

It also gains fcm: fn(service_account_env: String) -> FCM and web_push: fn(key_env: String, contact: String) -> WebPush. serve reads each variable through core.sys.getenv and parses it once with Push.jet's builders. It refuses the start on an unset, empty or malformed value.

Proof: jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter web_app/push_config_reads_named_variables, where local fakes check each signed request. A second row, web_app/push_config_missing_variable_refuses_start, checks the refusal.

options.name: One modifier per provider: .apns(...), .fcm(...), .web_push(...)
options.gist: Each provider is its own builder method on the app, naming its own environment variables.
options.detail:
The entry gains three builders, one per provider, with the same arguments as A's makers. A provider left out is skipped and logged.

Beginner path: paste the provider lines the app needs and list the names as secrets in env.jet, as in A. Expert path: as in A.

Mail keeps .mail(app.smtp(...)), so an entry names the mail transport with a builder and a maker, but names push providers with bare builders. That is two shapes for one meaning, naming how the app reaches people. Each builder also needs its own rule for a second call.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. core.app gains App.apns, App.fcm and App.web_push, each returning App, with A's argument lists and A's start-up checks. Proof: the same rows as A.

options.name: Typed secret fields in the environment file: push: Push{apns: APNs{key: Secret("APNS_KEY"), ...}} in env.jet
options.gist: The environment file declares typed push fields, Jetpack checks them before the program starts, and the server entry writes nothing.
options.detail:
Jetpack's environment schema gains Push, APNs, FCM, WebPush and Secret records. jet dev checks each secret's form before it starts the program, and the server takes the fields from the environment Jetpack prepared.

Beginner path: fill in the env.jet record; jet dev reports a bad key before the program runs. Expert path: a host that starts the program without Jetpack needs a second way to give the same fields. That means variables with names the framework fixes, or a file it reads.

The environment model is a plan model with no provider, store or network role (Docs/spec/architecture.md:975). Its typed records live in Environment.jet.schema (Jetpack/EnvModel/Source/ModuleEval/Schema/Environment.jet.schema:57-62). Putting push types there ties Jetpack to core.app. Mail would stay in code, so the app's transports would live in two places.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. Jetpack/EnvModel's schema gains the push records and a Secret marker, checked at environment evaluation; core.app reads the prepared environment when serve starts. The production path without Jetpack is not defined by this option and would need its own rule. Proof: jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter jetpack/env_push_fields_checked, plus a web_app row for the production path.

comparisons.note: The app passes its VAPID subject and keys, read from variables it names; the library fixes no names. Like A and B. Source: https://github.com/web-push-libs/web-push

The app gives a service-account credential from where it chooses; GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is one fixed fallback name, which #6800 refuses for Jet. Source: https://firebase.google.com/docs/admin/setup
One APNs token-auth app record holds the key, key ID, team ID and bundle ID, like A's app.apns. Source: https://github.com/rpush/rpush

recommendation.why: A names the push transport the way the ratified app shape (D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1) names the mail transport, with one builder and a maker per provider. Every key stays in a variable the app chose, read once and kept secret. B gives the same meaning a second shape. C needs a second path for every host that starts the program without Jetpack.
gains: One line in the server entry turns on all three providers, shaped like the mail line.
No variable name is fixed by Jet, and no key value appears in code or logs.
A missing or malformed key stops the start with the variable and the line, before any push is lost.

losses.loss: New public names in core.app: App.push, app.apns, app.fcm, app.web_push and their three value types.
losses.mitigation: They mirror .mail, app.smtp and Mail one for one, and they replace the token signing an app would otherwise write by hand.

losses.loss: A missing variable is found as the server starts, not by jet check.
losses.mitigation: The start stops before the port opens and names the variable and the line, so a deploy's health check fails at once. Local tests need no variables, because the test host uses fake providers.

losses.loss: A .p8 key and a service-account file span several lines, which some hosts handle badly in variables.
losses.mitigation: A variable may hold the file's base64 on one line; the server tells the two forms apart by the PEM header or the opening brace.

losses.loss: Changing a key needs a restart.
losses.mitigation: Provider tokens live an hour at most, so a live reload could not switch faster. A rolling restart loses no push, because a stopping server leaves unfinished push jobs for the next one.

whyNot.reason: Three builders give push a different shape from mail for the same meaning, and each needs its own rule for a second call.
Keys checked by Jetpack still need a second path on hosts that start the program without it, and the transports split between env.jet and code.

recommendation.tradeoff: A handful of new core.app names, mirroring mail, buy one checked line that turns on every push provider with names the app chooses.

decisions.title: Where an app's background jobs are kept: only in the app's own database, through a public store trait with a law kit, or through a trait whose promises jet check reads
decisions.situation: A background job is a piece of work a server does after it answers, such as sending a push when a task gets an assignee. Today Jet keeps each job as a row in the app's own database, written in the same step as the change that asked for it. A promise on the jobs card says a home-made job store that breaks the rules is refused when the code is checked. No public way to write a job store exists, so that promise has nothing to check. This vote decides whether apps may plug in their own job store, and how. We recommend A: jobs stay in the app's database, and the promise is reworded to the contract that store keeps.
decisions.gist: Should an app's jobs stay in its own database, or may an app plug in a job store through a tested trait or a trait with checked promises?
decisions.lesson: A job must be saved in the same step as the change that asked for it. Then a change that is undone sends nothing, and a crash never loses a job. Only the database that holds the change can save the job in that step.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A job is work the server does later, after a change is saved. A job store is where jobs wait until they run. A transaction is a group of database writes that all happen or none do; committing it saves them, and rolling it back undoes them.

At least once means a job may run twice after a crash, but never zero times. To acknowledge a job is to mark it done, so it is not run again. An adapter is code that plugs another system, such as Redis, into a slot the framework offers. A trait is a list of methods a type must have.
decisions.story:
Ana assigns a task to Ben in Crewboard. The assignment and a job that pushes to Ben are saved together.

Under A the job is a row in crewboard.db, written in the same transaction as the assignment. If the assignment rolls back, there is no job. If the server crashes after the commit, the row is still there, and the next server runs it. Mia never writes job-store code.

Under B Mia writes RedisJobs, six methods, and runs the law kit in her tests. Redis cannot join crewboard.db's transaction. So her adapter saves the job just after the commit, and a crash between the two loses Ben's push. The law kit passes, because it tests the adapter alone.

Under C she marks RedisJobs with its promises. jet check refuses it, because it cannot join the transaction, which is true of every store outside the database.
decisions.inWild:
# Oban (Elixir): jobs are rows in the app's Postgres, inserted in the caller's transaction.
# https://hexdocs.pm/oban/Oban.html
Ecto.Multi.new() |> Ecto.Multi.update(:task, changeset) |> Oban.insert(:push, PushWorker.new(%{id: id})) |> Repo.transaction()

# Rails Solid Queue: Active Job's backend in the app's own database.
# https://github.com/rails/solid_queue
config.active_job.queue_adapter = :solid_queue

# Sidekiq (Ruby): jobs live in Redis, outside the app's transaction, so enqueueing is a second write beside the commit.
# https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki
PushWorker.perform_async(task.id)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: whether core.app offers a public slot for a job store other than the built-in one. If it does, the ballot decides the slot's shape and how jet check refuses a store that cannot keep the contract. The contract has four parts: at-least-once delivery, acknowledgement only after the job finishes, a new delivery after a crash, and jobs that survive a restart.

It also decides the text of #6825 c9. Today c9 reads: "A queue store adapter that cannot keep the job store's durability and acknowledgement contract is refused at check time with a registered error naming what it lacks". Its proof row is jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter app_job_store_adapter_contract.

Main's ruling of 2026-11-16 on #6825 found no adapter seam an app can write. The only seam is core.app's priv(package) transactions module with CallOutbox, joined only by core.db. Refusing a service with jobs that holds no store would contradict Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:5692-5693. So c9 has no subject until a public slot exists, and adding one is owner-gated public API.

Today, at dev d6d482c5f7, Core/App/App.jet:766-772 says a queued job is kept in the outbox of the first store the call joined, in that store's transaction. CallOutbox (:780-811) is the hook: now, keep, done, failed, take and hold. The transactions module that joins it is priv(package) (:874), and so is the jobs module (:1160).

core.db fills the hook. db_join hands each store's outbox to the call as its transaction begins (Core/Db/Db.jet:1370-1383). db_outbox keeps a job as an INSERT into __jet_jobs on the connection that holds the call's open transaction (:1460-1501). The hold lasts five seconds and is renewed each second (App.jet:1108-1117).

Two parts of the contract depend on that shared transaction. A rolled-back write queues nothing (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:5662-5665, #6825 c1). A repeated run's writes are dropped, because each store records the job's key with the job's own writes (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:5686-5691, #6825 c6). A store outside the database cannot join that transaction.

Such a store must save the job either before the commit, so a rollback still runs it, or after it, so a crash in between loses it. That is the dual-write problem, which Oban, Solid Queue and the outbox pattern avoid by keeping jobs in the app's database.

Edge cases. An in-memory database keeps its jobs only as long as the process, the same as the rows that queued them; core.db never scans one for jobs at open (Db.jet:1268). A call that used no store runs its job at once without keeping it, as the ratified text says (core-library.md:5692-5693); no option changes that.

options.name: Jobs stay in the app's database: no public store slot, and c9 is reworded to that store's contract
options.gist: The job row is written in the same transaction as the change that queued it, and c9 states the contract every database engine must pass.
options.detail:
No new public surface. A job is a row of __jet_jobs in the first store the call used, written in that call's transaction, as today. A database engine that core.db adds later brings its outbox through core.db's internal hook, so apps change nothing.

c9 becomes: "Jobs are kept only in a core.db store's outbox, in the transaction of the call that queued them. core.app has no public job-store slot, so no app code can weaken the contract. Every engine core.db opens passes the contract rows of c1, c6, c7 and c8."

Its proof row becomes jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter web_app/job_store_contract_per_engine. It runs those four laws on a database file and states the in-memory case: jobs last as long as the rows that queued them.

Beginner path: mark a method #App.Job and call app.enqueue; there is nothing to configure. Expert path: to feed another system, such as a billing queue, a job sends to it. The outbox retries that hand-off until it succeeds, so it happens at least once.

The cost: job rows share the app's database, so a very busy queue adds write load there. Moving jobs to another system then means a new ballot, not a setting.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented: the c9 text and its proof row. CallOutbox, the transactions module and the jobs module stay priv(package) (Core/App/App.jet:780-811, :874, :1160). core.db stays the only caller (Core/Db/Db.jet:1383, :1465).

Proof: jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter web_app/job_store_contract_per_engine. It runs rollback-queues-nothing, redelivery after a dropped hold, restart survival and no-ack-on-stop against every engine core.db opens.

options.name: A public trait with required methods, app.JobStore, plus a law kit, app.job_store_laws
options.gist: An app writes six methods to plug in its own job store and proves the contract with a test kit.
options.detail:
CallOutbox's six members become a public trait, and the entry picks a store with .jobs(store). jet check refuses a store missing a method, with the ordinary error for an incomplete trait. app.job_store_laws runs the four laws against the store in the app's tests.

Its best case is a team that already runs Redis or a cloud queue. Job traffic then stays off the app's database, and job workers scale on their own, as Sidekiq's do.

Beginner path: unchanged, since the built-in store stays the default. Expert path: write the six methods, run the law kit, and pick the store in the entry.

The check-time refusal covers missing methods only. Durability and acknowledgement are behaviour, which the law kit tests at run time. A store outside the database cannot join the call's transaction, so c1's "a rolled-back write queues nothing" and c6's once-only writes break. The law kit cannot see that, because it tests the store alone.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. core.app gains the trait JobStore (keep, done, failed, take, hold, now), QueuedJob, JobStoreError, App.jobs and job_store_laws. core.db's outbox implements the trait. Proof: --profile ui --filter app_job_store_adapter_contract for the missing method, and --profile cases --filter web_app/job_store_laws for the kit.

options.name: A trait whose promises are marked: #App.JobStore(durable:, ack_after_run:, redelivers:, joins_transaction:)
options.gist: An adapter declares what it keeps, and jet check refuses one that lacks a promise, with a registered error naming it.
options.detail:
The trait is B's, and the marker lists four promises. jet check refuses a store whose marker sets one to false, or leaves one out, with a registered error naming the missing promise. This is c9's text read literally.

Beginner path: unchanged, as in B. Expert path: write the six methods and the marker.

The promises are the author's word: jet check reads the marker, not the behaviour. Only a store inside the app's database can truthfully set joins_transaction, so every outside store, such as Redis or SQS, is refused. What remains is option A with extra public names.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. B's surface plus the #App.JobStore marker and a registered error, jet.JobStoreLacks, at check time. Proof: jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter app_job_store_adapter_contract.

comparisons.note: Jobs are rows in the app's Postgres, inserted in the caller's transaction, so a rollback queues nothing. Like A. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/oban/Oban.html
comparisons.code: Ecto.Multi.new() |> Ecto.Multi.update(:task, changeset) |> Oban.insert(:push, PushWorker.new(%{id: id})) |> Repo.transaction()

comparisons.note: Active Job's database backend: jobs live in the app's own database. Like A. Source: https://github.com/rails/solid_queue

One adapter interface with many backends; durability and acknowledgement differ per backend, and nothing checks them. Like B without the law kit. Source: https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_job_basics.html

Jobs live in Redis, outside the app's transaction. Enqueued before the commit, a rolled-back change still runs its job; enqueued after it, a crash in between loses the job. The dual write that B and C face. Source: https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki
Write the message to an outbox table in the same transaction as the change, then relay it. What A does for every job. Source: https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
comparisons.code: INSERT INTO outbox (key, job, args) VALUES (...); -- same transaction as the change

recommendation.why: Only the database that holds a change can save its job in the same step, and two of the contract's four parts depend on that. A keeps that guarantee with no new public names, and it rewrites c9 so its proof runs the contract on every engine. B lets a store pass its tests and still lose jobs. C refuses every store outside the database, which is A with more names.
gains: A rolled-back change never sends anything, and a crash never loses a job.
Nothing to configure: marking a method #App.Job is the whole beginner path.
c9 gets a real subject and a proof row that runs the contract on every database engine.

losses.loss: An app cannot keep its jobs in Redis, SQS or another broker.
losses.mitigation: A job can send to any broker itself, and the outbox retries that hand-off until it succeeds, which is the transactional outbox pattern.

losses.loss: Jobs share the app database's write capacity.
losses.mitigation: A job costs one insert in a transaction already open and one delete when it runs, plus one hold statement per second per store. A future core.db engine brings its own outbox with no app change.

losses.loss: c9's ratified text and proof row change.
losses.mitigation: The new text keeps c9's intent, that no store can weaken the contract, by offering no slot to weaken it. Its proof row runs the contract on every engine core.db opens.

Promises are the author's word, and only a store inside the database can truthfully make the transaction promise, so C is A with more public names.

decisions.title: How an app gives each row a checked ID
decisions.situation: A row ID is the text that names one row, such as one task. Offline apps let the device make the ID itself: a UUIDv7, a random text that also records the time, so a task made on a train opens at once. The server must refuse IDs a client made up. Today a request with the ID "t1" is stored as is, because the decoder sees an ID type as a String. The vote decides how an app declares ID types and makes new IDs. We recommend one line per table and nothing per new row.
decisions.gist: How should an app declare and make row IDs, so they are checked UUIDv7 text with the least code?
decisions.lesson: An ID names one row. Offline apps make IDs on the device, so the server must refuse made-up ones like "t1" with 422 (bad input) before any method runs. The options differ in what an app writes for each table and each new row.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: the app writes one line per table, TaskID: distinct app.ID, and nothing else. On the client, TaskID.from_id(app.new_id()) makes a new ID. A crafted request with "t1" gets 422 at the id field, and the method never runs. The ID prints as its text, travels in JSON as a plain string, and is stored as one text column.

Expert path. Code can build an ID only from app.new_id() or by decoding checked text, so no TaskID ever holds "t1". A generic function can ask for any ID through the wrapped type. A legacy key that is not a UUIDv7 stays a plain distinct String, and an integer key stays Int. Neither option changes those.

Some things stay the same under every option: the ID's text, the 422 answer, the JSON string and the SQL text column. Passing a ProjectID where a TaskID belongs is a compile error under all three.
decisions.story: Ana's TaskList app makes a task on the train and gives it a fresh ID. Later Leo writes a script that sends {"id":"t1","title":"Ship it"} straight to the server. Today the server stores a task named t1, and the next client that makes its own t1 collides with it. Ana needs the server to refuse t1 before her code runs.
decisions.detail:
Code is truth, checked on today's dev with the gate jet. Each probe below is a file in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/inbox/Speed-3-ballot-app-id/.

jet run gap.jet prints "accepted id t1". A distinct String decodes any text.

jet run core_id_and_row_id.jet prints "A: t1 refused: [at `id`: expected a UUIDv7]". A struct with a hand-written bare-text codec already refuses t1. It also prints "A: uuid accepted, encodes {\"id\":\"0193a5e0-7c1a-7000-8000-000000000001\",\"title\":\"x\"}", so the ID travels as a plain string. Its last line, "C: x", shows that a generic struct whose parameter only names a row compiles today.

jet run distinct_over_struct.jet fails with E0311: "`TaskID` has no matching static method `from_id`". A distinct type over a struct does not derive its codec yet. That is a gap in D-CODABLE-DISTINCT1=A (a distinct type codes as its base), and A must close it.

The proposal (D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A, Docs/proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md, sections 3.2 and 4.8) writes TaskID: distinct String. It requires that an ID type's decoder accept only UUIDv7 text, with a test sending "t1". It never says what marks an ID type.

app.new_id() -[Rand, Time]> String is in Core/App/App.jet (SUB Speed-3-c6-server). It makes the text through core.crypto.uuid.v7, and its return type follows this vote. The same SUB makes Table.add on a taken key answer Exists or Denied, by whether the caller may read the row. Card #6867 c6.

options.name: A distinct ID with a fresh default
options.detail:
Core adds app.ID, whose decoder accepts only canonical UUIDv7 text and answers anything else with FieldError{path: "id"} and 422. Each table declares its own ID type in one line, TaskID: distinct app.ID, so a ProjectID can never be passed where a TaskID is expected. A distinct type codes as its base (D-CODABLE-DISTINCT1=A), so TaskID gets the check.

app.ID has one constructor, fresh(), which makes a new UUIDv7. A distinct type gets its base's constructors, typed as itself and made through its own conversion, the same path decoding takes. So the field default id: TaskID = .fresh() means a new row needs no ID code: Task{title: "Ship it"}.
options.technical:
Core: app.ID in Core/App/App.jet with Encode, Decode, Display, Equatable, Comparable and fresh(). Language: a distinct type forwards each static constructor of its base that returns the base, through its own conversion. A base whose conversion can fail, such as a range type, forwards none.

The generated codec fills a missing id from the default, so a request without one gets a server-made ID. The request key (#6867 c2) makes a retry return the first result instead of a second row. Under the app test host, fresh() draws from the test's seeded clock and random source, so tests stay deterministic. The derived codec of a distinct type over a struct base is fixed (today E0311).

options.name: A distinct ID, made by hand
options.detail: As A, without forwarded constructors: each new row writes TaskID.from_id(app.new_id()).
options.technical: Core only: app.ID and app.new_id(). No language rule changes.

options.name: One generic app.ID<Row>
options.detail: Core adds app.ID<Row>, named after the row it identifies. Apps declare no ID type, and every signature spells app.ID<Task>. An ID that names no row, such as a device or an upload, needs a stand-in row type.
options.technical: Core only: a generic struct whose parameter only names a row, its codec, and fresh().

comparisons.note: A newtype over the uuid crate's checked Uuid type; serde refuses bad text. This is A's shape.
The primary key is a field option, and a cast refuses non-UUID text. This is B's shape.
The column type does the check; the model has no ID type.

recommendation.why: The common path, making a row, needs no ID code, and every ID is checked and typed per table.
gains: Zero ID code per new row.
One line per table buys type-safe, checked IDs.

losses.loss: Distinct types gain a general rule: they get their base's constructors.
losses.mitigation: Constructors go through the type's own conversion, as decoding does, so no unchecked value can be made.

whyNot.reason: B makes every new row repeat two calls that A writes once in the field default.
C spells app.ID<Task> in every signature and needs stand-in rows for other IDs.

recommendation.tradeoff: One line per table, in exchange for IDs that are checked and typed everywhere.

decisions.title: Where a growing value lives when the code does not say
decisions.situation: Every Jet program keeps its lists, text and other growing values somewhere in memory. Today a value the code does not place goes to the general heap, which finds room for it and frees it piece by piece. The Goose language shows a faster way for values that end in the reverse order they began: stack them, and free a whole scope in one step. The vote decides whether Jet's compiler does that on its own, keeps it an explicit choice, or makes it the only default. We recommend the compiler choose, and use the heap whenever it cannot prove the order.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet put a growing value, like a list or text, when the code does not say where?
decisions.lesson: A scope stack hands out memory by moving one pointer and frees a whole scope in one step. It only works when values end in the reverse order they began. Today Jet uses the heap unless code picks an arena. Any winner still needs an adversarial review and measurements before it ships.
decisions.story: Noor writes a log tool that splits each line into words, counts them and drops the list. Each word and the list are separate heap requests and frees today. She will never write an arena, and her tool runs on servers and in the browser.

options.name: The compiler chooses
options.detail:
One rule decides, and a reader can apply it: a growing value goes on a scope stack unless it is stored in something that outlives it or sent to another task. A value a function returns is built on its caller's stack, so builder functions qualify too.

Each growing value gets its own stack, as in Goose, so it is freed at its last use with one pointer reset, not at its scope's end. Everything the rule leaves out uses the default heap of D-ALLOC-DEFAULT1 and costs exactly what it costs today. An allocator named by #Context (D-ALLOC-SITE1) always wins. No syntax, diagnostic or API is added; `jet inspect placement` names each heap value and the rule that sent it there.
options.technical:
Placement is a sema fact (I3), so O0, O1, O2 and the web place every value the same way (I9). Threads reserve address ranges for their stacks. Tasks and the web use chunked stacks instead, taken from the thread's pool on a task's first stacked value. So a task that stacks nothing costs nothing, and thousands of tasks reserve no address space. A task's stacks belong to the task, so a stacked value survives a wait.

Growth already compares length with capacity on the heap path; a chunked stack reuses that check, extending in place when the value is on top. A recursive function's growing locals use the heap, so recursion stays unrestricted (contrast goose-048). Scope stacks are separate from the native call stack, so Mem.Stack budgets are unchanged. #6469, stack slots for small boxes that never escape, is the scalar end of the same placement ladder.

options.name: Explicit only, as today
options.detail: Every value uses the default heap unless code names an allocator with #Context(allocator:), as D-ALLOC-SITE1=A ratified. The compiler keeps only the small, invisible optimizations it does today, such as stack slots for small boxes that never escape (#6469).
options.technical: No sema placement fact. Arena, Bump and Pool stay the explicit route (Docs/spec/spec.md, Allocator families).

options.name: Stacks by default, heap by hand
options.detail: Goose's model becomes Jet's default. Every growing value lives on a compiler-assigned stack. Some values have lifetimes that do not nest: a map of lists, a cache, a value kept past its scope. Code must place those on the heap explicitly, and the compiler refuses the stack-only forms with a diagnostic.
options.technical: C inherits Goose's restrictions. Each stack has one growing value on top, and growing values cannot be array elements (goose-023, goose-024). Recursion is restricted so the stack count stays constant (goose-048). Specialization is whole-program by root (goose-051), and web growth is checked (goose-143). About 60% of Goose's rejection tests are lifetime errors (goose-220), and Jet's beginners would meet them.

comparisons.note: Data stacks with a bump pointer, freed by one store at scope exit; growing values are restricted to keep the model sound. https://github.com/aardappel/goose rev 94cc64da; claims goose-001, goose-023, goose-024, goose-048, goose-143, goose-173.
comparisons.code: var scratch: u8[>..] = [];  // grow-only, pointer bump

comparisons.note: Region inference (ML Kit) later added a garbage collector for what regions leaked; Cyclone kept LIFO arenas only where callers know lifetimes (goose-144). Lesson: inferred stacking needs a heap fallback.
comparisons.code: (* ML Kit: regions inferred, plus a collector for the rest *)

recommendation.why: It gives stack speed to the common shapes with no new syntax, and the rest costs no more than today.
gains: No new syntax and no new errors.
The fast path reaches code nobody tuned.
One stated rule says which values are stacked.

losses.loss: Values stored in a longer-lived container stay on the heap.
losses.mitigation: They pay exactly today's cost, and `jet inspect placement` names each one and the rule that sent it there.

whyNot.reason: B is simplest but leaves common temporaries on the slower heap unless authors tune them.
C is fastest where it fits but rejects everyday code like maps of lists, and slows the web.

recommendation.tradeoff: Placement becomes a compiler decision users can predict and inspect but never write.

gains: Code stays the same; locals, temporaries and returned builders get stack speed.

decisions.title: Which screens a device loads ahead so they work offline
decisions.situation: A synced app keeps what it has read, so a screen still shows it offline. Today that covers only screens the person opened while online, so a field worker without signal cannot open a project they skipped this week. The vote decides how the device picks more screens to fetch ahead. We recommend it follow the links already in the code, with nothing to write.
decisions.gist: When an app works offline, which screens should a device fetch ahead of time, and who decides?
decisions.lesson: Offline, an app can show only what the device already holds. Today that is just the screens the person opened. Loading ahead means fetching, while online, the screens the person is likely to open next.
decisions.story: Mara leads a field crew and opens Crewboard in a basement with no signal. She needs the board of a project she has not opened this week. Today it fails.
decisions.inWild:
bucket_definitions:
  user_boards:
    parameters: SELECT id AS project_id FROM projects WHERE owner = token_parameters.user_id
    data:
      - SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE project_id = bucket.project_id
# https://docs.powersync.com (sync rules)

options.name: Follow the links
options.detail:
With .offline(.Queue), the device fetches ahead the screens the person can reach by links from the screens they opened. Nothing is written. A link names its screen and arguments in code, such as kit.link(logic.BoardView{project: card.id}, ...). So the device makes exactly the read the board will make, crew.board(card.id), and every fetched result is one a screen uses.

Fetching runs after the first screen shows, on an unmetered connection, nearest first: one link away, then two. It stops at the offline storage budget, 64 MiB unless the entry sets another. A screen that must never load ahead says preload: false on its .screen line. A screen that must work offline says offline: true, and the build fails if one of its reads cannot be fetched ahead, naming the read.
options.technical:
The compiler records each kit.link and app.go target whose arguments come from loaded results, and each screen's live reads whose arguments come from its view. That graph is the preload set (#6868 c12). jet inspect preload prints it per screen with the reason for each read.

Reads are one-shot and hold no subscription; a mounted screen with the same key takes the result over. One screen kind is one batched request in one read transaction, each result capped at LIVE_MAX_PAYLOAD. Re-checks every 15 minutes send row versions, so an unchanged result costs one version compare. The server runs each read's policies as if the person tapped the link.

options.name: List the reads in the entry
options.detail: The offline entry takes a warm function that lists reads to fetch ahead, with loops over earlier results. The compiler compares each listed read's key with the reads screens make, and a read no screen makes is a compile error.
options.technical: Batching, budget, metering and re-checks are as in A. Only listed reads are fetched; the list is kept in step with the screens by hand.

options.name: No loading ahead
options.detail: Offline, the device shows only what it already read. The docs say so. Apps that need more write their own fetching with ordinary calls.
options.technical: Nothing is added to the entry, the compiler or the sync protocol. #6868 c12 becomes a report of which screens were last read and when.

comparisons.note: Server-side sync rules choose a user's rows; the device keeps them in SQLite and any local query works offline. https://docs.powersync.com
comparisons.code:
data:
  - SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE project_id = bucket.project_id

comparisons.note: The client names queries to keep synced; Zero keeps their rows locally for a TTL, so queries named ahead work offline. https://zero.rocicorp.dev

recommendation.why: The links already say where a person can go next, so the common case needs no code and every fetched read is used.
gains: No code for the common case.
Fetched reads always match their screens.

losses.loss: Screens reached only by typed text, like search, cannot load ahead.
losses.mitigation: Offline they show their last results, and the build report names each one.

whyNot.reason: B makes every offline app write and maintain a list that A derives from code already written.
C leaves screens Mara never opened unusable offline.

recommendation.tradeoff: The device spends unmetered data and storage, within a budget, on screens the person may never open.

surface.lesson: Offline, an app can show only what the device already holds. Today that is just the screens the person opened. Loading ahead means fetching, while online, the screens the person is likely to open next.

current.note: Offline, Crewboard shows only boards Mara opened while online. Other boards fail.

decisions.title: Whether a predicted write may queue a job
decisions.situation: A predicted write updates the screen at once, before the server answers. D-OPTIMISTIC1 predicts a write only when it "has no other effects". Many writes also queue a job, such as telling the assignee about a task, with app.enqueue. The job runs on the server, and only after the write commits. You decide whether queuing a job stops a write from being predicted. In Crewboard, 6 of its 12 writes are predicted if it doesn't and 2 of 12 if it does. We recommend that it doesn't: the job still runs once, on the server, and only after the commit.
decisions.gist: May a write that queues a job still update the screen at once?
decisions.lesson: A prediction runs the write on the device's own copy of the rows and shows the result at once. The server then runs the same write, and its answer replaces the guess. A job queued with app.enqueue never runs on the device. It runs on the server after the write commits, and never runs if the write is refused. So the question is only whether the screen waits for the server.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: the app writes update_task once, with its app.enqueue line. Under A, the edit shows at once and the assignee is told after the server commits it. Under B, the edit shows a busy state until the server answers, unless the app moves the job into a second call.

Expert path: under both options, the job runs only on the server, once, after the commit (#3709 jobs). A refused write queues nothing. jet inspect choices lists each method as predicted or waiting, with the fact that decided it.

Under both options, a method that reads the clock or randomness, calls the network or writes files is never predicted.
decisions.story: Ana assigns a task to Leo on the train. Under A, the card shows Leo at once, and when Ana's phone reaches the server, the write commits and Leo gets his notification. If the server refuses it (Leo left the project), the card goes back and Ana sees why, and Leo is told nothing. Under B, the card spins until the phone reaches the server.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 77f7729b72. app.enqueue is `fn(call: Int, job: &&CallJob) Never!` in Core/App/App.jet:919, and it carries no effect. A job runs after the commit and never after a rollback (Tests/Cases/WebApp/job_runs_after_commit_and_never_after_rollback.case).

Crewboard (Docs/Proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md) has 12 writes a client can call. create_task and update_task queue tell_assignee through after_assign (line 1543). remove_member queues the unassign job, and leave calls remove_member. move_task and set_role queue nothing. The other six read the clock or randomness, write files, or make their ID on the server, so they wait under both options.

The count is in Docs/Audits/2026-11-16-d-optimistic1-review.md, claim 13 and the second re-review. The review's D8 has the client also run named row policies. Until member_policy stops reading the clock, set_role, remove_member and leave wait too. That makes the counts 3 of 12 under A and 1 of 12 under B. The ratio between the options stays the same.

options.name: Predict it; the job waits for the commit
options.detail: A write that queues a job is predicted like any other write. The device runs the method on its copy and skips the app.enqueue line. The server runs the method, commits, then runs the job once. In Crewboard, 6 of 12 writes update the screen at once: create_task, update_task, move_task, set_role, remove_member and leave.
options.technical: Prediction treats app.enqueue as a compiler-known call it skips, as it skips row policies. No new syntax. jet inspect choices says "predicted (queues tell_assignee after commit)".

options.name: Queuing a job makes the method wait
options.detail: A write that queues a job is not predicted. The screen shows the busy state until the server answers. In Crewboard, 2 of 12 writes update the screen at once: move_task and set_role. To get an instant edit, the app moves the job into a second method that the screen calls after the reply.
options.technical: Eligibility refuses a body that reaches app.enqueue. No new syntax. jet inspect choices says "waits (queues tell_assignee)".

comparisons.note: The client mutator updates the screen; server-only work runs in the server mutator after the client's guess is shown. This is A's shape.
A method stub runs on the client and skips server-only calls with isSimulation; the server sends the mail. This is A's shape.
The guess is hand-written in onMutate; whatever the server does after is invisible to it. Neither option's question arises.

recommendation.why: The job never runs on the device and runs on the server only after the commit, so a refused guess sends nothing and a committed one sends once. What the ballot's "no other effects" protects against, an outside effect before the server agrees, cannot happen. A predicts three times as many of Crewboard's writes with the same code.
gains: Crewboard: 6 of 12 writes are instant instead of 2.
No code is moved to get an instant edit.
A refused write still tells no one.

losses.loss: It widens the ratified "no other effects" to allow one effect that is deferred until after the commit.
losses.mitigation: jet inspect choices names the queued job beside each predicted method; the opt-out (D-PREDICT-PIN1) keeps any method waiting.

losses.loss: The screen shows the edit before the notification goes out, so for a moment the screen is ahead of the job.
losses.mitigation: That is true of every committed write too: a job always runs after the commit.

whyNot.reason: It makes 4 of Crewboard's 6 predictable writes wait. Its workaround, a second call after the reply, is more code and loses the job if the app closes between the calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: One deferred server effect allowed inside a prediction, for three times as many instant writes.

decisions.title: How a write method opts out of prediction, or pins it
decisions.situation: D-OPTIMISTIC1 predicts each write the compiler can predict, so the screen updates before the server answers. It promised an opt-out per action, spelled optimistic: false on app.action(...). The web app shape has no app.action. A write is a method of a service, marked #App.SignedIn or #App.Public, and those markers already take arguments, as in #App.Public(limit: 30, per: 1min). You decide how a method says "never predict me" (the opt-out) and "always predict me, and fail the build if you can't" (the pin). Most methods write neither. We recommend one argument on the marker: predict: .Never or predict: .Always.
decisions.gist: How does a write method say "never predict" or "must be predicted"?
decisions.lesson: With nothing written, the compiler decides, and jet inspect choices shows the decision and why. The opt-out keeps a method waiting for the server, for example a payment or logic the app wants to keep off the device. The pin is for experts: it fails the build when a change makes the method unpredictable, so an instant screen can't silently become a slow one.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write nothing. A method the compiler can predict is predicted; one it can't waits. jet inspect choices lists each with the fact that decided it, for example "move_task: predicted" or "invite: waits (reads the clock)".

Expert path: the opt-out and the pin are each one argument on the access marker the method already has. A pinned method that stops qualifying fails the build with a diagnostic naming the fact, such as the line that reads the clock.

Under every option the default is the compiler's choice, and no option adds a marker to methods that don't use it.
decisions.story: Ana's Crewboard predicts move_task, so a card moves the moment it is dropped. Later Leo adds a timestamp to move_task with time.now_utc(). Without a pin, the card quietly starts to spin. With the pin, Leo's build fails at that line and he passes the time in as an argument instead. Separately, Ana's pay method must never show a paid state before the bank agrees, so she opts it out.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 77f7729b72. Marker arguments exist on the access markers: #App.Public(limit: 30, per: 1min) (Core/App/App.jet:58; Tests/Cases/WebApp/MethodRateLimitAnswers429.fixture). #App.Job(retries: 2) and #App.Webhook(path:, signature:, key:) also take arguments.

The ratified D-OPTIMISTIC1 example is app.action("pay", pay, optimistic: false). The shape (Docs/Proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md) has no app.action and no spelling for the opt-out. jet inspect choices (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/InspectChoices.jet) has no prediction kind yet; #6555 c3 adds it. The review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-16-d-optimistic1-review.md, claim 11 and D6.

options.detail: The ratified ballot's word, carried to the marker as a Bool. optimistic: false keeps the method waiting. optimistic: true pins it, with the same build failure as A. With no argument, the compiler decides.
options.technical: One argument name, optimistic, on #App.SignedIn and #App.Public, typed Bool. The same two diagnostics as A.

options.name: Two markers of their own
options.detail: Two new markers stack beside the access marker: #App.Wait keeps the method waiting, and #App.Predicted pins it. With neither, the compiler decides.
options.technical: Two marker rows, App.Wait and App.Predicted, legal only beside #App.SignedIn or #App.Public, plus a diagnostic for both on one method and the same pin diagnostic as A.

decisions.title: Offer F32 complex values without requiring generic default syntax
decisions.situation: Complex currently stores two Float components. Signal buffers may need F32 components to reduce component storage and match other F32 data. The draft proposed Complex<T> while allowing plain Complex to mean Complex<Float>. That is also a public generic-default and literal-typing decision, not just a struct edit. We recommend one shared implementation with concrete Complex and Complex32 aliases. An explicit public generic family remains a strong alternative, with its language costs stated honestly.
decisions.gist: How should Jet offer a complex number with F32 components?
decisions.lesson: Complex32 here means two F32 components, not 32 bits in total. Sharing an implementation does not require exposing generic defaults to every caller.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: existing Complex code keeps Float components. Complex32{real: 3.0, imaginary: 4.0} asks for F32 components explicitly. Context supplies each literal's component type. No new imaginary literal inference rule is approved.

Expert path: share arithmetic and every existing Complex math method over an internal component parameter restricted to F32 or Float. Expose destination-owned from_complex conversions for both concrete aliases, using scalar conversion policy for each component. Narrowing is explicit and fallible; do not silently select a type from the operand values or promise twice the throughput.
decisions.story: Em edits a long signal buffer. F32 components halve the payload bits compared with two Float components, before considering padding or container overhead. She measures numerical error and actual throughput instead of treating smaller components as a universal speedup.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40404-40406 fixes both components to Float. :40414-40487 contains the full current arithmetic and elementary method surface, which any new precision must cover. missing.jet rejects Complex<F32>{...} with E0104. edges.jet rejects the audit's call-shaped Complex<F32>(...) with E0803, not its older E0119. Current z.abs() prints 5.0 and z*z prints -7 + 24i. The review does not infer successful F32 support from generic syntax or from another language.

D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A requires destination-owned source-named conversion. D-ARRAY-CONJ1 is an open companion ballot, not a ratified prerequisite or a current method. Public generic defaults and complex literal inference are not licensed by merely adding F32 storage. B explicitly requests a default type argument for this family and thus needs full syntax review. A needs no such default and must migrate compiler-protected Complex handling to the shared representation in one cutover, without a hidden legacy type.

options.name: Concrete aliases over one implementation
options.detail: Keep public Complex as the Float specialization and add Complex32 as the F32 specialization of one internal generic implementation. Both have identical operations at their own precision.
options.technical: The internal generic family is not a second public construction path. Preserve existing Complex meaning and literal behavior. Complex32 fields are F32, with normal aggregate alignment rather than a packed-ABI guarantee. Generate or share implementations for all existing methods, including transcendental functions, without silently calculating in Float then narrowing. from_complex infers the source specialization; widening is lossless and narrowing follows the established scalar fallible conversion policy. No implicit precision change.

options.name: Public Complex<T> with Float default
options.detail: Expose Complex<F32> and Complex<Float>, with bare Complex denoting the Float specialization. This is the original recommended model, with the default rule made explicit.
options.technical: Approve omitted component arguments for this family, not a general default-argument feature by implication. Explicitly annotated fields receive T; unannotated imaginary literals keep today's Float behavior rather than gaining value-driven inference. Restrict T to F32 or Float. Supply the full A operation and conversion set. Migrate every compiler identity check and existing caller; do not preserve an old non-generic Complex beside the new family.

options.name: Two concrete nominal types
options.detail: Keep today's nominal Complex and add a distinct Complex32 struct with F32 fields. Share private generic helpers or generated methods instead of duplicating algorithms by hand.
options.technical: Same mathematical coverage, conversion and precision rules as A. This avoids converting the existing protected type into an alias, but creates two nominal declarations and associated compiler registrations. It does not inherently double handwritten math. I8 permits implementation sharing; do not ship multiple public mechanisms for the same precision.

options.name: Float computation with F32 boundary pairs
options.detail: Keep Complex unchanged. Store compact buffers as fixed F32 pairs, widen components when reading, compute with Complex, and explicitly narrow when writing.
options.technical: A complete same-program route for storage-oriented work; it does not supply F32-precision complex arithmetic. Conversions and pair indexing remain caller code. This may be enough when buffer size matters more than F32 computation throughput, without a second complex API.

comparisons.note: complex64 has two f32 components; the name counts total bits. Odin also has complex32 and complex128, so Jet's Complex32 name must explain its different convention.
Complex<T> offers reusable generic algorithms; Complex32 and Complex64 aliases make common precisions easy. Layout compatibility does not guarantee by-value C calling convention compatibility.
Complex is parametric; ComplexF32 and ComplexF64 are concrete aliases. Promotion provides convenience beyond Jet's explicit conversion rule and has its own complexity.
SIMD's scalar parameter reuses vector algorithms across precisions. It is a representation example, not a claim that a two-lane SIMD value has complex multiplication semantics.

recommendation.why: Concrete aliases keep the beginner surface small and share one implementation. Public generic defaults and new complex literal inference are unnecessary to offer F32 components.
gains: One implementation across precisions.
Existing Complex meaning stays stable.
No public generic-default rule.

losses.loss: Two public precision names.
losses.mitigation: Document component widths explicitly, including the difference from Odin's total-bit names.

losses.loss: No public component-generic complex family.
losses.mitigation: Choose B if cross-precision generic APIs are a requirement, accepting its explicit default-type decision.

whyNot.reason: Strong for public generic numeric code, but couples the precision feature to omitted type arguments and compiler identity migration.
Avoids alias migration, but keeps two nominal declarations even when all operations share one implementation.
Sufficient for compact storage with Float math, but not F32-precision complex computation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Convenient concrete precisions now, without implicitly approving a broader generic-default feature.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT-6-1 Sol. Fresh agent: OdinBallotReview. Corrected diagnostics, naming conventions, migration costs and unsupported packed-layout or throughput claims.

Measure actual buffer layout and kernels before promising ABI size or speed; compare execution tiers.

surface.lesson: Complex32 means two F32 components here. Sharing implementation does not require exposing omitted generic arguments or changing complex literals.

decisions.title: Add Complex.conj without adding a synonym
decisions.situation: Jet has a Complex value with real and imaginary parts, but no conjugation method. A program can construct the conjugate by copying the real part and negating the imaginary part. The free math.conj currently accepts a Float and returns it unchanged. The approved quaternion API uses conj. We recommend the same short method name for Complex, without also adding conjugate. Extending the existing free function is a serious alternative for generic numeric code.
decisions.gist: Should complex conjugation use conj, conjugate, or the existing free function?
decisions.lesson: Conjugation keeps the real part and negates the imaginary part. It does not compute magnitude, inverse, transpose or a matrix adjoint.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: z.conj() returns a Complex. For 3 + 4i the result is 3 - 4i. This is a value operation; the receiver does not change.

Expert path: use the existing scalar negation on the imaginary component, including signed zero, infinities and NaNs. Do not replace a norm calculation with z*z.conj() under an exact floating-point identity: overflow and non-finite values can invalidate that shortcut. If both complex precisions are approved, the method preserves the receiver's component type.
decisions.story: Ivo needs the conjugate in a signal calculation. A named operation avoids repeating the two-field construction. His quaternion code uses the same operation name, but the quaternion surface is approved work, not an API demonstrated by today's compiler.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40404-40406 declares Float components; :40414-40487 gives magnitude, elementary methods and arithmetic, with no conj. :37547-37552 defines real/imag/conj for Float; conj returns its input. missing.jet reports E0102 for z.conj(), confirming audit Q4. current.jet prints z*z as -7 + 24i, magnitude 5.0, and real conj 3.0.

reference.jet's manual conjugate prints 3 - 4i and product 25 + 0i. Its reciprocal of conjugated positive imaginary zero prints -inf. These are finite and signed-zero witnesses, not a universal floating-point norm identity.

D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A ratifies quaternion conj(); it does not prove an implementation exists. D-ARRAY-COMPLEXT1 is a separate open precision question. This ballot approves scalar Complex conjugation, not complex matrices or automatic elementwise broadcasting. I8 does not inherently prefer methods to free functions; do not add both conj and conjugate for the same receiver.

options.name: Complex.conj
options.detail: Add conj() to Complex, preserving its component precision. Keep the approved quaternion operation name. Do not add a conjugate alias.
options.technical: Return Complex{real: self.real, imaginary: -self.imaginary} using ordinary scalar negation. No allocation, mutation, conjugate-transpose or norm shortcut is included. The existing Float free conj remains a real-number identity; this ballot adds no second Complex call path.

options.name: Complex.conjugate

options.technical: Same value and special-value semantics as A. Rename the quaternion operation in its approved spec and all implementation callers when landed; do not keep conj as a compatibility alias. Costs are the amendment and migration, not an intrinsic inability to write clear math.

options.name: Extend math.conj
options.detail: Extend the existing free function to Complex. Use one generic numeric entry point alongside the current real identity.
options.technical: No Complex method is added. This is attractive for code handling real and complex numbers under a shared function constraint. Existing overload and owning-package rules still apply. Quaternion method naming need not change because it is a different receiver surface; this does not automatically authorize a second Complex spelling.

options.name: Use explicit fields
options.detail: Add no API. Write the complete same-program operation using today's fields and scalar negation.
options.technical: Useful when conjugation is rare and requires no protected-type method work. Repeated field construction is less recognizable than a single named operation. Same numerical behavior as the proposed method, including signed-zero negation.
options.code: c: Complex{real: z.real, imaginary: -z.imaginary}

comparisons.note: The built-in conj operation works on complex values and the overview also documents quaternion conjugation. One mathematical name can serve multiple number families.
num-complex exposes conj as a method; nalgebra supports matrix conjugation separately. Scalar conjugation need not also approve matrix adjoints.
Free conj is familiar in numerical code and numpy applies it elementwise. numpy also has a conjugate alias, which Jet need not copy.

recommendation.why: The method fits Complex's existing numeric methods and the approved quaternion name. The free-function alternative is stronger for generic numeric code, not a semantic error.

One Complex spelling.

A strong generic-code choice; A favors the existing Complex method surface.
Already works, but repeats the definition instead of naming the mathematical operation.
