decisions.title: Convert fixed arrays with length-preserving map; lanes use their arrays
decisions.situation: Programs often need four integer counts as four floats, without losing the length. Today [Float#4]{counts} fails, and map produces a growable list. Lane values have array adapters but no element conversion. Jet already requires map to keep a fixed array's length. We recommend finishing that rule rather than giving braces another meaning. The alternatives add a converting head or a named conversion on the destination.
decisions.gist: How should a fixed array or lane value convert its elements?
decisions.lesson: Keep the length and apply the ordinary scalar conversion to each element. Shape-preserving map already has that contract; converting braces would be a new rule.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: counts.map(fn(n) { F32{n} }) keeps the fixed length under option A. This fixes an existing implementation gap, not a new map meaning. Until that fix lands, explicit indexed construction works.

Expert path: F32x4.from_array(ints.to_array().map(fn(n) { F32{n} })) uses the same conversion. Fixed map must not allocate a heap list. The scalar head keeps its exactness and failure rules; it does not silently round integers to fit F32. Failure handling belongs inside the callback, not a new checked(map(...)) rule.
decisions.story: Lena converts four tile counts for a shader. A length-preserving map keeps her conversion correct when the fixed length changes. She uses the same scalar expression in a lane array adapter.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40675-40686 defines F32x4 and its array adapters. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Literals.jet:597-600 checks literal length. missing.jet reports E0963 for [Float#4]{counts}, E0303 for F32x4{ints}, and E0102 for to_i32x4. current.jet runs map; its fixed-result type is checked separately. Audit A15/S10 identify real gaps, but old diagnostic spellings are not promises.

reference.jet stops with E3010 converting runtime Int 16777217 to F32: exactness, not just range, matters. A separate check rejects checked(F32{huge}) with E1005. No ballot may claim aggregate checked handling already follows from this implementation. Numeric.jet:7-8 and BuildTypes.jet:5067-5068 identify the exactness stop.

D-FIXARR1=A is ratified; Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:1631-1634 records map preserving N. D-DOTCTOR3's amendment (:1663-1683) distinguishes whole values from elements and permits scalar conversion. D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A requires destination-owned source-named conversions. B explicitly amends the aggregate head and checked rules. All option examples are proposed unless called current.

options.name: Length-preserving map
options.detail: Finish fixed map as ratified. Each element uses the existing scalar head. Lanes convert through fixed arrays; no new aggregate conversion operation is added.
options.technical: Map visits indexes in order, evaluates its receiver once and retains N, including N=0. Failure and cleanup follow the existing callback rules. Checked scalar conversions belong inside the callback; no outer checked-map feature is included. Nested arrays use nested maps, not an implicit recursive cast.

options.name: Converting type heads
options.detail: [F32#4]{counts} and F32x4{ints} convert each element using the scalar rule. Only equal lengths and numeric elements qualify.
options.technical: Explicitly amend D-DOTCTOR3. Same-type whole values retain priority, then eligible equal-length conversions, then literal notation. Cross array/lane representation conversion is excluded; use existing adapters. Length mismatch is a build error. Also extend checked to these aggregate heads: evaluate once in index order and return None at the first scalar failure, with no partial result. This is a new checked rule, not current behavior.

options.name: Destination-owned generic conversions
options.detail: Add from_array on fixed destinations and from_lanes on the ratified generic lane family. The source element type is inferred, avoiding a method for every width pair.
options.technical: [F32#4].from_array(counts) and Lanes<F32, 4>.from_lanes(ints) preserve shape. Narrowing is fallible under D-SHAPE-CONVERT1. This depends on generic lanes and number parameters, not today's twenty structs. Reuse the scalar conversion implementation rather than defining another rounding policy.
options.code:
weights: [F32#4].from_array(counts) ?? return
lanes: Lanes<F32, 4>.from_lanes(ints) ?? return

comparisons.note: Array casts include equal-depth nested arrays; less ceremony than A, with different scalar conversion policy.
@floatFromInt converts vector elements and rounds to the closest float; explicit operation names expose conversion policy.
Fixed array map retains length; nalgebra also offers element mapping across matrix shapes. These avoid converting construction syntax.
comparisons.code: let b = a.map(|n| n as f32);

comparisons.note: vec4(ivec4) is compact component conversion; integer-to-float precision loss is explicitly allowed, unlike exact checked integer conversions.

recommendation.why: It fulfills an existing shape rule and reuses scalar conversion. No additional aggregate head meaning or conversion-name family is needed.
gains: No new aggregate conversion rule.
Fixed length survives conversion.
Arbitrary scalar policies remain explicit.

losses.loss: Lane conversions need array adapters.
losses.mitigation: Keep adapters allocation-free; require focused code-generation evidence before claiming their cost disappears.

whyNot.reason: Compact, but adds aggregate conversion to a literal/assertion form and must settle precedence and nesting.
A strong alternative for lane-heavy code, but adds public conversion APIs and depends on generic lanes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Longer lane expressions in exchange for one reusable element-mapping path.

decisions.title: Add lane-scalar arithmetic through typed hooks, not broader mirroring
decisions.situation: A lane value currently needs an explicit splat before arithmetic with a scalar. Vec3 already supports a scalar on the right, so the two families feel inconsistent. We recommend scalar arithmetic on either side of exact lanes, using ordinary typed hooks. The draft incorrectly relied on D-OPMIX1 mirroring for fixed-width F32 and integer scalars. That rule mirrors only Int, Float and Decimal. Explicit reverse hooks can supply the feature without changing the mirror rule or adding a special broadcast parser.
decisions.gist: Should exact lane values support scalar arithmetic without an explicit splat?
decisions.lesson: A scalar is repeated across the lanes for +, -, * and /. Preserve operand order and scalar arithmetic policy; this is not a general array broadcast feature.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: lanes * gain means lanes * LaneType.splat(gain), where gain has the lane element type. gain - lanes means subtract each lane from gain, not the reverse. Scalar operands are evaluated once, in source order.

Expert path: add L.Add<E>, L.Sub<E>, L.Mul<E> and L.Div<E> for operations L already supports. Add the corresponding E hooks for a lane on the right in the owning Core package. Existing direct hooks win before D-OPMIX1 fallback. Exact lane type and element type remain unchanged; normal literal context applies, with no new cross-width coercion.
decisions.story: Kai changes brightness with a runtime F32 gain. He no longer writes a manual splat at every arithmetic site. He does not assume that a literal-only example proves a stored Decimal variable can silently narrow to F32.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40675-40686 gives F32x4.splat and adapters; :41486-41515 gives I32x4's four vector arithmetic operations. missing.jet reports E2511 for F32x4 * 2.0. current.jet runs explicit F32x4.splat(10.0) and Vec3 * 2.0; its earlier scalar-left Vec3 expression failed E0133. Ratified mixed operators are therefore not fully working today. Audit S3's gap is real.

D-OPMIX1=D ratifies typed hooks and mirrors only + and * from Int, Float or Decimal on the left. It does not automatically mirror F32, I32 or U8. Direct hooks win; operands evaluate left-to-right once. An unconstrained 2.0 is Decimal, not Float.

D-LANES1=A replaces the current named structs with exact generic lanes. A adds library hooks under existing rules; it does not amend lookup or extend fixed-array arithmetic. No performance identity is asserted without code-generation evidence.

options.name: Typed hooks on both sides
options.detail: Support +, -, * and / between an exact lane value and its element scalar, on either side, whenever that lane-lane operation exists. Implement each direction with ordinary owning-package hooks.
options.technical: Do not depend on fixed-width scalars entering D-OPMIX1's mirror set. Reverse subtraction and division retain source order. Match explicit splat arithmetic for overflow, division by zero, signed zero and NaN behavior. Receiver and scalar evaluate once, left-to-right. No comparison, mask, bitwise, shift, arbitrary array or sizeless-lane feature is included. Compound assignment follows existing direct-hook rules rather than gaining an automatic mirror.
options.code:
gain: F32{0.8}
bright: pixels * gain
inverted: F32{1.0} - pixels
ratio: F32{2.0} / pixels

options.name: Scalar on the right only
options.detail: Add lane-owned typed hooks, but no scalar-owned reverse hooks. Left-scalar expressions use an explicit splat.
options.technical: A smaller implementation and a visible direction for broadcasting, without a new lookup mechanism. Existing D-OPMIX1 mirroring still applies only where its actual permitted types and hooks match. Do not teach that every literal or fixed-width scalar automatically mirrors. Noncommutative reverse operations are written explicitly.
options.code:
bright: pixels * gain
inverted: F32x4.splat(F32{1.0}) - pixels
ratio: F32x4.splat(F32{2.0}) / pixels

options.name: Explicit splat only
options.detail: Keep the current representation conversion visible at every arithmetic site. This is a complete equivalent program with no new mixed hooks.
options.technical: Evaluate a stored scalar once, splat it to the exact lane type, then use existing lane-lane operators. This is Zig's strong explicit baseline, not an inherently slower program. Avoid claiming redundant machine copies without checking lowering for the actual target and optimization tier.
options.code:
bright: pixels * F32x4.splat(gain)
inverted: F32x4.splat(F32{1.0}) - pixels
ratio: F32x4.splat(F32{2.0}) / pixels

comparisons.note: Scalar operands are convenient for SIMD arithmetic and array programming. Jet can offer that convenience through existing typed operator hooks rather than a general broadcast rule.
Vectors and scalars cannot be mixed directly; @splat is explicit and exposes the repeated value. Its optimized cost need not exceed mixed-operator syntax.
Float SIMD supports scalar arithmetic on both sides. Integer SIMD deliberately rejects ordinary checked +, - and * in favor of wrapping operators; its overflow policy differs from Jet's.
Scalar-vector component arithmetic is familiar in shader expressions. That convenience does not settle CPU overflow or Jet's typed-hook ownership rules.
Broadcast syntax and array operations cover broader shape combinations. They solve more than exact-lane scalar arithmetic, at the cost of a larger shape and dispatch model.

recommendation.why: Ordinary typed hooks provide the requested convenience on both sides. Explicit reverse hooks preserve D-OPMIX1's narrow mirror set and ordered subtraction and division.
gains: Less repeated splat notation.
Both operand orders are supported.
No new operator lookup rule.

losses.loss: More hook instances to maintain.
losses.mitigation: Share elementwise implementations and test each supported direction against explicit splat.

losses.loss: Broadcast is less visible at the call.
losses.mitigation: Restrict it to exact element scalars and document the equivalent splat expression.

whyNot.reason: Smaller, but left-scalar subtraction and division remain asymmetric.
Strong explicit baseline with potentially identical code; A favors readability in repeated lane arithmetic.

recommendation.tradeoff: More Core operator instances in exchange for simpler expressions, without a compiler broadcast mechanism.

decisions.title: Keep matrix cropping, identity growth and reshape distinct
decisions.situation: A graphics program may copy a top-left block, extend a smaller transform with identity entries, or reinterpret the same count of entries under another shape. These are three different operations. Today Mat3 and Mat4 offer fixed column arrays, but no matrix resize or fixed reshape. Jet has ratified bracket places and destination-owned conversions. We recommend using those rules, with explicit source-named growth helpers and array-based reshape. A direct destination reshape is also a serious alternative.
decisions.gist: How should a matrix crop, grow or change shape?
decisions.lesson: A block selection borrows until copied. Growth adds identity entries. Reshape preserves entry count and column sequence; it is not a transpose.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: ~m4[0..<3, 0..<3] makes an owned top-left block under the ratified matrix-place rule. Without ~ it is a read place, not an owned Mat3. Mat4.from_mat3(m3) keeps the 3 by 3 corner and fills the rest as identity.

Expert path: Matrix<2, 8>.from_array(m4.to_array()) preserves the column-major sequence. This example is proposed fixed-matrix syntax, not a current compiler success. Current core.compute.reshape uses row-major Tensor data and copies it; do not infer that fixed matrices already share this representation or promise a zero-copy view.
decisions.story: Mira embeds a 3 by 3 rotation into a 4 by 4 homogeneous transform. A top-left block copied from an arbitrary transform can still contain scale or shear. It is not generally a rotation or the correct normal transform.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:39470-39510 defines Mat3 with nine Float values, column-indexed multiplication and copying to_array. :39536-39562 gives Mat4's sixteen values and copying adapter. current.jet prints the original and transposed column sequences. missing.jet rejects Mat4{m} with E0303; edges.jet rejects Mat3.reshape with E0102.

Audit M17/M18 identify missing fixed operations, not an ownership or copy law. Core/Compute/Compute.jet:173-179 checks element count and copies Tensor data for reshape; :192-203 transposes row-major data. Fixed matrices cannot inherit those storage rules merely through an alias spelling.

D-MATRIX-INDEX1=E makes bracket results places, with ~ selecting an owned copy. D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A owns named conversions on the destination. D-ARRAY-MAT21=A makes Mat2/3/4 aliases once fixed Matrix parameters exist. B amends aggregate heads; C amends destination ownership and S33's generic-call restriction. The alternatives therefore require full syntax review.

options.name: Places, source-named growth, array reshape
options.detail: Crop with an owned copy of a bracket block. Add Mat3.from_mat2, Mat4.from_mat2 and Mat4.from_mat3. Reshape equal-count fixed matrices through their fixed column arrays.
options.technical: Growth preserves the top-left square, writes one on newly added diagonal positions and zero elsewhere. No translation is invented. Cropping neither mutates nor converts the source, and ~ is required for ownership. Reshape requires equal counts at compile time and keeps scalar type and column sequence. No cross Tensor conversion is included. Coordinate with the generic Matrix alias cutover so these are not a second matrix family.
options.code:
corner: ~m4[0..<3, 0..<3]
grown: Mat4.from_mat3(m3)
flat: grown.to_array()
wide: Matrix<2, 8>.from_array(flat)

options.name: Destination head for all three
options.detail: Use Mat3{m4} to crop, Mat4{m3} to identity-extend, and a matrix head to reshape an equal entry count.
options.technical: Amend D-DOTCTOR3, with precedence required between equal-count reshape and resize. Different dimension pairs can otherwise imply both operations. The ballot must choose equal-count reshape first, then top-left copy and identity-fill for unequal counts. A head would now mean different mathematical transformations depending on shape.

options.name: Source resize and reshape methods
options.detail: Name the mathematical action at the source. A single resized dimension can cover the small square family, with explicit reshaped dimensions for equal counts.
options.technical: Amend D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 and S33, rather than calling this impossible. Reuse A's crop and growth math; require equal count for reshaped. No borrowed result is implied by either method. Explicit verbs are clearer than a dimension-dependent head, at the cost of a destination-type argument mechanism.
options.code:
corner: m4.resized<3>()
grown: m3.resized<4>()
wide: grown.reshaped<2, 8>()

options.name: Places, named growth, direct destination reshape
options.detail: Keep A's crop and growth rules, but add from_matrix for equal-count fixed matrices instead of requiring an array adapter round trip.
options.technical: Matrix<2,8>.from_matrix(m4) copies the column sequence and requires equal counts. The source-kind name follows D-SHAPE-CONVERT1. It cannot silently resize. This is a strong same-program alternative, not another spelling for growth or a new layout.
options.code:
corner: ~m4[0..<3, 0..<3]
grown: Mat4.from_mat3(m3)
wide: Matrix<2, 8>.from_matrix(grown)

comparisons.note: Matrix casts are compact and specify identity extension. Odin also distinguishes equal-count nonsquare reshapes in column order; short casts still need those rules.
Mat4::from_mat3 clearly names growth and establishes a homogeneous transform, without changing literal construction.
Reshape is a distinct equal-count operation. Julia shares data; numpy may return a view or copy, and its order parameter specifies index traversal.
Matrix storage and dimensions are independent choices; named reshape and block operations avoid assigning every transformation to a cast.

recommendation.why: It reuses ratified places and destination ownership. Separate operations expose whether data is cropped, identity-extended or merely reshaped.
gains: Ownership is explicit for crops.
Growth names its source shape.
Reshape preserves a documented sequence.

losses.loss: Array reshape is longer.
losses.mitigation: Keep fixed arrays inline; choose D if direct matrix reshaping earns its own public API.

losses.loss: Several small growth helpers are needed.
losses.mitigation: Provide all three widening pairs and migrate them with the generic Matrix aliases.

whyNot.reason: Compact, but overloads a head with distinct transformations and requires shape-dependent precedence.
Clear verbs, but reopens destination ownership and explicit call-site dimension arguments.
Strong and consistent; A avoids a separate reshape API until direct calls justify it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little adapter notation in exchange for fewer matrix-specific conversion mechanisms.

decisions.title: Keep small fixed matrices column-major; improve row input and packing
decisions.situation: People usually write matrices as rows on paper, while Jet's small fixed matrices store columns. Row-friendly input does not require a second stored layout. We recommend from_rows and row access for those fixed matrices, keeping their column-major representation. This is not a claim that every Jet matrix is column-major: core.compute stores row-major Tensor data. The alternative layout parameter has real benefits for row-oriented buffers and traversal, not twice as much handwritten math.
decisions.gist: Should small fixed matrices gain row-major storage, or just row-friendly input?
decisions.lesson: Input order, stored order and an external buffer's layout are separate choices. A shader also needs the right scalar width, padding and stride.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: Mat3.from_rows(r0, r1, r2) accepts three Vec3 values in visual row order and stores columns. row(i) returns an owned Vec3, not a place or writable alias. Existing new, from_array and to_array retain their column sequence.

Expert path: transpose().to_array() gives the original fixed matrix's scalars in row sequence. It is a copying adapter, not an ABI promise. Dedicated row-array packing could avoid an explicit transpose expression. Neither path makes nine Float values match an arbitrary F32 shader buffer or its alignment and matrix stride.
decisions.story: Nina types a rotation by rows, then passes it to a renderer. The row constructor fixes the typing problem. She still checks the renderer's declared buffer layout instead of assuming that column-major means GPU-ready.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:39470-39510 uses a nine-Float column array for Mat3; multiplication indexes k*3+row. :39536-39562 does the same for Mat4's sixteen values. current.jet runs both to_array and transpose().to_array(), printing their distinct column sequences. missing.jet reports E0311 for from_rows; edges.jet reports E0102 for row. Audit M19's API gap is real. Core/Compute/Compute.jet:13-20, :74-76 and :192-203 instead implement row-major Tensor matrices. A blanket one-layout claim would contradict today's code.

D-ARRAY-MAT21=A requires the small names to become Matrix<N,N> aliases once that family exists. D-MATRIX-INDEX1=E governs bracket places, not a row() method. Any generalization must preserve the owning fixed representation without silently migrating Tensor. D-LANES1 and D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 do not ratify a GPU matrix ABI. Option B would add a type-level layout parameter, so the whole ballot receives full syntax review. Options A and D require no new bracket or row-place mechanism.

options.technical: Bounds use the existing checked indexing behavior. Constructors accept exactly N rows, preserving scalar type. row() copies a value and is never an alternate writable place. Restrict the decision to small fixed matrices and their alias cutover; do not force row-major Tensor data to change. Use transpose().to_array() for row-sequence packing, with no zero-copy or GPU ABI promise.

Row and column indexing keep the same mathematics; kernels may share generic implementations. Costs are more type combinations, layout-sensitive FFI, conversion and test coverage, not necessarily twice the handwritten methods. This does not authorize implicit mixed-layout allocation or change Tensor layout.

options.technical: No API or representation changes. Small hand-written matrices cost more care, but callers can write a local row constructor. This is a complete same-program baseline, not a claim that row input is impossible.

Julia's ordinary arrays are column-major; numpy reshape has C/F index orders and may copy. Neither storage preference proves a shader ABI.
Both support row/column buffer layout choices. GLSL separates matrix stride and block layout; HLSL storage and constructor order are distinct.

decisions.title: Pick slots by number with shuffle, without promising one instruction
decisions.situation: A swizzle picks slots to make a new row, such as rgb to bgr. Jet currently supports letter swizzles on selected vector types, not fixed arrays or every lane type. Letters cannot name slot 7 or 15. Programs can already write indexed elements out by hand. We recommend shuffle with constant indexes on fixed arrays and exact lanes, sharing the operation name ratified for lanes. This chooses the call and result rules, not a machine-instruction count.
decisions.gist: How should arrays and exact lanes pick slots by number?
decisions.lesson: Write the source indexes in result order. Indexes may repeat; compile-time bounds checking does not imply that hardware can perform every permutation in one instruction.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: a.shuffle(2, 1, 0) produces those three slots. Fixed arrays return [T#K], where K is the argument count. The source is evaluated once. Existing letter swizzles remain available where supported.

Expert path: accept compile-time Int expressions, including named constants, rather than literal tokens only. Reject negative and out-of-range indexes. Exact lanes return Lanes<T, K> only when K is a legal exact width; otherwise report the unsupported width and show the fixed-array adapter. This does not add dynamic gather, two-source selection, writes or sizeless-lane shuffle.
decisions.story: Sam reverses the channels in a 32-byte pixel block. He lists all 32 destination picks, not just eight. A pick of 32 is out of bounds; 9 is valid. The target may need several instructions, especially across register sublanes.
decisions.detail:
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Places.jet:1448-1491 limits letter reads to Vec2/3/4, F32x4 and F64x2, using x/y/z/w. Core/Math/Math.jet:40695-40706 makes a three-slot F32x4 letter read a Float Vec3, not three F32 lanes. Numeric shuffle deliberately preserves the source element type. Literals.jet:1120-1122 and :1164-1167 establish bounds diagnostics E0965.

missing.jet reports E0311 for the audit W8 method; edges.jet gives E0302 for fixed-array letters. Planned #6177 c3 is not current support. D-LANES1=A ratifies shuffle on exact widths, but not this argument syntax or an instruction guarantee. The generic family replaces the current twenty names rather than preserving another family.

Numeric and letter forms must share selection semantics where their result types agree. This ballot needs full syntax review because it introduces constant-argument and result-shape rules, despite using ordinary method tokens.

options.technical: Bounds are 0 <= i < N. Constants may be expressions. Evaluation reads an unchanged source once; repeats are allowed. Non-copy element types are rejected rather than duplicated or implicitly moved out of a read place. Empty calls are errors, without inventing a Random API fix. Reuse the same selector lowering as letter projections; code generation chooses a legal instruction sequence.

options.technical: Amend D-LANES1's shuffle operation name in the same cutover. Do not ship both method names. All A bounds, copy, width and evaluation rules apply.

Index-vector subscripts allow reusable dynamic masks and wrap indexes modulo the input length. Jet's proposal instead rejects bad constants.
Letter swizzles are short for graphics vectors and support repeated reads. They do not express an arbitrary long-array permutation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small hand-written selector API, not a replacement for two-source shuffle or dynamic gather.

decisions.title: Adopt owned column buffers and extract them explicitly
decisions.situation: Two separate field buffers may already contain the data for a columnar list. Rebuilding rows copies that data. The draft proposed from_columns without distinguishing taking buffers from borrowing them, and treated read column windows as owned extraction. Those are different promises. We recommend an explicitly taking constructor plus consuming extraction, built into the approved compiler-provided Columns family. A borrowed join is a strong alternative when the original buffers must remain owned by their callers.
decisions.gist: Should Columns adopt separate owned buffers, borrow them, or copy rows?
decisions.lesson: A read column window borrows data; it is not an independent owned buffer. Joining borrowed slices and adopting whole lists require different ownership contracts.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: Columns

.from_columns(x: xs.move(), v: vs.move()) takes the two whole lists. Equal lengths are required. ps.x remains the ratified read window. ps.into_columns() consumes ps and returns owned field lists, with no element copying. Expert path: synthesize the constructor's labels and list types from P's stored fields as part of the existing compiler-provided Columns mechanism. Each parameter takes &&[FieldType]. This is not an ordinary Core function whose signature can be written once without field-dependent typing. Preserve each buffer's ownership and allocator; do not combine them into a single allocation.
decisions.story: Rae receives two independently allocated Float lists and wants one columnar owner. She hands both over, then later consumes the owner to retrieve them. If she only wanted a temporary borrowed view, option B would avoid transfer altogether.
decisions.detail:
Review missing.jet reports E0102 for zip_columns, agreeing with audit O5's missing helper. The audit's source shape is an older columnar spelling; D-SOA-SITE1=A instead ratifies compiler-provided Columns<T> and removes #Layout(columnar) at cutover. D-ARRAY-COLUMNS1=A supplies bare read windows, & write windows and ~ copies, with column(.len) for method-name collisions. Those windows cannot resize a single column and are not consuming extraction. Neither decision alone approves importing arbitrary owned buffers.

Current ownership is established by D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A and D-MOVE-SIGIL1=A: signatures use &&T for taking, calls are plain, and an early move uses x.move(). Historical ^ forms are retired. See Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:3581-3607 and Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/Copy.jet's ordinary ownership machinery. The review separately probes list-taking and disjoint field moves; no Columns implementation is inferred from those witnesses. Field-dependent named arguments and multi-buffer views require compiler work and full syntax review, even though their call tokens are ordinary.

options.name: Take lists; consume to extract
options.detail: from_columns takes one list per stored field. into_columns consumes the owner and returns a named record of the original owned lists. Ordinary field reads remain borrowed windows.
options.technical:
Each generated input is &&[FieldType], keyed by field name; unknown, missing and duplicate labels fail while compiling. Length mismatch returns ColumnError.LengthMismatch, consuming and dropping all taken inputs once. Callers needing preservation validate lengths before calling. Successful transfer allocates no element buffers and copies no elements.

Different capacities are allowed; reported capacity is their minimum. Growth preserves per-buffer allocation ownership. Empty-field T accepts from_columns() with length zero; ordinary pushes can represent nonzero rows. into_columns returns every field once and invalidates the owner; no live window may outlive extraction.

Preserve non-copy elements, destructors and each allocator. A field called len remains constructor label len; read collision uses column(.len). No reserved metadata label is added. For zero stored fields, capacity is zero on construction and follows ordinary capacity after growth.
options.code:
ps: Columns

.from_columns(x: xs.move(), v: vs.move()) read_x: ps.x // borrowed, not an owned split print(read_x[0]) owned: ps.into_columns() print(owned.x[0])

options.name: Borrowed column join
options.detail: over_columns borrows existing column windows and returns a read-only Columns view. Original buffers retain ownership and there is nothing to consume or unzip.
options.technical: Reuse ordinary read-window lifetime and conflict rules across all input owners. The generated view descriptor holds one column window per stored field and a shared length, with no element copying. It cannot grow, own its inputs, escape them, or support into_columns. Reject unequal lengths with ColumnError.LengthMismatch without consuming sources. Empty-field input gives length zero. This adds multi-owner Columns view support, not a second owning container or an already-working Core helper.
options.code:
view: Columns

.over_columns(x: xs, v: vs) print(view.x[0]) print(xs[0]) // xs still owns its list

options.name: Rebuild rows with existing list operations
options.detail: Add no join or extraction API. Validate lengths, push rows into the approved Columns list, and copy individual columns when separate owned lists are wanted.
options.technical: A complete Float-field baseline under the ratified Columns family, not today's implementation. It costs element copies and new buffers but introduces no field-dependent call signature. Non-copy fields require ownership-aware row moves and may not support the simple indexed version; do not claim equivalence for arbitrary owning elements.

options.name: Copying constructor; borrowed field access
options.detail: from_columns reads the field lists and copies them into owned Columns storage. Callers keep their originals; separate owned outputs use the existing ~ column-copy rule.
options.technical: Generated labels and shared-length validation are still compiler work. Restrict to copyable field values and propagate allocation failures through existing allocation policy. Unlike A, unequal lengths leave the source lists untouched. This matches the common non-consuming constructor intuition but is not zero-copy adoption and does not supply ownership transfer.
options.code:
ps: Columns

.from_columns(x: xs, v: vs) print(xs[0]) // originals remain owned here owned_x: ~ps.x

comparisons.note: soa_zip and soa_unzip operate on slices: useful zero-copy borrowed views without transferring ownership of independent dynamic arrays. That differs from an owning import/export pair.
MultiArrayList stores field regions inside one managed byte allocation and exposes slices. It is not a direct example of adopting independently allocated field lists.
Storage-generic matrix views show how borrowed storage can be separate from owned storage. Ownership constraints must be explicit; a borrowed view is not an owned unzip.
View-or-copy behavior is an explicit API concern, not implied by an operation's shape. reshape documents when copying is allowed and can reject a requested no-copy transformation.

recommendation.why: Adoption plus consuming extraction solves owned buffer interchange end to end. It reuses move and window rules instead of pretending that borrowed columns transfer ownership.
gains: No element copies on successful transfer.
Owned extraction is explicit.
No user reflection feature.

losses.loss: Failure consumes the imported lists.
losses.mitigation: State this in the signature and validate lengths before transfer when the caller needs recovery.

losses.loss: Field-dependent signatures need compiler support.
losses.mitigation: Implement them inside the approved Columns family and test field collisions and ownership together.

whyNot.reason: Best when callers must retain buffers; it does not provide an owning import/export path.
Complete for copyable fields, but rebuilds data and cannot simply copy arbitrary owning elements.
Preserves inputs and is easy to reason about, but pays the copying cost the motivating program avoids.

recommendation.tradeoff: Explicit ownership transfer and compiler-generated signatures, not an ordinary borrowed zip helper.

decisions.title: Complete small-matrix arithmetic without redundant adjoint names
decisions.situation: Jet's Mat3 and Mat4 compose, transform vectors and transpose today. Scalar scaling and several other named operations are missing. Mat2, identity, determinant and fallible inverse are ratified work, not present in the inspected dev source. Integer fixed arrays already support element-wise bit operations, but are not shape-checked integer linear maps. We recommend scalar hooks, three matrix methods and vector outer products. Inverse transpose stays a composition of existing operations; integer and complex matrix types remain an explicit competing choice, not an implied deliverable.
decisions.gist: Which matrix operations need public names, and which should stay compositions or array operations?
decisions.lesson: Scaling multiplies every cell; it does not fill only the diagonal. A minor is a determinant without a cofactor's sign. Adjugate is the transposed cofactor matrix, not the conjugate transpose.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: m * scale scales each cell, m.trace() adds the diagonal, and u.outer(v) makes cell (i,j) equal u[i]*v[j]. Integer masks use fixed arrays and ordinary bit operators. These are proposals, apart from the existing array operations.

Expert path: after the ratified inverse lands, m.inverse()?.transpose() computes inverse transpose and propagates its failure. For a nonsingular linear transform this carries normal directions; renormalize afterward. For an affine 3D transform use its linear 3x3 part, not a blanket rule for projective 4x4 matrices. Never replace an inverse failure with identity in a normal calculation.

A real matrix's Hermitian adjoint is its transpose. A complex matrix additionally needs element-wise conjugation, offered completely in C. A does not claim complex or integer linear-algebra parity with Odin.
decisions.story: Ines lights a mesh after uneven scaling. She transposes the inverse of its linear transform, handles failure, and normalizes the resulting normals. Another program needs cofactors even when the matrix is singular, where inverse times determinant is not a substitute.
decisions.detail:
Inspected dev 5a29fc351f486cafaf013c4780c5b8d9b96f3031. Core/Math/Math.jet:39470-39534 and :39536-39614 define column-major Float Mat3/Mat4. Vec3 scalar hooks are at :39276-39295. Neither matrix has identity, determinant, inverse or a private mat4_adjugate helper. D-ARRAY-MAT21=A and D-ARRAY-INVERSE1=A approve the missing base APIs; their approval is not a current implementation claim.

Gate-p240 matops-missing.jet reports E2511 for both scalar multiplication directions and matrix/scalar division. It reports E0102 for trace, adjugate, minor, inverse_transpose, Vec3.outer, determinant and inverse; identity is E0311 and qualified Mat2 is E1004. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions.jet:5682-5686 owns E2511. Audit M5 combines scalar-as-identity initialization with scaling: this ballot addresses scaling, not a scalar matrix constructor. M10 asks about integer matrices, M13 outer products, and M15 several operations with different domains.

FixedArithmetic.jet:48-70 and Expressions.jet:6193-6196 implement integer fixed-array bits. matops-integer.jet runs &, |, infix/prefix ~ and a scalar mask successfully. D-BIT-SIGILS1=A uses infix ~ for xor, not ^. Odin's runtime core:math/linalg supplies adjugate, trace, matrix_minor and inverse_transpose; they are not all compiler intrinsics. Its matrix_minor returns a determinant without the alternating cofactor sign.

D-MATRIX-MUL1=F keeps Matrix composition distinct from cell work. All hook options explicitly amend its left-type-only dot wording: a scalar pair gets ordinary scaling only, never a duplicate dotted scaling spelling. Matrix-matrix dot behavior is unchanged. D-OPMIX1=D still governs literal adaptation, mirrors, explicit reverse hooks and evaluation order. Existing Vec3 rejects a bound Int operand in both directions; a numeric literal is not the same case.

The executed reference computes trace 16, a nonsymmetric minor -4, asymmetric outer columns, and a nonzero adjugate for diag(1,1,0). Correctly transformed normals give tangent dot 0; using the model matrix gives -5. These are formula witnesses, not executions of proposed APIs or performance evidence.

options.name: Methods for primitives; compose inverse transpose
options.detail: Add scalar multiplication/division, trace, adjugate and minor to Mat2-4, plus outer on matching Vec2-4. Spell inverse transpose as inverse()?.transpose(). Keep integer masks as fixed arrays and real Hermitian adjoint as transpose.
options.technical:
Use Mul(Float), Div(Float) and the ordinary reverse Float.Mul(MatN) hook. Scaling applies ordinary scalar arithmetic directly to every cell; do not multiply by an allocated or constructed diagonal matrix. Matrix/scalar division follows Float division, including zero and non-finite operands; it is not matrix inversion. Scalar/matrix division and plain scalar addition remain refused. No bespoke Int conversion is added: literals and bound values follow the existing hook rules, with explicit Float conversion available.

Amend D-MATRIX-MUL1=F so dot eligibility depends on the operand pair, not merely a Matrix left operand. Matrix/scalar plain scaling has no dotted synonym. Matrix-matrix composition and dotted cell multiplication keep their approved distinction. Direct compound assignments use the existing result-type rule.

trace() returns Float with diagonal terms added in increasing index order. minor(row: Int, col: Int) returns the determinant after deleting that zero-based row and column, without the cofactor sign. On Mat2 it is the remaining cell. Out-of-range indices stop under the ordinary bounds policy; known-invalid facts may be rejected by existing proof rules, not a new literal-only method mechanism.

adjugate() returns the transpose of signed minors without inversion or a singular error. Ordinary Float overflow, infinities and NaNs remain possible. VecN.outer(VecN) returns MatN with column j equal to the first vector scaled by the second vector's jth cell; inputs are not conjugated. The approved Matrix<N,N> alias cutover retains these names and contracts.
options.code:
scale: Float{2.0}
bigger: tilt * scale
spin: tilt.trace()
normals: tilt.inverse()?.transpose()
cofactors: tilt.adjugate()
corner: tilt.minor(0, 1)
plane: up.outer(right)
mask: cells & 15

options.name: Free functions for the new named operations
options.detail: Keep A's scalar hooks, dot amendment and composed inverse transpose. Add core.math trace, adjugate, minor and outer functions instead of methods. Each operation has only one new entry point.
options.technical:
Use math.trace(m), math.adjugate(m), math.minor(m,row,col) and math.outer(u,v), with A's exact domains and numerical contracts. Free functions are attractive for generic algorithms, explicit imports and ports from numerical libraries. Odin's actual names include trace, matrix_minor and outer_product; this option chooses Jet's shorter names, not exact source compatibility.

Existing transpose, determinant and inverse remain methods. Different operations using different call styles do not by themselves violate I8. Do not also add method aliases for these same new operations. The cost is discovery across two call styles, not a second arithmetic mechanism.
options.code:
bigger: tilt * Float{2.0}
spin: math.trace(tilt)
normals: tilt.inverse()?.transpose()
cofactors: math.adjugate(tilt)
corner: math.minor(tilt, 0, 1)
plane: math.outer(up, right)
mask: cells & 15

options.name: Element-generic matrices, including complex cells
options.detail: Adopt Matrix<R,C,T>, with T defaulting to Float. Include Int, fixed-width signed/unsigned integers, F32, Float and the current Float-component Complex. Provide integer linear algebra as well as masking, and complete complex conjugate transpose.
options.technical:
Amend D-ARRAY-MAT21 and the Matrix/Grid family contracts, rather than creating parallel integer matrix structs. Mat2-4 become aliases of Matrix<N,N,Float>; existing two-parameter Matrix spelling keeps Float as its default. Shared scalar implementations serve the aliases, not parallel handwritten APIs. This is a broader owner choice, not justified merely by integer masks.

Addition and multiplication use the element's existing scalar rules. Matrix multiplication requires matching inner dimensions; scalar multiplication requires T under ordinary literal rules. Trace and minor return T; adjugate returns Matrix<N,N,T>. They require square matrices; integer calculations use ordinary checked scalar arithmetic. Scalar division and inverse remain Float-only, so integer truncation and new complex failure rules are not implied.

Integer Matrix cell bit work goes through its approved .cells() Grid view. The Grid uses &, |, infix ~ xor and prefix ~ complement; ^ is not introduced. This adds shape information and integer composition, unlike a flattened fixed array. It is not inherently an I8 violation to distinguish linear maps from their cells.

Use A's matrix method names with those generic signatures. For outer products use one generic math.outer([T#R],[T#C]) returning Matrix<R,C,T>, instead of also adding VecN.outer aliases; vector callers pass to_array(). Complex matrices gain conj() and use transpose().conj() for Hermitian adjoint. Real/integer matrices use transpose alone. Outer remains bilinear, without implicit conjugation. The scalar-pair dot amendment from A applies here too.
options.code:
grid: Matrix<3,3,U8>.from_array(cells)
mask: grid.cells() & U8{15}
product: grid * grid
spin: grid.trace()
plane: math.outer(up.to_array(), right.to_array())
hermitian: complex_matrix.transpose().conj()

options.name: Complete local formulas; no new public API
options.detail: Keep the same programs possible through existing arrays, scalar arithmetic and matrix constructors. Define local helpers for trace, minors, adjugate and outer. Compose the ratified inverse with transpose instead of adding its synonym.
options.technical:
Read cells through to_array(), in column-major order. Scaling already has a complete spelling: Mat3.from_array(m.to_array() * scale), because fixed-array arithmetic preserves length. Trace adds slots 0,4,8 for Mat3. Compute a minor by deleting its row and column and taking the determinant by scalar expansion. Build adjugate directly from signed minors in transposed order, including singular inputs; do not use an identity fallback or inverse times determinant.

Build outer-product cells as u[i]*v[j], column by column. The same finite expansion handles sizes 2,3,4, and integer or complex fixed-array data without inventing a public matrix type. Real Hermitian adjoint remains transpose; for complex cell arrays transpose the indices and negate each imaginary component. The executed 3x3 reference demonstrates the minor, adjugate, singular case and outer formulas.

This option adds no public hooks, dot amendment or helper names. Local helpers are application code, not promised Core APIs. Costs are repeated formulas, explicit indexing, copied to_array values and application-owned numerical tests. It is a real same-program route, not a claim that singular adjugate is impossible.
options.code:
bigger: Mat3.from_array(tilt.to_array() * Float{2.0})
a: tilt.to_array()
spin: a[0] + a[4] + a[8]
normals: tilt.inverse()?.transpose()
// Remaining complete local formulas are in matops-reference.jet.
mask: cells & 15

comparisons.note: Matrix syntax supports integer, floating and complex elements. outer_product is intrinsic-backed; trace, adjugate, matrix_minor and inverse_transpose are runtime library procedures. hermitian_adjoint is complex-only; inverse_transpose has no Jet-style singular error result.
comparisons.code:
t := linalg.trace(m)
n := linalg.inverse_transpose(m)
h := linalg.hermitian_adjoint(complex_m)

comparisons.note: Vectors combine primitive lanes, explicit @splat and reductions. Its best case is transparent element-wise work with compile-time sizes; that vector model alone is not a shape-checked matrix algebra API.
comparisons.code:
const lanes: @Vector(4, f32) = values;
const scaled = lanes * @as(@Vector(4, f32), @splat(scale));

comparisons.note: Concrete graphics matrices provide scalar multiplication, transpose, determinant and inversion, with focused Float types. That gives simple signatures without claiming integer or complex matrix coverage.
comparisons.code:
let bigger = m * 2.0f32;
let normals = m.inverse().transpose();

comparisons.note: One generic Matrix carries scalar, dimensions and storage parameters. Methods cover trace and complex adjoint; generic scalar constraints support broader algorithms without duplicating matrix families.
comparisons.code:
let t = m.trace();
let h = complex_m.adjoint();

comparisons.note: Scalar scaling uses operators; trace, transpose and complex adjoint use methods. Matrix versus Array distinguishes algebra from cells. Expression templates can combine work without requiring separate eager intermediates.
comparisons.code:
double t = m.trace();
auto h = complex_m.adjoint();

comparisons.note: Generic arrays and LinearAlgebra supply tr, inverse and lazy transpose/adjoint wrappers. Adjoint conjugates; on real matrices it equals transpose. Generic free operations and explicit cell work are a strong coherent alternative.
comparisons.code:
t = tr(m)
h = adjoint(m)
n = transpose(inv(m))

comparisons.note: Array functions offer broad element types and rectangular outer products, with an out parameter. np.outer flattens its inputs; that differs from an API requiring two genuine vectors.
comparisons.code:
p = np.outer(u, v, out=destination)
# p[i,j] = u[i] * v[j]

comparisons.note: HLSL matrix * is per-component and mul composes; GLSL matrix * composes and outerProduct is a built-in function. Both provide compact graphics formulas; GLSL inverse is undefined for singular or poorly conditioned matrices.
simd_float3x3 offers scalar operators and determinant, inverse and transpose properties over concrete column vectors. Its best case is a compact value API rather than a universal numeric matrix type.
comparisons.code:
let bigger = m * Float(2)
let normals = m.inverse.transpose

recommendation.why: Keep discoverable primitive operations near the matrix while using composition for inverse transpose and real Hermitian adjoint. Existing arrays already solve masking; C is the stronger choice when typed integer maps or complex matrices are required.

Scalar hooks match the vector model.
No redundant inverse-transpose or real-adjoint name.

Buys typed integer and complex algebra, but changes the approved matrix family beyond the real graphics workload.
Complete and works through existing primitives, but repeats indexing and numerical formulas in each application.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: Please reform the ballot using a2 & c beta (#context) as the baseline. Give me grammar options to pick from using those two choices. That is what I want to pick but need to ensure I like the syntax/grammar
questions.answer: Reformed and now RATIFIED. A2+Cβ fixed as the baseline; the grammar pick resolved to G2 — `#context(field: value) { … }`, reusing Jet's single `name: value` spelling (S61/S29), with `=` staying reassign-only. No single-field shorthand; bundle-spread deferred. Shipped as the c74 Smart Context feature.

questions.text: Option D but I dont want to defer the full implementation if avoidable. We are close to epoch 3 anyway, so what should we do to get this working? Propose a new approach in this decision.
questions.answer: Proposed Option D+ so nothing is deferred: an interpreter seam now (Phase 1) plus a Cranelift JIT this Epoch-3 (Phase 2, tiered — interpreter tier-0, Cranelift tier-1). I6 still holds because Cranelift is runtime-side, never in Source/. This needs your approval of the runtime-side Cranelift dependency (same posture as the regex dep). Recommendation: D+. Decision still open pending your call on the dep.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal
questions.answer: Not a blocker. `$` is plain ASCII and universal on physical keyboards; Jet already left the ISO-646-invariant subset behind by depending on `# @ { } [ ]`, so `$` adds nothing new. Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

questions.text: Please update this card so it isnt called "raw mode" AND we will have a separate library for TUI. This gives experts control but also provides batteries included TUI development features out of the box. Please update this question accordingly & give me alternatives to "raw mode"
questions.answer: Reformed the D-TERM1 card: dropped 'raw mode' (naming menu, rec `live { }`; alts direct_input/live_keys/keys/interactive/immediate/cockpit/takeover); confirmed a SEPARATE batteries-included `core.tui` library on top (old Option D is the library, not core), so experts get the low-level primitive and beginners get widgets out of the box; the card now decides only the primitive name + surface (A scoped block rec / B handle / C free fns).

questions.text: Break this into multiple cards, I cant choose multiple on one card
questions.answer: Split the old mega-card into three separate Focus Mode decisions: D-MIGRATE2A for migration operation vocabulary (`add`/`remove`/`change`/reorder), D-MIGRATE2B for where type-change converters come from (inline `via`, named `impl`, or both), and D-MIGRATE2C for `jet schema` CLI verbs (`status`, `squash --before`, and whether CI needs a separate `check`). c73 now links to all three IDs.

questions.text: I dont understand the downside. Please explain more precisely why we shouldn't just allow all core calls.
questions.answer: Updated D-CTCORE1 with the precise downside: allowing all Core at comptime turns pure compile-time evaluation into running a second runtime during compilation. That harms reproducibility, allows ambient side effects during builds (fs/env/process/net/secrets), forces the comptime interpreter to duplicate runtime behavior, complicates supply-chain policy, and creates machine-dependent compile failures. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

questions.text:
1) This was more a request for comprehensive and native builtin support for inline assembly and easy way to see generated assembly from jet source
2) too many downsides, must design away negatives
questions.answer:
Final integration: D-CODE-INSPECT2 recommends A: direct source assembly emission while preserving the ratified explicit capture workflow. B is the explicit alternative that removes retained capture. Fresh review found that capture was already ratified, not merely a new proposal; removing it must be an honest owner amendment.

The earlier Astra recommendation is preserved below as attributed design advice, not the final recommendation or ratification. The final source-view and three native-assembly ballots have completed independent beginner/adversarial review and pass the ballot readiness checker. They remain owner choices, not implemented features.

Astra answer — openai-codex/gpt-6-astra. This is a design recommendation, not a claim that the proposed commands already ship.

1. Native inline assembly and generated assembly viewing are separate needs. Keep the ratified #FFI(asm), core.mem and audited #Unsafe gates. Complete typed operands/results, register directions/classes, constants, symbols, local control flow, machine effects, target facts and applicable native execution modes through that one compiler contract. Do not add a competing asm! or mem.asm API. Existing ratified defects remain on #3017; the additional expressiveness is on #3042.

For ordinary Jet, propose jet emit --asm FILE: compile current source when needed and show compiler-emitted assembly without starting the application or requiring a prior recording. Propose jet inspect code for exact existing artifacts or identified live code. Source compilation may still perform its authorized compile-time/build work. #3016 owns this viewer.

2. The earlier ballot put recording infrastructure in the way. Remove the proposed --capture-code, --run and --generation workflow from this revision. Use one source-linked code representation for the simple view, exact inspection and export. Do not reconstruct vanished historical code and label it original; report unavailable/missing-code. An optimized function may have no standalone instructions, and mappings must come from real producer facts.

The remaining constraints are real: new source needs compilation, exact old code requires retained bytes, and hand-written instructions still require an audited unsafe promise and compatible hardware. Full ballot revisions are being reviewed separately; this answer neither ratifies them nor claims implementation or benchmark proof.

questions.text: Do not like either option. How is this handled elsewhere for other languages? I like the idea of one top level .jet folder that also includes things like build folder for anything generated by jet to keep things clean and tidy without polluting top level dir
questions.answer:
Yes. One top-level .jet directory is a reasonable design. My earlier ballot treated a local directory as clutter, but your concern is scattered directories, not one organized directory.

Other tools handle this in several ways:

- Rust/Cargo puts build outputs in workspace-root target/ by default. It separates profiles and target platforms below that root. [Cargo documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html).
- Dart shares .dart_tool/ for project tool caches. Its build tools use .dart_tool/build/. Downloaded packages remain in a shared user cache. Not every Dart output lives in .dart_tool/. [Dart documentation](https://dart.dev/tools/pub/package-layout#project-specific-caching-for-tools).
- Java/Kotlin with Gradle uses .gradle/ for project caches and build/ for build products. Shared caches also exist under the user's home directory. [Gradle documentation](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/directory_layout.html).
- .NET offers an opt-in artifacts/ directory containing every project's build outputs, grouped by kind and project. This is the closest direct precedent for gathering build outputs under one configurable root. [.NET documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/sdk/artifacts-output).

I revised B to mean one top-level .jet directory for all default project-generated files, including .jet/build/, .jet/cache/, and .jet/generated/. Existing records, receipts, reports, and locks also remain below that root. Nested source files share the root rather than creating their own directories. Default top-level build/ and .jet-build/ disappear.

Generated does not mean disposable. Saved replay claims, required evidence, and reproducibility metadata keep their protection. Routine cleanup and version-control ignore rules must target disposable contents, not all of .jet. Shared downloads, user credentials, application data, and explicitly requested export destinations remain separate.

The retained limitation is write permission: required local build output needs a writable destination. Optional cache and history writes keep their existing best-effort behavior.

I now recommend the expanded B. I updated the ballot and card #3421, but left the decision open for your ratification. No generated files were moved or deleted. The comparisons come from official documentation read on 2026-09-15; they are not newly executed peer builds.

questions.text: Dont we already reserve/use dunders for compiler stuff in jet? Why not just use that as a namespace? then build info, package info, compiler info can all be dunders and not pollute user namespaces and still be shorter than compiler.{...} format?
questions.answer:
Short answer: yes, Jet already reserves every name that starts with two underscores, but only as hidden machine space, not as a public namespace. Writing `__build` or `__package` in your code today is error E0067 ("double-underscore names belong to the compiler and tools"). The compiler uses that space for generated names (`__jet_...`) and internal markers such as `__core_intrinsic`.

Using dunders for build, package, and compiler info would work and is shorter than `compiler.build.os`. The costs: the same visual lane would then hold both hidden internals and a public API, and the two reservation rules (D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 and D-NAME-SIGIL1) must be amended with a closed list such as `__compiler`, `__build`, `__package`. Python is the usual precedent, but Python dunders are user-visible hooks, not compiler facts.

This is already option B on the family ballot D-COMPILER-NS1 (`__compiler.build.os`, `__compiler.type(T)`). Since `prep if`, `prep fn`, and `<prep N: Int>` are now ratified, that ballot really decides how compiler facts are spelled. I added your other idea there as option D: `$build.os`, `$package.version`, `$type(T)`. The recommendation stays A (`compiler.build.os`) because these facts are rare, and rare things can afford a clear word (friction in proportion to how common something is). `$` also already means an environment variable in config files and was Jet's first, retired compile-time mark.

Evidence: crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:624-634 (E0067); crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/predicates.rs:430-447 (every `__name` is reserved); crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs:62-64 (`__core_intrinsic` is compiler-only); Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6708-6720 (D-SHAPE-DUNDER2, D-NAME-SIGIL1); crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs:126-141 (retired `$` compile-time mark); Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6818 (D-ONCE-DOLLAR1: `$NAME` is a config environment variable); https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#special-method-names.

questions.text: I think parallel default wouldn't be a terrible idea with magic for beginners but it could make debugging difficult and make things less predictable with effective data races. So we would need a non default version as well for full expert control.
questions.answer:
Agree, and parallel by default does not create data races here. The scheduler (ResourceSchedule) only runs systems together when their checked access sets do not overlap: reads with reads, writes on disjoint resources or regions. Unknown aliases are treated as conflicts, and a system that needs parallel access with unknown or conflicting writes is rejected. Tests cover read/read, overlap, unknown alias, conflicting writes, and disjoint regions.

What can still vary: which system finishes first, the order of emitted commands, events, and logs, and float sums that combine in a different order. Fix these by merging commands and events in a fixed order (system declaration order) at the end of each stage.

Expert control, using the choose-explain-pin rule: Auto groups disjoint systems; `jet inspect` or `schedule.explain()` shows why; a Serial pin runs one at a time for debugging and fully repeatable runs; a Parallel pin fails compilation when facts become incomplete or conflicting. Bevy offers similar ambiguity reports.

Note: game callbacks still run directly today; D-SYSSCHED1 is open.

Evidence: crates/jet-foundation/src/ResourceSchedule.rs:62-114,289-306,772-829,1377-1497,1941-2017; crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Game.rs:303-352; Docs/proposals/memory-model-foundations-2026-09-27.md:376-392; https://docs.rs/bevy/latest/bevy/ecs/schedule/.

questions.text: I want to support both reactive & timed, please update accordingly
questions.answer:
Done. Option A is now both, sharing one key queue.

Timed: term.read_key_within(wait) returns a key, or None when the wait runs out. Closed input is an error, so a loop cannot spin.
Reactive: term.keys() returns a Receiver<Key> that joins the wait table beside process.signals and after arms. This is the same shape as the ratified D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1=A.

Both calls take keys from one queue that #Live owns. A receiver reads input only while the program waits on it, so each key goes to exactly one reader and none is lost. That removes a trap in Rust crossterm, which offers both styles but forbids mixing them. It also keeps one mechanism (I8): the timed call is the beginner path, and the receiver is the expert path.

Options are re-lettered. B is receiver only, where a time limit is an after arm. C is the earlier timed-only option. The earlier poll-then-read option is dropped, because the timed call already returns the key in one step. Recommendation: A. Its one loss is that two spellings can wait for a key with a time limit.
