questions.text: confusing, not in plain english. rework
questions.answer:
A shared object stays alive while something owns it. If two objects own each other, neither may ever be freed. Weak links avoid that problem because they do not keep objects alive.

The vote is about the compiler's judgment, not whether leaks are acceptable. The tested compiler rejects a harmless child built by a helper, but accepts the same child built directly at the insertion.

I recommend improving that judgment: accept helper-built trees when their owning links are proved safe. Keep real loops behind the existing explicit collection choice. Unknown cases must receive an honest explanation and a safe alternative, not unsafe acceptance.

The alternatives now say plainly what they sacrifice: stricter type rules reject even safe tree shapes; conservative write checks restrict helpers; automatic collection removes those restrictions but changes the approved opt-in rule. None promises free collection or universal proof.

questions.text: is recoverability the better path? is non-recoverability ever desired over recoverability? if recoverability is basically always better then we can make it recoverable by default with an opt in strict version. otherwise we should flip the paradigm. this just doesnt seem like a cohesive idiomatic clean solution
questions.answer:
Recoverability is not always useful or free. Cleanup and emergency reporting must work without more memory; the operating system may kill a process instead of reporting a refusal. Programs that cannot continue may reasonably stop.

But returning an ordinary error preserves that choice. Always stopping removes it. I recommend C: recoverable allocation by default, one operation name, and ordinary error propagation through libraries. A caller that wants to stop writes load() ?? panic("no memory"). A strict Never! function must prove or handle failure, not silently change its callees.

This is cleaner than letting a surrounding handler change what push returns. Common code stays short through existing inference and propagation.

The cost is real failure-path code and wider error contracts. The implementation must prove nonallocating error transfer, safe partial cleanup and unchanged collections on failed growth. Successful probes do not prove exhaustion recovery; the revised ballot says so.

questions.text: based just on the tradeoffs I am inclined to go with option a, but i dont understand fully. what is the context, what does this actually mean, what does it look like in practice? i dont understand
questions.answer:
Imagine your library has a generated promise sheet, package.api. It lists what other programs may call, what errors they must handle, and what permissions those calls require.

You publish greeting as 1.0.0. Later you add a clock read inside it. Its written parameters stay the same, but callers now need a new permission. Under A, your next check shows that exact promise change. You intentionally accept it, then commit the updated generated sheet with the source.

When publishing, Jet compares against the last released promise, not the newly accepted local sheet. It calculates the minimum version: 2.0.0 for this breaking change. You may choose something larger for behavioral changes the sheet cannot detect.

I still recommend A. It brings important changes into normal editing and review. It does not prove every compatibility promise: behavior, target coverage and release planning still need attention.

questions.text: why would functions not be able to read top level locals, that doesnt seem to make sense the way you present it. also I lean toward accepting this BUT if there is a fn run in the file, it errors. you must have EITHER top level scripting OR put all logic in the fn run entry point. if there is no fn run entry point, the file implicitly "wraps" the file with a run fn. do you understand? this way we either have a "scripting" mode or we have a clear mode. we cannot mix them, if you have an entry point explicitly defined, you cannot implicilty wrap in an entry point. if you dont, then you can. do you understand?
questions.answer:
Yes. A file gets exactly one entry: either its loose executable lines form an implicit run, or it declares run explicitly. Both together are an error. Files with neither remain libraries; imports do not launch script bodies.

You are also right about helpers. Their inability to see script locals is a consequence of the current compiler treating them as separate module functions, not a physical limitation.

I added and recommend lexical helpers: when a helper uses an implicit body's local, use the same checked captures as an ordinary closure inside explicit run. A helper can read total without making total global. Calls before initialization, escaping captures and task crossings still receive the normal safety checks.

This needs a general named-local-helper extension, not special script globals. The ballot states that scope clearly and contrasts it with passing parameters or using main-task file state.

questions.text: i really dont want to require copies unless it is PHYSICALLY necessary. is this really required or just the path of least resistance? we want the best way, the right way, and we have room to innovate & trailblaze. is this the best we can do?
questions.answer:
No: leaving a scratch block does not physically require copying.

The stronger option is to build surviving storage in its final destination from the start. Temporary pieces still use scratch. Compatible owned allocations may also transfer ownership without moving their bytes. I added and recommend F, rather than requiring .copy() on every escape.

There is a genuine physical limit: bytes cannot be reclaimed while a surviving pointer still uses them. A slice inside a packed, non-detachable arena cannot survive exact rewind. Either preserve its owner explicitly, choose final storage earlier, or copy independent data when that is genuinely necessary.

F does not hide that conflict behind an automatic deep copy. It reports incompatible lifetimes and lets the author restructure ownership. Uncertain lifetimes may need longer-lived allocation, so this is not a universal peak-memory or speed claim. The available compiler's successful text output does not prove allocator routing or copy elimination.

questions.text: i want a compact handler syntax like a ternary type thing, especially for the standard wrapped return type that can be a value, none, or error. remember the goal is to minimize friction proportionally to frequency of use. the more frequent the less friction there should be. we want to at least cover the pareto cases. reevaluate based on that and feel free to propose from a greenfield perspective the syntax/semantics that best solve the issue
questions.answer:
Agreed: deleting the compact handler without a replacement would make a frequent job harder.

I added and recommend F:

```jet
lookup(key) ? { .Val(n) -> n, .None -> 0, .Err(e) -> -1 }
```

It handles value, absence and failure in one expression. The subject runs once; only the chosen arm runs. Return and loop exits still leave the surrounding function or loop, not a callback.

This is the ordinary pattern table with a short head, available for other enums too. It adds no new result representation or runtime mechanism. Simple optional defaults and ordinary error propagation remain shorter when they fit.

The strongest smaller alternative is C: allow comma-separated arms but keep `if subject == { ... }`. Today's two-branch operator also works for this example, but handles absence inside its success arm. F is proposed syntax, not something the probe compiler already accepts.

questions.text: this ballot is not in plain english and the example used for each option does not help me understand anything
questions.answer:
The vote is about an explanation tool, not automatic parallel execution.

Suppose scale prints a message and multiplies a number. You wonder whether it can safely run many times on workers. Today you can add the kernel marker and receive an error, but the tested error points at the marker rather than the print.

A lets you ask first:

```text
jet explain kernel scale.jet:2
```

The proposed answer identifies the print and explains why output prevents this worker contract. You can move logging outside and check again. Missing proof must say “not proved,” not pretend to be a pass.

I recommend A: the same checker serves preview and enforcement. It does not launch work, select a GPU or promise speed. B requires temporarily marking the function; D improves only marked errors; C is a separate choice to allow automatic worker execution of eligible unmarked loops.

questions.text: ballot not in plain english and do not understand what i am even voting on or what the true tradeoffs are and why things would be beneficial
questions.answer:
The choice is how you ask another machine to do one job.

B uses a normal typed service request. A adds a task-shaped shortcut over that same service: pass a named function and plain data, receive a handle, then join it. C also permits checked captured closures.

I recommend A for one-shot jobs because it saves request-wrapper code without adding another transport or discovery system. Local tasks remain unchanged. Long-lived state still fits services or actors better.

The costs are not cosmetic: data must be encoded and sent, compatible code must exist remotely, and remote resources are different. A file operation accesses the worker's files, not yours. If a reply disappears, the job may already have performed its effects. The result must report that uncertainty; there is no automatic retry or rollback promise.

The probe only ran the local job. No remote execution or remote authority guarantee has been demonstrated.

questions.text: is this really required or just the path of least resistance? we want the best way, the right way, and we have room to innovate & trailblaze. is this the best we can do?
questions.answer:
No: authors should not have to hand-maintain a purity claim for every foreign function. That is not the best design.

I recommend A using Jet's already approved foreign descriptor. Derive effect facts from accepted source analysis or artifact-bound evidence where possible. Experts can supply audited evidence when inference is unavailable. Keep one contract, not a second manual effect database.

Naming the dependency in FFI.C("sqlite3") answers which library is authorized. Its justified effect information answers what callers must permit. These are different controls.

Neither contains arbitrary native code. A C library running in-process can bypass language checks. If enforced isolation is needed, use the existing sandbox placement with fully mediated host access. A separate process alone is not sufficient.

The rework distinguishes trusted claims from enforced limits and leaves unknown behavior unknown. The probe also corrected stale prose: named effects already parse on ordinary functions; effect arrows inside import declarations are still refused.

questions.text: ok i still dont think you get the point. how exactly does jet enforce, detect, verify, and implicitly determine which effects are used? this is a core critical element. we shouldnt depend on the user to define these things, but we should block the use of effects as desired, which is the !Effect syntax. if we can do that for jet why cant we do it for other languages?
questions.answer:
Sorry this sat unanswered. The ballot was reworked at 11:39 and you ratified A at 12:40, but the rework only narrowed the permission. It never answered your actual question, so here it is.

How Jet does it for Jet code. Nobody declares effects. Every effect starts in one place: the Core function that actually performs the operation (opening a file, connecting a socket, reading the clock) carries its effect, once. Sema builds the whole program's call graph and propagates upward, so a function's effects are everything it can reach. `!Net` on a function, or a deny in a package's authority, makes sema check that graph and refuse the build if any path reaches Net, naming the call chain. Enforcement is static: code that would do it doesn't compile. A call whose target sema can't see (an unknown function value, dynamic dispatch) counts as every effect, so unknown never passes as none.

Other languages today: sema treats every foreign call as opaque and gives it every effect (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Effects/Checks.jet, the foreign_opaque branch). So `!Net` already blocks foreign code, with no declarations, but bluntly: libc's abs() is refused as well.

Yes, we can do for other languages what we do for Jet, and we should. Foreign code acts on the world only through the operating system: system calls, almost always through libc. A compiled library's imported symbols (open, connect, send, clock_gettime…) plus its internal call graph (from the machine code, or from source when Jet builds it) show which of those each exported function can reach. Map each libc and system-call entry to a Jet effect once, in one table, the same way Core's primitives carry theirs, and propagate through the foreign call graph exactly as for Jet. abs() reaches nothing, so it's pure. sqlite3_open reaches open, fcntl and friends, so it's Files. That is the ratified D-FFI-FACTS1 rule ("every fact traced to a hashed source"), with the facts derived by the compiler rather than written by a person.

The honest limits:
- Where analysis can't see, the function stays every effect: raw system-call instructions, callbacks into unknown code, dlopen, JIT, self-modifying code.
- The facts are bound to the locked artifact's hash, so a changed library is analyzed again, never trusted.
- Static analysis of native code is a proof about honest code, not a guarantee against a hostile library: native code shares the process and can overwrite anything, including Jet's own checks. Where you need a guarantee, the kernel enforces it. The library runs in a sandboxed worker whose seccomp and Landlock filters deny the system calls behind `!Net` or `!Files`. That's the isolated placement the ballot mentions.

What's next: the derivation isn't built. I'm adding it as a criterion on #6366 (the foreign-contract card): the import and call-graph analysis, the one libc and system-call table, unknown staying every effect, and cases where abs() passes under !Net, a library that calls connect is refused under !Net with the chain into the library named, and a library with a raw system call stays every effect.

questions.text: I think the reworked ballot missed the second point completely. the original ballot was about allowing a python style script that doesnt have a defined entry point. a secondary question was about top level locals. we need this ballot to address the primary issue FIRST and the secondary issue, not throw out the first and only determine the second.
questions.answer:
You're right, and I'm sorry this went unanswered. The rework was deleted at 11:39 and dropped your second point.

Primary issue, a Python-style script with no entry point: this is built and in force, per your ruling. A file of only top-level statements runs as a script, with no `run` needed. A file with `run: fn` runs that. A file with both is refused (E0621, "Move the statements into run: fn, or remove run: fn"). A file with neither is a library, and importing a file never runs a script body.

Second issue, functions reading top-level locals: this is NOT resolved. I just checked on seed-b13:
    total: 5
    show: fn() { print(total) }
    show()
is refused with E0107: "`total` is a local of this file's top-level statements, which a function can't see". Writing it as a closure, `show := fn() { print(total) }`, prints 5. You said the refusal doesn't make sense, and the earlier answer agreed: it's a compiler artifact (named functions are compiled as separate module functions), not a real limit. The rework then dropped the fix.

What I'm doing: a new ballot for exactly this point. Its recommended option makes a named function in a script file a lexical helper that sees the script's locals, like a closure, with the normal checks (calling it before a local it reads is bound is an error, and so are capture escapes and task crossings). The alternative keeps E0107. It covers both behaviors with the same program, plus the edge cases: locals declared after the helper, helpers that assign to script locals, recursion, and helpers used by other helpers. It gets an adversarial review before it comes to you. Until you vote, E0107 stands.

questions.text: this does not seem like the best solution. remember beginner magic full expert control, two sides of the same coin. also this seems to make too many sacrifies and does not engineer away the downsides
questions.answer:
Sorry this sat unanswered. The ballot was reworked at 11:39, after this question, and you ratified F at 12:40, so the record here is late, not open. What the rework changed, against your points:
- Beginner side: no copies, no annotations. Storage that has to survive a scratch block is built in its final place from the start, and ownership of compatible allocations transfers without moving bytes. A beginner writes ordinary code, and no hidden deep copy happens.
- Expert side: full control of where values live (choosing the final storage, keeping the arena's owner alive, or an explicit copy), and the compiler reports exactly which lifetime conflicts.
- What's left is the one physical limit: bytes can't be reclaimed while a surviving pointer still uses them. F reports that conflict instead of hiding it behind a silent copy.
The build criterion is #6314 c10. If F still makes sacrifices you don't accept, tell me which case and I'll put it back on a ballot.

questions.text: why would this be a side effect? it is a piece of context implicitly included in all functions? i dont see why that would be an environmental effect or otherwise it is a core part of the language itself
questions.answer:
You're right that it isn't an environmental effect. Reading the context touches no file, socket or device, and it needs no permission. Under today's rules a package never grants it.
The row entry tracks a dependency, not a power. A function that reads context.deadline or context.thread depends on an input its arguments don't show. Three checks rely on knowing that:
1. #Memo caches a result by its arguments (E0938). A memoized function that reads the deadline would hand back a result computed under a different deadline.
2. A pure -[]> function promises its result depends only on its arguments.
3. A C callback has no task context to read.
The effect row is simply the tool Jet already has for inferring "what does this function depend on" through calls, function values, generics and traits. So the earlier votes reused it, plus a package deny.
If you see context as part of the language itself, I've added option F to the ballot. Context reads never appear in rows and aren't effects, so nobody writes, grants or denies them, and a function with a written `-[IO]>` row can read context freely. The compiler still infers context reads internally, so pure, #Memo and C-callback functions are still refused with a clear message.
F drops the package-level deny and amends the read-effect clauses of D-JAI-CONTEXT1 and D-CONTEXT1. A to E all keep the visible Context row; they differ only in where it is declared. F's cross-family adversarial review hasn't been done yet.

questions.text: What would be the tradeoffs of encoding & compression? wouldnt that be part of building a binary anyway? We are trying to win against every other language and hit hand optimized machine code level for bin size, speed, performance, etc. How do other languages handle this? Sweeping it under the rug rather than fixing it doesnt seem like a good solution
questions.answer:
You're right, and the recommendation (A, a report) was wrong. Reporting the cost leaves it in place. Here is the full answer, and what changes.

1. This program shouldn't carry the data at all. It only uses the two lengths. Hand-written machine code for it prints 100000000 and holds no string bytes. Zig, Rust and C++ get there as well: the length of a constant is itself a constant, so the bytes nothing reads are never emitted. Jet today stores both 50 MB runs and then rescans them at run time to count characters. That's an optimizer defect, not a policy question, so it gets fixed without a ballot: #6769 c4 (fold the length) and a new c5 (bytes no run-time code reads are not emitted; this program's binary must come out about as small as the version that reads the size at run time, 136 KB).

2. Data the program really reads goes in read-only pages, raw. That's what every peer does (C, C++, Rust, Go, Zig): constants sit uncompressed in .rodata. The kernel maps those pages from the file on demand, so only the pages actually touched use RAM, they're shared between processes running the same binary, and they can be dropped and reloaded without swap. Today Jet puts them in writable .data, which loses the sharing; #6769 c3 fixes that.

3. Compression is not part of building a binary in any mainstream toolchain. Compilers and linkers don't compress code or data; the one exception is debug sections (`--compress-debug-sections=zstd`), which never load at run time. Packers like UPX are a separate, opt-in step. The trade-offs:
- Size: large wins on repetitive data (50 MB of "x" compresses to a few bytes), about 2-4x on typical tables, nothing on data that's already dense.
- Speed: the data must be decoded before use. zstd decodes at roughly 1-2 GB/s per core and LZ4 at about 4 GB/s, so 50 MB costs tens of milliseconds at startup or at first use.
- Memory: decoded data lives in private anonymous memory. It's always resident, counted in RSS, never shared between processes, and can't be dropped without swap. Raw read-only data can be all of those things.
So compression swaps disk bytes for RAM and startup time. Under the gate (Jet must match hand-optimized code on cycles and bytes), it loses for data that is read, except where disk or download size is the actual target, such as embedded or web.

4. How the peers handle huge compile-time values: C++ can't keep a compile-time heap string at run time at all (allocations during constant evaluation must be freed before evaluation ends), and clang and GCC cap evaluation steps. Rust's const evaluation can't build a String. Zig can build a large array at compile time, needs an explicit evaluation budget for long loops, and stores the result raw. None compress it.

What I'm doing: c3, c4 and c5 on #6769 are built as fixes, with no vote. I'm withdrawing this ballot's current options and rewriting it around the only real choice left: whether Jet offers compressed storage for large read data, for size-targeted builds only (embedded, web), and how that's switched on. It comes back to you with measured numbers for each option, after an adversarial review.

questions.text: typeid seems like a solid direction but needs downsides engineered away
questions.answer: Agreed, and revised. The ballot keeps TypeId and removes four of its five costs. Type text computed from data, types only the app declares, and lists of a struct made earlier in the same build now go through one lookup, meta.find_type("Point"). It returns the compiler's identity for that one type, or None, and the text is never pasted into source, so "I64, extra: String" can no longer add a field. Written types use the two spellings a Type value already has: a bare name such as String, or braces for anything else, such as TypeId{[String]} or TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int}. So function types no longer need an alias. The checker work is now listed as build work, not a cost, and the Type-versus-TypeId split is older than this ballot. One cost remains, because the text only exists while the build runs: a type named by text is checked then. The lookup returns None for a miss, so the build must handle it. Written and reflected types never take this path. One note: the lookup loosens the ratified sentence that no string can make a TypeId. It can only find a type the compiler already declared, so it can't forge one.

questions.text: i thought jet tuples ARE positional with optional names? is that not the latest guidance? also, the recommended option does not have downsides engineered away so it is immediately rejected on both grounds
questions.answer: No. The latest guidance is the pair of record votes you ratified on 2026-11-06. Every group of values names its members and is written in braces, {min: 1, max: 9}. Paren tuples retire, and a destructure binds by name: {min, max}: bounds(xs). Written member order is now part of the type and decides comparison and printing. Neither vote adds positional binding or optional names. Neither is built yet: on today's compiler the brace spelling is still a parse error, and the old paren form (left: 7, right: -9) still works and destructures by name. You were right that the ballot was stale. It predated both votes, and with them two of A's costs disappear. Parts keep the plugin's order, so part10 no longer sorts before part2, and a one-part tuple becomes the one-member record {part0: 7}. The ballot now says record for Jet's side and tuple only for the plugin's positional group. One cost remains, and no named-only design can remove it: the plugin supplies no names, so the host types the names it wants once, {part0: left, part1: right}: guest.pair(). Writing {left, right} gets an error whose fix writes that line, and jet fix applies it. If you want Jet records to be positional with optional names everywhere, that reopens the brace-record vote for every program, so it needs its own ballot. Say so and it will be drafted; this question then goes away.

questions.text: the terminology youre using is confusing me, but either way, the downsides are not engineered away for the recommended option, therefore rejected
questions.answer: Sorry for the jargon. The ballot now uses two plain terms. A script variable is a value the script's own lines set up, such as count := 0. An extra parameter replaces what the draft called a hidden input. The whole idea is now one sentence: for each script variable a helper uses, Jet gives the helper a parameter with that name, passed by name, and the script fills it in at every call. That reuses Jet's existing label-only parameters, so tests can now call every helper by passing the variables themselves: note("fig", count: tally, limit: 3). Today's compiler already runs that form in a test. The same labeled call in the script's own lines currently crashes the compiler, a separate bug the ballot now lists. Hover shows the full signature. Two former costs were ordinary Jet rules that apply to written parameters too, so they are no longer listed. The one place a script and run: fn would differ is a closure bug, now listed separately. Two small costs remain, each kept for safety. A helper that changes a script variable can only be called directly, not handed to each or run as a task, because a function value must not hide a change or race. The error rewrites the call as a loop. Methods in a script can't use script variables, because a method can be called through a trait; the error offers a helper function.

questions.text: please do your best to engineer away the remaining downsides for the recommended option
questions.answer: Revised. A's four costs are down to two, and both are costs hand-written code pays too. Almost-runs staying raw is no longer listed, since it never makes a file bigger than today. The missing Core encoder is now part of A: core.archive.zstd gains a real encoder, so an author compresses a table at build time and decodes it at run time with no outside tool. A stored run now stays a short recipe for its length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches, hashing, printing and copies. Only handing the whole value to a function that takes [U8], or to foreign code, fills it into memory once, as hand-written code would. Irregular tables, which real lookup tables are, still stay full size unless the author compresses them. Compressing them automatically would cost decode time and unshared memory on every run. jet inspect decisions --estimate now shows what each large table would save, so the author decides with numbers.

questions.text: why would byte traits NOT be a good idea, sounds good to me
questions.answer: You are right: byte traits are the better design, and the reworked ballot now recommends them as A. The three costs the posted ballot charged do not hold up. Jet's Prelude already declares Reader and Writer byte-stream traits, though user code cannot name them as a bound yet, so A opens them. FileReader's read and read_into are compiler routes today, so FileReader implements the trait with two one-line methods. The 75 compiler lines are private routes the philosophy says Core must not use, so deleting them is a gain. The 7 names that seemed to need new paths stay put once crypto moves up beside files and data, CSV and WebSocket move up to services; the census on dev drops from 67 upward lines to 31, and the traits remove 25 of those. Two costs remain and are named: the trait shares the name Reader with core.term's binary cursor, told apart by path as Go's io.Reader and bufio.Reader are, and speed parity with today is expected but must pass the speed gate. The result is no public path change, codecs that read files, stdin or any user type, and JSON programs that no longer load the files code.

questions.text: what would best intended behavior be? we have advanced api features, so we could even detect the type and switch accordingly so that if an int is passed it stays int and if float is passed it stays float, if the user wants to convert they could wrap in Int{}
questions.answer: Your design is the best intended behavior, and the reworked ballot makes it option A. Every rounding returns the type it was given: a Float gives a whole Float, a Decimal a whole Decimal, a Fraction a whole Fraction, and an Int comes back unchanged. Int{...} is the one way to get an Int, and the one place a program can stop, on NaN, an infinity or an out-of-range value. A small Core trait, Roundable, lets each number type and any user number type join with one impl, built per type so Floats cost the same as today. It also fixes real problems: math.round(7 / 2) is refused today because 7 / 2 is an exact Fraction, the posted program's 0.125 is a Decimal the current round_even refuses, and today's math.round silently returns 0 for NaN and clamps infinities. Two dependencies are named on the ballot. The exact Int{float} conversion is a submission waiting in the inbox, which every option needs. A also needs Int{} over a whole Decimal or Fraction, which the seed refuses and no submission covers yet.

questions.text: I think this should be allowed per rec a. but should be communicated to the user with an inspect
questions.answer: Agreed, and the reworked ballot keeps A with a new report: jet audit retention, also reachable as jet inspect audit retention. It lists every place a program can keep growing data without a cap: each #Memo(bound: none) cache, each module Shared global whose type holds a list, map, set or String, and each loop that never ends by itself and keeps appending to an outside collection. A loop over a range or a finite list is not listed. The first two kinds are exact; the loop kind is a simple source check, so its rows say may grow. It sits beside the existing jet audit memory, which reads what earlier runs held, and follows the jet audit copies, writes and foreign commands, with a --json form a project can use to fail CI. It is a list you ask for rather than a warning, because Jet decided to have no warnings. A probe confirms the example program runs today and that no such command exists yet. The memory audit document the posted ballot cited is on no branch; card #6567 c4 still owes it.

questions.text: what is the best greenfield solution? seems like you would recommend d if not for the fact that we would need to update old code. that is NOT at all a valid reason to go with a worse solution EVER.
questions.answer: Yes, the posted D is the best greenfield design, and the reworked ballot recommends it as A. The child read stays and counts as part of Exec, because nothing else can tell a memory or open-file limit from any other failure. The vault drops its read of another program's /proc entry and uses a kernel file lock, the same flock core.files locks already use, which the system releases the moment the holder exits. That removes the ten-minute wait after a crash, and it fixes a real bug where a pid on a shared network folder names a process on another machine. A new Jet never steals an old-format lock file. The reverse cost is named plainly: the new lock file is never removed, so once a new Jet has written a vault, an older Jet build refuses to write it until the file is deleted. Under greenfield Jet owes its older builds no compatibility; if mixed builds ever must share a vault, unlinking the file on release with an identity recheck removes it between writes.

questions.text: are the downsides for a engineered away? any chance we can engineer away the others or is this essentially a theoretically perfect solution
questions.answer: Not as posted, but most of its downsides can be engineered away, and the reworked A does that. Before holding the file, Jet now asks the file system for a free private clone and maps that. On btrfs a probe cloned 1 GiB in 0.10 ms, and the mapping kept its old bytes after the original was overwritten and truncated. On btrfs, xfs, macOS APFS and Windows ReFS this means zero copy, no writer ever waits, no deadline and no reserved signal. Copies now go to an unnamed temp file, so files larger than memory still map. What cannot be removed is on file systems without block sharing, such as ext4, tmpfs and NTFS: there the first writer waits once while Jet copies, or the copy happens at map time. One cost holds everywhere and is now named: a clone or copy holds disk space, so a rewritten original frees nothing until the map is dropped. Those are limits of the file systems themselves, so A is as close to perfect as they allow.

questions.text: what is the best theoretical greenfield solution?
questions.answer: The best design is the posted B, improved, now listed as A: send fails with SendError, and err.value hands the unsent value back. The cost the posted ballot charged it, 282 lines to edit, goes away once Core declares that SendError converts into the general Err and into Closed. With that, a bare send in run, a task block or a plain function simply passes its failure up, and a probe shows that pattern working with a stand-in error. So no value is ever lost silently, a program that cares gets the value back, and send agrees with the already ratified try_send. Two things remain and are named: sends inside functions that promise never to fail need ??, and values still queued when the last receiver is dropped are freed, as in Rust, Go and Kotlin; freeing runs each value's drop, so what it holds is released. The build must also teach error conversions to apply to generic errors, which the seed does not do yet.

questions.text: delete this ballot. i do not want to decide on this now but dont want to rule it out forever
questions.answer: Done. The ballot is deleted, and the idea is kept on the ideas list ("Build the jet compiler itself from a record of real runs"), so it is not ruled out. The speed plan on #5479 does not depend on it.

questions.text: rewrite in plain english. downside should be engineered away.
questions.answer: The ballot is rewritten in plain English, and its one downside, two versions of each check that could disagree, is designed away. Under the new A, the fast vector scan never writes a message or computes an answer. It only marks which blocks of code might hold a mistake, and today's precise check runs on those blocks and writes everything, as it does now. This is the same split simdutf uses: it scans text 64 bytes at a time and rewinds to a scalar check to report the exact error position. The scan is written in plain, portable Jet using lane types whose meaning is the scalar operation lane by lane, so every machine runs the same code without unsafe intrinsics. A test runs every check with the scans on and off over all test programs and generated inputs, and any difference in messages or results fails it. The only remaining risk is a scan bug that wrongly clears a block. That risk is held down because each scan tests a wider, simpler condition than its check, and the on-and-off test catches any difference.

questions.text: is this really the best solution? engineer away downsides
questions.answer: No, the old A wasn't the best: it added a second walk over the program to sum up what each function needs, and Jet already has that walk. Jet can already prove a function never uses the heap (the -[!Mem.Alloc]> mark), and a probe shows that proof already follows calls into Core. The new A runs that one proof from the program's start whenever the chip has no heap, so Core and every package are checked the same way and nothing is skipped by name. The cost is the walk Jet already does: checking with and without the proof both took about 240 ms in a measured probe. Two downsides were designed away. Each error now lands on the programmer's own call, with the full path and the exact Core or package line in the note, which also fixes today's wrong caret for that proof. The probes also found two gaps in that proof, and A closes both: a list that starts empty and then grows is now caught, and generic or trait-value calls whose targets are all heap-free, such as math.round on a Float, are no longer wrongly refused. What remains is mitigated: a package's error shows at the caller's line with the package's line in the note, and broken heap-free marks that grow lists now fail.

questions.text: what are the long term ramifications of dropping an ast? that is an important phase of optimization. why would we completely remove it? is that safe? does that limit our ability to optimize the resulting binary? the recommended option should be the best greenfield solution with all downsides engineered away
questions.answer: No: the syntax tree is not an optimization phase, and its form cannot limit how well the finished program is optimized. All 17 of Jet's optimizer passes run on IR, the lower instruction form. The IR builder, the backend and the compile-time evaluator never read the syntax tree; they read the checked body (checked with git grep, Opt.jet:97). The tree's real cost is its shape: thousands of small boxes that are copied and freed. In one measured run, that work plus compile-time value copies was 20.5% of busy time. Dropping the tree outright is unsafe in practice. The formatter, the editor, generic code and the ownership check all need a stored outline, so they would need a second parser or repeated re-parsing. The reworked A keeps one flat outline per file, as Zig and Carbon do, which removes the boxes and copies while every tool shares one parser. The old wait-and-measure gate and the tree-free parser are gone, and A's only remaining cost is a small flat slice kept for generic bodies.

questions.text: downsides not engineered away. is this the best greenfield solution? is it idiomatic and cohesive with jet and jet's philosophy? make sure those are the case
questions.answer: No: the old A copied Rust's byte-first names, which broke the beginner's out.write("hi"), kept a write that can silently send only part of the bytes, and still disagreed with core.files. The new A takes the rule Jet already uses for files and the screen: on every stream, write takes text and write_bytes takes bytes, so Stdout, Stderr and the reference example don't change. Only pipes, sockets, FileWriter and the Reader trait rename their byte methods. Writer becomes write_bytes, which writes every byte or fails as Go's io.Writer requires, plus flush; default bodies add write(text) and write_line, so a user writer needs two methods (probe r3 runs this on the seed compiler). The partial write leaves the trait and stays on pipes and sockets as write_some, which removes the short-write trap that Clippy lints against in Rust and that Jet's own Doctor.jet hits today. Two costs are left: every writer writes a one-line flush, and Rust or Go habits like conn.write(bytes) get a compile error whose fix names write_bytes. The lost unfinished-log mark is gone from the list, because JSON Lines and RFC 4180 CSV both say a missing last line end means nothing.

questions.text: what is the BEST greenfield solution? downsides should be engineered away and it should be idiomatic and cohesive with jet and jet philosophy and be the best solution compared to all others for all other languages and ecosystems
questions.answer:
The best design is still A: Core keeps one server that answers every request with a single handler, and the web package owns all routing. Go, Deno, Node and Python all ship this split, with routers as libraries above one serve call.
This rework removes or narrows the old downsides instead of only naming them.
Literal routes, the common case, keep their E2804 clash error at check time; only a route built while the program runs is checked when added, and its stop still prints E2804 with why and fix.
The one-request test call is now a method on the server listen returns, the shape of Python's handle_request, rather than a second free function.
The folder helper now returns a ready handler, like Go's FileServer and Deno's serveDir, so serving a folder of files needs no package at all.
The request id loss is gone, because request ids were always an app choice and the web package still adds them.
Only a real match by Core can tag a request with its route, so no code can forge path values; what remains is four small public items in Core, each replacing a private call.

questions.text: what about if the if statement checks a single case and does not have follow up if statements? If it is a one off check i dont think that should require a full check because there is logic you may want to only do when one type of enum is selected. if you have more than one branch, then you should probably have to be exhaustive. still doesnt feel like an ideal situation, would like a greenfield idiomatic cohesive with jet and jet philosophy proposal for how to do this in the best way possible. we want to minimize logic bugs in code
questions.answer: Agreed on both rules, and none of A-F says them, so the ballot will be redesigned rather than voted as it stands. The direction: a one-off check of a single case (if order is .Paid { ... } with no else-if) stays free, because doing something only for one case is normal logic. As soon as two or more branches test the same enum value, the chain is a decision over that enum and must cover every case. It names each case, or says the rest explicitly with a spelling Jet can check (so adding a new case to the enum flags every chain that has not decided about it, which is the logic bug to prevent). Today the subject table cannot say the rest (E0641 forbids else there), and 11 of 18 real chains end in else, so the redesign has to give that rest a safe spelling rather than ban it. The new ballot will show one program in each option, cover the beginner and expert paths, pass an adversarial review, and come back to you as D-GUARD-LINT1 revised.

questions.text: What about using the pipe “hole” syntax <> inside the method parenthesis, crew.tell(<>)? Would that be better? Then it shows it is clearly a method and that it has a hole? I would say just include parenthesis but keep them empty but then that may make people think it is a call with no args
questions.answer: Good idea to check, but <> cannot take this job. In Jet, <> is the value of the enclosing |> step. Inside a step, crew.tell(<>) is already a call: 7 |> crew.tell(<>) prints "Lin tells 7" on dev 03d5f7b309. So crew.tell(<>) would be a call inside a pipe and a bound value outside one: one spelling, two meanings. One hole also reads as one argument, so a two-parameter method would need crew.tell(<>, <>), and crew.tell(<>, 3) is partial application, a larger feature. Empty parentheses would read as a call, as you say. Option D, crew.tell(..), keeps your goal (it clearly marks a method value with a hole for the rest) with a mark that is free everywhere and never means a call. I added this to option D on the ballot. If you want partial application with holes, that is its own ballot.

questions.text: Should the hole be <> instead of _ to match pipe syntax so that <> means the value is inserted here? I also am very confused by this ballot, no idea what it means plainly
questions.answer:
Plainly: a decision table is Jet's `if` with arms, like a match. Today you write `if light == { .Red -> 30  .Amber -> 5 }`: Jet compares `light` with each arm in turn. The hole form marks where each arm's value goes: `if n % _ == 0 { 15 -> "FizzBuzz"  3 -> "Fizz" }` means try `n % 15 == 0`, then `n % 3 == 0`. On 2026-09-11 you ruled that every table must have a hole, so `if light == {` would become `if light == _ {`. That migration never ran. The ballot asks which headers stay: (A) keep `if light == {` for plain comparisons and use a hole only when the test is more than one comparison; (B) migrate all ~16,000 tables to a hole; (C) allow both spellings; (D) require the hole everywhere but read the header once. The catch for B: your rule re-runs the header for each arm tried, so `if files.try_lock(path) == _ {` would call try_lock up to once per arm, and ~6,000 tables call a function in the header and would first need a named value.

On `<>`: yes, we recommend it. `<>` already means 'a value is inserted here' in pipes, so the hole reuses one idea instead of adding one. `_` already means 'ignore this' in patterns and the catch-all arm, and a hole table would hold both meanings at once (`if try_lock(p) == _ { .Val(_) -> ... }`). The one cost is nesting: a hole table directly inside a pipe step would see two `<>` values. The rule we'd propose: a hole table inside a pipe step names the pipe value first, and the compiler refuses the ambiguous form with that fix. The ballot will be rewritten in plain language with `<>` as the hole in every option and re-reviewed; the hole syntax that landed today (`_`) is a one-token parser change to switch.

questions.text: need to engineer the downsides away for recommended option
questions.answer: Redesigned; the ballot now shows each downside of A, what was tried and the result. The two listed losses are gone. First, speed no longer hinges on hidden proofs. One rule decides, and a reader can apply it: a growing value is stacked unless it is stored in something that outlives it or sent to another task. A value a function returns is built on the caller's stack, so builder functions qualify. Second, a value no longer outlives its last use. Each growing value has its own stack, so it is freed at its last use with one pointer reset. Two costs the old ballot never named are also designed away: thousands of tasks do not reserve address space (tasks take chunked stacks on first use, reusing the capacity check growth already does), and a value kept across a wait is safe (stacks belong to the task). What remains: a value kept in a longer-lived container, like a map of lists, stays on the heap at exactly today's cost, and jet inspect placement names it and the rule that sent it there. Any winner still gets the adversarial review and measurements before it is built.

questions.text: this does not feel like a good idiomatic cohesive solution
questions.answer: Agreed; the old A made every new row write TaskID.from_id(app.new_id()), two Core calls for the most common thing an app does. Redesigned by frequency. Making a row is the most common, so it needs no ID code at all: the row's field says id: TaskID = .fresh(), and Task{title: "Ship it"} makes a checked UUIDv7 ID, offline too. Declaring a table is less common, so it costs one line: TaskID: distinct app.ID. That line buys an ID that is checked ("t1" gets 422 before any method runs) and typed, so a ProjectID can never pass where a TaskID is expected. The one language rule that makes it work is cohesive with how distinct types already code: a distinct type gets its base's constructors, made through its own conversion, the same path decoding takes. A base whose conversion can fail, like a range type, forwards none, so no unchecked value can be made. Downsides designed away: a request without an id gets a server-made one, and the request key from #6867 c2 stops a retry making a second row. Tests stay deterministic, because fresh() uses the test host's seeded clock and random source. The marker option, which failed silently when forgotten, is dropped. The old hand-made form is now B, and the generic app.ID<Row> is C.

questions.answer: Rewritten around a real job instead of 14, "hi" and a Point. Plainly: sometimes one list must hold values of different types, and log fields are the everyday case. log.info("saved", 14, "notes.txt", 120ms) carries an Int, a text and a Duration. In Jet those types opt into a shared trait (Field), and printing each field already works. The missing piece is asking one field "are you a Duration?" and using it as one, say to print it as milliseconds. The recommendation, C, writes that question the way Jet already matches enum cases: inside loop f in fields, the table if f == { .Duration(d) -> print("took {d.ns / 1000000} ms")  else -> print(f) }. .Duration(d) means "if f is a Duration, call it d". It is checked when compiling: .Bool(b) is an error, because Bool never opted into Field, and the table needs else. In practice: you write the trait and one empty impl line per type once, then use ordinary arms wherever you need a type back. The other options: E adds Any (no opt-in lines, but a wrong question is found only when the program runs), and B gives the trait one method per type you want back (works today, but a library's users cannot add methods).

questions.text: yeah this is not good enough. we want to reduce friction proportionally to frequency, so most common things are easiest with least friction and more complex cases take slightly more friction. we want to minimize friction everywhere and make code easier to reason about, but that is our trade space
questions.answer: Redesigned around friction in proportion to frequency. Most common, testing one case (if order == .Paid { ... }), stays free. Next, testing a few cases and ending in else: you type else as today, in a chain of ifs or in a table, and jet run, jet dev and jet test accept it, so trying code costs nothing. Before shipping, jet check and jet build give a tidy error saying which cases the else stands for (.Line | .Dot), and jet fix writes them in one step. From then on, a case added later stops the build at every place that has not decided it, which is the logic bug we want to prevent. Rarer, a rest that should take every other case now and later, like a key handler, is spelled _ -> and is never stopped, so the intent is visible to readers. Nothing is forced into a new shape: chains and tables both stay and get the same rule. Today a table's else is already refused everywhere (E0641), so A lowers friction there too. The old table-plus-case-sets design is now B, and naming every case by hand from the first run is C.

questions.text: I dont understand the ballot and I dont think this is the best solution. solutions should be idiomatic, cohesive jet and with jet philosophy. they should minimize friction proportional to frequency of use, and all downsides must be engineered away
questions.answer: Rewritten from scratch; the old A made every offline app hand-write a list. Plainly: offline, an app shows only what the device already holds, and today that is just the screens the person opened. The new recommendation, A 'Follow the links': with .offline(.Queue) the device fetches ahead, on Wi-Fi, the screens reachable by links from what the person opened. Nothing is written, because the links are already in the code: kit.link(logic.BoardView{project: card.id}, ...) tells the compiler that each board, crew.board(card.id), is one tap away. Friction follows frequency: the common case is zero code, and the rare cases are one argument on the .screen line, preload: false (never fetch this screen ahead) or offline: true (the build fails if this screen cannot be fetched ahead, naming the read). Downsides designed away (the ballot lists each attempt): a fetched read always matches its screen, because it is the screen's own read; nothing is hidden, since jet inspect preload lists each read and the link it came from; data, battery and server cost are bounded by unmetered-only, nearest-first fetching within a 64 MiB budget, one batched request per screen kind, and version re-checks; deeper screens are reached nearest first within the budget. The one cost left: a screen reached only by typed text, like search, cannot be fetched ahead, because nobody knows the text in advance. Offline it shows its last results, and the build names it. The old warm list is now B, and C is no loading ahead.

Valen (https://verdagon.dev/blog/golden-spike-reviving-vale-valen) replaces Vale's generational references with Nick Smith's group borrowing (https://verdagon.dev/blog/group-borrowing; original gist https://gist.github.com/nmsmith/cdaa94aa74e8e0611221e65db8e41f7b). Mutable aliases to the same object stay valid; a mutation invalidates only references into its independently replaceable contents (child groups); signatures name which groups a function may mutate. Smith reports Mojo 1.0 adopted a variation as 'Interior Origins' (unverified here). For Jet this would let attack(&a, &d) accept the same entity twice without a runtime check, but it relaxes the exclusivity of & and needs an owner ballot after #4247 ships the runtime-check baseline and a paired cell exists.

Owner order: native-platform cards that need cross-platform work are split into Linux and other platforms; Linux is done in G9, the other platforms in G13.

Done. Twelve G9 cards now cover Linux and the web only: #6799 menus and tray, #6800 notifications (freedesktop notifications and Web Push), #6801 background work, #6802 files (the desktop portal), #6803 camera and location (PipeWire, GeoClue), #6804 deep links, #6805 share and clipboard, #6806 permissions, #6807 accessibility (AT-SPI), #6809 lifecycle, #6810 install (AppImage, Flatpak) and #6818 native sessions (Secret Service). briefings.title: Cycle p212: the TitleCase cutover's census failed; nothing landed
briefings.body:
# Cycle p212: the TitleCase cutover's census failed; nothing landed

**What ran:** the cutover (#6733) as one commit on d6d482c5f7, built by a bridge compiler, then the collect-all census. The census failed, so nothing landed, and dev stayed at d6d482c5f7.

**Failure classes the census found** (each one is fixed in the cutover scripts, not by hand):
- Lookup file names were renamed: UI fixtures' `main.jet`, `module.jet`, `stderr` and `stdout`, which the harness opens by name. They now keep their names.
- Tool-required folder layouts were renamed: tree-sitter `src/` and `test/`, Zed `languages/` and `grammars/`. They now keep their names and are listed in the AcronymPathCase guard's `PATH_CASE_TOOL_LAYOUTS`, each with the tool that requires it.
- References the path passes cannot see stayed stale: string interpolations (`{toolchain}/tests/...`), bare corpus names in guards and gate scripts (`core_declarations`), and the `root:tests` selector. A new post-pass rewrites these from the move list only.
- Guards still named old paths: closed-list baselines, allowlists, the example-names guard, and the manifest, corpus and closeout guards.

**Plan change:** the queued submissions land first, on the old layout (p213). The cutover is then regenerated from its scripts on the new tip, so no landing has to be rebased across 40,000 moved files. Every pass is idempotent and reads paths only from the move list.

**Next:** p213 lands the 24 queued submissions. The cutover is regenerated on its tip and validated in collect-all mode (bridge build, census, guards, every suite) before it lands.

**Suites against p209:** 104 rows fixed (the served-mux hang is gone, and its HTTP, web_app and TLS rows pass again) and 35 new failures. Each new failure was rerun alone on the p210 gate. Two roots explain all but five flakes:

1. **The AccountID cutover (6e63e77b08): `AccountID` has no static method `from_string` (E0311)** on the built compiler. It breaks TypedTable, the Core/App and Db Table tests, four row-policy cases and the new AccountID case. The job SUBs (7255c5cece, 50466dc57b) also fail their own cases: no job is redelivered after a restart. Speed-3-2 fixes both first.
2. **The enum template cutover (ccf4ad95e7): the code generated for enums with payload cases names bindings (`right_<Case>_value`) that don't exist (E0107).** It breaks the EnumCases example, NestedPayloadSafety, two enum cases, two pattern UI snapshots, and its own reflect golden (`Signal.Paint.Stroke`, E0119). Until then the providers build against an internal record.
- EnvModel's schema split (#6847 c16 b1-b7) is approved. Bare names in env files stay EnvModel syntax because they are resolved, not evaluated.

**Any ballot (D-PRIM-ANY1):** review 9 failed on three gaps, and round 9 fixed them. It adopted a hybrid arm rule (type position first, then the member's name), defined arms for two instances of one generic (`.Box<Int>(b)`), and stated the view's scope once: a tracked copy until #6839 c46 lands. It still recommends C. Review 10 is running. New criteria: #6839 c54 (a loan keeps its owner through every carrier) and c55 (no internal generic names in diagnostics); #6833 c5 (the hybrid rule, if C wins).

briefings.body:
# Cycle p209: 7 landings, 3 regressions traced to their owners

**Landed on dev** (b467d0da48 → a1c3325a65; the census was clean, the core suite passed 2433/2433, and guards pass):

| Commit | Change | Card |
|---|---|---|
| a403b6e912 | the comptime root loop waits for #run values | #6847 c9 |
| 06c5d8b172 | module values may hold named functions | #6847 c10 |
| c4f916ca2d | BodyCodec --check matches the generated codecs | #6847 c15 |
| 8987b1961d | law kit: a Core trait's laws run under jet test | #6855 c4 |
| 9fb22f4c60 | #App.Every runs once across replicas | #6825 c2 |
| 4977565c79 | jobs, schedules and webhooks run as the system and are listed by inspect choices | #6825 c4 |
| a1c3325a65 | union members of one name from two modules stay two members (an I1 fix) | #6839 c36 |

**Met:** #6847 c9 and c15, #6839 c36, #6825 c5.

**Suites against p207:** 108 new failures and 9 fixed. Each new failure was rerun alone on the p209 gate; three roots explain all but one flake:

1. **9fb22f4c60 hangs every served mux (about 100 rows: HTTP examples, web_app, server lifecycle, ws, tls, canvas).** `mux_serving` expected list `remove(0, .Slot)` to give None on an empty list. `.Slot` stops on an index out of range, as its ratified text keeps the bounds check. So every serving task died at its first serve, and clients timed out. Speed-3-2 sends the fix first in p210 and sweeps every `.Slot ?? return|default` caller in the repository (App.jet and Db.jet have two more).
2. **8987b1961d: `jet test` panics with "the law `law` does not parse"** (2 cases). MemKernel-6-2 fixes the law text and replaces the panic with a registered diagnostic.
3. **06c5d8b172: an ICE (exit 101) on a module value holding a named function** (1 case). PrecompiledCore-4 owns the fix.

Also: the `reflect_of_field_not_capturable` UI snapshot now reports resource state instead of the secret field. GoalsA-1-4 is finding its root (u36 is the first suspect). `ffi_missing_version` passed alone, so it was a flake.

**Decisions made tonight:**
- A run-time call of a `#run fn` is refused (E1019, #6847 n7).
- Jetpack's EnvModel stops being a second evaluator; its env schema becomes Jet types the compiler checks (#6847 c16).
- `auth.AccountID` replaces String accounts in one cutover (#6800 c4, as D-DB-TABLE1 ratified).
- Built-in enum case lists come from one table generated from the Core declarations, not from loading more of Core per program (#3147 n15).
- #6825 c9 (a store adapter contract) has no subject until a public adapter API exists. That API is owner-gated, so it waits for a ballot.

**Any ballot (D-PRIM-ANY1):** review 7 failed on four gaps, and round 7 fixed them, still recommending C. Review 8 is running.

**Next:** p210 lands the three root fixes plus 11 queued SUBs (#3147 c5 and n14, #6847 n1, n2 and n7, #6825 c1, n6, n7 and n8, the AccountID cutover, and the first EnvModel step).

Its proof case still fails, though: the value is never computed, so the case reports E0956 "the build could not compute ASSETS". PrecompiledCore-4 is fixing that first, and #6847 c9 stays open until the case passes.

**Suites against p206:**

- golden: 4965 pass, 4 fail.

Two new failures. `Examples/Interop/FFI/LibraryGrant.jet` (O0) is a load flake: it passes on O0, O1 and O2 when run alone. The other is the root-loop case above. No new exit-101 failures.

**Compile speed:** rcc 0.49–0.51 s at 316 MB, InspectBuild 8.59 s. Both are flat against p206.

**Lander change:** a conflict only in the diagnostic generators' outputs no longer bounces a SUB. The stack keeps one side, then reruns DiagnosticRows and DiagnosticCensus `--write` on the stacked sources and lands their output as one more commit. This unblocked p208's ten-SUB stack.

# Self-compile speed, cold A/B (16:15): sweep2 is 4% slower, and the runtime step is half the build

Both compilers built the same fresh copy of the sweep2 tree, one after the other, on a quiet machine. The command was `jet build --profile dev Compiler`, with no build directory or cache.

||seed-b15 (before)|seed-b16 (sweep2, now on dev)|
|---|---|---|
|Wall time|**2:32.8**|**2:39.7**|
|User CPU|187.0 s|195.9 s|
|Peak memory|9.22 GB|9.57 GB|
|The compiler image alone|59.2 s|62.8 s|
|Runtime step (runtime plus Core library lowering)|84.9 s|87.3 s|

Tree: 903,380 lines (Compiler 679,836 + Core 223,544). The compiler image compiles at about 15k lines/s of its own wall time. The earlier 4:30 stage-B figure came from a warm, contended run and does not reproduce.

**Result: no speed gain yet.** The first data-oriented slices (#6793 S1/S2a) only change identifiers. Other sweep2 work added new phases:
- sema.effects: +1.0 s
- sema.late: new, 1.1 s
- comptime.body.recheck: new, 12 s, inside comptime bodies
- comptime.load: +0.7 s
- ir.build: +0.4 s

The net is +6.9 s.

**Where the time goes:**
- The runtime step: 87 s, more than half of the whole build.
- sema.finalize, codecs and build.plan: about 33 s.
- comptime bodies: about 12 s.
- ir.opt: 12.8 s.

**Being fixed now** (G11Speed-5, #5479/#6793):
1. Cut the runtime step, which lowers the runtime and the Core library in a separate process.
2. Remove the new comptime.body.recheck pass, or make it incremental-free and cheap.
3. Remove the sweep2 additions to sema.effects and sema.late.
4. Land #6793 S2b, then S3, which replaces maps with dense arrays.

The proof each time is the same cold A/B. Raw data: `$JET_STATE_ROOT/lander3-tmp/ab/`.
